sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what AWS is in simple terms, how Regions and Availability Zones work, what the Free Tier covers and how DevOps teams use AWS to build and run systems.

AWS (Amazon Web Services) is a cloud computing platform that lets you rent servers, storage, databases, and networking on demand instead of buying and running your own hardware. You pay only for what you use, scale up or down in minutes, and let Amazon handle the underlying data centers.

AWS is Amazon's cloud platform: a catalog of on-demand infrastructure and managed services that replaces buying servers, storage arrays, and networking gear up front. Instead of waiting weeks for hardware, a DevOps engineer can create a VM, bucket, database, or pipeline in minutes, test ideas quickly, and shut resources down when they are no longer needed.

sections.title: What is AWS in simple terms?
paragraphs: Think of AWS like electricity from a utility company. You do not build your own power plant to turn on a light. You plug into the grid and pay for the kilowatt-hours you consume. AWS does the same thing for computing. Instead of buying a physical server, installing it in a room, cooling it, patching it, and replacing it when it fails, you request a virtual server through an API or web console and it appears in seconds. When you are done, you turn it off and stop paying. This shift, from owning fixed hardware to renting flexible capacity, is the single most important idea behind cloud computing and the reason AWS changed how software gets built.

Amazon launched AWS publicly in 2006 after realizing the tooling it built for its own teams could help other companies move faster. Since then AWS has become the largest cloud provider by market share, largely because it offers a wide service catalog, mature global infrastructure, and tooling that fits startups, enterprises, and regulated environments.

Three advantages matter immediately in DevOps work. First, global reach: you can deploy close to users in many geographic regions. Second, pay-as-you-go pricing: you pay for compute hours, requests, storage, and transfer rather than fixed hardware purchases. Third, managed services: AWS handles undifferentiated work such as patching database engines, maintaining control planes, and replacing failed hardware.

A useful way to think about AWS is that it gives you layers of abstraction. EC2 gives you virtual machines that feel close to traditional servers. Lambda removes server management almost entirely. S3 abstracts away disk management and exposes durable object storage through APIs. The right choice depends on how much control you need versus how much operational effort you want to avoid.

sections.title: How AWS is organized: Regions and Availability Zones
paragraphs: AWS runs physical data centers all over the world, and it groups them into a two-level hierarchy that you will reference constantly. A Region is a geographic area, such as us-east-1 (Northern Virginia) or eu-west-1 (Ireland), and you choose one based on where your users are, data-residency laws, and which services are available there. Inside each Region are multiple Availability Zones (AZs): isolated clusters of data centers with independent power and networking. Running your application across two or more AZs is the foundation of high availability on AWS, if one zone fails, the others keep serving traffic. Understanding this layout early prevents two classic beginner mistakes: launching everything in a single AZ (no resilience) and accidentally deploying resources in the wrong Region (where you then cannot find them).

sections.title: The AWS Free Tier
paragraphs: You can learn AWS without a big bill because of the Free Tier, which comes in three flavors. Always-free offers never expire. For example, one million AWS Lambda requests per month. 12-months-free offers apply for a year after you create an account, such as 750 hours per month of a small EC2 instance and 5 GB of S3 storage. Short-term trials unlock specific services for a limited window. The Free Tier is enough to complete every hands-on lab in a typical DevOps learning path, but set a billing alarm on day one: the fastest way to get a surprise charge is to leave a large instance or a NAT gateway running after an experiment.

sections.title: How DevOps teams use AWS
paragraphs: For a DevOps engineer, AWS is not just a place to run servers. It is the substrate the whole delivery pipeline sits on. Teams describe their infrastructure as code using Terraform or AWS CloudFormation, so an entire environment can be created, reviewed, and destroyed from a Git repository. They build and ship applications through CodePipeline, CodeBuild, or third-party CI/CD like GitHub Actions and GitLab CI, deploying to ECS or EKS (managed Kubernetes). They observe everything through CloudWatch metrics, logs, and alarms, and they control access tightly with IAM roles and policies so that both people and machines get only the permissions they need. The recurring theme is automation: anything a DevOps engineer does twice on AWS, they try to encode once so it becomes repeatable, reviewable, and safe.
Start next with AWS Global Infrastructure, then move into Setting Up AWS, AWS IAM, and AWS EC2. Those lessons build the mental model you need before touching more specialized services.

codeBlock.code:
aws --version
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws s3 ls

sections.title: Operational note
paragraphs: Early AWS success usually comes from repeatable habits rather than memorizing every service. Use tags, consistent naming, and a short checklist for account setup, region awareness, and access patterns so new environments feel predictable instead of improvised. That discipline makes later automation, cost control, and incident response much easier.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is AWS in simple terms?

Amazon Web Services rents computing resources on demand. Servers, storage, databases, networking and several hundred higher-level services. Charged by the hour, the second, or the request rather than bought outright. Instead of ordering hardware and waiting weeks, you call an API and get a server in ninety seconds. The trade is that you give up control of the physical layer and take on a pricing model that rewards paying attention and punishes ignoring it.
What is the difference between a Region and an Availability Zone?

A Region is a geographic location such as eu-west-1 (Ireland) or us-east-1 (N. Virginia), and it is the level at which you choose where data lives. An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centres within a Region, with independent power, cooling and networking, connected to the other zones by low-latency links. Deploying across two or more Availability Zones protects you from a single data centre failing; deploying across Regions protects against a whole Region failing and is considerably more work.
Which AWS Region should I choose?

The one closest to your users, for latency, unless data residency rules dictate otherwise. Two secondary considerations matter more than people expect: pricing differs between Regions, sometimes by 10 to 20% for the same instance, and new services appear in us-east-1 first and reach smaller Regions later. us-east-1 is also where a few global services are anchored. ACM certificates for CloudFront must be issued there regardless of where the rest of your infrastructure sits.
How do I avoid an unexpected AWS bill?

Set a budget with an alert before you create anything, that single step turns a runaway cost into a notification rather than a month-end surprise. Then be aware of the usual sources: NAT gateways charging hourly plus per gigabyte, CloudWatch log groups defaulting to never expire, EBS volumes still billing after their instances are gone, and data transfer out to the internet. The Free Tier covers a genuinely useful amount for learning, but several of its limits are twelve-month rather than perpetual.
What AWS services should I learn first?

For DevOps, the order that pays off fastest is IAM, then VPC, then EC2, S3 and RDS, then CloudWatch. IAM comes first because every other service defers to it and most confusing errors are permissions errors. VPC comes second because networking mistakes surface later as problems that look like application bugs. Once those four are comfortable, container services and Lambda build on them naturally rather than feeling like separate products.
Do I need certification to work with AWS?

No, though the Solutions Architect Associate syllabus is a reasonable map of what a working knowledge covers, and some employers use it as a filter. It is not a substitute for having built and broken things. Certification teaches breadth, while operating a real system teaches the failure modes that actually matter. If you are choosing between studying for an exam and deploying something real with Terraform, deploy something real.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how AWS is laid out: Regions, Availability Zones, Local Zones and edge locations. Choose a Region and see why cross-AZ traffic costs money.
AWS is a hierarchy of physical locations, and nearly every architectural decision about availability, latency, compliance and cost is really a decision about where in that hierarchy something sits.

sections.title: Regions
paragraphs: A Region is the boundary that matters most. Data stays in the Region you put it in unless you explicitly replicate it, which is what makes Region choice the answer to most data residency questions.

Regions are isolated from each other by design. A failure in us-east-1 does not affect eu-west-1, and resources do not implicitly span Regions: a VPC, an S3 bucket, an EBS volume all belong to exactly one.
Some Regions are opt-in and must be enabled before use, which catches people whose API calls fail with an authorisation error that does not mention the Region at all.
Four considerations, roughly in order:
Latency. Closest to your users. This dominates for anything interactive.
Compliance. Data residency rules may simply decide it for you.
Price. Regions differ, sometimes by 10 to 20% for identical resources. us-east-1 is usually among the cheapest; newer and smaller Regions are often the most expensive.
Service availability. New services launch in us-east-1 first and reach smaller Regions months or years later. Check before designing around something recent.
A handful of things are anchored to us-east-1 regardless of where you operate:
That first one catches almost everyone building a CDN in Europe or Asia.

codeBlock.code: aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[].RegionName' --output text

sections.title: Availability Zones
paragraphs: An Availability Zone is one or more data centres with independent power, cooling and physical security, connected to other zones in the Region by high-bandwidth, low-latency private links, typically single-digit milliseconds apart.

Deploying across at least two zones is the baseline for production. A subnet belongs to exactly one zone, so multi-AZ means one subnet per zone per tier, with a load balancer or a managed service spreading across them.

eu-west-1a in your account is not necessarily the same physical zone as eu-west-1a in someone else's. AWS randomises the mapping so that customers do not all crowd into whichever zone is alphabetically first.
For genuine physical identity. Coordinating with a partner account, or placing resources deterministically. Use the zone ID, which is consistent across accounts:
The practical consequence for infrastructure code is to query zones rather than hardcoding names.
This is the part that surprises people on the bill. Data transferred between Availability Zones is charged in both directions.

A chatty microservice architecture spread evenly across three zones can spend meaningfully on traffic that never leaves the Region. It is the cost of the availability, and usually worth paying, but worth knowing about rather than discovering.
Mitigations where the volume justifies them: topology-aware routing in Kubernetes, keeping tightly-coupled services zone-local, and caching to reduce chattiness.
Note that traffic within a single zone is free, and traffic to most AWS services through a VPC endpoint avoids both cross-AZ and NAT charges.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region eu-west-1 \
  --query 'AvailabilityZones[].{Name:ZoneName,ID:ZoneId}' --output table

sections.title: Local Zones and Wavelength
paragraphs: Local Zones place compute and storage in a metro area far from the parent Region, for workloads needing single-digit millisecond latency to a specific city. They offer a subset of services and are managed as an extension of the parent Region.
Wavelength Zones do the same inside telecom providers' 5G networks.
Both are niche. Most workloads are better served by choosing a nearby Region and using CloudFront for static content.

sections.title: Edge locations
paragraphs: Hundreds of points of presence serving CloudFront, Route 53, AWS Global Accelerator and AWS WAF. They cache content and terminate connections close to users, which reduces latency and, importantly, reduces data transfer costs, since egress from CloudFront is cheaper than egress from a Region.
Serving downloads and static assets through CloudFront rather than directly from S3 is usually both faster and cheaper.

sections.title: Designing for failure
paragraphs: Multi-AZ is the right default and multi-Region rarely is. Going multi-Region means replicating data with the consistency trade-offs that implies, duplicating infrastructure, handling DNS failover, and testing something that is difficult to test. For a failure mode that is genuinely rare. Most organisations that believe they need it would be better served by making their multi-AZ deployment actually reliable.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Two AWS accounts both deploy into eu-west-1a, expecting to be in the same physical data centre. Are they?
A team sees significant data transfer charges despite all traffic staying inside one Region. What is the most likely cause?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a Region and an Availability Zone?

A Region is a geographic area such as eu-west-1, and it is the boundary for data residency. Data stays there unless you replicate it deliberately. An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centres within a Region, with independent power, cooling and networking, connected to the other zones by low-latency private links. Deploying across multiple zones protects against a single data centre failure; deploying across Regions protects against a whole Region failing and is far more work.
Which AWS Region should I use?

Start with the one closest to your users for latency, unless data residency requirements decide it for you. Then check two things people often miss: pricing varies between Regions by as much as 10 to 20% for identical resources, and new services launch in us-east-1 first and reach smaller Regions much later. If you are building for a global audience, a nearby Region plus CloudFront usually beats trying to run in several.
Why does eu-west-1a mean something different in another account?

AWS randomises the mapping between zone names and physical zones for each account, so that everyone does not concentrate in whichever letter sorts first. The zone ID, such as euw1-az1, is consistent across all accounts and is what you compare when physical location genuinely matters. For example when two accounts need resources in the same facility to avoid cross-AZ transfer charges. describe-availability-zones returns both.
Why am I charged for data transfer inside one Region?

Traffic between Availability Zones is charged per gigabyte in both directions, because zones are physically separate facilities. An architecture with many small services distributed evenly across three zones can generate substantial internal transfer. Traffic within a single zone is free, as is traffic to most AWS services through a VPC endpoint. If cross-AZ charges are significant, topology-aware routing and keeping tightly-coupled services zone-local both help.
Do I need a multi-Region architecture?

Almost certainly not. Multi-AZ protects against the failure mode that actually occurs, a data centre problem, and is straightforward. Multi-Region protects against an entire Region failing, which is rare, and costs you data replication with its consistency trade-offs, duplicated infrastructure, DNS failover, and a disaster recovery process that is genuinely hard to test. Most teams considering it would get more reliability from making their multi-AZ deployment properly resilient first.
Why must my CloudFront certificate be in us-east-1?

CloudFront is a global service whose configuration is managed from us-east-1, so ACM certificates it uses must be requested there regardless of where your origin and the rest of your infrastructure live. This catches nearly everyone building a distribution in Europe or Asia. In Terraform it means an aliased provider block pinned to us-east-1 purely for the certificate resource, while everything else uses your normal Region.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Prepare a new AWS environment before you build: pick an account structure, harden root, set up identity, add billing guardrails, enable CloudTrail, tag early.
Everything below takes about an hour and is far easier now than after you have workloads running. The order matters: identity and billing guardrails first, because both are painful to retrofit.

sections.title: Decide the account structure first
paragraphs: The single decision with the longest consequences.

One account per environment, at minimum. Production separate from everything else. Accounts are the strongest isolation boundary AWS offers: a mistake in staging physically cannot touch production resources, IAM is entirely separate, and service quotas do not compete.
An IAM-only separation inside one account is weaker in every respect, and the temptation to use it comes from thinking accounts are expensive. They are free. You pay for resources, not for accounts.
Create them with AWS Organizations, which gives consolidated billing, service control policies as organisation-wide guardrails, and central account creation.
The management account should hold no workloads. It is the account that can do anything to every other one, so keeping it empty limits what a compromise there reaches.

codeBlock.code:
Management account          billing and Organizations only, no workloads
├── security                CloudTrail archive, GuardDuty
├── production
├── staging
└── development

sections.title: Harden the root user
paragraphs: Every account has a root user that cannot be restricted by any IAM policy or service control policy. It is the one identity with unconditional power.
Then do not use it. There are perhaps five tasks that genuinely require root, and none of them are daily work.

sections.title: Set up identity properly
paragraphs: Do this before creating a single IAM user, because once users exist they persist.

Enable IAM Identity Center in the management account and connect an identity source: the built-in directory for a small team, or Entra ID, Okta or Google Workspace if you have one. Then create permission sets and assign groups to accounts.
People sign in once and reach every account they are entitled to, with temporary credentials and no access keys anywhere.

A convention worth adopting from the start: production defaults to a read-only permission set, with a separate administrator profile selected deliberately. It makes a mistyped command in the wrong terminal fail at the IAM layer.

codeBlock.code: aws configure sso

sections.title: Billing guardrails
paragraphs: Before anything is created, not after the first surprise.
Also worth enabling immediately:

codeBlock.code:
aws budgets create-budget \
  --account-id 111122223333 \
  --budget '{"BudgetName":"monthly","BudgetLimit":{"Amount":"200","Unit":"USD"},"TimeUnit":"MONTHLY","BudgetType":"COST"}' \
  --notifications-with-subscribers '[{
    "Notification":{"NotificationType":"ACTUAL","ComparisonOperator":"GREATER_THAN","Threshold":80,"ThresholdType":"PERCENTAGE"},
    "Subscribers":[{"SubscriptionType":"EMAIL","Address":"platform@acme.com"}]}]'

sections.title: Turn on CloudTrail everywhere
paragraphs: CloudTrail records every API call. Without it, you cannot answer who did what, and you cannot add it retroactively for events that already happened.

Create an organisation trail covering all Regions and all accounts, delivering to an S3 bucket in a separate security account with restricted access. That separation means someone who compromises a workload account cannot erase the evidence.
Enable GuardDuty at the same time. It is close to zero-effort threat detection and costs little at low volume.

sections.title: Tag from the beginning
paragraphs: Retrofitting tags across an existing estate is tedious and never finishes. Decide the schema now:

Enforce it with provider-level defaults, default_tags in the Terraform AWS provider applies them to everything automatically, and with a service control policy or AWS Config rule for anything created outside IaC.

sections.title: Set a few account defaults
paragraphs: Small settings that are annoying to apply later:
Note that EBS encryption by default is per Region, so it must be set in each Region you use.

codeBlock.code:
# Encrypt every new EBS volume by default
aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default --region eu-west-1

# Block public S3 access at the account level, above any bucket setting
aws s3control put-public-access-block \
  --account-id 111122223333 \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"

sections.title: Install the tooling
paragraphs: Start with infrastructure as code rather than promising to adopt it later. Importing a hand-built estate into Terraform afterwards is a genuinely unpleasant project.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team is deciding between separate AWS accounts per environment or one account with IAM separation. What is the strongest argument for separate accounts?
Why deliver organisation CloudTrail logs to an S3 bucket in a separate security account rather than in each workload account?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I use one AWS account or several?

Several, at minimum, production separate from everything else. An account is the strongest isolation boundary AWS provides: IAM is entirely separate, service quotas do not compete, and a mistake in one account cannot reach resources in another. Accounts are free, and AWS Organizations consolidates billing so there is no administrative penalty. A common structure is a management account holding only billing and Organizations, a security account for CloudTrail and GuardDuty, and one account per environment.
What should I do first with a brand new AWS account?

Enable hardware MFA on the root user and delete any root access keys, since root cannot be restricted by any policy. Set a budget with an alert before creating anything, so a mistake becomes a notification rather than a month-end surprise. Enable CloudTrail across all Regions. Then set up IAM Identity Center before creating any IAM users, because once users exist they tend to persist for years.
How do I avoid an unexpected AWS bill?

Create a budget with an alert at 80% of your expected spend before you build anything, and enable Cost Anomaly Detection, which flags unusual patterns without needing a threshold. Then be aware of the common sources: NAT gateways charging hourly plus per gigabyte, CloudWatch log groups defaulting to never expire, EBS volumes still billing after their instances are terminated, and data transfer out to the internet. Activating cost allocation tags early makes attribution possible later.
Do I need AWS Organizations for a small team?

It is worth it even for two accounts. You get consolidated billing, which combines usage for volume discounts and Free Tier, central account creation, and service control policies that set guardrails no member account can override. Such as denying the ability to disable CloudTrail or restricting which Regions may be used. There is no cost to enabling it, and retrofitting an Organization onto existing standalone accounts is more work than starting with one.
Should I create IAM users when setting up AWS?

No. Enable IAM Identity Center and connect an identity source instead, so people sign in with corporate credentials and receive temporary role sessions with no access keys. IAM users hold permanent credentials that do not expire and are the most common source of leaked AWS credentials. Doing this before any users exist saves a migration later, since users created for convenience early on tend to stay for years.
What tagging strategy should I use from the start?

At minimum Environment, Owner, Project and ManagedBy. Enforce them automatically, default_tags in the Terraform AWS provider applies them to every resource without repetition, and add an AWS Config rule or service control policy for resources created outside infrastructure as code. Remember to activate cost allocation tags in the billing console, otherwise they exist on resources but never appear in Cost Explorer. Retrofitting tags across a live estate is a project that rarely gets finished.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Secure a new AWS account: lock down the root user with MFA, set billing alarms, turn on CloudTrail and fix the settings that are painful to change later.
A new AWS account arrives with a root user, no guardrails, and a credit card attached. This page covers what to do in the first hour. The things that are quick now and awkward later.

sections.title: The root user is the whole problem
paragraphs: When you create an account, you get a root user identified by the email address you signed up with. It has unconditional power over the account and cannot be restricted by any IAM policy or service control policy.
That makes it the highest-value credential in your organisation, and it should be treated accordingly.

Hardware MFA is the right choice for anything that matters. A physical security key kept where access is controlled. A virtual authenticator app is acceptable for personal or learning accounts, but it lives on someone's phone.
AWS now supports multiple MFA devices on root, which removes the old single-point-of-failure problem of one lost token locking you out. Register two.
There is no legitimate reason for root to have programmatic credentials. Check and remove them:
A result of 1 means root access keys exist. Delete them from the security credentials page.
Sign up with a shared mailbox, aws-root@acme.com, not an individual's address. People leave, and recovering an account whose root email belongs to a former employee is genuinely difficult.
The same applies to the phone number used for account recovery.
Root should be used perhaps a handful of times ever. Any sign-in is worth knowing about, via CloudTrail and an EventBridge rule on ConsoleLogin where the user identity type is Root.

Very little: closing the account, changing the account name or root email, changing the support plan, restoring an IAM policy that locked everyone out, and a small number of billing operations. Nothing in that list is daily work.

codeBlock.code: aws iam get-account-summary --query 'SummaryMap.AccountAccessKeysPresent'

sections.title: Set the account contacts
paragraphs: Frequently skipped and genuinely important. AWS uses these to reach you about security issues, billing problems and service events:
Set SECURITY, BILLING and OPERATIONS, each to a team address. A security notification sent to a personal mailbox that nobody reads is the same as no notification.

codeBlock.code:
aws account put-alternate-contact \
  --alternate-contact-type SECURITY \
  --name "Security Team" \
  --title "Security" \
  --email-address security@acme.com \
  --phone-number "+441234567890"

sections.title: Billing guardrails before anything else
paragraphs: Create these before launching a single resource.
A budget with an alert, so overspend is a notification rather than a discovery:
Set both an ACTUAL alert at 80% and a FORECASTED alert, since the forecast warns you mid-month rather than after the fact.
Cost Anomaly Detection needs no threshold tuning and catches the pattern budgets miss. A sudden change in one service while the total stays plausible.

Activate cost allocation tags in the billing console. Tags exist on resources from the moment you create them, but they do not appear in Cost Explorer until activated, and activation is not retroactive.
Enable IAM access to billing data, otherwise only root can see the billing console, which pushes people toward using root for routine work.

codeBlock.code:
aws budgets create-budget \
  --account-id 111122223333 \
  --budget '{"BudgetName":"monthly","BudgetLimit":{"Amount":"100","Unit":"USD"},"TimeUnit":"MONTHLY","BudgetType":"COST"}' \
  --notifications-with-subscribers '[{
    "Notification":{"NotificationType":"ACTUAL","ComparisonOperator":"GREATER_THAN","Threshold":80,"ThresholdType":"PERCENTAGE"},
    "Subscribers":[{"SubscriptionType":"EMAIL","Address":"billing@acme.com"}]}]'

sections.title: Understand the Free Tier honestly
paragraphs: Three different things share the name:
The twelve-month ones expiring is a common source of a surprising thirteenth-month bill. Set a calendar reminder at month eleven.
Note also that Free Tier limits are per consolidated billing family, not per account, so additional accounts under one Organization do not multiply the allowance.

sections.title: Turn on CloudTrail and GuardDuty
paragraphs: CloudTrail records every API call, and it cannot be applied retroactively. Events before it was enabled are simply not recorded.

Create a multi-Region trail delivering to S3. In an Organization, create an organisation trail from the management account and send logs to a separate security account, so someone who compromises a workload account cannot erase the evidence.

GuardDuty analyses CloudTrail, VPC flow logs and DNS logs for threats. It takes one click, costs little at low volume, and catches things nobody is watching for. Cryptomining on a compromised instance, credentials used from an unusual location, communication with known-malicious addresses.

codeBlock.code: aws cloudtrail describe-trails --query 'trailList[].{Name:Name,MultiRegion:IsMultiRegionTrail}'

sections.title: Account-level defaults
paragraphs: Two settings that apply above individual resources:
EBS encryption by default must be set in every Region you use, which is easy to forget when expanding to a second one later.

codeBlock.code:
# Block public S3 access for the whole account, overriding any bucket setting
aws s3control put-public-access-block \
  --account-id 111122223333 \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"

# Encrypt every new EBS volume. Note this is PER REGION
aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default --region eu-west-1

sections.title: Closing an account
paragraphs: Worth knowing before you need it. A closed account enters a 90-day post-closure period during which it can be reopened, after which it is permanently gone along with all its data.

Closing does not stop charges already incurred, and resources continue to be billed until they are actually deleted, so delete resources first, confirm the bill has settled, then close. In an Organization, an account must be removed from the Organization or closed from the management account.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Can a service control policy or IAM policy limit what the AWS root user can do in an account?
Resources have been tagged with Project since the account was created, but Cost Explorer shows no Project dimension. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What should I do first with a new AWS account?

Enable hardware MFA on the root user and delete any root access keys, since root cannot be restricted by any policy. Set a budget alert before creating resources. Enable CloudTrail across all Regions, because it does not record anything retroactively. Set the security, billing and operations alternate contacts to team addresses rather than an individual's. Then set up IAM Identity Center before creating any IAM users, which saves a migration later.
How do I secure the AWS root user?

Register two hardware MFA devices, now that AWS supports multiple. Delete any access keys. There is no legitimate programmatic use for root. Use a shared mailbox for the root email address and a phone number that is not an individual's, because recovering an account whose contact details belong to a former employee is genuinely painful. Set a CloudTrail and EventBridge alert on root sign-in, and use it only for the handful of tasks that require it.
How do I set up a billing alarm in AWS?

Create an AWS Budget with a notification, ideally two: an ACTUAL alert at around 80% of expected spend, and a FORECASTED alert so you hear about a problem mid-month rather than afterwards. Also enable Cost Anomaly Detection, which needs no threshold and catches a sudden change in one service even when the total looks plausible. Do both before creating resources. A guardrail added after the first surprise is too late for that surprise.
What does the AWS Free Tier actually include?

Three separate things. Twelve-month offers that expire a year after signup, including EC2 micro instance hours, 30 GB of EBS and 5 GB of S3. Always-free offers that never expire, such as a million Lambda requests a month and 25 GB of DynamoDB. And short trials for specific services. The twelve-month expiry is the common surprise, so set a reminder at month eleven. Note also that Free Tier applies per consolidated billing family, not per account.
Why can't my IAM users see the billing console?

Access to billing data is disabled for IAM principals by default and must be enabled by the root user in the account settings. Until then only root can view costs, which perversely encourages people to use root for routine work. Enable IAM access to billing information, then grant the relevant permissions through a policy so the people responsible for cost can actually see it without elevated access.
What happens when I close an AWS account?

It enters a 90-day post-closure period during which it can be reopened; after that it is permanently gone along with all data. Closing does not stop charges already incurred, and resources keep billing until they are genuinely deleted, so delete resources first, confirm the final bill has settled, then close. If the account belongs to an AWS Organization, close it from the management account or remove it from the Organization first.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Navigate the AWS Console quickly: use the search bar, avoid Region mistakes, open CloudShell, find resources with Tag Editor and know when to skip it.
The console is where most people meet AWS, and it is genuinely good for exploring, reading state and diagnosing problems. It is a poor place to build anything you intend to keep.
This page covers using it well, and knowing when to stop.

sections.title: The search bar does almost everything
paragraphs: Pressing / or Alt+S focuses the unified search bar, and it is by far the fastest way to move around. It searches services, documentation, the AWS Marketplace and, usefully, your own resources.
Typing an instance ID, a bucket name or a function name jumps straight to that resource. Typing a partial service name gets you there in three keystrokes, which is quicker than any menu.
Learn this one thing and console navigation stops being a chore.

sections.title: The Region switcher is the thing to watch
paragraphs: Top right, and it determines which resources you see. Almost every "my resources have disappeared" moment is the wrong Region.
A few services are global and ignore the switcher entirely:
That S3 row is a common confusion: the bucket list is global, but each bucket lives in a Region and its contents are served from there.

Resource Explorer searches across Regions and resource types at once, which answers "where did I create that?" without switching through each Region manually. It needs enabling first, and is worth doing on day one.

sections.title: CloudShell
paragraphs: The terminal icon in the top bar opens a browser shell with the AWS CLI already installed and already authenticated as your console identity. No credential configuration, no access keys.
It is genuinely useful:
It includes 1 GB of persistent home directory storage per Region, and sessions time out after about 20 minutes of inactivity.

sections.title: Reading state efficiently
paragraphs: Where the console beats the CLI:
Service dashboards give a visual overview. An ECS service's deployment progress, an RDS instance's Performance Insights graphs, a VPC's resource map, that would take several CLI calls to assemble.
CloudWatch dashboards and Logs Insights are considerably nicer in the browser than through the API.
Cost Explorer is console-only in practice. Ten minutes there answers most "why is the bill high" questions.
Trusted Advisor surfaces idle resources, unattached volumes and security findings in one place.

sections.title: Tag Editor and Resource Groups
paragraphs: Tag Editor finds resources across Regions and services by tag, and can bulk-apply tags to the results. Retrofitting a missing Owner tag across a few hundred resources is one of the few bulk operations the console does better than scripting.
Resource Groups collect resources matching a tag query into a named view, which is a practical way to see everything belonging to one application.

sections.title: Keyboard and layout
paragraphs: Pinning your six most-used services to the favourites bar removes most menu navigation. Recently visited on the console home covers the rest.
The unified settings page sets your default Region, visual mode and language, which is worth doing once.

sections.title: When not to use the console
paragraphs: This is the part that matters more than any navigation tip.
Never build production infrastructure by clicking. The problems are not hypothetical:
Use Terraform, CloudFormation or CDK for anything that should still exist next week.

A practical pattern: explore in the console, then write the Terraform. Clicking through a service to understand it and then codifying the result is a legitimate and efficient workflow. Leaving the clicked version running is not.

sections.title: Make production read-only
paragraphs: The strongest safeguard available, and it takes five minutes.

With IAM Identity Center, give yourself a read-only permission set for production by default, and a separate administrator one selected deliberately. Browsing production then cannot change it, and making a change is a conscious act of switching roles.
That removes an entire category of accident, the mistaken click in the wrong tab, at the IAM layer rather than relying on care.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An engineer created an EC2 instance yesterday and today the console shows none. What is the most likely explanation?
Someone changes a security group rule in the console on infrastructure managed by Terraform. What happens next?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why can't I see my AWS resources in the console?

Almost always the Region selector in the top right. Most AWS services are regional, so the console only shows resources in the currently selected Region, and it can differ between browser sessions or from what a colleague is looking at. IAM, Route 53 and CloudFront are global and always visible. Enabling Resource Explorer lets you search every Region and resource type at once, which answers the question in one step rather than by clicking through Regions.
What is AWS CloudShell and when should I use it?

A browser-based terminal with the AWS CLI preinstalled and already authenticated as your console identity, so there are no credentials to configure. It is useful for running a quick command without leaving the browser, working from a machine where you cannot install the CLI, and checking what a command does before committing it to a script. It provides 1 GB of persistent storage per Region and times out after roughly 20 minutes of inactivity.
Should I build infrastructure in the AWS console?

Not for anything you intend to keep. Console-built infrastructure is not reproducible, not reviewable, not versioned, and it causes drift when it touches resources managed by Terraform or CloudFormation. Use infrastructure as code for anything that should still exist next week. The console is genuinely good for learning a service's shape, reading state, and diagnosing problems. A common and sensible workflow is to explore in the console and then write the Terraform.
What is the fastest way to navigate the AWS console?

Press / or Alt+S to focus the unified search bar, then type a service name or a resource identifier. It searches services, documentation and your own resources, so typing an instance ID or bucket name jumps straight there. Pin your most-used services to the favourites bar with the star icon, and set a default Region in the unified settings. Between them, those three things remove most console navigation.
Which AWS services are global rather than regional?

IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, and WAF when used with CloudFront. Everything else is regional, including EC2, VPC, RDS, Lambda, ECS and EKS. S3 is a partial exception worth knowing: the bucket list is global so all your buckets appear regardless of Region, but each bucket lives in a specific Region and its data stays there. Certificates in ACM are regional, which is why CloudFront requires one issued specifically in us-east-1.
How do I avoid accidentally changing production from the console?

Make production read-only by default. With IAM Identity Center, assign yourself a read-only permission set for the production account and a separate administrator one that you select deliberately when you intend to make a change. Browsing production then cannot modify anything, and a mistaken click in the wrong browser tab fails at the IAM layer rather than succeeding. It takes a few minutes to set up and removes a whole category of accident.

Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Install the AWS CLI and set it up with SSO instead of long-lived access keys. Create named profiles, learn the credential chain and stay in the right account.

The AWS CLI is how you check what is actually true in an account, and it is the tool every other AWS workflow falls back on. Setting it up well, particularly the credentials part, takes about ten minutes and avoids a category of problems later.

sections.title: Install
paragraphs: Use v2. Version 1 is still installable and lacks SSO support, auto-prompt and several output improvements.
If that reports aws-cli/1.x, you have v1. Uninstall it first, since having both on the PATH causes confusing behaviour.

codeBlock.code:
# macOS
brew install awscli

# Linux
curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o awscliv2.zip
unzip awscliv2.zip && sudo ./aws/install

# Windows
winget install Amazon.AWSCLI

sections.title: Configure with SSO, not access keys
paragraphs: aws configure prompts for an access key and secret. Prefer not to use it. Long-lived access keys sitting in ~/.aws/credentials are the credential most likely to end up somewhere it should not.
If your organisation uses IAM Identity Center, and it should, configure SSO instead:
This writes a profile that fetches temporary credentials through your browser session. Nothing long-lived is stored. When the session expires:
For personal accounts with no SSO, aws configure with an access key is the fallback, but create the key on a dedicated IAM user with narrow permissions, and delete it when you stop using it.

codeBlock.code: aws configure sso

sections.title: Named profiles
paragraphs: One profile per account or role. This is what makes multi-account work manageable:

Note the pattern in those last two: production defaults to read-only, with a separate admin profile used deliberately. That means a mistyped command in the wrong terminal fails at the IAM layer rather than changing production.
Select a profile per command or per shell:
For assuming a role from a base profile:
The CLI handles the AssumeRole call and prompts for MFA automatically.

codeBlock.code:
# ~/.aws/config
[default]
region = eu-west-1
output = json

[profile acme-staging]
sso_session = acme
sso_account_id = 111122223333
sso_role_name = PowerUserAccess
region = eu-west-1

[profile acme-prod]
sso_session = acme
sso_account_id = 444455556666
sso_role_name = ReadOnlyAccess    # read-only by default is a good habit
region = eu-west-1

[profile acme-prod-admin]
sso_session = acme
sso_account_id = 444455556666
sso_role_name = AdministratorAccess

[sso-session acme]
sso_start_url = https://acme.awsapps.com/start
sso_region = eu-west-1
sso_registration_scopes = sso:account:access

sections.title: The credential chain
paragraphs: The CLI looks for credentials in this order, and knowing it resolves most "wrong account" confusion:
A stale AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID exported in one terminal overrides your carefully configured profile, which produces genuinely baffling behaviour. When something is wrong, check the environment first:

codeBlock.code: env | grep AWS

sections.title: Always confirm your identity
paragraphs: This is the single most useful AWS command. It answers which account and which identity, and nothing else in the CLI output tells you. Run it before anything destructive. Pointing at the wrong account is the most expensive AWS mistake available.
Showing the active profile in your shell prompt is worth setting up if you work across accounts.

codeBlock.code: aws sts get-caller-identity

sections.title: Output and querying
paragraphs: The --query flag takes a JMESPath expression and filters server-side output before it reaches you, which beats piping gigabytes into jq:
--filters is applied by the AWS API; --query is applied locally by the CLI. Prefer --filters where available, since it reduces what is transferred.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 describe-instances --output table
aws ec2 describe-instances --output yaml

sections.title: Settings worth enabling
paragraphs: The pager setting in particular removes a persistent annoyance, by default v2 pipes output into less, which breaks scripting expectations.

codeBlock.code:
aws configure set cli_pager ""              # stop paging every output
aws configure set cli_auto_prompt on-partial # suggest commands as you type

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A command run with --profile acme-staging keeps acting on the production account. What is the most likely cause?
A team configures acme-prod with ReadOnlyAccess and a separate acme-prod-admin with AdministratorAccess for the same account. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I use aws configure or aws configure sso?

Use aws configure sso if your organisation has IAM Identity Center, which it should. It stores no long-lived credentials. You authenticate through a browser and the CLI receives temporary credentials that expire, refreshed with aws sso login. Plain aws configure writes a permanent access key and secret to ~/.aws/credentials, which is the credential most likely to leak into a repository, a screenshot or a former laptop. Reserve it for personal accounts with no SSO available.
How do I work with multiple AWS accounts?

Define one named profile per account or role in ~/.aws/config, then select with --profile per command or export AWS_PROFILE per shell. A worthwhile pattern is making the default production profile read-only and creating a separate admin profile used deliberately, so an accidental command fails at the IAM layer rather than changing production. Always confirm with aws sts get-caller-identity before anything destructive.
Why is the AWS CLI using the wrong account?

Almost always the credential chain. Command-line flags come first, then environment variables, then the credentials file, then config, then container and instance metadata. A stale AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID or AWS_PROFILE exported earlier in the shell overrides your profile silently. Run env | grep AWS to see what is set, and aws sts get-caller-identity to confirm which identity is actually being used.
What is the difference between --query and --filters?

--filters is applied by the AWS API before the response is sent, so it reduces the data transferred and is supported only on commands that offer it. --query is a JMESPath expression applied locally by the CLI after the full response arrives, and works on every command. Use --filters where available for efficiency, then --query to shape the output, often combined, as in filtering to running instances server-side and selecting specific columns locally.
How do I get a single value out for a shell script?

Combine --query with --output text, as in aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text, which returns the bare value with no quotes or JSON structure. This is the idiomatic way to capture an AWS value into a shell variable. Using --output json and piping through jq -r works too but adds a dependency the CLI does not need.
Why does the AWS CLI page its output?

CLI v2 sends output through a pager by default, which is helpful interactively and unhelpful everywhere else. It breaks scripts and requires a keypress to dismiss. Disable it permanently with aws configure set cli_pager "", or set the AWS_PAGER environment variable to an empty string. This is one of the first settings most people change after installing v2.

Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how AWS IAM decides who can do what: users, groups, roles and policies, policy anatomy, the evaluation order behind AccessDenied and least privilege.
IAM is the permission system that decides who can do what in an AWS account. Every other service defers to it, which makes it the one AWS service you cannot avoid understanding.

It is also the one people get wrong most expensively, because the failure modes are asymmetric: an over-permissive policy works perfectly until it is abused, while an under-permissive one fails loudly and gets fixed.
IAM: Identity & Access Model
Deny always overrides Allow. Explicit deny wins in every evaluation

sections.title: Four building blocks
paragraphs: The distinction that matters most is user versus role. A user carries permanent credentials that exist until someone deletes them. A role issues temporary credentials that expire on their own, typically within an hour.

That difference is why the modern guidance is blunt: do not create IAM users for people. Use IAM Identity Center, or federate from your existing identity provider, so humans sign in with corporate credentials and receive a temporary role session. There are no access keys to leak, and offboarding happens in one place.
Keep IAM users only for the cases that genuinely need a long-lived credential and cannot use a role, and treat each one as a liability to be reviewed.

sections.title: Anatomy of a policy
paragraphs: Two details cause most S3 policy failures. s3:ListBucket acts on the bucket ARN while s3:GetObject acts on the object ARN. They are different resources and both are usually needed. And "Version": "2012-10-17" is a policy language version, not a date you should change; omitting it silently disables condition variables.
Condition is where least privilege becomes practical. Rather than enumerating every resource, you can require a matching tag, a source VPC endpoint, MFA, or a specific request region.

sections.title: How a request is actually evaluated
paragraphs: This is the part worth memorising, because it explains every AccessDenied you will ever see.

The practical consequence: an AdministratorAccess policy does not mean you can do everything. An SCP or a permissions boundary above it silently caps what that allow is worth, and the resulting denial names neither.
simulate-principal-policy is underused and answers the question directly instead of by trial and error.

codeBlock.code:
# Which principal am I actually? First question, always.
aws sts get-caller-identity

sections.title: Roles have two policies, not one
paragraphs: Every role carries two documents, and confusing them is the most common IAM stumbling block.
The trust policy says who may assume the role:
The permissions policy says what the role can do once assumed.

An AccessDenied on sts:AssumeRole is a trust policy problem. An AccessDenied on s3:GetObject after successfully assuming the role is a permissions policy problem. The error tells you which, if you read which action was denied.
The --role-session-name appears in CloudTrail, so putting a build number or username there turns an anonymous role session into an auditable one.

sections.title: How workloads should get permissions
paragraphs: Never embed access keys in an application. Every AWS compute service can assume a role automatically:

That last row deserves emphasis. OIDC removes long-lived AWS keys from CI entirely. The pipeline presents a signed token, AWS exchanges it for temporary credentials, and the trust policy restricts which repository and branch may do so. If your CI still holds an AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, this is the highest-value IAM change available to you.

sections.title: Getting to least privilege without guessing
paragraphs: Starting from AdministratorAccess "for now" never gets narrowed. Start from nothing and add what fails, but use the data AWS already has rather than guessing:

IAM Access Analyzer goes further: it reviews CloudTrail history for a role and generates a policy containing only the actions actually used. That is a far better starting point than a hand-written guess, and it is the fastest route from a permissive policy to a defensible one.
Access Advisor in the console shows services a principal has not touched in months, usually the easiest permissions to remove safely.

codeBlock.code:
# What has this role actually used, and when?
aws iam generate-service-last-accessed-details --arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DeployRole

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A user with the AdministratorAccess policy attached gets AccessDenied when creating an S3 bucket in eu-west-1. The policy is definitely attached. What is the most likely cause?
A CI pipeline fails with AccessDenied on sts:AssumeRole when trying to use a deployment role. Which document should you check?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?

A user is a long-lived identity with permanent credentials. A console password, and often access keys that remain valid until someone deletes them. A role is an identity that anyone or anything permitted by its trust policy can assume temporarily, receiving credentials that expire automatically, typically within an hour. Roles are safer because there is no lasting secret to leak, and they are what EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECS tasks and CI pipelines should use. Current AWS guidance is to avoid creating IAM users for people at all, using IAM Identity Center or federation instead.
Why am I getting AccessDenied when my policy allows the action?

Work through the evaluation order. An explicit Deny anywhere, in an identity policy, a resource policy, or a service control policy, beats every allow. A service control policy in an AWS Organization sets a ceiling that even AdministratorAccess cannot exceed, and region restrictions are a common form of this. A permissions boundary on the principal does the same. Run aws sts get-caller-identity to confirm which principal you actually are, then aws iam simulate-principal-policy to see whether the call would be permitted and what decides it.
What is the difference between a trust policy and a permissions policy?

Both attach to a role and answer different questions. The trust policy names the principals allowed to assume the role: a service such as ec2.amazonaws.com, another account, or a federated identity provider. The permissions policy defines what the role may do once assumed. If you are denied on sts:AssumeRole, the trust policy is refusing you; if you assume the role successfully and are then denied on an action, the permissions policy is the problem. Reading which action was denied tells you which document to open.
How do I give an EC2 instance or Lambda function access to S3?

Attach a role, never access keys. For EC2 that means an instance profile; for Lambda an execution role; for ECS a task role; for EKS, Pod Identity or IRSA. The SDK on that compute picks the credentials up automatically from the instance metadata service or the environment, with no configuration in your code. Embedding access keys in an application or an AMI is the single most common way AWS credentials leak, because they end up in images, repositories and logs.
How do I remove AWS access keys from my CI pipeline?

Use OIDC federation. Register your CI provider, GitHub Actions, GitLab, and most others support this, as an OIDC identity provider in your AWS account, then create a role whose trust policy accepts tokens from it with conditions restricting which repository and branch may assume it. The pipeline exchanges a short-lived signed token for temporary AWS credentials at run time. Nothing long-lived is stored anywhere, there is nothing to rotate, and a leaked pipeline log contains no reusable secret.
How do I actually achieve least privilege without breaking things?

Use the data AWS already collects rather than guessing. IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from a role's real CloudTrail activity, giving you a starting point containing only actions genuinely used. Access Advisor shows which services a principal has not touched in months, which are the safest permissions to remove first. Apply changes in a non-production account and watch CloudTrail for denials before promoting. Starting broad with the intention of narrowing later almost never results in narrowing.

Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how IAM users and groups work, why AWS recommends against IAM users for people, how to keep access keys safe and how to move to IAM Identity Center.
An IAM user is a long-lived identity with permanent credentials. A group is a container that carries policies and applies them to its members.

Both are foundational to understanding IAM, and current AWS guidance is that you should not create users for people. That tension is worth resolving up front, because most material on this topic predates the recommendation.

sections.title: Users
paragraphs: A user has an ARN, optionally a console password, and optionally up to two access keys:
The secret is shown exactly once. There is no way to retrieve it again. Losing it means creating a new key and deleting the old one.
Those credentials remain valid until someone deletes them. They do not expire, they work from anywhere in the world, and they are trivially copied. That is the entire problem.

codeBlock.code:
aws iam create-user --user-name ci-legacy-uploader
aws iam create-access-key --user-name ci-legacy-uploader

sections.title: Groups
paragraphs: A group holds policies; users in it inherit them. Groups have no credentials and cannot be assumed.

Attach policies to groups, never directly to users. Per-user policies produce an estate where nobody can answer "what can this person do" without inspecting each account individually, and where offboarding means finding every attachment.
A user can belong to up to ten groups, and permissions are the union of all of them.
Groups cannot be nested, there is no group-within-a-group, which is one of several reasons Identity Center exists.

codeBlock.code:
aws iam create-group --group-name developers
aws iam attach-group-policy \
  --group-name developers \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/PowerUserAccess
aws iam add-user-to-group --user-name alice --group-name developers

sections.title: Why AWS recommends against users for people
paragraphs: The failure mode with IAM users is not theoretical. Access keys end up in Git repositories, in CI configuration, in Slack messages, on former employees' laptops, and in Docker images. Public scanners find exposed AWS keys within minutes.
IAM Identity Center removes the category entirely: people sign in with corporate credentials and receive a temporary role session.

codeBlock.code: aws configure sso

sections.title: Where users still make sense
paragraphs: A small number of genuine cases remain:
Treat each as a liability with a named owner and a review date. Everything else, EC2, Lambda, ECS, EKS, CI pipelines, should use a role.

sections.title: Access key hygiene
paragraphs: If you must have keys, manage them properly.
The report lists every user with MFA status, key age, and when each key was last used. Two things to act on:
Keys unused for 90 days should be deleted, not rotated. An unused key is pure risk with no benefit.
Rotation uses the two-key allowance:
Deactivating before deleting is the part people skip, and it is what turns a botched rotation from an outage into a one-command revert.

codeBlock.code:
aws iam generate-credential-report
aws iam get-credential-report --query Content --output text | base64 -d | column -t -s,

sections.title: MFA
paragraphs: Enforce it with a policy condition rather than trusting people to enable it. Denying everything except MFA management when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false is the standard pattern.

codeBlock.code:
aws iam list-users --query 'Users[].UserName' --output text | \
  xargs -n1 -I{} sh -c 'echo -n "{}: "; aws iam list-mfa-devices --user-name {} --query "length(MFADevices)"'

sections.title: Migrating to Identity Center
paragraphs: Step 6 matters. Deactivate rather than delete first, so anything you missed fails visibly and reversibly rather than permanently.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Why is attaching policies to groups rather than directly to individual users considered best practice?
What is the correct sequence for rotating an IAM access key that is in active use?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I create IAM users for my team?

No. Current AWS guidance is to use IAM Identity Center or federate from an existing identity provider, so people sign in with corporate credentials and receive temporary role sessions. IAM users hold permanent credentials that do not expire, work from anywhere, and are easily copied, which is why exposed AWS access keys are found in public repositories within minutes of being committed. Identity Center also centralises offboarding and MFA enforcement across every account.
What is the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?

A user is a long-lived identity with permanent credentials. A password and possibly access keys that remain valid until deleted. A role has no permanent credentials; it is assumed temporarily by a person, a service or another account, issuing credentials that expire automatically, typically within an hour. Roles are safer because there is no lasting secret, and they are what EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECS tasks and CI pipelines should use.
I lost my AWS secret access key. Can I recover it?

No. The secret is displayed exactly once, at creation, and AWS does not store it in retrievable form. Create a new access key, deploy it wherever the old one was used, then deactivate and finally delete the old key. Since a user may hold two active keys, this can be done without downtime. If the lost key is no longer needed anywhere, simply delete it.
How often should I rotate access keys?

Frequently enough that a leaked key has limited value: 90 days is a common policy. But rotation is a mitigation for a problem better solved by removal: a key unused for 90 days should be deleted rather than rotated, and workloads should use roles so there is no key at all. Generate a credential report regularly to find both stale keys and users without MFA. Rotation matters most for the small number of keys that genuinely cannot be eliminated.
Can IAM groups be nested?

No. A group cannot contain another group, so hierarchies such as "all engineers" containing "backend engineers" are not possible in IAM. You would attach overlapping policies or add users to multiple groups instead. A user can belong to up to ten groups and receives the union of their permissions. This limitation is one of several reasons IAM Identity Center exists, since its permission sets and directory groups model organisational structure far better.
How do I migrate from IAM users to Identity Center?

Enable Identity Center in the management account, connect an identity source such as Entra ID, Okta or Google Workspace, then create permission sets and assign groups to accounts. Have people reconfigure their CLI with aws configure sso. Before deleting anything, deactivate the old access keys and watch CloudTrail for authentication failures, that surfaces any automation still using them in a way you can reverse with a single command. Delete the users only once the account has been quiet for a while.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand IAM roles and policies: trust vs permission policies, assuming roles with STS, managed vs inline policies, boundaries and AssumeRole errors.
A role is an identity with no permanent credentials. Something assumes it, receives temporary credentials, and acts with its permissions until they expire.
That is why roles are preferred almost everywhere: there is no lasting secret to leak, rotate, or find committed to a repository.

sections.title: Every role has two policies
paragraphs: This trips up nearly everyone at first, and keeping them straight makes IAM errors far easier to read.
The trust policy: who may assume this role:
The permissions policy: what the role can do once assumed:
The error message tells you which one failed:

sections.title: Principals in a trust policy
paragraphs: Naming :root means "any principal in that account whose own IAM policy allows it", not the root user. It is broader than most people intend; naming a specific role is better.
Conditions narrow it considerably, and for cross-account access an external ID protects against the confused deputy problem:
For OIDC federation, the condition is what stops any repository on the provider assuming your role:
Omitting that sub condition is a serious mistake, without it, any GitHub repository anywhere can assume the role.

sections.title: Assuming a role
paragraphs: --role-session-name appears in CloudTrail, so putting a build number or username there turns an anonymous session into an auditable one. Use it meaningfully.

Sessions default to one hour and can be extended up to the role's maximum session duration, which itself caps at twelve hours. Role chaining, assuming a role from within an assumed role, is limited to one hour regardless.
In practice you rarely call assume-role by hand. A named profile does it for you:

codeBlock.code:
aws sts assume-role \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DeployRole \
  --role-session-name ci-build-482

sections.title: Policy types
paragraphs: Prefer customer-managed policies to inline ones. An inline policy does not appear when you list policies, cannot be attached elsewhere, and is easy to miss in an audit. AWS managed policies are convenient starting points and almost always grant more than needed, AmazonS3FullAccess on a role that reads one prefix is a real risk with no benefit.
Customer-managed policies are versioned, with up to five versions kept, so rolling back a bad change is straightforward:

codeBlock.code:
aws iam list-policy-versions --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:policy/PaymentsRead
aws iam set-default-policy-version --policy-arn <arn> --version-id v3

sections.title: Permissions boundaries
paragraphs: A boundary sets the maximum permissions a principal can have. The effective permissions are the intersection of its policies and its boundary. A boundary never grants anything.
The main use is safe delegation: letting a team create roles for their own workloads without being able to escalate to administrator.
That condition means they may create roles only if they attach your boundary, so anything they create is capped by it.
This is also a common cause of confusing denials. A principal with AdministratorAccess and a restrictive boundary is not an administrator, and nothing in the error says so.

sections.title: How workloads get roles
paragraphs: The ECS distinction is worth stating clearly because it causes a lot of confusion: the task execution role is used by the ECS agent to pull the image from ECR and write logs; the task role is what your application code uses to call AWS. Putting your application's S3 permissions on the execution role does not work.
The SDK finds these credentials automatically through the default provider chain, so application code should never reference them explicitly.

sections.title: Debugging
paragraphs: Run both list-attached-role-policies and list-role-policies. The second returns inline policies, which the first does not, and an unnoticed inline policy is a classic source of "where is this permission coming from".
Common causes, in the order worth checking:

codeBlock.code:
# Who am I actually?
aws sts get-caller-identity

# Would this be allowed?
aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DeployRole \
  --action-names s3:PutObject \
  --resource-arns 'arn:aws:s3:::acme-artifacts/build.zip'

# What is attached?
aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name DeployRole
aws iam list-role-policies --role-name DeployRole          # inline ones
aws iam get-role --role-name DeployRole --query 'Role.AssumeRolePolicyDocument'

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A GitHub Actions OIDC trust policy conditions only on the audience claim, not on sub. What is the consequence?
An ECS task pulls its image and writes logs successfully, but the application gets AccessDenied calling S3. S3 permissions were added to the task execution role. What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a trust policy and a permissions policy?

Both attach to a role and answer different questions. The trust policy names which principals are allowed to assume the role: an AWS service, another account, a federated identity provider. The permissions policy defines what the role can do once assumed. When you get AccessDenied, the action named in the error tells you which to look at: a denial on sts:AssumeRole is a trust policy problem, while a denial on anything else means you assumed the role successfully and its permissions are lacking.
How do I assume an IAM role from the CLI?

Either explicitly with aws sts assume-role --role-arn <arn> --role-session-name <name>, which returns temporary credentials, or, much more conveniently, by configuring a named profile in ~/.aws/config with role_arn and source_profile, after which aws s3 ls --profile prod-deploy handles the assumption transparently. Adding mfa_serial to the profile prompts for an MFA code automatically. Always set a meaningful session name, since it appears in CloudTrail and is what makes role activity attributable to a person or a build.
What is the difference between managed and inline policies?

A managed policy is a standalone object that can be attached to many principals, is versioned so changes can be rolled back, and appears when you list policies. An inline policy is embedded in a single principal, cannot be reused, has no version history, and does not show up in policy listings, which makes it easy to miss during an audit and a frequent source of unexplained permissions. Prefer customer-managed policies. AWS managed policies are useful starting points but are generally far broader than a specific workload needs.
What is a permissions boundary and when do I need one?

A permissions boundary caps the maximum permissions a principal can have; effective permissions are the intersection of its policies and the boundary. It never grants anything. The main use is safe delegation. Allowing a team to create IAM roles for their own workloads while requiring that every role they create carries your boundary, so nothing they create can exceed it. It is also a common cause of confusing denials, since a principal with AdministratorAccess and a restrictive boundary is not an administrator and the error message does not mention the boundary.
Why does my ECS task get AccessDenied when calling AWS APIs?

Almost certainly because the permissions are on the wrong role. ECS uses two: the task execution role, assumed by the ECS agent to pull images from ECR and write logs to CloudWatch, and the task role, which your application code uses via the SDK. If image pulls and logging work but your application's API calls fail, the permissions were added to the execution role and need to be on the task role instead.
How do I set up cross-account role access safely?

Name the specific role in the other account rather than using :root, which grants to any principal in that account whose own IAM permits it. Add an external ID condition when a third party will assume the role, which protects against the confused deputy problem where another customer of that third party could otherwise have them assume your role. Remember both sides must allow it, the trust policy on your role and an IAM policy in the calling account, and if the target resource uses KMS encryption, the key policy needs the external principal as well.
