sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Harden IAM: replace IAM users with Identity Center, drop long-lived CI keys, lock down root, reach least privilege from usage data and set boundaries.

IAM failures are asymmetric. An over-permissive policy works perfectly until it is abused; an under-permissive one fails immediately and gets fixed. That asymmetry is why permissions drift outward over time unless something deliberately pushes back.
These are ordered by impact, not by how often they appear on checklists.

sections.title: 1. Stop creating IAM users for people
paragraphs: This is the highest-impact change available and the one most often skipped.

An IAM user holds permanent credentials, a console password and often access keys, that remain valid until someone deletes them. They get committed to repositories, pasted into scripts, kept on former employees' laptops, and forgotten.

Use IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO), or federate from your existing identity provider. People then sign in with corporate credentials and receive a temporary role session. There are no access keys to leak, offboarding happens in one place, and access across multiple accounts is managed centrally.
Keep IAM users only where a long-lived credential is genuinely unavoidable, and treat each as a liability with a named owner.

codeBlock.code:
# Find the users you still have
aws iam list-users --query 'Users[].[UserName,CreateDate,PasswordLastUsed]' --output table

sections.title: 2. Remove long-lived access keys from CI
paragraphs: The second-largest exposure. A pipeline holding AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY has a credential that works from anywhere, forever, until rotated.
OIDC federation removes it entirely. Register your CI provider as an OIDC identity provider, create a role whose trust policy accepts its tokens, and condition on the specific repository and branch:
That sub condition is not optional. Without it, any repository on GitHub can assume your role. It is a genuine and not-uncommon misconfiguration.
Find keys that still exist:
The report shows every user, whether MFA is enabled, and when each key was last used. Keys unused for 90 days should be deleted, not rotated.

sections.title: 3. Lock the root user away
paragraphs: The root user cannot be restricted by IAM policy or by a service control policy. It is the one identity that can do anything.

sections.title: 4. Get to least privilege from data, not guesswork
paragraphs: Starting with AdministratorAccess "for now" never gets narrowed. But hand-writing a minimal policy is slow and usually wrong in both directions.
Use what AWS already records:

IAM Access Analyzer policy generation goes further. It reviews CloudTrail history for a role and generates a policy containing only the actions genuinely used. That is a far better starting point than a guess, and it turns least privilege from a research project into a review task.
Access Advisor in the console shows services a principal has not touched in months. Those are the safest permissions to remove first.
Apply reductions in a non-production account and watch CloudTrail for denials before promoting.

codeBlock.code:
# What has this role actually used, and when?
aws iam generate-service-last-accessed-details --arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/DeployRole

sections.title: 5. Prefer customer-managed policies
paragraphs: Inline policies are the ones that surprise people during an audit, because list-attached-role-policies does not show them:
Customer-managed policies keep up to five versions, so a bad change rolls back in one command.

codeBlock.code:
aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name DeployRole   # managed
aws iam list-role-policies --role-name DeployRole            # inline. Run both

sections.title: 6. Use conditions rather than enumerating resources
paragraphs: Conditions make least privilege practical at scale:

Attribute-based access control, matching a principal's tag against a resource's tag, scales where enumerating every ARN does not. Other high-value conditions require MFA for sensitive actions, restrict access to a VPC endpoint, or limit a role to specific regions.

sections.title: 7. Permissions boundaries for safe delegation
paragraphs: A boundary caps the maximum permissions a principal can have. Effective permissions are the intersection of its policies and the boundary; a boundary never grants anything.
The main use is letting teams create their own roles without being able to escalate:
Note the flip side: a boundary is a silent cause of denials. A principal with AdministratorAccess and a restrictive boundary is not an administrator, and nothing in the error says so.

sections.title: 8. Service control policies for organisation-wide guardrails
paragraphs: SCPs apply across an AWS Organization and cannot be overridden by any account-level policy, including root. They set ceilings rather than granting anything.
Common guardrails: deny the ability to leave the organisation, deny disabling CloudTrail or GuardDuty, deny regions you do not operate in, deny deleting specific backup resources.

sections.title: 9. Audit on a schedule
paragraphs: Access Analyzer is worth enabling regardless of whether you suspect a problem. It continuously reports which resources are accessible from outside the account, which is a question most teams cannot otherwise answer.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A GitHub Actions OIDC trust policy conditions only on the aud claim. What is the risk?
An audit lists a role's attached policies and finds nothing granting S3 access, yet the role can read buckets. What was missed?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I still create IAM users?

Not for people. Current AWS guidance is to use IAM Identity Center or federate from an existing identity provider, so humans sign in with corporate credentials and receive a temporary role session with no permanent access keys to leak. Offboarding then happens in one place rather than across every account. Reserve IAM users for the narrow cases where a long-lived credential is genuinely unavoidable, and give each one a named owner and a review date.
How do I remove AWS access keys from my CI/CD pipeline?

Use OIDC federation. Register your CI provider as an OIDC identity provider in AWS, create a role whose trust policy accepts its tokens, and condition on the specific repository and branch. The pipeline exchanges a short-lived signed token for temporary credentials at run time, so nothing long-lived is stored and there is nothing to rotate. The critical detail is conditioning on the sub claim, without it, any repository on that provider can assume your role.
How do I actually achieve least privilege?

Use the data AWS already collects rather than guessing. IAM Access Analyzer generates a policy from a role's real CloudTrail activity, giving a starting point containing only actions genuinely used. Access Advisor shows which services a principal has not touched in months, which are the safest permissions to remove first. Apply reductions in a non-production account and monitor CloudTrail for denials before promoting. Starting broad with the intention of narrowing later almost never results in narrowing.
What is a permissions boundary and when should I use one?

A boundary caps the maximum permissions a principal can have. Effective permissions are the intersection of its policies and the boundary, and the boundary never grants anything itself. The main use is safe delegation: allowing a team to create IAM roles for their own workloads while requiring that every role they create carries your boundary. Be aware it is also a silent cause of denials, since a principal with AdministratorAccess and a restrictive boundary is not an administrator and the error does not say why.
How should I secure the AWS root user?

Enable hardware MFA, delete any access keys it has, and use it only for the small number of tasks that genuinely require root. Closing the account, changing the support plan, certain billing operations. Set up a CloudTrail and EventBridge alert on root sign-in so any use is noticed immediately. Root is the one identity that cannot be restricted by IAM policies or service control policies, which is precisely why it should be locked away rather than managed.
What should I audit regularly in IAM?

Run a credential report to find users without MFA and access keys unused for 90 days, which should be deleted rather than rotated. Use Access Advisor to find permissions never exercised. Enable IAM Access Analyzer, which continuously reports which resources are reachable from outside the account. A question most teams cannot otherwise answer. Alert on root sign-in. And check both attached and inline policies, since inline ones do not appear in the attached-policies listing and are easy to miss entirely.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how EC2 works: instance families and sizing, pricing models, EBS vs instance store, IMDSv2, Session Manager instead of SSH, and stop vs terminate.

sections.title: Amazon EC2
paragraphs: EC2 gives you virtual machines. That sounds unremarkable until you consider that the decisions around them, which family, which pricing model, which storage, how you get a shell, account for a large share of most AWS bills and most AWS security findings.
EC2: Instance Lifecycle
Stopped instances retain their EBS root volume. You only stop paying for compute

sections.title: Reading an instance type
paragraphs: m6i.xlarge decomposes into four parts:

Two easy wins hide in that table. Always use the newest generation available. An m7i typically costs less than an m5 and performs better. And Graviton instances are roughly 20% cheaper for equivalent performance; if your workload is a container, an interpreted language or anything with an ARM build, the migration is often trivial and the saving is permanent.

sections.title: Burstable instances have a credit system
paragraphs: t family instances earn CPU credits while below their baseline and spend them above it. Run out and the instance is throttled hard, sometimes to 20% of a core, which presents as an application that is inexplicably slow while CloudWatch shows low CPU.

unlimited mode lets them burst past the balance for an extra charge, which is fine until a runaway process produces a surprising bill. For anything with sustained load, an m family instance is both cheaper and more predictable.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUCreditBalance \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abc123 \
  --start-time 2026-09-11T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-09-12T00:00:00Z \
  --period 3600 --statistics Average

sections.title: Pricing
paragraphs: Compute Savings Plans are the pragmatic default for steady workloads: they commit to an hourly spend rather than a specific instance type, so they keep applying as you change families, sizes and regions. Reserved Instances are more rigid and usually only worth it for a workload you are certain will not change.

Spot is the largest single saving available and is underused. Anything fault-tolerant. CI runners, batch jobs, stateless web tiers behind a load balancer, Kubernetes worker nodes. Can run on Spot with a mixed-instances policy that falls back to On-Demand. Handle the two-minute interruption notice and the risk is manageable.

sections.title: Storage: EBS and instance store
paragraphs: EBS is network-attached block storage that persists independently of the instance.
Moving gp2 volumes to gp3 is typically around 20% cheaper and faster, because gp3 no longer ties performance to volume size. It is a live change with no downtime:

Instance store is physically attached NVMe. It is far faster and entirely ephemeral: stopping the instance loses it permanently. Use it for caches, scratch space and temporary build output, never for anything you need to keep.
Two EBS defaults worth changing: enable encryption by default at the account level, and note that the root volume is set to delete on termination while additional volumes are not.

codeBlock.code: aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0abc123 --volume-type gp3

sections.title: Getting a shell: use Session Manager, not SSH
paragraphs: The traditional approach, a key pair, port 22 open, a bastion host, has a lot of moving parts to get wrong. SSM Session Manager replaces all of it:

No open inbound ports, no key pairs to distribute or rotate, no bastion to maintain. Access is controlled by IAM, every session is logged to CloudTrail, and it works for instances in private subnets with no public IP at all.
It needs the SSM agent (preinstalled on current Amazon Linux and Ubuntu AMIs) and an instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. That is the whole setup.
If you still need SSH, at least restrict the security group to a known CIDR rather than 0.0.0.0/0. An open port 22 is found by automated scanners within minutes.

codeBlock.code: aws ssm start-session --target i-0abc123

sections.title: User data and metadata
paragraphs: User data runs on first boot:

It runs once, as root, on the first start only. A common confusion when people expect it on every reboot. Output goes to /var/log/cloud-init-output.log, which is the first place to look when an instance comes up wrong.
The instance metadata service provides instance identity and, importantly, the temporary credentials from its IAM role. Require IMDSv2:

IMDSv1 answered a plain GET, which meant a server-side request forgery bug in your application could be used to read the instance's AWS credentials. IMDSv2 requires a session token obtained by PUT, which closes that path. New instances default to requiring it; older ones need this change.

sections.title: Stop, terminate, hibernate
paragraphs: Two things catch people. A stopped instance still bills for its EBS volumes. Stopping saves the compute charge only. And a stopped instance gets a new public IP when restarted, which breaks anything pointing at the old one; attach an Elastic IP, or better, put a load balancer in front.
Enable termination protection on anything that matters:

codeBlock.code: aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id i-0abc123 --disable-api-termination

sections.title: Treat instances as replaceable
paragraphs: The pattern that saves the most operational pain: define the instance in a launch template, bake or bootstrap it reproducibly, and put it in an Auto Scaling group even if the desired capacity is one.
Then a failed instance is replaced automatically rather than repaired by hand at 3am, and nothing has state that only exists on one machine.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A t3.medium web server becomes very slow under moderate load, but CloudWatch shows CPU utilisation around 20%. What is the likely cause?
What class of vulnerability does requiring IMDSv2 on an EC2 instance mitigate?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I choose an EC2 instance type?

Start with the family that matches the bottleneck, m for balanced workloads, c when CPU-bound, r when memory-bound, t only for genuinely bursty or low-traffic work. Then pick the newest generation available, since newer generations are typically both faster and cheaper. Consider Graviton (g in the name, such as m7g) for around 20% saving where your workload runs on ARM, which most containerised and interpreted applications do. Size from measurement rather than estimate, and use Compute Optimizer, which recommends right-sizing from real utilisation data.
What is the difference between stopping and terminating an instance?

Stopping halts the instance and ends compute charges, but the root EBS volume is preserved and still billed, and you can start it again. Terminating destroys the instance and, by default, deletes its root volume permanently. Two details surprise people regularly: a stopped instance still costs money for its storage, and restarting a stopped instance assigns a new public IP unless an Elastic IP is attached. Data on instance store volumes is lost on stop as well as on terminate.
How do I connect to an EC2 instance without SSH keys?

Use SSM Session Manager: aws ssm start-session --target i-0abc123. It needs the SSM agent, which is preinstalled on current Amazon Linux and Ubuntu AMIs, and an instance profile with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy. There are no inbound ports to open, no keys to distribute or rotate, and no bastion host. Access is granted through IAM and every session is recorded in CloudTrail. It works for instances in private subnets with no public IP at all.
How can I reduce my EC2 costs?

In order of impact: buy Compute Savings Plans for baseline steady-state usage, which discount up to around 72% while remaining flexible across instance families and regions. Move fault-tolerant workloads, CI runners, batch processing, stateless web tiers, Kubernetes nodes, to Spot for up to 90% off. Migrate to Graviton where the workload supports ARM. Upgrade to the newest instance generation and convert gp2 volumes to gp3. Then find idle and oversized instances with Compute Optimizer, and stop non-production instances outside working hours.
What is IMDSv2 and should I enforce it?

The instance metadata service provides instance identity and the temporary credentials from the instance's IAM role. IMDSv1 served these over a plain GET request, which meant a server-side request forgery flaw in your application could be used to read those credentials and act as the instance in AWS. IMDSv2 requires a session token obtained via PUT, which closes that route. Enforce it, aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --http-tokens required, on every instance. New instances default to requiring it, but older ones do not.
Why doesn't my user data script run when I restart the instance?

Because user data executes only on the first boot by design. Cloud-init records that it has run and skips it thereafter, so changes to the script have no effect on an existing instance. For configuration that must apply on every boot, use a systemd unit or a configuration management tool instead. When a first boot does not produce the expected result, /var/log/cloud-init-output.log on the instance contains the script's output and is almost always where the answer is.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Launch an EC2 instance properly: pick an AMI without hardcoding IDs, use a launch template and user data, enforce IMDSv2 and debug a bad start.

Launching an instance needs six decisions: which image, which size, which network, which credentials, what runs at boot, and how you will reach it. Getting them right the first time is considerably easier than fixing them afterwards.

sections.title: Do not hardcode the AMI ID
paragraphs: AMI IDs are Region-specific and change with every release, so a hardcoded ID is both unportable and steadily more out of date, which means steadily more unpatched.
AWS publishes current images as SSM public parameters:
Terraform and CloudFormation can both resolve these at deploy time, so templates never carry a stale ID.

The trade-off is that a new AMI release changes the resolved value, which can trigger instance replacement. That is manageable behind a launch template and an Auto Scaling group, and a reason to pin deliberately for a pet instance.

codeBlock.code:
AMI=$(aws ssm get-parameter \
  --name /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 \
  --query Parameter.Value --output text)
echo $AMI

sections.title: Launch with the settings that matter
paragraphs: Four of those deserve attention.

--metadata-options HttpTokens=required enforces IMDSv2. IMDSv1 answered a plain GET to a well-known address, which meant a server-side request forgery bug in your application could read the instance role's AWS credentials. IMDSv2 requires a token obtained by PUT, closing that path. New instances default to requiring it, but set it explicitly so the intent is in your code.
--iam-instance-profile is how the instance gets AWS permissions. Never bake access keys into an AMI or user data. The SDK picks up role credentials from the metadata service automatically.
No key pair in that command, deliberately. Use Session Manager instead, which needs no inbound port and no key to distribute.
Encrypted: true on the root volume, or better, enable EBS encryption by default at the account level so no launch can forget:

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id "$AMI" \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --subnet-id subnet-private-a \
  --security-group-ids sg-application \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=app-instance-profile \
  --metadata-options "HttpTokens=required,HttpEndpoint=enabled" \
  --block-device-mappings '[{"DeviceName":"/dev/xvda","Ebs":{"VolumeSize":30,"VolumeType":"gp3","Encrypted":true,"DeleteOnTermination":true}}]' \
  --user-data file://bootstrap.sh \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=payments-api},{Key=Environment,Value=production}]'

sections.title: Use a launch template
paragraphs: run-instances is fine for learning. For anything real, put the configuration in a launch template:

Templates are versioned, so changes are auditable and reversible. More importantly, they are what Auto Scaling groups consume, and putting even a single instance behind an Auto Scaling group with min=max=1 means a failed instance is replaced automatically rather than repaired by hand.
That single change converts an instance from a pet into cattle, and it is the difference between a node failure being an alert and being an incident.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-launch-template \
  --launch-template-name payments-api \
  --launch-template-data '{
    "ImageId":"'"$AMI"'",
    "InstanceType":"t3.micro",
    "IamInstanceProfile":{"Name":"app-instance-profile"},
    "MetadataOptions":{"HttpTokens":"required"},
    "SecurityGroupIds":["sg-application"],
    "UserData":"'"$(base64 -i bootstrap.sh)"'"
  }'

sections.title: User data runs once
paragraphs: Three things to know:
set -euxo pipefail at the top is worth the habit: without -e, a failing command is ignored and the instance boots half-configured with no obvious error.
For anything substantial, bake the image with Packer instead. Boot time drops and the result is reproducible rather than dependent on package repositories being reachable and unchanged.
Setting user_data_replace_on_change in Terraform makes a script change replace the instance, which is usually what you actually want.

codeBlock.code:
#!/bin/bash
set -euxo pipefail

dnf update -y
dnf install -y nginx amazon-cloudwatch-agent

systemctl enable --now nginx

sections.title: Reaching it
paragraphs: No key pair, no inbound port 22, no bastion. It works for instances in private subnets with no public IP. Requirements are the SSM agent, preinstalled on current Amazon Linux and Ubuntu AMIs, and the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy on the instance profile.
If you do use SSH, restrict the security group to a known CIDR. An open port 22 is found by scanners within minutes.

codeBlock.code: aws ssm start-session --target i-0abc123

sections.title: When it comes up wrong
paragraphs: Two status checks, and which one fails tells you where to look:
A stop and start moves the instance to different physical hardware and resolves most system status failures. A reboot does not, since it stays on the same host.
Console output is the closest thing to a monitor attached to the machine, and it shows kernel messages and boot failures that no agent could report.
Two more things that catch people: a stopped instance gets a new public IP when restarted unless an Elastic IP is attached, and instance store data is lost on stop.

codeBlock.code:
# Is it actually running and passing checks?
aws ec2 describe-instance-status --instance-ids i-0abc123 \
  --query 'InstanceStatuses[0].{Instance:InstanceStatus.Status,System:SystemStatus.Status}'

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An instance fails its system status check but passes the instance status check. What is the right first action?
A team edits an instance's user data to install an extra package and reboots. The package is not installed. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I avoid hardcoding AMI IDs?

Read them from AWS's public SSM parameters, which always resolve to the current image, /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 for Amazon Linux, with equivalents published for Ubuntu and other distributions. Terraform and CloudFormation can both resolve these at deploy time. AMI IDs are Region-specific and change with every release, so a hardcoded value is unportable and becomes progressively more unpatched.
Should I use run-instances or a launch template?

A launch template for anything beyond experimentation. Templates are versioned so changes are auditable and reversible, and they are what Auto Scaling groups consume, which matters because putting even a single instance behind an Auto Scaling group with min and max of one means a failed instance is replaced automatically. That converts a node failure from an incident into a non-event, and it is the single biggest operational improvement available when launching instances.
Why doesn't my user data script run after a reboot?

Because it is designed to run only on first boot. Cloud-init records that it has executed and skips it thereafter, so editing the script on an existing instance achieves nothing. For configuration that must apply on every boot, use a systemd unit instead. When a first boot produces the wrong result, /var/log/cloud-init-output.log on the instance contains the script's full output and almost always explains it.
How do I give an EC2 instance permission to access AWS services?

Attach an IAM instance profile at launch. The SDK inside the instance picks up temporary credentials automatically from the instance metadata service, with no configuration in your application. Never bake access keys into an AMI, user data or application configuration. Those are permanent credentials that end up in images, snapshots and repositories. Also require IMDSv2, which prevents a server-side request forgery bug from being used to read those role credentials.
Do I need a key pair to launch an EC2 instance?

No, and for new instances you generally should not use one. SSM Session Manager gives you a shell with no key pair, no inbound port 22 and no bastion host, working even for instances in private subnets with no public IP. It needs the SSM agent, which is preinstalled on current Amazon Linux and Ubuntu images, and the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy on the instance profile. Access is granted through IAM and every session is logged to CloudTrail.
What is the difference between the two EC2 status checks?

The system status check monitors AWS infrastructure. The physical host, its networking and power. The instance status check monitors your instance's own health, covering things like a kernel panic, a full root volume or a broken network configuration. A system check failure is fixed by stopping and starting the instance, which relocates it to different hardware; a reboot keeps it on the same failing host. An instance check failure means looking at the guest, starting with get-console-output.

Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Read an EC2 instance type name, learn what each family is for, understand burstable credits and Graviton savings, and size instances from data, not guesses.

There are several hundred EC2 instance types. The naming is systematic, so once you can decode it the choice narrows quickly, and two simple rules ("newest generation" and "consider Graviton") capture most of the available savings.

sections.title: Reading the name
paragraphs: m6i.xlarge has four parts:
So c7g.4xlarge is compute-optimised, seventh generation, Graviton, four times the base extra-large size.
Sizes scale predictably, 2xlarge has twice the vCPU and memory of xlarge, and roughly twice the price. That linearity means there is rarely a cost advantage in picking an awkward size.

sections.title: The families
paragraphs: Start from the bottleneck. If the workload is waiting on CPU, c. If it is holding a large dataset in memory, r. If neither dominates, m.

sections.title: Two rules that capture most of the savings
paragraphs: Use the newest generation available. An m7i typically costs less than an m5 and performs better. Upgrading generation is usually a stop and start, and it is close to free money. Check what is available in your region:

Consider Graviton. AWS's ARM processors are roughly 20% cheaper for equivalent performance and often faster. For containers, interpreted languages, and anything with an ARM build, migration is frequently a base image change and a rebuild.

It applies well beyond EC2. RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch and Lambda all have Graviton options, and switching an RDS instance class to db.m6g is a maintenance-window change with an immediate permanent saving.
The constraint is genuine but narrow: compiled binaries need an ARM build, and a few commercial agents remain x86-only. Test rather than assume.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 describe-instance-type-offerings \
  --location-type availability-zone \
  --filters Name=instance-type,Values=m7i.large \
  --region eu-west-1

sections.title: Burstable instances and the credit trap
paragraphs: The t family is cheap because it does not give you a full core continuously. Each instance has a baseline percentage of a vCPU and earns CPU credits while running below it, spending them to burst above.

Run out of credits and the instance is throttled hard, sometimes to 20% of a core. The symptom is an application that is inexplicably slow while CloudWatch shows low CPU utilisation, because the utilisation figure is of the throttled allowance.
A credit balance trending toward zero means the workload does not fit the family.

Unlimited mode lets it burst past the balance for a surcharge, which is fine until a runaway process produces a surprising bill. For anything with sustained load, an m instance is both cheaper and more predictable than a t instance in unlimited mode.
Use t for genuinely bursty or idle workloads. Do not use it for production services with steady traffic.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUCreditBalance \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abc123 \
  --start-time 2026-09-14T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-09-15T00:00:00Z \
  --period 3600 --statistics Minimum

sections.title: Size from data, not guesswork
paragraphs: Over-provisioning is close to universal, because sizing is usually a guess made once and never revisited.
AWS Compute Optimizer analyses real CloudWatch utilisation and recommends a size, including cross-family and Graviton options:

Two caveats worth knowing. Memory utilisation is not visible to CloudWatch without the CloudWatch agent, so recommendations are CPU-weighted unless you have installed it. And it needs at least 14 days of data to be meaningful.

codeBlock.code:
aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations \
  --query 'instanceRecommendations[].{Instance:instanceArn,Current:currentInstanceType,Finding:finding,Recommended:recommendationOptions[0].instanceType}' \
  --output table

sections.title: Changing instance type
paragraphs: Not a live operation. The instance must be stopped:
Two things to expect. Instance store data is lost on stop. And the instance gets a new public IP on restart unless an Elastic IP is attached.
If the workload sits behind a launch template and an Auto Scaling group, which it should, changing the type is a template update and an instance refresh, with no manual stop at all.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0abc123
aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --instance-ids i-0abc123
aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id i-0abc123 --instance-type m7i.large
aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-0abc123

sections.title: Pricing shorthand
paragraphs: Commit to your baseline with a Compute Savings Plan, and run anything fault-tolerant on Spot.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A t3.medium web server is slow under moderate load, but CloudWatch reports CPU utilisation around 20%. What is happening?
A team is running m5.large instances and discovers m7i.large costs less per hour. How is a newer generation cheaper?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I read an EC2 instance type name?

m6i.xlarge breaks into family, generation, attributes and size. The letter is the family, t burstable, m balanced, c compute-optimised, r memory-optimised, i storage-optimised, p and g accelerated. The number is the generation, where higher is newer. Trailing letters indicate the processor and features: i Intel, a AMD, g Graviton, d local NVMe storage, n enhanced networking. The suffix is the size, scaling roughly linearly in both resources and price.
Which EC2 instance family should I choose?

Start from the bottleneck. c for CPU-bound work such as build agents and batch processing, r for memory-bound workloads like databases and caches, m when neither dominates, and t only for genuinely bursty or mostly-idle workloads. Then pick the newest generation available and check whether a Graviton variant works for you. Size from Compute Optimizer recommendations rather than estimating, since over-provisioning is close to universal.
Are Graviton instances worth switching to?

Usually yes, around 20% cheaper for equivalent performance, and often faster. For containerised workloads and interpreted languages such as Python, Node and Ruby, the migration is frequently a base image change and a rebuild. Compiled code needs an ARM build, which is normally straightforward but worth testing. The saving extends beyond EC2 to RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch and Lambda, so switching a database instance class to db.m6g is a quick permanent win.
When should I use t3 or t4g burstable instances?

For workloads that are genuinely idle most of the time and occasionally busy. Development environments, internal tools, low-traffic services. They are poor for production services under steady load, because once CPU credits are exhausted the instance is throttled to its baseline, producing slowness that is hard to diagnose since reported CPU stays low. Unlimited mode removes the throttle for a surcharge, but at sustained load an m family instance is usually both cheaper and more predictable.
How do I know if my instance is the right size?

Use AWS Compute Optimizer, which analyses real CloudWatch utilisation over at least 14 days and recommends a size, including cross-family and Graviton alternatives. Note that memory usage is invisible to CloudWatch unless the CloudWatch agent is installed, so without it recommendations are weighted toward CPU and may suggest a size too small for a memory-bound workload. Installing the agent as part of your base image makes the recommendations considerably more trustworthy.
Can I change an instance type without downtime?

Not for a standalone instance. It must be stopped, modified and started, which loses any instance store data and assigns a new public IP unless an Elastic IP is attached. If the workload runs behind a launch template and an Auto Scaling group, changing the type is a template update followed by an instance refresh, which replaces instances gradually with no downtime. That is one of several reasons to put even single instances behind an Auto Scaling group.

aws-ec2-security-groups.subtitle: Learn how EC2 security groups work as stateful firewalls: rule structure, referencing groups instead of CIDRs, default outbound rules and blocked traffic.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS EC2 Security Groups must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Learn how EC2 security groups work as stateful firewalls: rule structure, referencing groups instead of CIDRs, default outbound rules and blocked traffic.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how EC2 security groups work as stateful firewalls: rule structure, referencing groups instead of CIDRs, default outbound rules and blocked traffic.

A security group is a stateful firewall attached to a network interface. It is the primary network control in AWS, and it behaves differently enough from a traditional firewall that the differences are worth being precise about.

sections.title: Stateful means you write half the rules
paragraphs: Allow inbound TCP 443 and the response traffic is automatically permitted, on whatever ephemeral port the client used. You never write a return rule.

This is the key difference from a network ACL, which is stateless and requires explicit rules in both directions. Most "my traffic is mysteriously blocked" problems in AWS are NACL statelessness, not security groups.

sections.title: Allow-only, and implicitly deny
paragraphs: A security group contains only allow rules. There is no deny.

Anything not explicitly allowed is denied, and rules are additive. Attaching three groups to an instance gives it the union of all their allow rules. You cannot use one group to subtract permission granted by another. That is what NACLs are for.

sections.title: Default behaviour
paragraphs: The permissive outbound default is deliberate and usually sensible. Tightening it is a real security improvement. An instance that can only reach what it needs limits what a compromise can do, but it breaks package installs, agent check-ins and AWS API calls in ways that are tedious to diagnose. Restrict outbound only where the value justifies the effort, and expect to add VPC endpoints when you do.

sections.title: Rule structure
paragraphs: Each rule is a protocol, a port range, and a source (inbound) or destination (outbound):
Always set a Description. Six months later, an undocumented rule allowing an unfamiliar CIDR is one nobody dares remove, so it stays forever.

sections.title: Reference other security groups, not CIDRs
paragraphs: This is the single most useful thing security groups do, and it is underused.

The rule now means "any instance carrying sg-application", which keeps working as instances are created, replaced and scaled. A CIDR-based equivalent has to be maintained by hand and breaks the moment the fleet changes.
That gives you a clean tiered design:
Nothing in that diagram contains a hardcoded IP address, and no rule needs updating when the application scales.
Security group references work within a VPC, and across peered VPCs in the same region.

codeBlock.code:
# The database accepts Postgres only from the application tier
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-database \
  --protocol tcp --port 5432 \
  --source-group sg-application

sections.title: Things not to do
paragraphs: 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 or 3389. Automated scanners find an open SSH port within minutes of it opening. Restrict to a known CIDR, or better, remove SSH entirely and use SSM Session Manager, which needs no inbound rule at all.
0.0.0.0/0 on a database port. 5432, 3306 and 27017 open to the internet is how databases get ransomed. Databases belong in private subnets with a security group reference.
Opening a wide port range because the exact port is unclear. Find the port.
AWS Config and Security Hub can flag these continuously, which is better than remembering to audit.

codeBlock.code:
# Audit for the obvious problems
aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --filters Name=ip-permission.cidr,Values=0.0.0.0/0 \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[].{ID:GroupId,Name:GroupName,Ports:IpPermissions[?contains(IpRanges[].CidrIp, `0.0.0.0/0`)].[FromPort,ToPort]}'

sections.title: Limits worth knowing
paragraphs: Most are adjustable, but the 60-rule limit is reached surprisingly quickly by teams that list individual office IPs. That is a signal to use a prefix list. A managed, named collection of CIDR blocks referenced as a single rule, and updated in one place.

sections.title: Debugging blocked traffic
paragraphs: Security groups produce timeouts, not refusals. A blocked packet is dropped silently, so the client hangs until it gives up. A fast "connection refused" means the packet arrived and nothing was listening, which is an application problem, not a security group one.
That distinction alone saves a lot of time.
VPC Reachability Analyzer does the whole check automatically and names the blocking component, which beats working through the list by hand:
And VPC flow logs record REJECT entries, so you can confirm whether traffic arrived and was dropped rather than never arriving.

codeBlock.code:
# What rules does it actually have?
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-database \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[0].IpPermissions'

# Which interfaces use this group?
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --filters Name=group-id,Values=sg-database \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[].{ID:NetworkInterfaceId,Desc:Description}'

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A client connecting to an EC2 instance gets an immediate "connection refused" rather than hanging. What does that tell you about the security group?
An Auto Scaling group replaces application instances regularly. What is the best way to let them reach the database?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a security group and a network ACL?

A security group attaches to an instance or network interface, is stateful so return traffic is automatically allowed, and contains only allow rules. A network ACL attaches to a subnet, is stateless so each direction requires its own rule, and supports both allow and deny evaluated in numbered order. Use security groups as the primary control and NACLs only for coarse subnet-level blocking. The stateless behaviour of NACLs is the most common cause of confusing half-working connectivity in AWS.
Why can't I add a deny rule to a security group?

Because security groups are allow-only by design. Everything not explicitly permitted is denied implicitly, and rules from multiple attached groups combine additively, so there is no mechanism to subtract permission that another group granted. If you genuinely need to block specific traffic, such as a known-bad CIDR range, that belongs in a network ACL at the subnet level, which does support explicit deny rules.
Should I restrict outbound rules?

It is a real security improvement, since an instance that can only reach what it needs limits what an attacker can do after a compromise, including preventing data exfiltration to arbitrary destinations. It is also genuinely fiddly: package repositories, agent check-ins, and AWS API calls all break in ways that take time to diagnose, and you will usually need VPC endpoints to compensate. Restrict outbound on high-value workloads where the effort is justified, and leave the permissive default elsewhere.
How do I let one security group talk to another?

Use the other group as the source rather than a CIDR: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-database --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group sg-application. The rule then applies to any network interface carrying that group, so it keeps working as instances are replaced and scaled without any rule maintenance. This works within a VPC and across peered VPCs in the same region, and it is the foundation of a clean tiered network design.
My connection times out. Is it the security group?

Probably, because security groups drop disallowed packets silently and a client hangs until it times out. Check the destination's inbound rules first, then the source's outbound rules, then route tables, then NACLs in both directions. A fast "connection refused" instead means the packet arrived and nothing was listening, which points at the application rather than networking. VPC Reachability Analyzer tests the whole path and names the blocking component, which is quicker than checking each layer manually.
How many rules can a security group have?

Sixty inbound and sixty outbound by default, with up to five security groups per network interface, and each referenced group counts as a rule. Most of these limits can be raised on request. Reaching the rule limit usually means you are listing individual IP addresses, for example, every office and VPN endpoint, which is better handled with a managed prefix list, a named collection of CIDR blocks referenced as a single rule and maintained in one place.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how EC2 key pairs work, create one for SSH, recover an instance after losing the key, and see why Session Manager is a better default than SSH.
A key pair is how SSH authentication to an EC2 instance traditionally works: AWS holds the public key, you hold the private key, and the public key is written into the instance at first boot.
It works, and for most workloads there is now a better option. This page covers both, because inherited infrastructure rarely gets to choose.

sections.title: How it actually works
paragraphs: When you launch an instance with a key pair, cloud-init writes the public key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for the default user, ec2-user on Amazon Linux, ubuntu on Ubuntu, admin on Debian.
That single sentence explains most key pair behaviour:

sections.title: Creating one
paragraphs: Use ed25519 rather than RSA. It is faster, the keys are shorter, and it is the modern default. RSA remains available for older tooling that needs it.
That chmod 400 is not optional. SSH refuses to use a private key readable by others:
The private key is shown once, at creation. There is no way to download it again.
Alternatively, import a key you already have, so AWS never sees a private key at all:
This is the better approach for personal keys.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-key-pair \
  --key-name acme-prod \
  --key-type ed25519 \
  --query 'KeyMaterial' --output text > ~/.ssh/acme-prod.pem

chmod 400 ~/.ssh/acme-prod.pem

sections.title: Connecting
paragraphs: Getting the right username is a common first stumble:
Beyond the key, SSH needs a security group allowing inbound 22 from your address, a route to the instance, and a public IP if you are outside the VPC.

codeBlock.code: ssh -i ~/.ssh/acme-prod.pem ec2-user@<public-ip>

sections.title: Prefer Session Manager
paragraphs: The key pair model has real drawbacks: a private key to distribute and protect, port 22 open somewhere, a bastion host for private subnets, and no audit trail of who connected.
SSM Session Manager removes all of it:
The requirements are modest: the SSM agent, preinstalled on current Amazon Linux and Ubuntu AMIs, and an instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
For anything new, this should be the default. Launch instances with no key pair at all.
You can even use it as an SSH transport, which keeps your SSH tooling while removing the open port:

codeBlock.code: aws ssm start-session --target i-0abc123

sections.title: EC2 Instance Connect
paragraphs: A middle option: push a temporary public key valid for 60 seconds, authorised by IAM.

No permanent key on the instance, and access controlled by IAM. It still needs network reachability on port 22, which is why Session Manager is generally the better choice, though the EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint variant removes that requirement too.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2-instance-connect send-ssh-public-key \
  --instance-id i-0abc123 \
  --instance-os-user ec2-user \
  --ssh-public-key file://~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ec2-user@<public-ip>

sections.title: Recovering an instance with a lost key
paragraphs: AWS cannot recover a private key, but the key is only a file on a volume, so access is recoverable.
The easy route, if the SSM agent is running: connect with Session Manager and append a new public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. No downtime.
The easy route on a modern AMI: EC2 Instance Connect, if the instance supports it.
The manual route, when neither is available:
Tedious but reliable. An alternative is replacing the instance entirely from an AMI with the new key, which is often faster if the instance is cattle rather than a pet.

sections.title: Key pairs are regional
paragraphs: A key pair exists in one region. Launching in a second region requires creating or importing it there:
Importing the same public key into several regions keeps one private key working everywhere, which is why importing is more convenient than generating per region.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 import-key-pair --key-name acme-prod \
  --public-key-material fileb://~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub \
  --region us-east-1

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: You stop an instance and try to associate a different key pair so you can SSH with a new key. It does not work. Why?
What does SSM Session Manager require in order to give you a shell on an EC2 instance in a private subnet with no public IP?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: I lost my EC2 private key. Can AWS recover it?

No. AWS never stores private keys and has no way to retrieve one. Access is still recoverable, though. If the SSM agent is running, connect with aws ssm start-session and append a new public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, which needs no downtime. If not, stop the instance, detach its root volume, attach it to another instance you can reach, mount it and add your key to the file, then reattach. Replacing the instance from an AMI is often faster if it holds no unique state.
How do I change the key pair on an existing EC2 instance?

You cannot change it through the AWS API in any meaningful way. The public key is written into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys by cloud-init on first boot and never touched again, so the key pair association is effectively historical metadata afterwards. To add a new key, edit that file on the instance. Through Session Manager, EC2 Instance Connect, or by mounting the root volume elsewhere. Then remove the old key from the file if you want to revoke it.
Should I use SSH keys or Session Manager?

Session Manager, for anything new. It requires no key pairs, no inbound port 22, and no bastion host; it works for instances in private subnets with no public IP; access is granted through IAM and revoked the same way; and every session is recorded in CloudTrail with optional full session logging. The requirements are just the SSM agent, preinstalled on current AMIs, and an instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. Launch new instances with no key pair at all.
Why does SSH reject my .pem file with "permissions too open"?

SSH refuses to use a private key that other users on the machine could read, as a safety measure. Run chmod 400 your-key.pem so only your user can read it. On Windows the equivalent is removing inherited permissions and granting access only to your account. This is one of the first errors nearly everyone hits, and the message is at least explicit about the cause.
What username do I use to SSH into an EC2 instance?

It depends on the AMI: ec2-user for Amazon Linux and RHEL, ubuntu for Ubuntu, admin for Debian, bitnami for Bitnami images. Using root almost always fails, since most AMIs disable direct root login and print a message telling you the correct user. If you are unsure, attempt a connection as root and read the error. It usually names the right account.
Are EC2 key pairs regional?

Yes. A key pair created in eu-west-1 does not exist in us-east-1, so launching there requires creating or importing one in that region. Importing the same public key into each region is more convenient than generating separate pairs, since one private key then works everywhere, and importing has the further advantage that AWS never handles a private key at all.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Build an AWS VPC step by step: CIDR and subnet sizing, public vs private subnets, NAT gateway costs, VPC endpoints, security groups vs NACLs and flow logs.

sections.title: Amazon VPC
paragraphs: A VPC is your own isolated network inside AWS. Almost everything else runs inside one, which means VPC mistakes surface later as connectivity problems that look like application bugs, and as a NAT gateway line on the bill that nobody can explain.
VPC Network Architecture
Private subnets use a NAT Gateway (in the public subnet) for outbound internet access

sections.title: CIDR and subnet sizing
paragraphs: A VPC gets a private CIDR block, conventionally something like 10.0.0.0/16: 65,536 addresses.

Size generously. The primary CIDR cannot be changed after creation. You can attach secondary CIDR blocks later, but that is a workaround rather than a fix, and overlapping ranges make future VPC peering or a Transit Gateway connection impossible. A /16 costs nothing extra.
Then split into subnets, each bound to one Availability Zone:
Two sizing details that bite:
AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet: network address, VPC router, DNS, a reserved address, and broadcast. A /28 gives you 11 usable addresses, not 16.
On EKS, every pod consumes a VPC IP. A /24 private subnet sounds ample until 200 pods exhaust it and new pods fail to start. Use /20 or larger for anything running Kubernetes.

codeBlock.code:
10.0.0.0/16          VPC
├── 10.0.0.0/20      public-a     (eu-west-1a)
├── 10.0.16.0/20     public-b     (eu-west-1b)
├── 10.0.32.0/20     private-a    (eu-west-1a)
├── 10.0.48.0/20     private-b    (eu-west-1b)
└── 10.0.64.0/20     database-a   (eu-west-1a)

sections.title: What actually makes a subnet public
paragraphs: Nothing about the subnet itself. A subnet is public if its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway. That is the whole definition.
A resource in a public subnet also needs a public IP to be reachable. The route makes the subnet public, the IP makes the instance reachable.

A subnet with no explicit route table association uses the VPC's main route table, which is a frequent cause of a "private" subnet that unexpectedly has internet access, or a public one that does not.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abc123 \
  --query 'RouteTables[].{ID:RouteTableId,Routes:Routes[].{Dest:DestinationCidrBlock,Target:GatewayId}}'

sections.title: NAT gateways are where the money goes
paragraphs: A NAT gateway lets private subnets reach the internet outbound while remaining unreachable inbound. It is also one of the most expensive small components in AWS: an hourly charge per gateway plus a per-GB data processing charge, on top of normal data transfer.
Run one per Availability Zone for high availability and you are paying three hourly charges before a single byte moves. Teams routinely find NAT is their largest networking cost.
Three ways to reduce it, in order of payoff:

1. VPC endpoints for AWS services. Traffic to S3 and DynamoDB through a Gateway endpoint is free and bypasses NAT entirely. If your workload pulls container images from ECR, writes logs to CloudWatch, or reads from S3, that traffic is otherwise flowing through NAT and being charged per gigabyte.

Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) cover most other AWS services. They carry their own hourly and per-GB charge, so they pay off when they displace meaningful NAT volume. ECR and CloudWatch Logs usually qualify.
2. One NAT gateway instead of three in non-production. You lose AZ redundancy, which is an acceptable trade for a dev environment and not for production.
3. Check what is actually using it with flow logs before assuming.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-0abc123 \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-0abc123

sections.title: Security groups and NACLs
paragraphs: Two independent layers, and the differences matter.

Use security groups as your primary control. They are stateful, which removes a whole class of error, and they can reference each other, so "the database accepts traffic from the application tier" is expressed directly rather than by hardcoding IP ranges:
That rule keeps working as instances come and go, which a CIDR-based rule does not.

NACLs are stateless, and that is the classic trap: allowing inbound 443 without also allowing outbound on the ephemeral port range (1024 to 65535) means requests arrive and responses cannot leave. Symptoms look like a hung connection rather than a rejection. Use NACLs only for coarse subnet-level denies, blocking a known-bad CIDR, and leave the default allow-all otherwise.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-database \
  --protocol tcp --port 5432 \
  --source-group sg-application

sections.title: Connecting VPCs
paragraphs: Peering is not transitive, if A peers with B and B with C, A cannot reach C. Beyond three or four VPCs, a Transit Gateway is the right answer.
All of these require non-overlapping CIDR blocks, which is why the sizing decision at the very beginning matters so much.

sections.title: Flow logs
paragraphs: Not enabled by default, and the only way to answer "what is actually talking to what":

Send them to S3 and query with Athena rather than paying CloudWatch Logs ingestion rates for high-volume data. They are how you find which workload is driving NAT charges, and they record ACCEPT and REJECT, so a REJECT entry tells you a security group or NACL blocked something, which beats guessing.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-flow-logs \
  --resource-type VPC --resource-ids vpc-0abc123 \
  --traffic-type ALL \
  --log-destination-type s3 \
  --log-destination arn:aws:s3:::acme-flow-logs

sections.title: Debugging connectivity, in order
paragraphs: When something cannot reach something else, check in this sequence:
VPC Reachability Analyzer does this automatically and names the blocking component:
It is much faster than manual inspection and worth reaching for first.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-network-insights-path \
  --source i-0source --destination i-0dest \
  --protocol tcp --destination-port 5432

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A NACL allows inbound TCP 443 to a subnet. Clients connect but every request hangs and eventually times out. The security group allows all outbound. What is wrong?
A team sees large NAT gateway data processing charges. Their workload runs in private subnets and pulls container images and writes logs to AWS services. What is the most effective fix?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What makes a subnet public or private in AWS?

Only its route table. A subnet is public when its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway, and private when it does not, typically routing that traffic to a NAT gateway for outbound access instead. Nothing about the subnet object itself marks it either way. A resource in a public subnet also needs a public IP to be reachable from outside, so "public subnet" and "publicly reachable instance" are two separate conditions.
How do I reduce NAT gateway costs?

Add VPC endpoints for the AWS services your workload uses. Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and remove that traffic from NAT entirely, which often covers a surprising share of the volume since ECR image layers live in S3. Interface endpoints for services such as ECR APIs and CloudWatch Logs carry their own hourly and per-GB charges but typically cost less than the NAT processing they replace. In non-production, running a single NAT gateway rather than one per Availability Zone cuts the hourly charge at the cost of redundancy. Enable flow logs first to see what is actually flowing.
What is the difference between a security group and a network ACL?

A security group attaches to an instance or network interface, is stateful so return traffic is automatically permitted, contains only allow rules, and can reference other security groups as a source. A network ACL attaches to a subnet, is stateless so each direction needs its own rule, supports both allow and deny, and is evaluated in numbered order. Use security groups as the primary control and NACLs only for coarse subnet-level blocking. The stateless behaviour of NACLs is the most common source of confusing half-working connectivity.
What CIDR block should I choose for my VPC?

Something large and unlikely to overlap anything you may later connect to, 10.0.0.0/16 is the common default, giving 65,536 addresses at no extra cost. The primary CIDR cannot be changed after creation, and overlapping ranges make VPC peering, Transit Gateway attachments and VPN connections to on-premises networks impossible. If you run multiple environments or accounts, allocate distinct ranges to each from the outset. Remember AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet, and that EKS consumes one VPC IP per pod.
Why can't my EC2 instance reach the internet?

Work through it in order. Is there a 0.0.0.0/0 route in the subnet's route table, pointing at an Internet Gateway for a public subnet or a NAT gateway for a private one? Is the subnet associated with the route table you think it is, rather than falling back to the VPC's main table? Does the security group allow outbound traffic? For a public subnet, does the instance actually have a public IP? And if a NACL has been customised, does it allow outbound on the port and inbound on the ephemeral range? VPC Reachability Analyzer checks all of this and names the blocking component.
When should I use VPC peering versus a Transit Gateway?

Peering is simple and cost-effective for a small number of VPCs, but it is not transitive. Each pair needs its own connection, so the number of connections grows quadratically and becomes unmanageable past three or four VPCs. A Transit Gateway acts as a hub, so each VPC attaches once and routing is managed centrally. It has its own hourly and per-GB charges, so peering is cheaper at small scale. Both require non-overlapping CIDR blocks.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Design VPC subnets properly: what makes a subnet public, CIDR sizing and the five reserved IPs, one subnet per AZ, required tags and running out of addresses.

A subnet is a slice of your VPC's address range, bound to exactly one Availability Zone. Subnet design is one of the few AWS decisions that is genuinely hard to undo, so it is worth a little thought before the first terraform apply.

sections.title: A subnet is public because of its route table
paragraphs: Nothing about the subnet object makes it public or private. A subnet is public if its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway. That is the entire definition.
A resource in a public subnet also needs a public IP to be reachable. The route makes the subnet public; the IP makes the instance reachable. Those are two separate conditions and both are required.
A subnet with no explicit route table association falls back to the VPC's main route table, which is a common cause of a subnet that behaves unexpectedly. Associate every subnet explicitly.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-0abc123 \
  --query 'RouteTables[].Routes[?DestinationCidrBlock==`0.0.0.0/0`]'

sections.title: One subnet, one Availability Zone
paragraphs: A subnet cannot span zones. To be multi-AZ you create one subnet per zone per tier:
Three tiers across three zones is the standard shape: public for load balancers and NAT gateways, private for application workloads, and a separate isolated tier for databases.
Query zones rather than hardcoding them, since zone names differ per account:

codeBlock.code:
10.0.0.0/16                 VPC
├── 10.0.0.0/20    public-a     eu-west-1a
├── 10.0.16.0/20   public-b     eu-west-1b
├── 10.0.32.0/20   public-c     eu-west-1c
├── 10.0.48.0/20   private-a    eu-west-1a
├── 10.0.64.0/20   private-b    eu-west-1b
├── 10.0.80.0/20   private-c    eu-west-1c
├── 10.0.96.0/22   database-a   eu-west-1a
└── 10.0.100.0/22  database-b   eu-west-1b

sections.title: AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet
paragraphs: So a /28 gives you 11 usable addresses, not 16. On small subnets this matters a great deal, and it is a frequent surprise when a /28 intended for four instances runs out sooner than arithmetic suggested.

sections.title: Size generously: you cannot resize
paragraphs: A subnet's CIDR block is immutable. Changing it means creating a new subnet and migrating everything into it, which for anything with attached resources is a project rather than an edit.
Since private address space costs nothing, the sensible default is /20 per subnet in a /16 VPC. That leaves room for growth and for subnets you have not thought of yet.

On EKS this is not optional. The AWS VPC CNI gives every pod a real VPC IP address, so pod density is bounded by subnet size. A /24 sounds ample until 200 pods exhaust it and new pods fail with failed to assign an IP address to container:
Check that Free column before scaling anything, and enable prefix delegation on the CNI to raise pod density substantially.
If you do exhaust the VPC, you can attach a secondary CIDR block, but ranges must not overlap anything you might later peer with, which is why the initial choice matters.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 describe-subnets \
  --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abc123 \
  --query 'Subnets[].{ID:SubnetId,AZ:AvailabilityZone,CIDR:CidrBlock,Free:AvailableIpAddressCount}' \
  --output table

sections.title: Tags that are functionally required
paragraphs: Some AWS services discover where to place resources by reading subnet tags. Miss them and things fail quietly.
An Ingress stuck in pending with no useful error is very often a missing subnet tag. The AWS Load Balancer Controller logs say it could not discover subnets, which is the clue.
Tag by purpose too, Tier = public, Tier = private, so automation and cost reporting can distinguish them.

sections.title: Auto-assign public IP
paragraphs: Enable it on public subnets so instances get an address automatically. Leave it off on private subnets. Enabling it there does not grant internet access, since there is no Internet Gateway route, but it does consume public IPv4 addresses, which are now chargeable.
That charge is worth knowing about: AWS bills for every public IPv4 address, attached or not. Instances that do not need one should not have one.

codeBlock.code: aws ec2 modify-subnet-attribute --subnet-id subnet-0abc123 --map-public-ip-on-launch

sections.title: Database subnets
paragraphs: A third isolated tier for databases is worth the extra structure. It has no route to the internet at all, not even through NAT, so a compromised application cannot exfiltrate data outward from the database tier.
RDS requires a DB subnet group spanning at least two Availability Zones, even for a single-AZ instance, so you always need at least two database subnets.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A /28 subnet is created for 12 instances but only 11 can launch. Why?
An instance in a subnet named "public-a" has a public IP but cannot reach the internet. What should you check?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What makes a subnet public or private in AWS?

Only its route table. A subnet is public when its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway, and private when it does not, typically routing that traffic to a NAT gateway instead. There is no property on the subnet itself that marks it either way, and the name is just a tag. A resource in a public subnet additionally needs a public IP to be reachable from outside, so "public subnet" and "reachable instance" are two separate conditions.
How many IP addresses does an AWS subnet actually provide?

Five fewer than the CIDR suggests. AWS reserves the network address, the VPC router, the DNS resolver, one address for future use, and the broadcast address in every subnet regardless of size. So a /28 provides 11 usable addresses rather than 16, a /24 provides 251, and a /20 provides 4,091. The reservation is proportionally most painful on small subnets.
What size should my subnets be?

Larger than feels necessary, because CIDR blocks are immutable and private address space costs nothing. A /20 per subnet inside a /16 VPC is a sensible default, leaving room for growth. This matters especially for EKS, where the VPC CNI assigns every pod a real VPC IP address. A /24 that looks generous will stop pods scheduling once a few hundred are running. Check AvailableIpAddressCount before scaling.
Can I change a subnet's CIDR block after creating it?

No. Subnet CIDR blocks are immutable, so changing one means creating a new subnet with the desired range and migrating resources into it, which for anything with attached network interfaces, load balancer registrations or database subnet group membership is a project rather than an edit. If the VPC itself runs out of space you can attach a secondary CIDR block, provided the new range does not overlap anything you might peer with later.
Why is my EKS Ingress stuck in pending?

Almost always missing subnet tags. The AWS Load Balancer Controller discovers where to place a load balancer by looking for kubernetes.io/role/elb=1 on public subnets and kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1 on private ones. Without them it has nowhere to put the load balancer and fails quietly. Check the controller logs, kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/aws-load-balancer-controller, which will say it could not discover subnets.
Should I enable auto-assign public IP on private subnets?

No. It does not grant internet access, since that comes from the route table, but it does allocate a public IPv4 address to every instance launched there, and AWS charges for every public IPv4 address, attached or not. Enable it on public subnets where instances genuinely need to be reachable, and leave it off everywhere else. Instances in private subnets reach the internet through a NAT gateway using only their private address.
