verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS VPC Route Tables must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: How VPC route tables route traffic: the local route, longest prefix match, the main route table trap, one table per AZ and debugging no connectivity.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: How VPC route tables route traffic: the local route, longest prefix match, the main route table trap, one table per AZ and debugging no connectivity.
A route table is a list of destinations and where to send traffic for each. Every subnet uses exactly one, and that association is what makes a subnet public, private or isolated.
Most VPC connectivity problems are route table problems.

sections.title: The local route
paragraphs: Every route table is created with one route you cannot remove:

This is what lets every subnet in the VPC reach every other subnet, with no configuration. It cannot be deleted or overridden, which is why you never need to add routes between your own subnets. A frequent misunderstanding when someone adds a route for another subnet and wonders why it appears to do nothing.

codeBlock.code:
Destination        Target
10.0.0.0/16        local

sections.title: Adding routes
paragraphs: A target can be an internet gateway, NAT gateway, virtual private gateway, transit gateway, VPC peering connection, network interface, or a gateway VPC endpoint.
The presence of a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an internet gateway is the entire definition of a public subnet. Nothing else marks it.

codeBlock.code:
# Public: send internet-bound traffic to the Internet Gateway
aws ec2 create-route \
  --route-table-id rtb-public \
  --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 \
  --gateway-id igw-0abc123

# Private: send internet-bound traffic to a NAT gateway
aws ec2 create-route \
  --route-table-id rtb-private-a \
  --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 \
  --nat-gateway-id nat-0abc123

sections.title: Longest prefix match wins
paragraphs: When several routes could match, the most specific one is used. Regardless of order in the table.
Traffic to 10.1.5.20 takes the transit gateway; traffic to 10.1.9.20 takes the peering connection; everything else goes to NAT.
This is how you route selected destinations differently without disturbing the default path, and it is worth knowing because the behaviour is not order-dependent the way firewall rules are.
The local route always wins within the VPC CIDR, whatever else is listed.

codeBlock.code:
0.0.0.0/0          nat-0abc123        ← general
10.1.0.0/16        pcx-0peering       ← more specific, wins for 10.1.x.x
10.1.5.0/24        tgw-0transit       ← most specific, wins for 10.1.5.x

sections.title: The main route table trap
paragraphs: Every VPC has a main route table. A subnet with no explicit association uses it, which is the single most common cause of a subnet behaving unexpectedly.

The typical failure: someone creates a "private" subnet, does not associate it with anything, and it silently inherits the main table. If the main table happens to have an internet gateway route, that private subnet is quietly public.
Two habits prevent it entirely: associate every subnet explicitly, and leave the main route table with only the local route so an unassociated subnet is isolated rather than accidentally connected.

codeBlock.code:
# Which subnets are relying on the main table?
aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abc123 \
  --query 'RouteTables[?Associations[?Main==`true`]].RouteTableId'

# What is a specific subnet actually using?
aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-0abc123 \
  --query 'RouteTables[].{ID:RouteTableId,Routes:Routes[].[DestinationCidrBlock,GatewayId,NatGatewayId]}'

sections.title: One table per AZ for private subnets
paragraphs: Public subnets can share a single route table, since they all point at the same internet gateway.
Private subnets cannot, if you run a NAT gateway per Availability Zone. Each private subnet needs its own table pointing at the NAT gateway in its own zone:

Pointing all three at one NAT gateway works, and sends traffic across zones. Incurring cross-AZ charges and creating a dependency on that zone staying healthy. It is a reasonable saving in development and a poor choice in production.

codeBlock.code:
rtb-private-a   0.0.0.0/0 → nat-zone-a
rtb-private-b   0.0.0.0/0 → nat-zone-b
rtb-private-c   0.0.0.0/0 → nat-zone-c

sections.title: Gateway endpoints add routes
paragraphs: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 or DynamoDB works by adding a prefix list route to the route tables you specify:

Traffic to S3 then bypasses the NAT gateway entirely, which is free and removes a per-gigabyte charge. The endpoint must be associated with every route table that needs it. Associating only one table means the other subnets keep paying for NAT.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-0abc123 \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-private-a rtb-private-b

sections.title: Route propagation
paragraphs: A virtual private gateway can propagate routes learned over BGP from a VPN or Direct Connect connection, so you do not maintain them by hand:
Propagated routes appear alongside static ones. Where both exist for the same destination, the static route wins.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 enable-vgw-route-propagation \
  --route-table-id rtb-private-a \
  --gateway-id vgw-0abc123

sections.title: Debugging
paragraphs: Work through in this order:
A route with target blackhole means the thing it pointed at no longer exists. A deleted NAT gateway or a removed peering connection. The route remains and silently discards traffic:
VPC Reachability Analyzer tests the whole path and names the blocking component, which is faster than checking each layer:

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --query 'RouteTables[].Routes[?State==`blackhole`]'

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A subnet created for private workloads turns out to have internet access, though no route table was configured for it. How?
A route table shows a 0.0.0.0/0 route with state "blackhole". What does that mean?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the main route table and why does it matter?

Every VPC has one, and any subnet not explicitly associated with another route table uses it. That default is the most common cause of a subnet behaving unexpectedly. A "private" subnet that inherits an internet gateway route from the main table is quietly public. The two habits that prevent it are associating every subnet explicitly and leaving the main table containing only the local route, so an unassociated subnet is isolated rather than accidentally connected.
Do I need routes between subnets in the same VPC?

No. Every route table is created with a local route covering the VPC CIDR, and it cannot be removed or overridden. All subnets in a VPC can therefore reach each other at the routing layer by default. If traffic between two subnets is being blocked, the cause is a security group or network ACL rather than routing. Adding a route for the other subnet's CIDR achieves nothing.
How does AWS choose between multiple matching routes?

By longest prefix match. The most specific route wins, regardless of the order entries appear in the table. A /24 beats a /16, which beats 0.0.0.0/0. This is how you send particular destinations through a peering connection or transit gateway while everything else goes to a NAT gateway. The local route always takes precedence within the VPC CIDR. Where a static and a propagated route match the same destination, the static one wins.
Why do I need a separate route table per private subnet?

Because each should point at the NAT gateway in its own Availability Zone. If all private subnets share one table pointing at a single NAT gateway, traffic from other zones crosses zones to reach it. Incurring cross-AZ data charges and making every private subnet dependent on that one zone staying healthy. Public subnets can share a table, since they all point at the same internet gateway.
What does a blackhole route mean?

The route exists but its target has been deleted, so matching traffic is silently discarded. It usually follows a NAT gateway being replaced, since the new one has a different ID and the old route is not updated automatically, or a VPC peering connection being removed. Find them with a query filtering routes on State == 'blackhole'. They are worth checking for whenever connectivity breaks after infrastructure changes, because nothing reports an error.
How do gateway VPC endpoints interact with route tables?

A gateway endpoint for S3 or DynamoDB works by adding a prefix list route to the route tables you associate it with, sending that traffic directly rather than through a NAT gateway. It is free and removes a per-gigabyte NAT charge, so there is no reason not to have one. The important detail is that it only affects the route tables you explicitly associate. Attach it to every private route table, or the subnets you missed keep routing S3 traffic through NAT and paying for it.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: See what an AWS NAT gateway does, why it is often the largest networking cost on your bill, and how VPC endpoints and design changes reduce it.
A NAT gateway lets resources in a private subnet reach the internet outbound while remaining unreachable inbound. It is a managed, highly available service with no instances to patch.
It is also, on a great many AWS bills, the single largest networking line item, and usually the one nobody can immediately explain.

sections.title: What it does
paragraphs: Private subnets have no route to an Internet Gateway, which is what makes them private. But the workloads in them still need to download packages, call third-party APIs, pull container images and reach AWS service endpoints.
The NAT gateway sits in a public subnet and translates outbound traffic from private subnets to its own public address. Responses come back; unsolicited inbound connections do not get in.
Two placement details people get wrong:

codeBlock.code:
private subnet ──0.0.0.0/0──► NAT gateway ──► Internet Gateway ──► internet
  (10.0.32.0/20)              (in public subnet)

sections.title: The cost model
paragraphs: A NAT gateway charges two ways, and the second is the one that gets out of hand:

That per-GB processing charge applies to traffic that stays entirely inside AWS. A workload in a private subnet pulling container images from ECR, writing to CloudWatch Logs, or reading from S3 is paying a per-gigabyte NAT charge on traffic that never touches the internet.

And for high availability you want one gateway per Availability Zone, because a NAT gateway is zonal, if its AZ fails, private subnets routed to it lose outbound access. Three AZs means three hourly charges before a byte moves.

sections.title: Reducing it
paragraphs: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free. They add a route so traffic to those services goes directly rather than through NAT:
There is no reason not to create these. They cost nothing, take one command, and often remove a large share of NAT volume, including ECR image pulls, because image layers are stored in S3.
Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) cover most other AWS services and carry their own hourly and per-GB charges. They pay off when they displace meaningful NAT volume; the usual candidates are:
Note that an interface endpoint is charged per AZ it is deployed into, so the arithmetic is worth doing rather than creating them reflexively.
Do not guess. Flow logs will tell you:
Query with Athena, grouping by destination, and the top talkers are usually obvious, and usually AWS services that an endpoint would handle for free or cheaper.
The NatGatewayAddressCount and BytesOutToDestination CloudWatch metrics give a quicker top-level view.
One NAT gateway shared by all AZs costs a third as much and loses AZ redundancy. That is a reasonable trade in development and a bad one in production.
Be aware of the second-order effect: private subnets in other AZs then send traffic cross-AZ to reach it, which incurs cross-AZ data transfer charges. At high volume that can erode the saving.

Some workloads in private subnets have no genuine need for outbound internet access once VPC endpoints cover the AWS services they use. Removing the route removes the charge entirely, and tightens security, since the workload can no longer reach arbitrary destinations.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-0abc123 \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-private-a rtb-private-b

sections.title: NAT gateway or NAT instance?
paragraphs: A NAT instance is an EC2 instance doing the same job with software.

For production, use the NAT gateway. The managed availability and automatic scaling are worth the price, and a self-managed NAT instance becomes a single point of failure that someone has to maintain.
A NAT instance can genuinely be cheaper for a low-traffic development environment, since a small instance has no per-GB charge, but it is an operational item to own, so weigh that against the saving.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
paragraphs: Private instances cannot reach the internet. Work through:

ErrorPortAllocation in metrics means the gateway has exhausted its ports to a single destination. A NAT gateway supports a large but finite number of simultaneous connections per destination IP, and a workload opening very many connections to one endpoint can hit it. Spreading across multiple destinations, or using an interface endpoint for that service, resolves it.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --filter Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abc123 \
  --query 'NatGateways[].{ID:NatGatewayId,State:State,Subnet:SubnetId}'

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A NAT gateway is created in a private subnet and the other private subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to it. Instances still cannot reach the internet. Why?
A workload in private subnets writes large volumes to S3 and the NAT data processing charge is high. What is the most cost-effective change?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What does a NAT gateway actually do?

It allows resources in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet while remaining unreachable from it. Outbound traffic is translated to the gateway's public address, responses return to the originating instance, and unsolicited inbound connections are not possible. This is how workloads without public IPs download packages, call external APIs and reach AWS service endpoints while staying private.
Why is my NAT gateway so expensive?

Two charges combine: an hourly rate per gateway, which applies continuously, and a per-gigabyte data processing charge on everything that passes through, including traffic to AWS services that never leaves the AWS network. Since high availability means one gateway per Availability Zone, a three-AZ setup pays three hourly charges before any data moves. The per-gigabyte component is usually what makes the bill surprising, and it is almost always dominated by traffic to S3, ECR and CloudWatch Logs.
How do I reduce NAT gateway costs?

Add VPC endpoints. Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are completely free and remove that traffic from NAT, which typically covers a large share. Container image pulls included, since ECR layers live in S3. Interface endpoints for ECR, CloudWatch Logs, SSM and STS carry their own charges but usually cost less than the NAT volume they replace. Enable flow logs first so you optimise against real traffic rather than assumptions, and consider consolidating to a single gateway in non-production.
Do I need a NAT gateway in every Availability Zone?

For production, yes. A NAT gateway is a zonal resource, so if its Availability Zone becomes unavailable, every private subnet routed to it loses outbound access, which turns a single-AZ problem into a multi-AZ outage. In development, a single shared gateway saves roughly two thirds of the hourly cost, at the price of that redundancy. Note that traffic from other AZs then crosses zones to reach it, incurring cross-AZ data transfer charges that partly offset the saving at volume.
What is the difference between a NAT gateway and a NAT instance?

A NAT gateway is fully managed, redundant within its Availability Zone, scales bandwidth automatically, and charges hourly plus per gigabyte. A NAT instance is an EC2 instance running NAT software, so you patch and monitor it, its throughput is bounded by the instance type, and it is a single point of failure unless you build failover yourself, but it has no per-gigabyte charge. Use a NAT gateway in production. A NAT instance can be cheaper for a low-traffic development environment if you accept owning it.
Can I use a NAT gateway for inbound traffic?

No, and that is the point of it. A NAT gateway only supports connections initiated from inside the VPC; it has no mechanism for forwarding unsolicited inbound connections to private instances. To accept inbound traffic, put a load balancer in a public subnet with targets in private subnets, which keeps the instances unreachable directly while still serving requests.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how Amazon S3 works: buckets and keys, storage classes, lifecycle rules, encryption, public access, versioning, presigned URLs and cost control.

sections.title: Amazon S3
paragraphs: S3 stores objects in buckets and addresses them by key. There is no filesystem, no mounting, and no directories, which is what lets it scale effectively without limit, and also what surprises people who treat it like a disk.
For DevOps it ends up everywhere: build artifacts, logs, backups, Terraform state, static sites, and the landing zone for data before anyone decides where it really belongs.
S3: Object Storage Structure
Lifecycle rules automate transitions between storage classes over time

sections.title: Buckets, keys and the folder illusion
paragraphs: A bucket is the top-level container. Its name must be globally unique across all of AWS, not just your account, which is why bucket creation fails with a name someone else took years ago. Names must be lowercase, DNS-compatible, and 3 to 63 characters.
Include your account ID or organisation name to avoid collisions:
us-east-1 is the exception that catches everyone: it must not have a LocationConstraint, and passing one fails.

An object has a key, content and metadata. A key like logs/2026/09/app.log looks like a path but is a single flat string. There are no folders. The console renders them as folders for convenience, which is why:

Prefixes do matter for one real reason: S3 scales request rate per prefix, at roughly 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second each. A high-throughput workload writing everything under one prefix will throttle; spreading keys across prefixes fixes it.

codeBlock.code:
aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket acme-artifacts-111122223333 \
  --region eu-west-1 \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=eu-west-1

sections.title: Storage classes
paragraphs: Those minimum duration charges are the trap. Delete a Standard-IA object after five days and you are billed for thirty. A lifecycle rule that moves objects to Glacier after seven days, on data routinely deleted at day twenty, costs more than leaving it in Standard.

Intelligent-Tiering is the honest default when you do not know the access pattern. It moves objects between tiers automatically for a small per-object monitoring fee, with no retrieval charges and no minimum duration surprises.
One Zone-IA stores in a single Availability Zone. Use it only for data you can regenerate.

sections.title: Lifecycle rules
paragraphs: That second rule is worth adding to every bucket. Failed multipart uploads leave orphaned parts that are billed as storage but never appear in a normal listing. Teams discover them years later as an unexplained line on the bill.

sections.title: Public access and encryption
paragraphs: Both defaults improved substantially and it is worth knowing what you now get for free on new buckets:
For sensitive data, move to SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key so you control the key policy and see key usage in CloudTrail:

BucketKeyEnabled matters commercially, without it, every object operation is a separate KMS API call, and on a high-volume bucket the KMS bill can exceed the S3 bill. It typically cuts those calls by over 99%.

sections.title: Versioning and Object Lock
paragraphs: Versioning keeps every version of an object, so an overwrite or delete is recoverable:

Two consequences to plan for. A "delete" becomes a delete marker with the real data still stored and still billed, so lifecycle rules need NoncurrentVersionExpiration or the bucket grows forever. And versioning cannot be turned off once enabled, only suspended.

Object Lock goes further, making objects genuinely immutable for a retention period, even the root user cannot delete them in compliance mode. It must be enabled at bucket creation and is the right tool for backups you want protected against ransomware and against your own mistakes.

codeBlock.code:
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket acme-artifacts-111122223333 \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

sections.title: Controlling cost
paragraphs: S3 bills for storage, requests, and data transfer out. The usual surprises:
S3 Storage Lens gives a free account-wide dashboard of usage and cost by bucket and prefix, and is the fastest way to find what is actually driving the bill.

codeBlock.code:
# What is actually in there?
aws s3 ls s3://acme-artifacts-111122223333 --recursive --summarize --human-readable | tail -3

sections.title: Presigned URLs
paragraphs: The right way to let someone upload or download without giving them AWS credentials:

The URL grants access to that one object for that period. It is how applications hand files to users without proxying the bytes through their own servers, and how users upload directly to S3 without the application handling the data at all.

codeBlock.code: aws s3 presign s3://acme-artifacts-111122223333/reports/q3.pdf --expires-in 3600

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team moves build artifacts to Standard-IA after 7 days to save money. Artifacts are deleted at day 20. The bill went up. Why?
Versioning is enabled on a bucket. A job deletes old files nightly, but storage costs keep climbing. What is happening?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does my S3 bucket name fail with "already exists"?

Bucket names are globally unique across every AWS account, not just yours, so a common name was almost certainly claimed long ago. Names must also be lowercase, 3 to 63 characters and DNS-compatible. Include your account ID or organisation prefix, acme-artifacts-111122223333, which makes collisions essentially impossible. Note also that creating a bucket in us-east-1 must omit LocationConstraint, while every other region requires it.
What S3 storage class should I use?

Standard for actively accessed data. Intelligent-Tiering when the access pattern is unknown or varies, since it moves objects automatically for a small monitoring fee with no retrieval charges or minimum duration penalties. Standard-IA or Glacier only when you are confident objects will live well beyond their minimum duration, 30 days for IA, 90 for most Glacier tiers, 180 for Deep Archive, because deleting earlier still incurs the full charge. One Zone-IA saves money but stores in a single Availability Zone, so reserve it for data you could regenerate.
How do I reduce my S3 bill?

Start with S3 Storage Lens, which shows free account-wide usage by bucket and prefix and usually reveals the cause immediately. Then: add an AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule to every bucket, since orphaned parts are billed but invisible in listings; expire old noncurrent versions if versioning is on; move genuinely cold data to Glacier where it will outlive the minimum duration; serve public downloads through CloudFront rather than directly, as internet egress is often the largest line; and keep compute in the same region as the bucket.
Is S3 data encrypted by default?

Yes. All new objects are encrypted with SSE-S3 automatically at no cost. For sensitive data, configure SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key so you control the key policy and can see usage in CloudTrail. If you do, enable BucketKeyEnabled, without it every object operation makes a separate KMS API call, and on a busy bucket the KMS charges can exceed the S3 charges entirely.
How do I safely make files publicly available?

Usually you should not make the bucket public at all. Put CloudFront in front with an Origin Access Control, keep Block Public Access enabled, and let the distribution read from the private bucket. You get caching, HTTPS, a custom domain and lower egress costs as well as better security. For individual files shared with specific people, use a presigned URL, which grants time-limited access to one object without credentials or any public configuration.
Can I turn off versioning once it is enabled?

No. Versioning can be suspended but never returned to the unversioned state, and suspending it does not delete versions already stored. They remain and continue to be billed. If storage is growing unexpectedly on a versioned bucket, the cause is almost always retained noncurrent versions and delete markers. Add a lifecycle rule with NoncurrentVersionExpiration and one to remove expired delete markers.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create and configure an S3 bucket correctly: naming rules, the us-east-1 exception, settings to apply at creation, Object Lock and deleting a stuck bucket.
A bucket is the top-level container for objects. Creating one takes a single command; creating one you will not regret takes about six settings.

sections.title: Naming rules
paragraphs: Bucket names are globally unique across every AWS account, not just yours. That is why obvious names fail. Someone claimed logs and backups in 2006.

Avoid dots entirely. A bucket name containing a dot breaks virtual-hosted-style HTTPS access, because the wildcard certificate does not match multi-level subdomains, which produces a TLS error that looks nothing like a naming problem.
The practical convention is to include your account ID or organisation name:

codeBlock.code:
acme-artifacts-111122223333
acme-prod-logs-eu-west-1

sections.title: Creating one
paragraphs: us-east-1 is the exception. It must not have a LocationConstraint, and passing one fails with InvalidLocationConstraint:
This inconsistency exists because us-east-1 was the original region and its API behaviour predates the concept.

codeBlock.code:
aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket acme-artifacts-111122223333 \
  --region eu-west-1 \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=eu-west-1

sections.title: Region matters more than people expect
paragraphs: A bucket lives in one region and the data stays there. Three consequences:
Put the bucket in the same region as whatever reads it most.

sections.title: The settings to apply at creation
paragraphs: Some of these cannot be added later, and the rest are tedious to retrofit.

Good news on defaults: Block Public Access is on by default for new buckets, ACLs are disabled by default under Bucket owner enforced ownership, and SSE-S3 encryption is applied automatically. The commands above are worth running anyway to make the intent explicit in code rather than relying on a default that could differ across accounts.

The lifecycle rule for incomplete multipart uploads belongs on every bucket. Failed uploads leave parts billed as storage that never appear in a listing, and teams find them years later as an unexplained cost.

codeBlock.code:
BUCKET=acme-artifacts-111122223333

# 1. Block all public access. Four settings, all on
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket $BUCKET \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"

# 2. Disable ACLs. The mechanism behind most historic S3 exposures
aws s3api put-bucket-ownership-controls --bucket $BUCKET \
  --ownership-controls 'Rules=[{ObjectOwnership=BucketOwnerEnforced}]'

# 3. Versioning. Cannot be undone, so decide deliberately
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket $BUCKET \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# 4. Encryption with a bucket key to keep KMS costs sane
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket $BUCKET \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration '{
    "Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"},"BucketKeyEnabled":true}]}'

# 5. Lifecycle, at minimum, clean up failed multipart uploads
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket $BUCKET \
  --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json

sections.title: Object Lock is creation-only
paragraphs: If you need genuine immutability, ransomware protection, regulatory retention, Object Lock must be enabled when the bucket is created. It cannot be added afterwards, and retrofitting means creating a new bucket and copying everything.

codeBlock.code:
aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket acme-backups-111122223333 \
  --region eu-west-1 \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=eu-west-1 \
  --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket

sections.title: Folders do not exist
paragraphs: The console shows folders, but S3 has none. logs/2026/09/app.log is a single flat key that happens to contain slashes.

Prefixes do matter for one real reason: S3 scales request rate per prefix, at roughly 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second each. A high-throughput workload writing everything under one prefix will throttle.

sections.title: Deleting a bucket
paragraphs: A bucket must be empty before it can be deleted, which is a useful accident-preventer.
That --force deletes every object first. On a versioned bucket it is not enough. Versions and delete markers remain, and rb still fails:
A gentler alternative for large buckets is a lifecycle rule expiring everything, then deleting the bucket a day later. S3 does the deletion in the background at no request cost.
Note that a deleted bucket name is not immediately reusable, and in a different region it may take time to become available.

codeBlock.code:
# Delete objects and the bucket in one step
aws s3 rb s3://$BUCKET --force

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: The same create-bucket command works in eu-west-1 but fails with InvalidLocationConstraint in us-east-1. Why?
aws s3 rb s3://my-bucket --force reports the bucket is not empty, but a listing shows no objects. What is going on?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does my S3 bucket name fail with "already exists"?

Bucket names are globally unique across every AWS account, so a short or obvious name was almost certainly claimed years ago, and you get the same error whether it belongs to you or to a stranger. Names must also be 3 to 63 characters, lowercase, and DNS-compatible. Including your account ID or organisation prefix, as in acme-artifacts-111122223333, makes collisions essentially impossible and also makes ownership obvious when browsing a long list.
Why does creating a bucket in us-east-1 behave differently?

us-east-1 was the original S3 region and predates the LocationConstraint parameter, so the API treats it as the implicit default and rejects an explicit value with InvalidLocationConstraint. Every other region requires the parameter. Scripts written for one region and reused for another hit this constantly, so it is worth handling explicitly if you provision across regions.
Should I use dots in bucket names?

No. A name containing a dot breaks virtual-hosted-style HTTPS access, because AWS's wildcard certificate does not match multi-level subdomains, so requests fail with a TLS error that gives no hint about naming. Dots were historically used to match a custom domain for static website hosting, but the modern approach is CloudFront in front of a private bucket, which removes the reason entirely. Use hyphens.
What settings should I apply to a new S3 bucket?

Block Public Access on all four settings, Bucket owner enforced ownership to disable ACLs, default encryption with a bucket key enabled, and a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads. Most of these are now defaults for new buckets, but applying them explicitly in your infrastructure code makes the intent visible and protects against differences between accounts. Decide about versioning and Object Lock at creation, since Object Lock cannot be added later and versioning cannot be undone.
How do I delete a bucket that will not empty?

If versioning is or was ever enabled, aws s3 rb --force is not enough. It removes current objects but leaves noncurrent versions and delete markers, which block deletion while being invisible in a normal listing. Delete them explicitly using list-object-versions piped into delete-objects for both Versions and DeleteMarkers. For very large buckets, a lifecycle rule expiring everything is cheaper and easier: S3 removes the objects in the background at no request cost, and the bucket deletes cleanly a day or two later.
Do folders exist in S3?

No. The console renders folders for convenience, but a key like logs/2026/app.log is a single flat string containing slashes. Deleting a folder means deleting every object with that prefix, renaming one means copying and deleting every object, and an empty folder only exists if someone created a zero-byte object to represent it. Prefixes do matter for performance, though: S3 scales request rate per prefix, so spreading high-volume writes across prefixes avoids throttling.

keyConcepts.explanation: Understand how S3 decides access: IAM vs bucket policies, Block Public Access, disabled ACLs, cross-account access, presigned URLs and debugging AccessDenied.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand how S3 decides access: IAM vs bucket policies, Block Public Access, disabled ACLs, cross-account access, presigned URLs and debugging AccessDenied.
S3 access is decided by several mechanisms evaluated together, and an AccessDenied never tells you which one refused. Knowing the order turns a guessing game into a checklist.

sections.title: The mechanisms
paragraphs: Within one account, an IAM policy alone is sufficient. You do not need a bucket policy for your own principals. Bucket policies come into their own for cross-account access, for enforcing conditions on everyone regardless of their IAM, and for the narrow cases of genuine public read.

sections.title: How a request is evaluated
paragraphs: The consequence worth internalising: Block Public Access wins over a bucket policy that grants public read. A team that adds a public-read policy and still gets 403 is nearly always hitting this, and the fix is not to disable BPA. It is to put CloudFront in front.

sections.title: Bucket and object are different resources
paragraphs: This is the most common S3 policy mistake by a distance.

s3:ListBucket acts on the bucket ARN with no trailing /*. s3:GetObject acts on the object ARN, which requires it. Writing one statement with both actions against one ARN fails in a way that looks arbitrary: listing works but downloads do not, or vice versa.

A related confusion: a missing s3:ListBucket makes a GetObject on a non-existent key return 403 rather than 404, because S3 will not confirm whether an object exists to a principal that cannot list. People chase a permissions bug when the real problem is a typo in the key.

sections.title: Block Public Access
paragraphs: Four independent settings, all on by default on new buckets:
Leave all four on. For content that genuinely must be public, the correct pattern is CloudFront with an Origin Access Control, where the bucket stays private and only the distribution can read it:
That gives you HTTPS, a custom domain, caching and cheaper egress as well as a private bucket.

codeBlock.code: aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket acme-artifacts

sections.title: ACLs are disabled, and that is good
paragraphs: Since 2023, new buckets default to Bucket owner enforced object ownership, which disables ACLs entirely. Every well-known S3 exposure incident traced back to an object ACL someone set without realising.
If you encounter a bucket with ACLs enabled, move it:

Check first that nothing relies on them. Some older tooling sets --acl bucket-owner-full-control on upload, which fails once ACLs are disabled (and becomes unnecessary, since the bucket owner then owns everything automatically).

codeBlock.code:
aws s3api put-bucket-ownership-controls \
  --bucket acme-artifacts \
  --ownership-controls 'Rules=[{ObjectOwnership=BucketOwnerEnforced}]'

sections.title: Cross-account access
paragraphs: Two halves, and both are required:
The bucket policy grants the other account:
The other account's IAM policy must also allow it. A grant from the bucket alone is not enough. The principal's own account must permit the action too.

Two further details. If the bucket uses SSE-KMS, the KMS key policy must also grant the external principal kms:Decrypt, which is the most common reason cross-account reads fail after the S3 side looks correct. And RestrictPublicBuckets can interfere with cross-account patterns, so check BPA if a correct-looking policy is refused.

sections.title: Enforcing conditions on everyone
paragraphs: A bucket policy applies to all principals, which makes it the right place for organisation-wide rules IAM cannot guarantee:
That denies any request not over HTTPS, for everyone, regardless of their IAM permissions. Similar conditions can require a specific KMS key, restrict access to a VPC endpoint, or require MFA.
Explicit Deny beats every allow, which is exactly what makes this pattern reliable, and also why a stray Deny in a bucket policy can lock out principals you did not intend, including yourself.

sections.title: Presigned URLs
paragraphs: The right way to grant temporary access to one object without credentials:

The URL carries the signature of whoever generated it, so it can only grant permissions that principal already has. A presigned URL from a role without GetObject on that key does not work. The maximum lifetime depends on the signing credentials: a URL signed with temporary role credentials expires when those credentials do, regardless of --expires-in, which surprises people using presigned URLs from Lambda.

codeBlock.code: aws s3 presign s3://acme-artifacts/reports/q3.pdf --expires-in 3600

sections.title: Debugging AccessDenied
paragraphs: Then work through the usual causes in order:
IAM Access Analyzer for S3 reports which buckets are accessible externally, which is worth running whether or not anything is currently broken.

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Who am I?
aws sts get-caller-identity

# 2. Would it be allowed, and what decides?
aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/AppRole \
  --action-names s3:GetObject \
  --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::acme-artifacts/path/file.txt

# 3. What does the bucket say?
aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket acme-artifacts --output text | jq .
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket acme-artifacts

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A role can list objects in a bucket but every GetObject returns AccessDenied. The policy allows both actions on "arn:aws:s3:::acme-artifacts". What is wrong?
A bucket policy grants s3:GetObject to Principal "*", but anonymous requests still return 403. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between an IAM policy and a bucket policy for S3?

An IAM policy attaches to a principal and answers what that user or role may do. A bucket policy attaches to the bucket and answers who may access it. Within a single account, an IAM policy alone is sufficient and no bucket policy is needed. Bucket policies matter for cross-account access, for granting anonymous access in the rare cases that is appropriate, and for enforcing conditions on every principal regardless of their IAM. Such as denying any request that does not arrive over HTTPS.
Why do I get AccessDenied when the object exists?

Check the resource ARNs first. s3:GetObject requires an object ARN ending in /* while s3:ListBucket requires the bare bucket ARN, and mixing them up produces exactly this. There is also a subtler cause: without s3:ListBucket, S3 returns 403 rather than 404 for a key that does not exist, because it will not reveal whether an object is present to a principal that cannot list. So an apparent permissions failure is sometimes a misspelled key. aws iam simulate-principal-policy settles it directly.
Why doesn't my public bucket policy work?

Block Public Access is enabled, and it overrides any policy that would grant public access. All four BPA settings are on by default for new buckets at both account and bucket level. Rather than disabling it, serve public content through CloudFront with an Origin Access Control: the bucket stays private, only the distribution can read it, and you gain HTTPS, a custom domain, caching and cheaper egress. Turning BPA off should be a deliberate and rare decision.
How do I give another AWS account access to my bucket?

Both sides must permit it. Add a bucket policy naming the external principal, ideally a specific role ARN rather than the whole account, and allow the actions on both the bucket ARN and the object ARN. The other account must also grant its principal those actions in its own IAM policy. If the bucket is encrypted with SSE-KMS, the KMS key policy must additionally allow the external principal kms:Decrypt, which is the most frequent reason a correct-looking S3 configuration still fails.
Should I use S3 ACLs?

No. ACLs are legacy and are disabled by default on new buckets under Bucket owner enforced ownership, which is the right setting. Object-level ACLs were behind most well-known S3 data exposure incidents, because a single object could be made public independently of the bucket's configuration. Use IAM policies and bucket policies instead. If you inherit a bucket with ACLs enabled, disable them after confirming nothing depends on them. Some older upload tooling sets bucket-owner-full-control, which becomes both unnecessary and invalid.
How long can a presigned URL last?

--expires-in accepts up to seven days, but the effective lifetime is capped by the credentials that signed it. A URL signed with temporary role credentials, which is the case in Lambda, ECS, EC2 with an instance profile, and anywhere else using a role. Expires when those credentials do, typically within an hour, regardless of what you requested. For genuinely long-lived links, sign with credentials that live long enough, or generate the URL on demand rather than in advance.

Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Enable S3 versioning to survive overwrites and deletes. Learn how delete markers work, hidden storage costs, lifecycle rules, MFA delete and Object Lock.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Enable S3 versioning to survive overwrites and deletes. Learn how delete markers work, hidden storage costs, lifecycle rules, MFA delete and Object Lock.
Versioning keeps every version of every object in a bucket. An overwrite creates a new version rather than replacing the old one, and a delete hides the object rather than removing it.
It is the difference between "someone overwrote the production config" being a five-minute recovery and being an incident.

codeBlock.code:
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket acme-artifacts \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

sections.title: It cannot be turned off
paragraphs: Once enabled, versioning can be suspended but never returned to the unversioned state. Suspending stops new versions being created; it does not delete the versions already stored, which remain and continue to be billed.
That is worth knowing before enabling it on a bucket holding terabytes of frequently-overwritten data.

sections.title: Deletes create a marker, not a deletion
paragraphs: This is the mechanism to understand, because it explains both the protection and the cost.

A DELETE on a versioned bucket does not remove anything. It adds a delete marker, a zero-byte object that becomes the current version, so the object appears gone from a normal listing while every previous version is still stored.
To restore, delete the delete marker:
The object reappears immediately. That asymmetry, deleting a delete marker undeletes the object, is initially confusing and is the whole recovery mechanism.
Deleting a specific --version-id of the actual data is permanent.

codeBlock.code:
# Looks deleted
aws s3 ls s3://acme-artifacts/config.json

# Actually still there
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket acme-artifacts --prefix config.json

sections.title: The cost surprise
paragraphs: Every version is billed at full storage price. A 100 MB file overwritten daily for a year is 36 GB of storage, not 100 MB.
This catches almost everyone: versioning is enabled for safety, nightly jobs overwrite objects, and storage grows steadily for months while a normal aws s3 ls shows a bucket that looks small.
The fix is a lifecycle rule, and every versioned bucket should have one:
Three parts, all worth having:

codeBlock.code:
# What is actually stored, versions included
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket acme-artifacts \
  --query 'sum(Versions[].Size)' --output text

sections.title: Listing gets slower
paragraphs: list-object-versions returns every version and every delete marker, so a bucket with millions of accumulated versions is slow and expensive to enumerate. Lifecycle expiry keeps this manageable; without it, listing performance degrades quietly over years.

sections.title: MFA delete
paragraphs: For high-value buckets, MFA delete requires a hardware or virtual MFA token to permanently delete a version or to change the versioning state:

Two constraints make it awkward: it can only be configured by the root user of the account, and it cannot be enabled through the console. That limits it to genuinely critical buckets, but for those it is a strong protection. An attacker with compromised credentials still cannot permanently destroy data.

codeBlock.code:
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket acme-critical \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled,MFADelete=Enabled \
  --mfa "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:mfa/root-account-mfa-device 123456"

sections.title: Object Lock for true immutability
paragraphs: Versioning protects against accident. Object Lock protects against intent.

With Object Lock in compliance mode, an object cannot be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including the root user, until its retention period expires. This is what ransomware protection and regulatory retention actually require.
It must be enabled when the bucket is created and requires versioning. It cannot be added to an existing bucket, which is a decision to make up front for anything holding backups.
Governance mode is the softer variant, allowing users with a specific permission to override retention, which suits internal policy rather than compliance.

sections.title: Versioning and replication
paragraphs: Cross-region replication requires versioning on both source and destination buckets. It is worth noting that replication copies new objects going forward, existing objects need a separate batch replication job, and that delete markers are only replicated if you configure it explicitly.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An object was deleted from a versioned bucket. How do you restore it?
A versioned bucket holds a 100 MB file overwritten by a nightly job. After a year, aws s3 ls shows 100 MB but the bill reflects far more. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I restore a deleted object in S3?

Find the delete marker with aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket <name> --prefix <key>, then delete that marker by its version ID. Removing the marker makes the previous version current and the object reappears immediately. If the specific data version itself was deleted with a version ID rather than a plain delete, it is permanently gone, only a delete marker is reversible.
Why is my versioned S3 bucket so expensive?

Because every version is stored and billed at full price, and a normal listing shows only current versions so the growth is invisible. A file overwritten nightly accumulates a year of copies. Check the real total with aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket <name> --query 'sum(Versions[].Size)'. The fix is a lifecycle rule with NoncurrentVersionExpiration to remove old versions after a retention window, plus ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker to clean up orphaned markers.
Can I turn off S3 versioning?

Not completely. Versioning can be suspended, which stops new versions being created, but a bucket can never return to the unversioned state. Suspending also does not delete existing versions. They remain stored and billed until a lifecycle rule expires them. Enable versioning deliberately, particularly on buckets holding large, frequently-overwritten objects, and pair it with a lifecycle policy from the start.
What is a delete marker?

A zero-byte object that S3 adds as the new current version when you delete an object in a versioned bucket. It makes the object appear absent from normal listings while every previous version remains stored. Delete markers themselves consume negligible space but accumulate as clutter, slow down version listings, and are worth cleaning up with the ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker lifecycle action once their underlying versions have expired.
What is the difference between versioning and Object Lock?

Versioning protects against accidents. An overwrite or delete is recoverable, but anyone with permission can still permanently remove a specific version. Object Lock protects against intent: in compliance mode an object cannot be deleted or modified by anyone, including the root user, until its retention period expires. Object Lock requires versioning and must be enabled when the bucket is created, so it is a decision to make up front for backups and anything with regulatory retention requirements.
Should I enable MFA delete?

For genuinely critical buckets, yes. It requires an MFA token to permanently delete a version or change the versioning configuration, so compromised credentials alone cannot destroy data. Two constraints limit its use: it can only be configured by the account's root user, and not through the console. That makes it impractical as a blanket policy but worthwhile for a small number of high-value buckets. For broader immutability, Object Lock is usually the more manageable option.

aws-rds.title: AWS RDS
aws-rds.subtitle: Learn Amazon RDS: Multi-AZ vs read replicas, backups and point-in-time recovery, settings you cannot change later, why Lambda needs RDS Proxy, and cost.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS RDS must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Learn Amazon RDS: Multi-AZ vs read replicas, backups and point-in-time recovery, settings you cannot change later, why Lambda needs RDS Proxy, and cost.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn Amazon RDS: Multi-AZ vs read replicas, backups and point-in-time recovery, settings you cannot change later, why Lambda needs RDS Proxy, and cost.

sections.title: Amazon RDS
paragraphs: RDS runs relational databases so you do not have to. Patching, backups, replication and failover are handled for you. What remains yours is schema, queries, connection management, and a handful of configuration decisions that cannot be changed after creation.
Those irreversible decisions are where most RDS regret comes from.

sections.title: Engines
paragraphs: RDS supports MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle and SQL Server. Aurora is a separate AWS-built engine that is wire-compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL, with a distributed storage layer giving faster failover, up to 15 read replicas and storage that scales automatically.

Choose standard RDS for straightforward workloads and full engine compatibility. Choose Aurora when you need its scaling and failover characteristics and can accept a different cost model, and note Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity with load, which suits variable or unpredictable workloads.

sections.title: Multi-AZ and read replicas solve different problems
paragraphs: These two are constantly confused, and the confusion causes both wasted money and missed outages.
A Multi-AZ standby is not a read replica. In the classic instance deployment you cannot query it; it exists purely to take over. Teams sometimes enable Multi-AZ expecting read capacity and get none.
A read replica is not high availability. It is asynchronous, so promoting one after a primary failure can lose recent writes, and promotion is a manual decision.
Production databases usually want both: Multi-AZ for availability, plus read replicas if reads need scaling.
The newer Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment gives two readable standbys and faster failover, which narrows the distinction, but the classic deployment remains the default and behaves as above.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --db-instance-class db.m6g.large \
  --engine postgres --engine-version 16.4 \
  --allocated-storage 100 --storage-type gp3 \
  --multi-az \
  --storage-encrypted \
  --backup-retention-period 14 \
  --no-publicly-accessible \
  --deletion-protection

sections.title: The settings you cannot change later
paragraphs: Get these right at creation:
Everything else, instance class, storage size, backup retention, parameter groups, can be changed, usually with a brief interruption or during a maintenance window.

sections.title: Backups and recovery
paragraphs: Two separate mechanisms with different lifecycles:

Automated backups run daily and capture transaction logs, enabling point-in-time recovery to any second within the retention window. Retention is 0 to 35 days, and 0 disables backups entirely: which also disables PITR and read replicas.
Manual snapshots persist until you delete them, independent of retention or even of the instance.

The detail that catches people during an incident: a restore creates a new instance with a new endpoint. It does not roll the existing database back. Recovery therefore means restoring, verifying, then repointing the application, which takes longer than people plan for and is worth rehearsing before you need it.
Deleting an instance offers a final snapshot. Take it. Combine with --deletion-protection on anything that matters, so deletion requires a deliberate two-step.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time \
  --source-db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --target-db-instance-identifier payments-restored \
  --restore-time 2026-09-12T08:30:00Z

sections.title: Connections, and why Lambda needs RDS Proxy
paragraphs: Relational databases have a hard connection limit, and each connection consumes memory. A db.t3.medium PostgreSQL instance supports a few hundred connections.

That works fine for a handful of application servers with connection pools. It fails badly with Lambda, where every concurrent execution opens its own connection: 500 concurrent invocations means 500 connection attempts, and the database refuses them.
RDS Proxy sits in front and pools connections:
Besides pooling, it shortens failover time for clients and supports IAM authentication, which removes the database password from your application entirely.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds create-db-proxy \
  --db-proxy-name payments-proxy \
  --engine-family POSTGRESQL \
  --auth '[{"AuthScheme":"SECRETS","SecretArn":"arn:aws:secretsmanager:...","IAMAuth":"REQUIRED"}]' \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/rds-proxy-role \
  --vpc-subnet-ids subnet-0aaa subnet-0bbb

sections.title: Maintenance and upgrades
paragraphs: RDS applies patches during your maintenance window, and on Multi-AZ it patches the standby first, fails over, then patches the former primary, so expect a short failover rather than sustained downtime.

--auto-minor-version-upgrade is on by default and generally worth keeping. Major version upgrades are always deliberate: test against a restored snapshot first, because extension compatibility and query plan changes routinely produce surprises.
Every engine version reaches end of standard support, after which AWS forces an upgrade or moves you to paid extended support. Track it rather than being surprised.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team enables Multi-AZ hoping to offload read queries to the standby. Reads do not get faster. Why?
A Lambda function querying RDS starts failing with "too many connections" during traffic spikes. The database has capacity to spare. What is the fix?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between Multi-AZ and a read replica?

Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone purely for availability. It is not readable in the classic instance deployment, and it takes over automatically in about 60 to 120 seconds if the primary fails, with no data loss. A read replica is an asynchronous copy that is readable, used to scale read traffic, and can live in another region. Because replication is asynchronous, promoting a replica after a failure can lose recent writes and is a manual decision. Production systems commonly use both.
Can I enable encryption on an existing RDS instance?

No. Encryption at rest must be enabled when the instance is created. To encrypt an existing database you take a snapshot, copy that snapshot specifying a KMS key, restore a new instance from the encrypted copy, and cut over, which means either downtime or a replication and switchover exercise. Since there is no additional charge for encryption, the sensible default is to enable it on every instance at creation and never face the migration.
How does point-in-time recovery work in RDS?

Automated backups capture a daily snapshot plus continuous transaction logs, allowing restoration to any second within the retention window of up to 35 days. The important detail is that a restore creates a new instance with a new endpoint rather than rewinding the existing database, so recovery involves restoring, verifying the data, then repointing your application. That takes longer than teams expect during an incident, which is why it is worth rehearsing. Setting backup retention to 0 disables this entirely, along with read replicas.
Why is my Lambda function exhausting RDS connections?

Because each concurrent Lambda execution runs in its own isolated environment and opens its own database connection. A spike to 500 concurrent invocations attempts 500 connections, and relational databases have a hard limit far below what a Lambda burst can produce. RDS Proxy solves this by pooling connections and multiplexing many clients onto few database connections, and it additionally shortens failover time and supports IAM authentication. Setting reserved concurrency on the function provides a secondary cap.
Should I use Aurora or standard RDS?

Standard RDS for straightforward workloads and full engine compatibility, including extensions or features Aurora does not support. Aurora when you need its distributed storage layer: faster failover, up to fifteen read replicas, storage that grows automatically, and better performance under heavy load. Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity with demand, which suits variable or unpredictable workloads well. Aurora generally costs more for small steady databases and can cost less at scale, so compare against your actual usage rather than list prices.
How do I reduce RDS costs?

Buy Reserved Instances for production databases, which discount up to around 70% and suit a workload that is about as predictable as they come. Use Graviton instance classes such as db.m6g, which are cheaper than equivalent Intel classes. Right-size deliberately and remember storage can only grow, so over-provisioning is permanent. Disable Multi-AZ in non-production, since it roughly doubles instance cost. Stop development instances outside working hours, bearing in mind RDS restarts a stopped instance automatically after seven days.

aws-rds-setup.title: AWS RDS Setup
aws-rds-setup.subtitle: Create an RDS instance with the right choices up front: subnet groups, settings you cannot change later, parameter groups, private access and first checks.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS RDS Setup must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Create an RDS instance with the right choices up front: subnet groups, settings you cannot change later, parameter groups, private access and first checks.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create an RDS instance with the right choices up front: subnet groups, settings you cannot change later, parameter groups, private access and first checks.
Creating an RDS instance takes one command. Creating one you will not regret takes a handful of decisions, several of which are permanent.

sections.title: What you need first
paragraphs: A DB subnet group. RDS requires subnets in at least two Availability Zones, even for a single-AZ instance, because it needs somewhere to fail over to if you later enable Multi-AZ.
Use private subnets with no route to an internet gateway. A database should not be reachable from the internet under any circumstances.
A security group that references your application's security group rather than a CIDR range:
Referencing the application's security group means the rule keeps working as instances are replaced and scaled, which a CIDR-based rule does not.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds create-db-subnet-group \
  --db-subnet-group-name payments-db \
  --db-subnet-group-description "Private database subnets" \
  --subnet-ids subnet-db-a subnet-db-b subnet-db-c

sections.title: Creating the instance
paragraphs: Several of those are worth explaining.

--manage-master-user-password has RDS create and rotate the master password in Secrets Manager automatically. There is then no password in your shell history, your Terraform state or anyone's notes. Use it.
db.m6g is Graviton, around 20% cheaper than the Intel equivalent for the same performance.
--max-allocated-storage enables storage autoscaling, so the instance grows when it approaches full rather than failing at 3am. Storage can only ever grow, so set the ceiling thoughtfully.
--storage-encrypted must be set now. See below.
--deletion-protection requires an explicit disable before the instance can be deleted, which is a cheap guard on something irreversible.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --db-instance-class db.m6g.large \
  --engine postgres --engine-version 16.4 \
  --master-username dbadmin \
  --manage-master-user-password \
  --allocated-storage 100 \
  --max-allocated-storage 500 \
  --storage-type gp3 \
  --storage-encrypted \
  --db-subnet-group-name payments-db \
  --vpc-security-group-ids sg-database \
  --multi-az \
  --backup-retention-period 14 \
  --preferred-backup-window "02:00-03:00" \
  --preferred-maintenance-window "sun:04:00-sun:05:00" \
  --enable-performance-insights \
  --no-publicly-accessible \
  --deletion-protection

sections.title: The settings you cannot change later
paragraphs: Encryption is the one that catches people. It costs nothing, so there is no reason not to enable it on every instance, and no convenient path back if you forget.

sections.title: Parameter and option groups
paragraphs: The default parameter group cannot be modified. To change any database setting you need your own:
Create one at instance creation even if empty, because attaching one later requires a reboot.

Parameters are either dynamic (applied immediately) or static (requiring a reboot). describe-engine-default-parameters tells you which, and a static parameter change silently waits until the next reboot, which is confusing if you expect an immediate effect.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds create-db-parameter-group \
  --db-parameter-group-name payments-pg16 \
  --db-parameter-group-family postgres16 \
  --description "Payments tuning"

aws rds modify-db-parameter-group \
  --db-parameter-group-name payments-pg16 \
  --parameters "ParameterName=log_min_duration_statement,ParameterValue=1000,ApplyMethod=immediate"

sections.title: Connecting
paragraphs: The instance is in a private subnet, so connecting from a laptop needs a tunnel. Session Manager port forwarding does this without a bastion host:
Always use the endpoint DNS name, never a resolved IP. The address changes on failover, and an application caching the IP will fail in a way that looks like a network problem.

codeBlock.code:
# The endpoint
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].Endpoint.{Address:Address,Port:Port}'

# The managed password
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value \
  --secret-id $(aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
      --query 'DBInstances[0].MasterUserSecret.SecretArn' --output text) \
  --query SecretString --output text | jq -r .password

sections.title: Use IAM authentication where you can
paragraphs: Applications then request a short-lived token instead of holding a password:
Tokens last 15 minutes, so there is no long-lived database credential in your application at all.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds modify-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --enable-iam-database-authentication \
  --apply-immediately

sections.title: Maintenance and backups
paragraphs: Both windows are worth setting explicitly rather than accepting a random assignment.

Put the backup window before the maintenance window, and both during genuinely low traffic. On Multi-AZ, backups are taken from the standby so there is no performance impact on the primary. One of the less-known benefits of Multi-AZ.

Minor version upgrades apply during the maintenance window with --auto-minor-version-upgrade enabled, which is the default and generally worth keeping. Major version upgrades are always deliberate: test against a restored snapshot first, because extension compatibility and query plan changes routinely surprise people.

sections.title: First-run checks
paragraphs: That second command is worth running in a non-production environment at least once. Failover takes 60 to 120 seconds and your application's reconnection behaviour during it is something to discover deliberately rather than during an incident.

codeBlock.code:
# Is it actually available?
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].{Status:DBInstanceStatus,MultiAZ:MultiAZ,Encrypted:StorageEncrypted,Public:PubliclyAccessible}'

# Prove failover works, before you need it to
aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier payments-prod --force-failover

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A production RDS instance was created without encryption. What is required to encrypt it?
After a Multi-AZ failover, an application cannot reach the database until it is restarted. What is the likely cause?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does RDS need subnets in two Availability Zones?

Because a DB subnet group defines where RDS may place the instance and any future standby, and it requires at least two zones even for a single-AZ deployment. That way enabling Multi-AZ later needs no network changes. Use private subnets with no route to an internet gateway. A database should never be reachable from the internet, and --no-publicly-accessible enforces that on the instance itself.
Can I enable encryption on an existing RDS instance?

No. Encryption at rest is set at creation and cannot be changed. To encrypt an existing database you snapshot it, copy the snapshot specifying a KMS key, restore a new instance from the encrypted copy, and cut over, which means downtime or a replication exercise. Since there is no extra charge for encryption, enable it on every instance at creation as a matter of course.
How should I manage the RDS master password?

Use --manage-master-user-password, which has RDS generate the password, store it in Secrets Manager and rotate it automatically. Nothing sensitive then appears in your shell history, your Terraform state or a colleague's notes. For application connections, go further and enable IAM database authentication, where applications request a 15-minute token instead of holding a password at all.
How do I connect to an RDS instance in a private subnet?

Through a tunnel. Session Manager port forwarding does it without a bastion host: start a session against any instance with the SSM agent using the AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost document, pointing at the RDS endpoint, then connect your client to localhost. This needs no open inbound ports, no SSH keys, and access is controlled by IAM with every session logged to CloudTrail.
What is a parameter group and do I need a custom one?

A parameter group holds the database engine's configuration settings. The default group attached to a new instance cannot be modified, so changing any setting requires creating your own. Create one at instance creation even if it initially matches the defaults, because attaching a parameter group to an existing instance requires a reboot. Note that static parameters only take effect after a reboot, which is a common source of confusion when a change appears to have done nothing.
What should the maintenance and backup windows be set to?

Both during your genuinely lowest-traffic period, with the backup window scheduled before the maintenance window. Setting them explicitly is better than accepting the random assignment AWS makes, which may land in the middle of your business day. On Multi-AZ instances backups are taken from the standby, so there is no performance impact on the primary. A useful and often overlooked benefit of Multi-AZ beyond the availability itself.

Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
