sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Secure an RDS database: network isolation, encryption at rest and in transit, IAM authentication, secret rotation, audit logs and deletion protection.

A database holds the data everything else exists to serve, which makes it the most valuable target in most architectures. The controls below are layered deliberately. Each assumes the ones before it might fail.

sections.title: Network isolation first
paragraphs: Never make an RDS instance publicly accessible. It is a setting, it defaults to off for instances in private subnets, and it is occasionally turned on during troubleshooting and forgotten.
A publicly accessible database is found by automated scanners within hours. Combined with a weak password or a known engine vulnerability, that is how databases get ransomed.
Place instances in private subnets with no route to an internet gateway, and reference the application's security group rather than a CIDR range:
The rule then survives instance churn and expresses the intent, the application tier may reach the database tier, rather than encoding a set of addresses that will change.
For the strongest isolation, put databases in a third subnet tier with no internet route at all, not even through NAT. A compromised database then cannot exfiltrate outward.

codeBlock.code:
# Audit every instance in the account
aws rds describe-db-instances \
  --query 'DBInstances[].{ID:DBInstanceIdentifier,Public:PubliclyAccessible,Encrypted:StorageEncrypted}' \
  --output table

sections.title: Encryption at rest
paragraphs: Must be enabled at creation. It cannot be added later, and the migration path, snapshot, copy encrypted, restore, cut over, means downtime.
It costs nothing, so there is no reason any instance should be unencrypted.

A customer-managed KMS key rather than the default aws/rds key gives you a key policy as a second access control layer and visibility of key usage in CloudTrail. It also means you can revoke access to the data by revoking the key.

Encryption covers the instance, its automated backups, snapshots and read replicas. Note that a snapshot of an unencrypted instance is unencrypted, and sharing an encrypted snapshot cross-account requires sharing the KMS key too. A frequent stumbling block.

codeBlock.code: aws rds create-db-instance ... --storage-encrypted --kms-key-id alias/payments-rds

sections.title: Encryption in transit
paragraphs: Encryption at rest protects a stolen disk. It does nothing for traffic on the wire.
Then connect with verification, not merely encryption:

sslmode=require encrypts but does not verify the server, which leaves the connection open to interception. verify-full is the one that actually protects you, and it needs the RDS CA bundle for your Region.
Those CA certificates expire. AWS announces rotations well in advance, but an unrotated client trust store fails to connect on the day. It is worth tracking rather than discovering.

codeBlock.code:
# PostgreSQL. Require SSL via a parameter group
aws rds modify-db-parameter-group \
  --db-parameter-group-name payments-pg16 \
  --parameters "ParameterName=rds.force_ssl,ParameterValue=1,ApplyMethod=pending-reboot"

sections.title: Credentials
paragraphs: Three approaches, in increasing order of preference.
A password in Secrets Manager, created and rotated by RDS itself:
IAM database authentication, where there is no long-lived password at all:

Tokens last 15 minutes. Access is granted and revoked through IAM like any other permission, and there is nothing in the application to rotate or leak. The limitation is a connection-rate cap, which is why it pairs well with RDS Proxy.

RDS Proxy with IAM auth is the strongest combination: the proxy holds the credential, the application authenticates with IAM, and connection pooling solves the Lambda connection-exhaustion problem at the same time.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds modify-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --manage-master-user-password --apply-immediately

sections.title: Least privilege inside the database
paragraphs: IAM controls who can reach the database. It says nothing about what they can do once connected, that is the database's own permission system, and it is frequently ignored.
Applications should not connect as the master user. Create a role with only the privileges it needs:
A compromised application credential then cannot drop tables.

sections.title: Audit logging
paragraphs: Database engine logs are not enabled by default and are the only record of what happened inside the database:
For PostgreSQL, pgaudit gives structured audit logging of statements. For MySQL, the MariaDB audit plugin does the same. Both are enabled through the option or parameter group.
Send logs to CloudWatch and set retention, otherwise they accumulate and are billed indefinitely.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds modify-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --cloudwatch-logs-export-configuration '{"EnableLogTypes":["postgresql","upgrade"]}' \
  --apply-immediately

sections.title: Protecting against deletion
paragraphs: Deletion protection requires an explicit disable before an instance can be removed, which turns an irreversible one-step mistake into a deliberate two-step action. Always take a final snapshot when deleting.

Automated backups are deleted with the instance; manual snapshots are not. For anything you must be able to recover, take periodic manual snapshots and copy them to another account. A backup in the same account as the thing it backs up is not protection against a compromised account.
AWS Backup with a vault lock provides genuinely immutable backups that even an administrator cannot delete.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds modify-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --deletion-protection --apply-immediately

sections.title: An audit in one command
paragraphs: Any Public: true, Encrypted: false, DeleteProtect: false or Backups: 0 is worth investigating immediately. AWS Config and Security Hub can check these continuously rather than relying on someone remembering.

codeBlock.code:
aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[].{
  ID:DBInstanceIdentifier,
  Public:PubliclyAccessible,
  Encrypted:StorageEncrypted,
  IAMAuth:IAMDatabaseAuthenticationEnabled,
  DeleteProtect:DeletionProtection,
  Backups:BackupRetentionPeriod,
  MultiAZ:MultiAZ}' --output table

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An application connects to RDS with sslmode=require. Is the connection secure against interception?
Why copy critical RDS snapshots to a separate AWS account?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should an RDS instance ever be publicly accessible?

Essentially never. A public database is discovered by automated scanners within hours, and combined with a weak credential or an unpatched engine vulnerability that is how databases get ransomed. Place instances in private subnets with no internet gateway route, set --no-publicly-accessible, and reach them through a bastion, Session Manager port forwarding, or a VPN. Audit the whole account periodically, because the setting is occasionally enabled during troubleshooting and forgotten.
What is the difference between sslmode=require and verify-full?

require guarantees the connection is encrypted but performs no verification of the server's identity, so an attacker able to intercept traffic can present their own certificate and read everything. verify-full validates the certificate chain against the RDS CA bundle for your Region and confirms the hostname matches. Since downloading the bundle is a one-off step, verify-full should be the default for anything carrying real data.
How does IAM database authentication work?

You enable it on the instance and grant the rds_iam role to a database user. Applications then call generate-db-auth-token to obtain a 15-minute token and use it as the password. There is no long-lived credential in the application, access is granted and revoked through IAM like any other permission, and every token request appears in CloudTrail. The main limitation is a cap on new connections per second, which makes it a natural pairing with RDS Proxy.
Can I enable encryption on an existing RDS instance?

No. It is fixed at creation. The migration is snapshot, copy the snapshot specifying a KMS key, restore from the encrypted copy and cut over, which means downtime or a replication exercise. Because encryption adds no cost, every instance should be created encrypted. Using a customer-managed KMS key rather than the default also gives you a key policy as a second access layer and visibility of key usage in CloudTrail.
Should my application connect as the RDS master user?

No. The master user typically has broad privileges including DDL, so a compromised application credential can drop tables rather than merely read data. Create a dedicated database role granting only what the application needs, usually SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on specific schemas, and often not DELETE. IAM controls who can reach the database; the database's own permission system controls what they can do once connected, and skipping the second layer wastes the first.
How should I back up an RDS database securely?

Automated backups give point-in-time recovery within a retention window of up to 35 days, but they are deleted along with the instance. Manual snapshots persist independently, so take them for anything you must be able to recover. Critically, copy important snapshots to a separate AWS account. A backup in the same account as the database shares its blast radius, so whoever can delete one can usually delete both. AWS Backup with a locked vault provides immutability that even an administrator cannot override.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how AWS Lambda works: the execution model, memory as CPU, cold starts, the concurrency limit, timeouts and retries, VPC networking and surprise costs.
Lambda runs your code in response to events without you managing servers. You supply a function, AWS supplies the compute, and you pay for the time it runs rather than for an instance sitting idle.
The model is genuinely different from a server, and most Lambda problems come from carrying server assumptions into it.
Lambda: Event-Driven Execution
Lambda scales to zero. You pay only for the milliseconds your code actually runs

sections.title: The execution model
paragraphs: An execution environment is a small, isolated sandbox that runs one invocation at a time. Ten simultaneous requests mean ten environments. There is no in-process concurrency to share.
What matters operationally is that AWS reuses environments. After an invocation finishes, the environment is kept warm for a while and reused for the next request. That has two consequences:
Code outside the handler runs once per environment, not once per invocation. This is the single most useful optimisation available:
Creating the client inside the handler adds its initialisation cost to every request.

State persists between invocations in the same environment. Warm environments retain globals and /tmp contents. That is excellent for connection reuse and caching, and a real source of bugs when a function accidentally carries state, a mutated global, a leftover file, into an unrelated request.

sections.title: Memory is how you buy CPU
paragraphs: Lambda has one performance dial, from 128 MB to 10,240 MB, and CPU scales proportionally with it. Around 1,769 MB you get one full vCPU; beyond that, more.

This means the intuitive cost trade-off is often backwards. Doubling memory doubles the per-millisecond price but can more than halve the duration, so the invocation ends up cheaper as well as faster:

Do not guess at this. AWS Lambda Power Tuning runs your function across memory settings and produces the cost and duration curve, and it routinely finds that the lowest memory setting was the most expensive choice.

codeBlock.code:
128 MB  × 8,000 ms  = 1,024 MB-s
512 MB  × 1,600 ms  =   819 MB-s   ← faster AND cheaper
1024 MB ×   900 ms  =   922 MB-s

sections.title: Cold starts
paragraphs: A cold start happens when no warm environment is available: AWS provisions a sandbox, downloads your code, starts the runtime, and runs your initialisation. Typically tens to a few hundred milliseconds; considerably more for heavy runtimes and large dependency trees.
What genuinely helps:
What usually does not help: a scheduled "warmer" invocation. It keeps one environment alive while a traffic spike needs fifty.
For most asynchronous and event-driven work, cold starts do not matter. They matter for user-facing synchronous requests, and that is where to spend effort.

sections.title: Concurrency, and the limit that causes incidents
paragraphs: The account has a default concurrent execution limit of 1,000 across all functions in a region. Exceeding it throttles invocations.

Reserved concurrency caps a function and guarantees it that capacity. Setting it protects the rest of the account from one runaway function. The classic incident being a function triggered by S3 events that consumes the whole account limit and takes down unrelated APIs.
Setting it to 0 disables a function entirely, which is the fastest way to stop a misbehaving one without deleting it.
Provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments, at an hourly cost.
Watch the Throttles metric. Throttling looks like intermittent failures rather than a clear error, so it is easy to misdiagnose as an application bug.

codeBlock.code:
aws lambda put-function-concurrency \
  --function-name image-processor \
  --reserved-concurrent-executions 100

sections.title: Timeouts and retries
paragraphs: Maximum timeout is 15 minutes, default 3 seconds. Set it deliberately. Too high and a hung function burns money, too low and legitimate work is cut off mid-way.
Retry behaviour depends on how the function was invoked, and this catches people:

That third row is a genuine outage generator: one poison-pill record in a Kinesis shard is retried indefinitely and nothing behind it processes. Set MaximumRetryAttempts and an OnFailure destination on the event source mapping.
Because retries exist, functions must be idempotent. The same event will be delivered more than once, and a handler that charges a card or sends an email needs a deduplication key.

sections.title: Lambda in a VPC
paragraphs: A function only needs VPC configuration to reach private resources. An RDS instance, an internal service. If it only calls public AWS APIs, leave it out; a VPC-attached function has no internet access by default.

That last point surprises people regularly: attaching a Lambda to a VPC removes its default internet access. Reaching a public endpoint then requires a NAT gateway, or a VPC endpoint for the AWS service in question.
The old penalty of many seconds of cold-start ENI setup is gone. VPC networking now uses shared network interfaces and adds very little. The connectivity trade-off remains.

sections.title: Cost
paragraphs: Billing is requests plus GB-seconds of duration, with a perpetual free tier that covers a great deal of light usage.
Where costs actually go wrong:

sections.title: When not to use Lambda
paragraphs: Worth stating plainly. Lambda is a poor fit for long-running processes beyond 15 minutes, sustained high-throughput workloads where an always-on container is cheaper, applications needing large local state or persistent connections, and anything with hard sub-10ms latency requirements. ECS Fargate or EKS is often the better answer.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A function at 128 MB runs for 8 seconds. At 512 MB it runs for 1.6 seconds. Which costs less per invocation?
A Lambda consuming a Kinesis stream stops making progress. One record consistently causes an unhandled error. What is happening?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What causes Lambda cold starts and how do I reduce them?

A cold start occurs when no warm execution environment is available, so AWS must create a sandbox, load your code and run initialisation. Reduce them by shrinking the deployment package, lazy-loading dependencies that are not needed on every code path, increasing memory, which also increases the CPU available during initialisation, and choosing a lighter runtime where possible. Java benefits enormously from SnapStart. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments permanently warm and eliminates cold starts for that capacity, at an hourly charge regardless of traffic.
How much memory should I give my Lambda function?

More than feels intuitive. CPU is allocated in proportion to memory, so a CPU-bound function at 128 MB may run eight times longer than at 512 MB, and since you are billed for memory multiplied by duration, the higher setting can be both faster and cheaper. Use AWS Lambda Power Tuning, which runs your function across a range of settings and plots cost against duration. Guessing low to save money is the most common and most expensive Lambda mistake.
Why is my Lambda function being throttled?

You have hit a concurrency limit. The account default is 1,000 concurrent executions across all functions in a region, shared between them, so one busy function can throttle others. If the function has reserved concurrency, it is capped at that number regardless of account headroom. Check the Throttles CloudWatch metric and aws lambda get-account-settings for the account limit. Setting reserved concurrency on high-volume functions protects everything else from being starved.
Does Lambda retry failed invocations?

It depends entirely on how it was invoked. Synchronous invocations, API Gateway, or a direct call, are not retried; the caller decides. Asynchronous invocations from S3, SNS or EventBridge are retried twice automatically before going to a dead-letter queue or failure destination. Stream sources such as Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams retry the batch until it succeeds or the data expires, blocking that shard meanwhile. SQS returns messages to the queue until maxReceiveCount is reached. Because duplicates are normal in all of these, functions must be idempotent.
Should I put my Lambda function in a VPC?

Only if it needs to reach private resources such as an RDS instance or an internal service. Attaching a function to a VPC removes its default internet access, so calls to public endpoints then require a NAT gateway or a VPC endpoint for the relevant AWS service. A frequent surprise. The cold-start penalty that used to make VPC Lambda painful is essentially gone thanks to shared network interfaces, so connectivity, not performance, is the deciding factor now.
When should I use ECS or EKS instead of Lambda?

When the workload runs longer than the 15-minute maximum, when throughput is high and sustained enough that always-on compute is cheaper than per-invocation billing, when the application needs persistent connections or significant local state, or when you need latency guarantees that cold starts cannot meet. Lambda is strongest for event-driven, spiky and intermittent work where paying nothing while idle is the dominant advantage. A steady workload running continuously is usually cheaper on Fargate.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Write, package and deploy Lambda functions: handler signatures, zip vs container image packaging, layers, versions and aliases, and testing locally.
A Lambda function is a handler, a runtime, and a set of configuration. This page is about writing and shipping one; the execution model, concurrency and cost behaviour are covered in AWS Lambda.

sections.title: The handler
paragraphs: Where you put initialisation matters more than anything else in this file. Code at module scope runs once when the execution environment is created and is reused across invocations; code inside the handler runs every time. Creating the boto3 client inside the handler adds its setup cost to every request.
The handler takes two arguments:
The handler is configured as file.function, index.handler for index.py, or src/app.lambda_handler for a nested file.

codeBlock.code:
import json
import os
import boto3

# Module scope. Runs ONCE per execution environment, reused across invocations
s3 = boto3.client("s3")
BUCKET = os.environ["BUCKET_NAME"]

def handler(event, context):
    # Runs on every invocation
    key = event["Records"][0]["s3"]["object"]["key"]
    obj = s3.get_object(Bucket=BUCKET, Key=key)

    return {
        "statusCode": 200,
        "body": json.dumps({"size": obj["ContentLength"]}),
    }

sections.title: Packaging
paragraphs: Three options, in increasing order of heft.
The default. Your code plus any dependencies not in the runtime:
Limits: 50 MB zipped for direct upload, 250 MB unzipped including layers. Upload via S3 for anything above 50 MB.

Dependencies with compiled components, anything wrapping C libraries, must be built for Amazon Linux on the target architecture, not for your laptop. Building on macOS and deploying produces an import error at runtime that looks unrelated. Build in a container matching the runtime, or use the AWS SAM build process which handles it.
A layer is a zip of shared dependencies, mounted at /opt and reusable across functions:
Up to five layers per function, counting toward the same 250 MB unzipped limit. They keep your function package small and avoid shipping identical dependencies with every function.
The trade-off is a second versioned artifact to manage, and layers are frequently over-used. For a single function they add ceremony with no benefit.
Up to 10 GB, which is the reason to use them:
Worth it for large machine learning dependencies, or when you want one build process for both Lambda and container workloads. Cold starts are comparable to zip for reasonably sized images.

codeBlock.code:
pip install -r requirements.txt -t package/
cd package && zip -r ../function.zip . && cd ..
zip -g function.zip index.py

aws lambda update-function-code \
  --function-name payments-processor \
  --zip-file fileb://function.zip

sections.title: Configuration
paragraphs: Three choices in there deserve attention.
--architectures arm64 selects Graviton, which is around 20% cheaper and usually faster. Use it unless a dependency requires x86.

--memory-size also sets CPU, which scales proportionally. More memory frequently makes a function both faster and cheaper, because you are billed for memory multiplied by duration. Measure with AWS Lambda Power Tuning rather than assuming the smallest is cheapest.
--timeout defaults to 3 seconds and maxes at 15 minutes. Set it deliberately: too high and a hung function burns money, too low and legitimate work is cut off.

Environment variables are fine for configuration. For secrets, they are visible in the console and in get-function-configuration, so prefer reading from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store at initialisation:

Module scope means this runs once per environment rather than per invocation. Better still, use the AWS Parameters and Secrets Extension, which caches locally so repeated reads never leave the execution environment.

codeBlock.code:
aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name payments-processor \
  --runtime python3.12 \
  --architectures arm64 \
  --handler index.handler \
  --role arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/payments-lambda-role \
  --zip-file fileb://function.zip \
  --memory-size 512 \
  --timeout 30 \
  --environment 'Variables={BUCKET_NAME=acme-artifacts,LOG_LEVEL=info}'

sections.title: Versions and aliases
paragraphs: By default you deploy to $LATEST, which is mutable, so an invocation during a deploy can hit either version.
Publish a version to get an immutable numbered snapshot, then point an alias at it:
Triggers reference the alias, so deploying is an alias move and rolling back is moving it back. Instant, with no code upload.
Aliases also support weighted routing for canary deploys:
Ten percent of traffic to version 43. Watch the metrics, then shift.

codeBlock.code:
VERSION=$(aws lambda publish-version --function-name payments-processor --query Version --output text)

aws lambda update-alias \
  --function-name payments-processor \
  --name prod \
  --function-version "$VERSION"

sections.title: Testing locally
paragraphs: For local iteration, AWS SAM runs the function in a container matching the runtime:
That --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out flag is needed on CLI v2 for a plain JSON payload, and its absence produces a confusing decoding error.

codeBlock.code:
# Invoke deployed
aws lambda invoke --function-name payments-processor \
  --payload '{"key":"test.txt"}' --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out out.json

# Tail the logs
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/payments-processor --follow

sections.title: Deploying properly
paragraphs: Update a function with the CLI once, to see how it works. After that use SAM, Terraform, CDK or the Serverless Framework: a Lambda in production needs its IAM role, triggers, environment, alias and log group managed together, and doing that by hand does not survive a second function.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A function creates its boto3 client inside the handler. What is the effect of moving it to module scope?
A function packaged on macOS fails in Lambda with an error importing a library that works locally. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Where should I initialise clients and connections in a Lambda function?

At module scope, outside the handler. That code runs once when the execution environment is created and is reused for every subsequent invocation on that environment, so SDK client construction, connection pools and configuration loading happen once rather than per request. Since most invocations reuse a warm environment, this is the highest-value optimisation available and takes seconds to apply. Only per-request logic belongs inside the handler.
Why does my Python dependency fail to import in Lambda?

Because it contains compiled components built for the wrong platform. Libraries wrapping native code ship binaries specific to an operating system and CPU architecture, so a package installed on macOS or Windows will not load on the Amazon Linux environment Lambda runs. Build the package inside a container matching the Lambda runtime, use sam build --use-container, or install with pip's platform and architecture options targeting manylinux and the architecture you configured.
What are the Lambda deployment package size limits?

50 MB for a zip uploaded directly, larger if you upload via S3, and 250 MB unzipped including any layers. Container images can be up to 10 GB, which is the usual reason to choose them. Machine learning dependencies in particular exceed the zip limits easily. Layers do not increase the total, since they count toward the same 250 MB unzipped budget; they simply let several functions share the same dependencies.
What are Lambda versions and aliases for?

A version is an immutable numbered snapshot of your code and configuration; an alias is a movable pointer to one. Without them you deploy to $LATEST, which is mutable, so an invocation during a deploy can hit either the old or new code. Publishing a version and pointing an alias at it makes deployment an alias move and rollback the same move in reverse. Instant, with no upload. Aliases also support weighted routing for canary releases.
Should I use Lambda layers?

For shared dependencies across several functions, yes. They keep each deployment package small and avoid shipping identical libraries repeatedly. For a single function they add a second versioned artifact to manage with little benefit, and they are frequently over-used for that reason. Note that layers count toward the same 250 MB unzipped limit as your function code, so they are an organisational convenience rather than a way to fit more in.
How do I test a Lambda function locally?

AWS SAM runs your function in a container matching the Lambda runtime: sam local invoke MyFunction --event events/test.json for a single invocation, or sam local start-api to emulate API Gateway. This catches packaging and dependency problems that only appear in the Lambda environment. For invoking a deployed function, use aws lambda invoke with --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out, which CLI v2 requires for a plain JSON payload and whose absence produces a confusing decoding error.

Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Compare ECS and EKS on cost, complexity, portability and ecosystem, see where Fargate and App Runner fit, and get a short decision rule for your team.

AWS gives you two container orchestrators. They solve the same problem and the choice between them is mostly about team and ecosystem rather than capability. Both will run your containers reliably at scale.
The honest summary: ECS is simpler and cheaper; EKS is portable and has a far larger ecosystem.

sections.title: Choose ECS when
paragraphs: ECS is frequently the right answer and frequently dismissed for the wrong reason, which is that Kubernetes is what people have heard of. A team of four running a dozen services does not need Kubernetes, and will spend real time on it.

sections.title: Choose EKS when
paragraphs: The ecosystem argument is the strongest one. Almost every infrastructure tool ships a Helm chart; far fewer ship an ECS task definition.

sections.title: Core concepts side by side
paragraphs: The two IAM roles are the thing people get wrong. The task execution role is used by the ECS agent to pull the image from ECR and write logs to CloudWatch. The task role is what your application code uses to call AWS. Putting your application's S3 permissions on the execution role does not work, and the symptom, image pulls and logging succeed while your code gets AccessDenied, is confusing until you know the split.

sections.title: Fargate: no servers either way
paragraphs: Both ECS and EKS can run on Fargate, which removes node management entirely. You specify CPU and memory per task or pod; AWS provisions the compute.

Fargate's constraints are real. No DaemonSets means most observability agents cannot run as designed, which catches teams out on EKS. You need a sidecar or a different collection approach. No privileged containers means no Docker-in-Docker builds.

The pricing crossover is roughly this: bursty, intermittent or low-volume workloads are cheaper on Fargate because you pay nothing between tasks. Steady 24/7 load is cheaper on reserved or Spot EC2 capacity.

sections.title: What EKS actually costs
paragraphs: The $0.10/hour control plane charge is per cluster, which shapes architecture. A cluster per team per environment adds up quickly. Six clusters is around $440/month before a single pod runs.
Add worker nodes, a NAT gateway, load balancers and cross-AZ transfer, and a modest production EKS setup typically lands around $300 to 500/month. ECS has no equivalent baseline.
That difference matters most at small scale. At large scale it disappears into the compute bill.

sections.title: What you actually operate
paragraphs: This is the part that decides how much time the choice costs you.
ECS: task definitions, services, capacity providers. Upgrades are AWS's problem. There is genuinely not much else.

EKS: everything above, plus Kubernetes version upgrades roughly annually before support expires, the CNI and its IP address arithmetic, an ingress controller, cluster autoscaling with Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler, RBAC and access entries, add-on lifecycle, and a steady stream of ecosystem components to keep current.
None of that is hard individually. Together it is a part-time job, and it needs an owner.

sections.title: The third option
paragraphs: App Runner deploys a container or a repository directly to a managed URL with automatic scaling and TLS. No cluster, no task definitions, no load balancer configuration.

For a straightforward HTTP service it is dramatically less work than either ECS or EKS, and it is worth ruling out deliberately before reaching for an orchestrator. The limits are real. Less control over networking, fewer configuration options, per-request pricing that suits variable traffic, but a great many web services fit inside them.

sections.title: A decision in one paragraph
paragraphs: If a single containerised web service is all you need, try App Runner. If you are AWS-only and want minimal operational load, use ECS with Fargate. If you need portability or the Kubernetes ecosystem and have someone to own a cluster, use EKS. Do not choose EKS because Kubernetes is on job adverts. Choose it because you need what it does.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An ECS task pulls its image and writes logs fine, but the application gets AccessDenied calling S3. The S3 permissions are on the task execution role. What is wrong?
A team moves an EKS workload to Fargate and their monitoring agent, deployed as a DaemonSet, stops collecting. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I use ECS or EKS?

Use ECS if you are AWS-only, want minimal operational overhead, and the team has no Kubernetes experience. It is simpler, has no control plane charge, and there is genuinely little to run. Use EKS if you need portability across clouds, want the Kubernetes ecosystem of Helm charts, operators and tooling, or already have Kubernetes expertise. Both run containers reliably at scale; the decision is about team and ecosystem rather than capability.
How much does EKS cost compared to ECS?

The EKS control plane is about $0.10 per hour per cluster, roughly $73 a month, before any compute. ECS has no control plane charge at all. Both then charge for the underlying compute, whether EC2 or Fargate, plus load balancers, NAT gateways and data transfer. The difference matters most for small deployments and for organisations running many clusters. Six EKS clusters cost around $440 a month in control plane fees alone. At large scale the gap disappears into the compute bill.
What is the difference between the ECS task role and task execution role?

The task execution role is assumed by the ECS agent to pull container images from ECR and write logs to CloudWatch. It is infrastructure-level. The task role is assumed by the code inside your container to call AWS APIs. If image pulls and logging work but your application gets AccessDenied, the permissions were added to the execution role and belong on the task role. This is the single most common ECS configuration mistake.
Should I use Fargate or EC2 for my containers?

Fargate when you want no node management and your workload is spiky, intermittent or low-volume, since you pay nothing between tasks. EC2 when load is steady around the clock, where reserved or Spot instances are meaningfully cheaper, or when you need something Fargate does not support. DaemonSets, privileged containers, GPU workloads, or very large instance sizes. Many teams run a mix, with Fargate for bursty jobs and EC2 for the steady baseline.
Can I migrate from ECS to EKS later?

Yes, but it is a rewrite of your deployment layer rather than a lift and shift. The containers themselves are unchanged, the same image runs on both, but task definitions become Kubernetes manifests, ECS services become Deployments and Services, and your CI/CD, service discovery, secrets injection and monitoring all need reworking. Plan it as a project. If portability is a genuine near-term requirement, starting on EKS is cheaper than migrating to it.
Is there a simpler option than either?

AWS App Runner deploys a container image or a source repository directly to a managed HTTPS endpoint with automatic scaling, no cluster, no task definitions and no load balancer to configure. For a single web service it is dramatically less work than either orchestrator. The trade-offs are less networking control, fewer configuration options and per-request pricing, but a great many straightforward web applications fit comfortably within them. It is worth ruling out deliberately before choosing an orchestrator.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand ECS task definitions and services: task role vs execution role, networking modes, health checks, deployments and fixing a task that will not start.
Two objects do most of the work in ECS. A task definition describes what to run; a service keeps a number of tasks running and handles deployments.

sections.title: Task definitions
paragraphs: A versioned, immutable blueprint. Registering a change creates a new revision. You never edit one in place:
The most common ECS mistake, and worth stating plainly:
If image pulls and logging work but your code gets AccessDenied, the permissions are on the execution role and belong on the task role.
Note that the secrets block is resolved by the execution role, not the task role, so the execution role needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and, if the secret is KMS-encrypted, kms:Decrypt.

On Fargate it is the only option, and on EC2 it is the one to choose. Each task gets its own elastic network interface and private IP, so tasks are addressable like instances and get their own security group.
That IP consumption is the constraint: a large ECS deployment can exhaust a subnet just as EKS can. Size subnets accordingly.
The alternatives, bridge and host, exist for EC2 launch type and involve port mapping on the host, which complicates running several copies of the same task on one instance.

Fargate accepts only specific CPU and memory combinations. 512 CPU units (half a vCPU) permits 1, 2, 3 or 4 GB of memory, and nothing else. An invalid pair is rejected at task definition registration with a message listing the valid values.
Set runtimePlatform.cpuArchitecture to ARM64 for Graviton, which is around 20% cheaper.

sections.title: Services
paragraphs: A service keeps N tasks running, replaces failures, registers targets with a load balancer, and manages rolling deployments:
Three settings there earn their place.

deploymentCircuitBreaker with rollback is the most valuable. Without it, a deployment of a broken image retries indefinitely while the service sits degraded. With it, ECS detects repeated task failures, stops, and reverts to the previous task definition automatically.
minimumHealthyPercent=100 with maximumPercent=200 means capacity never dips during a deploy. New tasks start before old ones stop, at the cost of briefly running double.

healthCheckGracePeriodSeconds stops the load balancer killing tasks that are still starting. Set it above your real start-up time, or a slow-booting application will be terminated and restarted in a loop that looks like a crash.
services-stable blocks until the deployment settles, which is what a CI pipeline should wait on rather than assuming success.

codeBlock.code:
aws ecs create-service \
  --cluster production \
  --service-name payments-api \
  --task-definition payments-api:42 \
  --desired-count 3 \
  --launch-type FARGATE \
  --network-configuration 'awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[subnet-0aaa,subnet-0bbb],securityGroups=[sg-0abc],assignPublicIp=DISABLED}' \
  --load-balancers 'targetGroupArn=arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...,containerName=api,containerPort=8080' \
  --health-check-grace-period-seconds 60 \
  --deployment-configuration 'deploymentCircuitBreaker={enable=true,rollback=true},maximumPercent=200,minimumHealthyPercent=100'

sections.title: Debugging a task that will not start
paragraphs: stoppedReason is the field to read first, and it is usually explicit:

That second one is a frequent Fargate problem: a task in a private subnet with no NAT gateway and no VPC endpoints cannot reach ECR or Secrets Manager, so it fails before your code runs at all. Interface endpoints for ecr.api, ecr.dkr, secretsmanager and logs, plus a gateway endpoint for S3, resolve it, and cost less than NAT.
ECS Exec needs enableExecuteCommand on the service and ssmmessages permissions on the task role. It is the ECS equivalent of kubectl exec and worth enabling before you need it.

codeBlock.code:
aws ecs describe-tasks --cluster production \
  --tasks $(aws ecs list-tasks --cluster production --desired-status STOPPED \
            --query 'taskArns[0]' --output text) \
  --query 'tasks[0].{Stopped:stoppedReason,Containers:containers[].{Name:name,Reason:reason,Exit:exitCode}}'

sections.title: Service discovery and scaling
paragraphs: Service Connect or Cloud Map give services stable DNS names so they can find each other without a load balancer per service.
Application Auto Scaling adjusts desiredCount on CloudWatch metrics, typically average CPU, or ALBRequestCountPerTarget, which tracks load far better than CPU for an I/O-bound service.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Fargate task in a private subnet fails with ResourceInitializationError before any application log appears. What is the usual cause?
A service is updated with a broken image. New tasks crash on start, and ECS keeps launching replacements for hours. What would have prevented this?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between an ECS task definition and a service?

A task definition is an immutable, versioned blueprint describing what to run: the image, CPU and memory, environment, IAM roles, logging and health checks. A service takes a task definition and keeps a specified number of copies running, replacing failures, registering them with a load balancer and managing rolling deployments. You can run a task once without a service, which suits batch jobs, but anything long-lived should be behind a service.
What is the difference between the ECS task role and task execution role?

The execution role is assumed by the ECS agent to pull the image from ECR, write logs to CloudWatch and resolve values in the secrets block. The task role is assumed by your application code for AWS API calls. If image pulls and logging succeed but your code gets AccessDenied, the permissions were added to the execution role and belong on the task role. Note that secrets injection specifically uses the execution role, which surprises people.
Why does my Fargate task fail with ResourceInitializationError?

It cannot reach the AWS services needed before your container starts, typically ECR for the image, Secrets Manager for secrets, or CloudWatch for logs. In a private subnet with no NAT gateway and no VPC endpoints there is no route to any of them. Add interface endpoints for ecr.api, ecr.dkr, secretsmanager and logs, plus a free gateway endpoint for S3 since image layers live there. That is usually cheaper than a NAT gateway as well as faster.
How do I get a shell inside a running ECS task?

aws ecs execute-command --cluster <c> --task <task-id> --container <name> --interactive --command "/bin/sh". It requires enableExecuteCommand on the service and ssmmessages permissions on the task role, both of which are easier to add before an incident than during one. It is the ECS equivalent of kubectl exec and works on Fargate as well as EC2.
How do I deploy a new version of my ECS service?

Register a new task definition revision with the updated image, then aws ecs update-service --task-definition <family>:<revision>. To redeploy the same revision, for instance after moving a mutable image tag, use --force-new-deployment. Always follow with aws ecs wait services-stable in CI so the pipeline fails on a bad deploy rather than reporting success while tasks crash. Enable the deployment circuit breaker with rollback so a broken image reverts automatically.
Why do my ECS tasks keep restarting?

Read stoppedReason from describe-tasks first. It usually names the cause directly. If it says the essential container exited, the application itself is failing and the CloudWatch logs will show why. If it reports failed ELB health checks, the target group check is not passing; the frequent cause is a health check grace period shorter than real start-up time, so the load balancer kills the task before it is ready. OutOfMemoryError means the container exceeded its memory allocation.

quickReference.command: aws ecs wait services-stable --cluster production --services payments-api

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Use CloudWatch metrics, logs, alarms and dashboards well. Covers missing EC2 metrics, log groups that never expire, alarm states and the bill.

sections.title: Amazon CloudWatch
paragraphs: CloudWatch is where AWS puts metrics, logs and alarms. Most of it works automatically, which is convenient and also why two specific defaults quietly cost teams money and visibility for years.
CloudWatch: Observability Pipeline
CloudTrail records API calls; CloudWatch monitors performance metrics and logs

sections.title: Metrics
paragraphs: A metric is identified by a namespace (AWS/EC2), a name (CPUUtilization) and dimensions (InstanceId=i-0abc123). AWS services publish theirs automatically at no charge.
This catches nearly everyone. EC2 publishes CPU, network and disk I/O by default, but not memory usage and not disk space used. The hypervisor cannot see inside the instance.
So the two numbers you most want during an incident are absent unless you install the CloudWatch agent:
Teams routinely discover this mid-incident, having assumed memory was being collected all along. Install the agent as part of your base image or launch template, not as a reaction.
The agent publishes these as custom metrics, which are billed per metric per month, so publish the handful you will actually alarm on rather than everything available.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abc123 \
  --start-time 2026-09-11T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-09-12T00:00:00Z \
  --period 300 --statistics Average Maximum

sections.title: Logs
paragraphs: Log groups hold streams; streams hold events. Lambda, ECS and many services write here automatically.

A new log group's retention is "Never expire." Logs accumulate forever and are billed for storage forever. On a busy account this becomes one of the larger CloudWatch line items, entirely by default and entirely invisibly.
Set retention on every log group. Thirty days suits most application logs; ninety or more for audit trails. For long-term retention, export to S3, where storage is far cheaper than CloudWatch Logs.
A query language over your logs, and far more capable than scrolling a stream:
That second query on a Lambda log group tells you whether the function is near its memory limit and how duration is trending. The two things you need to size it correctly.
Insights bills per gigabyte scanned, so narrow the time range before running broad queries across large groups.
Turn a log pattern into a metric you can alarm on. Useful when an application emits an error line but no metric:

codeBlock.code:
# Find the offenders
aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --query 'logGroups[?!retentionInDays].[logGroupName,storedBytes]' --output table

# Fix one
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/lambda/my-fn --retention-in-days 30

sections.title: Alarms
paragraphs: An alarm watches one metric and moves between three states:
Three settings there deserve attention:

--treat-missing-data decides what happens when a metric stops reporting. The default, missing, leaves the alarm in its current state, so an alarm on a metric that vanishes because the service died may sit quietly in OK. For a metric that should always have data, breaching is safer; for one that is naturally sparse, notBreaching prevents false alarms.
--datapoints-to-alarm with --evaluation-periods gives an "M out of N" rule, which tolerates a single noisy data point without missing a real problem.
INSUFFICIENT_DATA is not a failure. It commonly means the resource is idle and the metric is simply not being emitted.
Composite alarms combine several alarms with boolean logic, which is the right way to stop one incident paging five times:

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name payments-api-5xx \
  --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/payments/abc123 \
  --statistic Sum --period 60 \
  --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 \
  --threshold 10 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --treat-missing-data notBreaching \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:eu-west-1:111122223333:oncall

sections.title: Where the bill comes from
paragraphs: CloudWatch costs surprise people because each component is individually cheap:

The dimension point is the one that produces shocking bills. A custom metric with a user_id dimension creates one billable metric per user. Dimensions should be low-cardinality: environment, service, region, never an identifier.
Practical controls: set retention on every log group, drop debug logging in production, publish only metrics you alarm on, and export long-term logs to S3.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An EC2 instance is running out of memory, but no memory metric appears in CloudWatch. Why?
A team publishes a custom metric for request latency with dimensions for service, environment and user_id. The CloudWatch bill is far higher than expected. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why is there no memory metric for my EC2 instance?

Because EC2 only publishes what the hypervisor can observe from outside the guest. CPU, network, and disk I/O. Memory usage and filesystem utilisation live inside the operating system and require the CloudWatch agent to be installed and configured on the instance. It publishes them as custom metrics, which carry a per-metric monthly charge, so configure it to send the few you will actually alarm on. Building the agent into your AMI or launch template avoids discovering the gap during an incident.
How do I stop CloudWatch Logs costing so much?

Set a retention policy on every log group. New groups default to "Never expire", so logs accumulate and are billed indefinitely. This is usually the single largest avoidable CloudWatch cost. Find them with aws logs describe-log-groups --query 'logGroups[?!retentionInDays].logGroupName' and set something sensible, typically thirty days for application logs. Also reduce ingestion by disabling debug logging in production, since ingestion is charged per gigabyte, and export anything needing long retention to S3 where storage is far cheaper.
What does INSUFFICIENT_DATA mean on an alarm?

The alarm does not have enough data points in the evaluation window to decide. Most often this means the resource is idle and simply is not emitting the metric. A load balancer with no requests, or a queue with no messages. It is not inherently a problem. If it matters that a metric should always be present, set --treat-missing-data breaching so a metric that stops reporting triggers the alarm rather than leaving it silent, which is the safer configuration for anything that should always be alive.
How do I search across CloudWatch Logs?

Use Logs Insights, which provides a purpose-built query language over one or more log groups. Filtering with filter, aggregating with stats, and bucketing over time with bin(). It is far more effective than scrolling individual streams, and it is the practical way to answer questions like how latency is trending or how close a Lambda is to its memory limit. Queries are billed per gigabyte scanned, so narrow the time range before running something broad across a large group.
What is the difference between a metric filter and Logs Insights?

A metric filter continuously matches a pattern in incoming log events and publishes a CloudWatch metric from the matches, so you can alarm on something that only appears in logs. Logs Insights is an ad-hoc query tool for investigating logs after the fact. Use a metric filter when you need alerting on a log pattern, and Insights when you are exploring. The two complement each other: Insights to discover a pattern worth watching, a metric filter to alarm on it.
Should I use CloudWatch or Prometheus and Grafana?

CloudWatch is the path of least resistance on AWS, with automatic metrics from every service, no infrastructure to run, and native integration with alarms and EventBridge. Prometheus and Grafana offer a far richer query language, cheaper high-cardinality metrics, and portability across clouds, at the cost of running and scaling them yourself. Many teams use both. CloudWatch for AWS service metrics and alarms, Prometheus for application metrics where cardinality would make CloudWatch custom metrics prohibitively expensive.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand CloudWatch metrics: namespaces, dimensions, statistics, the EC2 metrics AWS does not publish (memory, disk), custom metric costs and metric math.
A metric is a time-ordered set of data points. Every AWS service publishes its own automatically, and you can publish your own, which is where both the value and the surprising bills come from.

sections.title: What identifies a metric
paragraphs: Three things together:

The crucial detail: a metric is defined by its name plus its complete set of dimension values. CPUUtilization with InstanceId=i-001 and CPUUtilization with InstanceId=i-002 are two separate metrics, billed separately if they are custom.
That is the whole cardinality story, and the reason custom metric bills get out of hand.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch list-metrics --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abc123

sections.title: Statistics
paragraphs: CloudWatch stores aggregates, not raw events. When you query, you choose how the data points within each period are combined:

Use percentiles for latency, not averages. An average response time of 200ms can hide a p99 of 8 seconds, which is the experience of your slowest and often most valuable requests. Averages conceal exactly the behaviour you need to see.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name TargetResponseTime \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/payments/abc123 \
  --start-time 2026-09-14T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-09-15T00:00:00Z \
  --period 300 --extended-statistics p50 p99

sections.title: The EC2 metrics that do not exist
paragraphs: EC2 publishes CPU, network and disk I/O automatically. It does not publish memory usage or disk space used, because the hypervisor cannot see inside the guest operating system.
So the two numbers most useful during an incident are absent unless you install the CloudWatch agent:
Teams routinely discover this mid-incident, having assumed memory was being collected all along. Put the agent in your base AMI or launch template.
Note that agent metrics are custom metrics and are billed per metric per month, so configure it to publish the few you will actually alarm on rather than everything it can collect.
The same gap affects Compute Optimizer, whose right-sizing recommendations are CPU-weighted unless the agent is supplying memory data.

codeBlock.code:
sudo dnf install -y amazon-cloudwatch-agent
sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \
  -a fetch-config -m ec2 -c ssm:AmazonCloudWatch-linux -s

sections.title: Resolution and retention
paragraphs: Standard resolution is one minute. High resolution is one second, costs considerably more, and is rarely worth it outside genuinely latency-critical systems.
Retention is automatic and lossy over time:

This matters for capacity planning. You cannot go back a year and look at minute-level detail, because it no longer exists. If you need long-term high-granularity history, export to S3 or use Prometheus with its own retention.

sections.title: Custom metrics, and the cardinality trap
paragraphs: Custom metrics are charged per metric per month, where a metric is one unique combination of name and dimension values.
Now add user_id as a dimension and you have one metric per user. A hundred thousand users is a hundred thousand billable metrics, and a bill that arrives as a genuine shock.

Dimensions must be low-cardinality. Environment, service, region, instance type. Values from a small fixed set. Anything that is an identifier belongs in logs, where you can query it without a per-value charge.
A better pattern for application metrics. Write a specially-structured JSON log line and CloudWatch extracts metrics from it automatically:

Note what happens here: Service is declared as a dimension so it becomes a metric, while requestId and userId stay as log fields. Queryable in Logs Insights but not multiplying your metric count. That separation is exactly what you want, and EMF makes it natural rather than something you have to remember.
It also avoids a synchronous PutMetricData API call on the request path.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-data \
  --namespace Acme/Payments \
  --metric-name TransactionLatency \
  --dimensions Environment=production,Service=payments \
  --value 142 --unit Milliseconds

sections.title: Metric math
paragraphs: Compute new series from existing ones without publishing anything:

An error rate is far more useful to alarm on than an error count, since ten errors means something different at ten requests per second than at ten thousand. Metric math produces it with no extra instrumentation.
ANOMALY_DETECTION_BAND() builds an expected range from historical patterns, which handles workloads with daily or weekly cycles that a static threshold cannot.

codeBlock.code:
[
  { "Id": "errors", "MetricStat": { "Metric": { "Namespace": "AWS/ApplicationELB",
      "MetricName": "HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count", "Dimensions": [{"Name":"LoadBalancer","Value":"app/payments/abc"}]},
      "Period": 300, "Stat": "Sum" }, "ReturnData": false },
  { "Id": "requests", "MetricStat": { "Metric": { "Namespace": "AWS/ApplicationELB",
      "MetricName": "RequestCount", "Dimensions": [{"Name":"LoadBalancer","Value":"app/payments/abc"}]},
      "Period": 300, "Stat": "Sum" }, "ReturnData": false },
  { "Id": "error_rate", "Expression": "errors / requests * 100", "Label": "Error rate %" }
]

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team adds a request_id dimension to a custom latency metric. The CloudWatch bill increases dramatically. Why?
A service shows an average response time of 180ms, but users report frequent slowness. What should you look at?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why is there no memory metric for my EC2 instance?

Because EC2 only publishes what the hypervisor can see from outside the guest. CPU, network and disk I/O. Memory usage and filesystem utilisation are internal to the operating system and require the CloudWatch agent to be installed and configured on the instance. The agent publishes them as custom metrics, which carry a per-metric monthly charge, so configure it for the few you will actually alarm on. Installing it in your base AMI avoids discovering the gap during an incident.
How are CloudWatch custom metrics priced?

Per metric per month, where a metric is one unique combination of metric name and dimension values. Three services in two environments publishing one metric name is six metrics. The trap is high-cardinality dimensions: adding a user or request ID creates one metric per user or request, which turns a handful of metrics into hundreds of thousands. Keep dimensions to small fixed sets and put identifiers in logs instead.
Should I use average or percentile statistics?

Percentiles for anything latency-related, averages for throughput and utilisation. An average response time is dominated by fast requests and routinely hides a p99 that is an order of magnitude worse, which is the experience of your slowest users. CloudWatch supports p50, p90, p99 and arbitrary percentiles through --extended-statistics, and alarms can be set on them directly.
How long does CloudWatch keep metric data?

Fifteen months, but with decreasing granularity: one-minute data points for 15 days, five-minute for 63 days, one-hour for 455 days, then deletion. The aggregation is automatic and irreversible, so you cannot go back six months and inspect minute-level detail. It no longer exists. For long-term high-resolution history, export to S3 or use a system such as Prometheus with retention you control.
What is the Embedded Metric Format and why use it?

EMF is a structured JSON log format that CloudWatch parses to extract metrics automatically. You write one log line containing both your metric values and any contextual fields, declaring which fields are dimensions. The fields you do not declare remain queryable in Logs Insights without becoming billable metrics, which cleanly separates low-cardinality dimensions from high-cardinality context. It also avoids a synchronous PutMetricData call on the request path.
What is metric math and when do I need it?

Metric math computes new time series from existing metrics without publishing anything new. Most usefully turning counts into rates. Alarming on "more than 10 errors" means something different at ten requests per second than at ten thousand, whereas an error rate expressed as a percentage is meaningful at any volume. It also provides ANOMALY_DETECTION_BAND(), which learns daily and weekly patterns and flags deviations that a static threshold would either miss or fire on constantly.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
