aws-codepipeline.subtitle: Build a CI/CD pipeline with AWS CodePipeline: stages, source providers, artifacts, manual approvals and deploy actions, plus CodePipeline vs GitHub Actions.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS CodePipeline must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Build a CI/CD pipeline with AWS CodePipeline: stages, source providers, artifacts, manual approvals and deploy actions, plus CodePipeline vs GitHub Actions.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Build a CI/CD pipeline with AWS CodePipeline: stages, source providers, artifacts, manual approvals and deploy actions, plus CodePipeline vs GitHub Actions.
CodePipeline orchestrates a release process as a sequence of stages. It does not build or deploy anything itself. It coordinates other services that do, passing artifacts between them.
Understanding that division is what makes the rest of it make sense.

sections.title: Structure
paragraphs: Stages run in order. Actions within a stage run in parallel unless you give them runOrder values, which sequence them.
Every stage must have at least one action, and the first must be a source action.

codeBlock.code:
Source ──► Build ──► Deploy-Staging ──► Approve ──► Deploy-Prod
(GitHub)   (CodeBuild)  (ECS)          (manual)     (ECS)

sections.title: Source
paragraphs: For GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, use a CodeStar connection rather than an OAuth token or a webhook you manage:

The connection is created in PENDING and must be authorised in the console. A one-time browser step that cannot be scripted. Until then, pipelines using it fail with a permissions error that does not mention the connection state.
Source actions can also be S3, ECR, or CodeCommit, though CodeCommit is closed to new customers, so new pipelines should assume an external Git provider.

codeBlock.code:
aws codeconnections create-connection \
  --provider-type GitHub \
  --connection-name acme-github

sections.title: Artifacts
paragraphs: Every artifact passes through an S3 bucket that CodePipeline manages. Actions declare input and output artifacts by name, and CodePipeline handles the upload and download.
The bucket is a security boundary. Build output lives there, sometimes including configuration. Encrypt it, block public access, and restrict who can read it.
Artifacts accumulate. Every pipeline execution stores its outputs, and nothing removes them. Add a lifecycle rule or the bucket grows forever:

sections.title: Manual approval
paragraphs: The simplest and most valuable gate:
Approval actions time out after 7 days and fail the pipeline, which surprises teams who leave one pending over a holiday.
Control who can approve with the codepipeline:PutApprovalResult permission scoped to that pipeline's ARN. Otherwise anyone with pipeline access can approve their own change.

sections.title: Deployment actions
paragraphs: The ECS rolling provider is the simplest: point it at a cluster and service with an imagedefinitions.json artifact from the build, and it updates the service.

CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS is more work and genuinely better for anything user-facing. It stands up a replacement task set alongside the existing one, shifts traffic between two target groups gradually, and can roll back automatically on a CloudWatch alarm. A bad deploy becomes a reverted deploy rather than an incident.

sections.title: Variables between stages
paragraphs: Actions can emit namespaced variables that later stages consume:
Downstream: #{BuildVars.IMAGE_TAG}. CodeBuild exports these via exported-variables in its buildspec, which is how a generated image tag reaches the deploy stage without being written to a file.

sections.title: Should you use it?
paragraphs: Worth being direct, because CodePipeline is frequently chosen by default on AWS and is not always the right answer.

If your code is on GitHub or GitLab, their native CI is usually the better choice. The configuration lives beside the code, the ecosystem is far larger, and OIDC gives keyless AWS access that removes CodePipeline's main historical advantage.

CodePipeline makes sense when you are deeply AWS-native, need approval workflows and deployment orchestration tied into IAM, are deploying with CodeDeploy's blue/green capabilities, or have compliance requirements that keep the pipeline inside your AWS account boundary.
A common and sensible hybrid: build and test in GitHub Actions, then use CodeDeploy for the deployment itself.

sections.title: Debugging
paragraphs: That second row catches people repeatedly: CodePipeline and CodeBuild have separate service roles, and a permissions error inside a build is almost always the CodeBuild role rather than the pipeline's.

codeBlock.code:
aws codepipeline get-pipeline-state --name payments-pipeline \
  --query 'stageStates[].{Stage:stageName,Status:latestExecution.status,Error:actionStates[?latestExecution.errorDetails].latestExecution.errorDetails.message}'

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A new pipeline fails at the source stage with a permissions error. The CodeStar connection exists and the IAM role looks correct. What should you check?
A build step fails with AccessDenied reading an S3 bucket. The CodePipeline service role has full S3 access. Why does it still fail?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between CodePipeline, CodeBuild and CodeDeploy?

CodePipeline orchestrates. It defines the stages and passes artifacts between them, but performs no build or deployment itself. CodeBuild runs build and test commands in a managed container. CodeDeploy handles the deployment mechanics for EC2, ECS and Lambda, including blue/green traffic shifting and automatic rollback. A typical pipeline uses all three: CodePipeline coordinating, CodeBuild producing the artifact, and CodeDeploy releasing it.
Should I use CodePipeline or GitHub Actions?

If your code is on GitHub or GitLab, their native CI is usually the better choice. The configuration lives beside the code, the community ecosystem is vastly larger, and OIDC federation gives keyless access to AWS, which removes the integration advantage CodePipeline used to have. CodePipeline still makes sense for deeply AWS-native teams, for CodeDeploy's blue/green capabilities, and where compliance requires the pipeline to stay inside the AWS account boundary. A common hybrid is building in GitHub Actions and deploying with CodeDeploy.
Why does my CodeStar connection not work?

It is almost certainly still in PENDING status. Creating a connection via the API or infrastructure-as-code only creates a placeholder. Completing it requires a one-time browser authorisation with the Git provider that cannot be scripted. Until then, pipelines using it fail with a permissions error that gives no hint about the connection state. Check with aws codeconnections list-connections and finish the handshake in the console.
How do I add a manual approval step?

Add an action with category Approval and provider Manual in its own stage before production. It can send an SNS notification, include custom text for the reviewer, and link to a staging URL for verification. Two details matter: approval actions expire after seven days and fail the pipeline, and you should scope the codepipeline:PutApprovalResult permission to specific pipelines. Otherwise anyone with access can approve their own changes, which defeats the gate.
Where do CodePipeline artifacts go?

Into an S3 bucket CodePipeline creates and manages, with each execution storing its output artifacts there. Two things follow. The bucket is a security boundary, since build output may contain configuration. Encrypt it, block public access, and restrict who can read it. And nothing cleans it up, so add a lifecycle rule expiring objects after a few weeks or it grows indefinitely and becomes a quiet line on your bill.
Why does my build fail with AccessDenied when the pipeline role has permissions?

Because CodeBuild has its own service role, and that is the identity your build commands run as. The CodePipeline role only orchestrates the pipeline and moves artifacts; it is not used inside a build at all. Permissions your buildspec needs, pulling from ECR, reading a parameter, deploying with Terraform, belong on the CodeBuild project's role. This separation accounts for a large share of the permission problems people hit with CodePipeline.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-codebuild.title: AWS CodeBuild
aws-codebuild.subtitle: Write a CodeBuild buildspec.yml that works: phases and failure behavior, caching, Docker image builds, VPC access, exported variables and build diagnosis.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS CodeBuild must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Write a CodeBuild buildspec.yml that works: phases and failure behavior, caching, Docker image builds, VPC access, exported variables and build diagnosis.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Write a CodeBuild buildspec.yml that works: phases and failure behavior, caching, Docker image builds, VPC access, exported variables and build diagnosis.
CodeBuild runs commands in a managed container and charges by the minute. There are no build servers to patch and no capacity to plan. You define the environment and the commands, and it runs them.

sections.title: The buildspec
paragraphs: A buildspec.yml in your repository root defines everything:
Several things in there are worth calling out.

parameter-store and secrets-manager fetch values at build time, so nothing sensitive sits in the buildspec or in project environment variables. The CodeBuild service role needs permission to read them, and kms:Decrypt if they are encrypted with a customer-managed key.
exported-variables makes a value available to later CodePipeline stages. This is how a generated image tag reaches the deploy stage without writing it to a file.
reports parses JUnit XML into a test report visible in the console, showing which tests failed rather than requiring you to read the log.
post_build runs even when build fails. Guard anything that should only happen on success with $CODEBUILD_BUILD_SUCCEEDING, or you will push an image from a failed build.

codeBlock.code:
version: 0.2

env:
  variables:
    NODE_ENV: production
  parameter-store:
    NPM_TOKEN: /build/npm-token
  secrets-manager:
    DB_PASSWORD: prod/payments/db:password
  exported-variables:
    - IMAGE_TAG

phases:
  install:
    runtime-versions:
      nodejs: 22
    commands:
      - npm ci

  pre_build:
    commands:
      - export IMAGE_TAG=${CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION:0:7}
      - aws ecr get-login-password --region $AWS_REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $ECR_REGISTRY

  build:
    commands:
      - npm run lint
      - npm test -- --ci
      - docker build -t $ECR_REGISTRY/payments-api:$IMAGE_TAG .

  post_build:
    commands:
      - docker push $ECR_REGISTRY/payments-api:$IMAGE_TAG
      - printf '[{"name":"api","imageUri":"%s"}]' "$ECR_REGISTRY/payments-api:$IMAGE_TAG" > imagedefinitions.json

reports:
  unit-tests:
    files: ['junit.xml']
    file-format: JUNITXML

artifacts:
  files:
    - imagedefinitions.json

cache:
  paths:
    - '/root/.npm/**/*'

sections.title: Phases and failure behaviour
paragraphs: That last row is the one that catches people. A failing test does not prevent post_build from executing:

codeBlock.code:
post_build:
    commands:
      - |
        if [ "$CODEBUILD_BUILD_SUCCEEDING" = "1" ]; then
          docker push $ECR_REGISTRY/payments-api:$IMAGE_TAG
        else
          echo "Build failed, not pushing"
        fi

sections.title: Building Docker images
paragraphs: A CodeBuild container has no Docker daemon by default. docker build fails with "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon" until you enable privileged mode:

Privileged mode is required and is a genuine trade-off. A privileged container can reach the host kernel. CodeBuild environments are ephemeral and single-tenant, which makes this far less dangerous than privileged mode on a shared runner, but it is still worth being deliberate about which projects have it.
Docker Hub rate limits will bite a busy pipeline. Either authenticate to Docker Hub with credentials from Secrets Manager, or mirror base images into ECR and pull from there.

codeBlock.code:
aws codebuild update-project \
  --name payments-build \
  --environment 'type=LINUX_CONTAINER,image=aws/codebuild/standard:7.0,computeType=BUILD_GENERAL1_MEDIUM,privilegedMode=true'

sections.title: Caching
paragraphs: Builds start from a clean container every time, so dependency installation is repeated on every run unless you cache.
Local caching is fastest but only helps when the same build host is reused:
S3 caching persists across hosts, at the cost of upload and download time:

Cache the package manager's download directory rather than the installed tree, /root/.npm rather than node_modules. Restoring a download cache and running npm ci is more reliable than restoring a partially-populated dependency directory across different base images.
Measure it. A large cache over a slow link can cost more than it saves.

codeBlock.code: --cache 'type=LOCAL,modes=[LOCAL_DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE,LOCAL_SOURCE_CACHE,LOCAL_CUSTOM_CACHE]'

sections.title: VPC access
paragraphs: By default CodeBuild runs outside your VPC, with internet access and no route to private resources. To reach an RDS instance or an internal service, configure VPC access:

A build in a VPC has no internet access by default, so it needs a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints. Otherwise it cannot pull dependencies, reach ECR, or write logs, and it fails in ways that look unrelated to the network change. This is the same trap as VPC-attached Lambda.
Use private subnets; a public subnet does not give a CodeBuild ENI internet access.

codeBlock.code:
aws codebuild update-project --name payments-build \
  --vpc-config 'vpcId=vpc-0abc123,subnets=[subnet-private-a,subnet-private-b],securityGroupIds=[sg-build]'

sections.title: Compute and cost
paragraphs: Billing is per build minute at a rate that scales with compute type. Counterintuitively, a larger instance is often cheaper overall, because a build that takes half as long on twice the compute costs about the same and returns feedback sooner.
ARM compute types are cheaper still where your build supports them.
Build timeout defaults to 60 minutes and caps at 8 hours. Set it to something realistic. A hung build otherwise burns an hour of billing before failing.

sections.title: Diagnosing failures
paragraphs: Build logs go to CloudWatch:
For anything you cannot reproduce from logs, break the session into an interactive shell:
With session debugging enabled on the project, the build pauses and you can connect via SSM to inspect the environment. It is considerably faster than adding echo statements and re-running.

codeBlock.code: aws logs tail /aws/codebuild/payments-build --follow

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Tests fail in the build phase, yet the Docker image is still pushed to ECR by post_build. Why?
A working build starts failing to install npm packages immediately after VPC access was configured on the project. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a buildspec file and where does it go?

buildspec.yml in the root of your repository defines the build: environment variables, runtime versions, and the commands to run in each phase. Keeping it in the repository means the build definition is versioned and reviewed alongside the code it builds. You can also define it inline in the project or point at a different path, but the repository file is the default and the better practice.
Why does docker build fail in CodeBuild?

Because a CodeBuild container has no Docker daemon unless you enable privilegedMode on the project's environment. Without it, docker build reports "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon". Privileged mode is required for Docker-in-Docker builds and is a real trade-off, though less risky here than on shared runners since CodeBuild environments are ephemeral and single-tenant. Enable it only on projects that genuinely build images.
Why does my build run even though tests failed?

Because post_build executes regardless of whether earlier phases succeeded, that is deliberate, so it can publish logs and notifications after a failure. Anything that should only happen on success needs to check the $CODEBUILD_BUILD_SUCCEEDING environment variable, which is 1 on success and 0 on failure. Forgetting this guard is how an image from a failed build ends up pushed to a registry.
How do I pass secrets into a CodeBuild build?

Use the parameter-store or secrets-manager blocks in the buildspec's env section, which fetch values at build time and expose them as environment variables. Nothing sensitive then appears in the buildspec, the project configuration or your repository. The CodeBuild service role needs permission to read them, plus kms:Decrypt if they are encrypted with a customer-managed key, and that is the role to check when access is denied, not the CodePipeline role.
Why did my build lose internet access after enabling VPC configuration?

Because outside a VPC, CodeBuild runs on AWS-managed networking with internet access included; attaching it to your VPC puts it behind your routing rules. A private subnet without a NAT gateway has no route to public package registries, and without VPC endpoints it cannot reach ECR, Secrets Manager or CloudWatch Logs either. Add a NAT gateway, or add interface endpoints for the AWS services and NAT for anything public. Use private subnets. A public subnet does not give the build ENI internet access.
How do I make CodeBuild faster?

Cache dependencies, using the package manager's download directory rather than the installed tree. Consider a larger compute type, which is frequently cheaper overall because the build finishes in less than half the time at roughly twice the rate. Use ARM compute where your build supports it. Mirror frequently-pulled base images into ECR to avoid Docker Hub rate limits and pull latency. And set a realistic build timeout, since the 60-minute default lets a hung build bill for an hour before failing.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-cost-optimization.subtitle: Cut your AWS bill in a sensible order: find where the money goes, use Savings Plans, Spot and Graviton, and fix hidden data transfer and NAT gateway charges.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Cost Optimization must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Cut your AWS bill in a sensible order: find where the money goes, use Savings Plans, Spot and Graviton, and fix hidden data transfer and NAT gateway charges.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Cut your AWS bill in a sensible order: find where the money goes, use Savings Plans, Spot and Graviton, and fix hidden data transfer and NAT gateway charges.

Most AWS overspending is not exotic. It is idle resources nobody turned off, on-demand pricing for workloads that never change, oversized instances chosen by guesswork, and data transfer charges nobody knew existed.
The order below is roughly by payoff per hour of effort.

sections.title: First, find out where the money goes
paragraphs: Optimising before measuring wastes effort on the wrong things.

Cost Explorer, grouped by service, then by usage type, answers most of it in ten minutes. Group by tag if your tagging is good enough, and if it is not, that is the first thing to fix, because untagged spend cannot be attributed to anyone who might reduce it.

Enable default_tags in Terraform or provider-level tagging so everything created carries an owner, environment and project. Retrofitting tags across an existing estate is tedious; doing it from the start costs nothing.
Set a budget with an alert before anything else. A billing surprise caught on day two is an annoyance; caught on day thirty it is a conversation with finance.

codeBlock.code:
aws ce get-cost-and-usage \
  --time-period Start=2026-08-01,End=2026-09-01 \
  --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE \
  --query 'ResultsByTime[0].Groups[?Metrics.UnblendedCost.Amount>`100`].[Keys[0],Metrics.UnblendedCost.Amount]' \
  --output table

sections.title: The big levers
paragraphs: For any workload running continuously, on-demand pricing is the most expensive option available.

Compute Savings Plans are the pragmatic default. The extra few percent from the more rigid options is rarely worth losing the freedom to change instance family, which you will, when a newer generation arrives.
Commit to your baseline, not your peak. Cover the load that is always there and let bursts run on-demand or Spot. Over-committing is the one way a Savings Plan loses money.
Up to 90% off, and the largest single saving most teams leave untouched.

Spot capacity can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice, which rules out stateful singletons and rules in a great deal else: CI runners, batch processing, data pipelines, stateless web tiers behind a load balancer, and Kubernetes worker nodes.

The practical pattern is a mixed-instances policy. A base of on-demand capacity for reliability with Spot on top, diversified across several instance types so reclamation of one type does not take everything. On EKS, Karpenter handles this well.

AWS's ARM processors are around 20% cheaper for equivalent performance, and often faster. If your workload is a container, an interpreted language, or anything with an ARM build, the migration is frequently a base image change and a rebuild.

It applies well beyond EC2. RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch and Lambda all offer Graviton options. Switching an RDS instance class to db.m6g is a maintenance-window change with an immediate permanent saving.
An m7i typically costs less than an m5 and performs better. Upgrading generation is usually a restart, and it is close to free money.

sections.title: The charges people do not expect
paragraphs: This is where audits find surprises.
Data transfer out to the internet is often the largest single line on a mature bill. Serving through CloudFront is cheaper at volume and faster.

Cross-AZ traffic is charged in both directions. A chatty microservice architecture spread across three Availability Zones can spend meaningfully on traffic that never leaves the region. Topology-aware routing helps.

NAT gateway data processing charges per gigabyte, including for traffic to AWS services that never touches the internet. A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and DynamoDB is free and removes that entirely, including ECR image pulls, since layers live in S3. This is a one-command change with an immediate effect.
CloudWatch Logs default to "Never expire." Logs accumulate and are billed forever. Setting retention on every log group is frequently the single largest avoidable line item.
Unattached EBS volumes and old snapshots keep billing after their instances are gone.
Idle load balancers cost an hourly charge whether or not anything is behind them.
Elastic IPs not attached to a running instance are charged.
S3 incomplete multipart uploads are billed as storage and do not appear in a normal listing.

codeBlock.code:
aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --query 'logGroups[?!retentionInDays].[logGroupName,storedBytes]' --output table

sections.title: Turn things off
paragraphs: The least sophisticated lever and often the largest in percentage terms.

Non-production environments typically run 168 hours a week and are used for about 45. Stopping development instances, RDS databases and scaling Auto Scaling groups to zero outside working hours saves roughly 70% on those resources. AWS Instance Scheduler automates it.
Note RDS restarts a stopped instance automatically after seven days, so a scheduler rather than a manual stop is the reliable approach.

sections.title: Storage tiering, carefully
paragraphs: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically for a small monitoring fee, with no retrieval charges and no minimum duration penalties. It is the safe default when access patterns are unknown.

Manual lifecycle transitions to Standard-IA or Glacier are cheaper still, but carry minimum duration charges: 30 days for IA, 90 for most Glacier tiers, 180 for Deep Archive. Transitioning data that gets deleted after twenty days costs more than leaving it in Standard. Match the policy to the real lifecycle.

sections.title: Tooling worth using
paragraphs: Compute Optimizer is the one to run first after Cost Explorer. It uses actual CloudWatch metrics rather than guesswork, and oversizing is close to universal.

sections.title: A sensible order of work
paragraphs: Steps 1 to 5 are quick and need no commitment. Steps 8 and 9 are the largest but want accurate measurement first, which is why they come last.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team finds CloudWatch Logs is one of their largest AWS charges, though they never configured log storage. What is the most likely cause?
A workload runs 10 instances constantly and bursts to 25 during business hours. How much should a Compute Savings Plan cover?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the fastest way to reduce an AWS bill?

Open Cost Explorer grouped by service first. Optimising before measuring wastes effort. Then the quick wins that need no commitment: set retention on CloudWatch log groups, which default to never expiring; add free S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints to remove NAT data processing charges; delete unattached EBS volumes, old snapshots, idle load balancers and unassociated Elastic IPs; and schedule non-production environments to shut down outside working hours, which saves around 70% on those resources.
What is the difference between Savings Plans and Reserved Instances?

Both discount steady usage in exchange for a one or three year commitment. Compute Savings Plans commit to an hourly dollar spend and apply across any instance family, size and region, and also cover Fargate and Lambda, so they keep applying as your architecture changes. Reserved Instances are tied to specific attributes and offer a slightly deeper discount, with the option to sell unused capacity on the marketplace. For most teams the flexibility of a Compute Savings Plan is worth the few percent difference.
Should I use Spot instances in production?

Yes, for anything fault-tolerant. Spot offers up to 90% off and is well suited to CI runners, batch jobs, data processing, stateless web tiers behind a load balancer, and Kubernetes worker nodes. Capacity can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice, so it is unsuitable for stateful singletons or anything that cannot be interrupted. Use a mixed-instances policy with an on-demand base and Spot diversified across several instance types, so reclamation of one type does not remove all your capacity.
Why is my AWS data transfer bill so high?

Three usual causes. Data transfer out to the internet is charged per gigabyte and is often the largest line. Serving through CloudFront is cheaper at volume. Cross-Availability-Zone traffic is charged in both directions, so a chatty architecture spread across three zones spends meaningfully on traffic that never leaves the region. And NAT gateway data processing charges per gigabyte even for traffic to AWS services, which free gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB eliminate.
How much can Graviton actually save?

Around 20% for equivalent performance, and frequently better performance as well. It applies across EC2, RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch and Lambda, so the opportunity is broader than people assume. For containerised workloads and interpreted languages the migration is often just a base image change and a rebuild, making it one of the best returns on effort available. Compiled languages need an ARM build, which is usually straightforward but worth testing.
Is S3 Intelligent-Tiering worth it?

When access patterns are unknown or variable, yes. It moves objects between tiers automatically for a small per-object monitoring fee, with no retrieval charges and none of the minimum duration penalties that make manual tiering risky. If you know the access pattern precisely, explicit lifecycle rules to Standard-IA or Glacier are cheaper, but only when objects genuinely outlive the minimum duration, which is 30 days for IA, 90 for most Glacier tiers and 180 for Deep Archive. Transitioning data deleted after twenty days costs more than doing nothing.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-elastic-load-balancing.subtitle: Choose between ALB, NLB and GWLB, then set up target groups, listener rules, health checks and TLS, and debug 502 and 503 errors from the load balancer.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Elastic Load Balancing must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Choose between ALB, NLB and GWLB, then set up target groups, listener rules, health checks and TLS, and debug 502 and 503 errors from the load balancer.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Choose between ALB, NLB and GWLB, then set up target groups, listener rules, health checks and TLS, and debug 502 and 503 errors from the load balancer.

Elastic Load Balancing distributes traffic across targets in multiple Availability Zones and takes unhealthy ones out of rotation. AWS offers three types, and picking the wrong one is a decision you feel months later when you need a feature the other one has.

sections.title: Choosing a type
paragraphs: The short version: ALB for HTTP, NLB for everything else. Two things push an HTTP workload to an NLB anyway. A client that requires a fixed IP to allowlist, and a need for extreme throughput at minimal latency.
The Classic Load Balancer still exists. Don't start anything new on it.

sections.title: Structure
paragraphs: Three objects make up a load balancer, and understanding the split makes the rest straightforward:
Health checks belong to the target group, not the load balancer. Two target groups behind one ALB can check different paths with different thresholds.
An ALB requires subnets in at least two Availability Zones, each with a minimum of 8 free IP addresses. It scales by adding nodes, and it can't scale into a subnet with no room.

codeBlock.code:
# Target group
aws elbv2 create-target-group \
  --name payments-tg \
  --protocol HTTP --port 8080 \
  --vpc-id vpc-0abc123 \
  --target-type ip \
  --health-check-path /healthz \
  --health-check-interval-seconds 15 \
  --healthy-threshold-count 2 \
  --unhealthy-threshold-count 2

# Load balancer across at least two AZs
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer \
  --name payments-alb \
  --type application \
  --subnets subnet-0aaa subnet-0bbb \
  --security-groups sg-0abc123 \
  --scheme internet-facing

sections.title: Listener rules
paragraphs: This is where ALBs earn their price. One load balancer fronting many services:

Rules evaluate by priority, lowest number first, and the default action catches anything unmatched. Beyond forwarding, rules can redirect (HTTP to HTTPS in one rule, no application code), return a fixed response, or authenticate against Cognito or an OIDC provider before traffic ever reaches your service.
Weighted target groups make canary deploys straightforward. Send 5% of traffic to the new version, watch the metrics, then shift.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 create-rule \
  --listener-arn $LISTENER_ARN \
  --priority 10 \
  --conditions Field=path-pattern,Values='/api/payments/*' \
  --actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=$PAYMENTS_TG

sections.title: Health checks
paragraphs: Most load balancer incidents are really health check misconfigurations.
Time to detection is interval × unhealthy threshold, so the settings above take 30 seconds to pull a dead target. That's a real availability decision, not a default to leave alone.

Point the check at an endpoint that reflects whether the instance can actually serve traffic, but not one that checks every downstream dependency. A health check that fails when the database is slow will remove every target simultaneously and turn a degraded system into a total outage. Check that the process is alive and can serve; let dependency failures surface as errors.
/healthz should not require authentication, should not be logged at high volume, and should be cheap.

codeBlock.code:
Interval:            15s     how often each target is checked
Timeout:             5s      must be less than the interval
Healthy threshold:   2       consecutive passes to return to service
Unhealthy threshold: 2       consecutive failures to remove
Success codes:       200

sections.title: Draining connections
paragraphs: When a target deregisters, a deploy, a scale-in, the load balancer stops sending it new connections but lets existing ones finish. That window is the deregistration delay, 300 seconds by default:

300 seconds makes deploys crawl. Set it slightly above your longest normal request; 30 seconds suits most APIs. Set it too low and you cut off in-flight requests, which shows up to users as failed requests during every deploy.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes \
  --target-group-arn $TG_ARN \
  --attributes Key=deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds,Value=30

sections.title: TLS
paragraphs: Terminate TLS at the load balancer with an ACM certificate. ACM certificates are free and renew automatically:

Choose the security policy deliberately. The default on older load balancers still permits TLS 1.0. A modern policy that requires TLS 1.2 or better is what you want unless you have a specific legacy client.
Redirect HTTP to HTTPS at the listener rather than in application code:

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 create-listener \
  --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN \
  --protocol HTTPS --port 443 \
  --certificates CertificateArn=$CERT_ARN \
  --ssl-policy ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 \
  --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=$TG_ARN

sections.title: Debugging 5xx errors
paragraphs: The status code tells you which side failed, which narrows it immediately:
Start with the target group, always:
The Reason field is precise and worth reading carefully:

The security group case deserves special mention because it produces a healthy-looking application that never receives traffic: the target's security group must allow inbound from the load balancer's security group on the target port. Referencing the load balancer's security group by ID rather than a CIDR is the correct form.

codeBlock.code: aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn $TG_ARN

sections.title: Sticky sessions
paragraphs: Available, but treat them as a workaround:
Stickiness produces uneven load, breaks graceful deploys, and means one lost target loses real user state. Externalising session state to Redis or DynamoDB is nearly always the better fix.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes \
  --target-group-arn $TG_ARN \
  --attributes Key=stickiness.enabled,Value=true \
                Key=stickiness.type,Value=lb_cookie \
                Key=stickiness.lb_cookie.duration_seconds,Value=3600

sections.title: Access logs
paragraphs: Off by default. Turn them on before you need them:
Logs land in S3 and query cleanly from Athena, which is how you answer "which client caused that spike" after the fact. Pair them with a lifecycle policy so the bucket doesn't grow forever.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 modify-load-balancer-attributes \
  --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN \
  --attributes Key=access_logs.s3.enabled,Value=true \
                Key=access_logs.s3.bucket,Value=my-alb-logs

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An ALB starts returning 503 for all requests. The application instances are running and healthy when curled directly from a bastion host. What is the most likely cause?
Should the /healthz endpoint verify that the database is reachable?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between an ALB and an NLB?

An ALB works at layer 7 and understands HTTP, so it can route on path, host, header, method or query string, terminate TLS, redirect, and authenticate against an identity provider. An NLB works at layer 4 and only sees TCP, UDP and TLS, so it routes on port alone, but it handles far higher throughput at lower latency, supports a static Elastic IP per Availability Zone, and preserves the client source IP natively rather than through an X-Forwarded-For header. Use an ALB for HTTP applications and an NLB for non-HTTP protocols, extreme throughput, or when a client needs a fixed IP address to allowlist.
Why is my ALB returning 502 Bad Gateway?

The load balancer reached a target but could not parse the reply. The two most common causes are the application crashing or closing the connection partway through a response, and a protocol mismatch. The target group set to HTTP while the application only speaks HTTPS on that port, or the reverse. Also check that your application's keep-alive timeout is longer than the ALB's idle timeout; if the target closes an idle connection the ALB still considers open, the next request on it produces a 502.
Why do my targets show as unhealthy when the application works fine?

Run aws elbv2 describe-target-health and read the Reason field before anything else. Target.Timeout usually means the target's security group does not allow inbound traffic from the load balancer's security group on the health check port. Reference the load balancer's security group by ID rather than a CIDR range. Target.ResponseCodeMismatch means the endpoint returned something outside the success codes, often a 302 redirect because the health check path sits behind authentication.
How do I make deploys faster without dropping requests?

Lower the deregistration delay from its 300-second default to just above your longest normal request: 30 seconds works for most APIs. That is how long the load balancer waits for in-flight requests to finish after a target starts draining. Setting it too low cuts off active requests and users see errors on every deploy; leaving it at 300 means every rolling deploy waits five minutes per batch for no benefit.
Should I use sticky sessions?

Only as a temporary measure. Stickiness distributes load unevenly, complicates rolling deploys because draining a target strands its sessions, and means losing one target loses real user state. The durable fix is to keep session state outside the application, in ElastiCache for Redis or DynamoDB, so any target can serve any request. If you must enable stickiness, prefer the load balancer cookie and keep the duration short.
Do I need one load balancer per service?

No, and you generally should not. A single ALB can front many services using listener rules that route on host or path, which saves both the hourly charge and a great deal of DNS and certificate management. Separate load balancers make sense when services need genuinely different configurations. Different security policies, WAF rules, or internal versus internet-facing schemes, or when you want hard blast-radius isolation between them.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-elb-alb.title: AWS Application Load Balancer
aws-elb-alb.subtitle: Create an Application Load Balancer, set up target group health checks and priority-ordered listener rules, read 502 and 503 errors and compare ALB with NLB.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Application Load Balancer must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Create an Application Load Balancer, set up target group health checks and priority-ordered listener rules, read 502 and 503 errors and compare ALB with NLB.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create an Application Load Balancer, set up target group health checks and priority-ordered listener rules, read 502 and 503 errors and compare ALB with NLB.

An ALB operates at layer 7, so it understands HTTP. That is what lets it route on path, host, header and method, terminate TLS, and check the health of targets with a real HTTP request rather than a TCP handshake.

The structure is always the same: a listener accepts connections on a port, rules on that listener decide where each request goes, and each rule forwards to a target group containing the instances, IPs or Lambda functions that serve it.

sections.title: Creating one
paragraphs: An ALB needs at least two subnets in different availability zones. This is not optional, and it is the first error people hit:
Note the port mismatch: the listener is on 443 and the target group on 8080. The ALB terminates TLS and speaks plain HTTP to your targets, which is the normal arrangement.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --name web-alb \
  --subnets subnet-0a1b2c3d subnet-4e5f6a7b \
  --security-groups sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --scheme internet-facing --type application

sections.title: Health checks decide everything
paragraphs: A target that fails its health check receives no traffic. That is the whole point, and it is also why a bad health check takes a service down more reliably than a bad deployment.
The Reason field names the cause, and it is the first thing to read:

Two things worth getting right. Give the check a dedicated path that does not touch the database, a /healthz returning 200 unconditionally, because a health check that fails when a dependency is slow removes every target at once and turns a degraded dependency into a total outage. And match the expected codes if your app redirects: a health check hitting / that receives a 301 to HTTPS is marked unhealthy unless you set --matcher HttpCode=200,301.
The deregistration delay also matters during deploys:
The default is 300 seconds, so a rolling deployment waits five minutes per target. Set it slightly above your longest request.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "$TG_ARN" \
  --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[].[Target.Id,TargetHealth.State,TargetHealth.Reason]' \
  --output table

sections.title: Listener rules are evaluated in priority order
paragraphs: Lowest priority number wins, and evaluation stops at the first match. A broad rule at priority 5 shadows everything below it. The usual cause of "my new rule is being ignored". List them in order before debugging anything else:
Rules can do more than forward. Redirect and fixed responses avoid a round trip to your servers entirely:

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 create-rule --listener-arn "$LISTENER_ARN" --priority 10 \
  --conditions '[{"Field":"path-pattern","Values":["/api/*"]}]' \
  --actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn="$API_TG_ARN"

aws elbv2 create-rule --listener-arn "$LISTENER_ARN" --priority 20 \
  --conditions '[{"Field":"host-header","Values":["admin.example.com"]}]' \
  --actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn="$ADMIN_TG_ARN"

sections.title: Reading the errors
paragraphs: 502 Bad Gateway: the ALB reached your target and could not understand the response. Almost always the application: it closed the connection, crashed mid-request, returned malformed headers, or its own keep-alive timeout is shorter than the ALB's 60-second idle timeout, so the target closes a connection the ALB is about to reuse. Setting your server's keep-alive above the ALB idle timeout fixes a surprising number of intermittent 502s.
503 Service Unavailable: no healthy targets. Not an application error at all; go straight to describe-target-health.
504 Gateway Timeout: the target did not respond within the idle timeout. Either the request is genuinely slow or the timeout is too low:

Connection refused with healthy targets: the target's security group must allow the ALB's security group on the target port. Referencing the ALB's security group as the source, rather than a CIDR, is the correct pattern.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 modify-load-balancer-attributes --load-balancer-arn "$ALB_ARN" \
  --attributes Key=idle_timeout.timeout_seconds,Value=120

sections.title: Sticky sessions
paragraphs: Stickiness pins a client to one target with a cookie. It works, and it is usually a workaround for state held in memory that should be in ElastiCache or a database. The costs are real: uneven load distribution, and a target's removal dropping sessions. Treat it as a stopgap while making the application stateless.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes --target-group-arn "$TG_ARN" \
  --attributes Key=stickiness.enabled,Value=true \
    Key=stickiness.type,Value=lb_cookie \
    Key=stickiness.lb_cookie.duration_seconds,Value=86400

sections.title: Client IP and access logs
paragraphs: The ALB terminates the connection, so your application sees the ALB's IP. The real client is in X-Forwarded-For, and X-Forwarded-Proto tells you whether the original request was HTTPS, which matters for generating correct absolute URLs and for redirect loops.
Enable access logs before you need them:
They record target_processing_time separately from request_processing_time, which is how you establish whether slowness is yours or the balancer's. Query them with Athena.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 modify-load-balancer-attributes --load-balancer-arn "$ALB_ARN" \
  --attributes Key=access_logs.s3.enabled,Value=true \
    Key=access_logs.s3.bucket,Value=my-alb-logs

sections.title: ALB or NLB
paragraphs: Use an ALB for HTTP and HTTPS. Use an NLB for other protocols, when you need a static IP, or for extreme throughput with minimal latency.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An ALB returns 503 Service Unavailable for all requests. The application runs fine when tested directly on the instances. Where should you look?
A new rule at priority 50 routes /api/v2/* to a new target group, but those requests keep going to the old one. An existing rule at priority 10 matches /api/*. What is happening?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between an ALB and an NLB?

An ALB works at layer 7, so it parses HTTP and can route on path, host header, HTTP header and method, terminate TLS, and perform HTTP health checks. An NLB works at layer 4, forwarding TCP and UDP without inspecting content, which makes it faster, gives it a static IP per availability zone, lets it carry non-HTTP protocols, and means it preserves the client's source IP. Use an ALB for web traffic, and an NLB when you need a static IP, a non-HTTP protocol, or extreme throughput.
Why is my ALB returning 502 Bad Gateway?

The ALB reached your target and could not use the response, so the cause is nearly always on the target side: the connection was closed early, the application crashed mid-request, or the response headers were malformed. The subtle and common case is a keep-alive mismatch, if your server's keep-alive timeout is shorter than the ALB's 60-second idle timeout, the target closes a connection the ALB is about to reuse, producing intermittent 502s under no particular load. Set the server's keep-alive above the ALB's idle timeout.
Why is my ALB target unhealthy when the app works fine?

Read the Reason in describe-target-health. Target.ResponseCodeMismatch usually means the health check path returns a redirect to HTTPS or a 404. Fix the path or widen --matcher to accept it. Target.FailedHealthChecks typically means the target's security group does not allow the ALB's security group on the target port. Target.Timeout means nothing is listening or the path is too slow. Testing the app from your laptop does not exercise any of those.
What should an ALB health check endpoint do?

Return 200 quickly and check nothing external. A health check that queries the database seems more thorough but is actively dangerous: when the database slows, every target fails simultaneously and the ALB removes all of them, converting a degraded dependency into a complete outage. Use a /healthz that confirms the process is serving requests, and monitor dependencies separately with real alarms. If you need a dependency-aware check, keep it on a different path used for readiness gating rather than for load balancer membership.
How do I get the real client IP behind an ALB?

Read the X-Forwarded-For header. The ALB terminates the connection, so the source IP your application sees is the load balancer's. Take the value your ALB appended rather than trusting the whole chain, since clients can send their own. X-Forwarded-Proto is equally important: it tells you whether the original request was HTTPS, which matters for building absolute URLs and for avoiding redirect loops when your app decides it needs to force HTTPS.
Why are my deployments slow behind an ALB?

The deregistration delay, which defaults to 300 seconds. When a target is deregistered the ALB stops sending it new requests but waits that long for in-flight ones to complete before considering it drained, so a rolling deployment pauses five minutes per target. Set deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds to a little above your longest expected request, commonly 30 seconds, and rolling deployments get dramatically faster without cutting anything off mid-request.

Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-elb-nlb.title: AWS Network Load Balancer
aws-elb-nlb.subtitle: Set up a Network Load Balancer for layer 4 traffic: static IPs, client IP preservation, the hairpin problem, cross-zone charges, TLS listeners and NLB vs ALB.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Network Load Balancer must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Set up a Network Load Balancer for layer 4 traffic: static IPs, client IP preservation, the hairpin problem, cross-zone charges, TLS listeners and NLB vs ALB.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Set up a Network Load Balancer for layer 4 traffic: static IPs, client IP preservation, the hairpin problem, cross-zone charges, TLS listeners and NLB vs ALB.
An NLB forwards TCP and UDP without looking inside. It cannot route on a URL path, because it never parses HTTP, and that limitation is exactly what buys you the four things an ALB cannot give you:
If your traffic is HTTP and you need none of those, an ALB is the better tool.

sections.title: Creating one
paragraphs: You can pin the addresses rather than letting AWS choose, which is the point of an NLB for many people:
Those Elastic IPs never change, so you can hand them to a partner's firewall team once and not revisit it.
A TCP health check only proves something accepted a connection. Where the protocol allows it, an HTTP health check tells you considerably more:

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --name db-nlb \
  --type network --scheme internal \
  --subnet-mappings 'SubnetId=subnet-0a1b2c3d' 'SubnetId=subnet-4e5f6a7b'

sections.title: Client IP preservation and the hairpin problem
paragraphs: By default, an NLB with --target-type instance or ip passes the client's source IP straight through. Your application sees the real client with no X-Forwarded-For needed, which is excellent, until a target tries to reach the load balancer that is in front of it.

The failure looks like this: an EC2 instance behind the NLB connects to the NLB's own DNS name, the NLB routes that connection back to the same instance, and the instance receives a packet whose source IP is its own. The TCP stack drops it. The connection simply hangs, with nothing in any log.
Use --target-type alb and put an ALB behind the NLB, which terminates connections.
Have the instance talk to the service directly rather than via the load balancer, which is usually the right answer anyway.
This is the single most common NLB surprise, and it is a design consequence rather than a bug.

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Turn preservation off. Targets then see the NLB's IP
aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes --target-group-arn "$TG_ARN" \
  --attributes Key=preserve_client_ip.enabled,Value=false

sections.title: Security groups work differently
paragraphs: For a long time NLBs had no security group at all, and traffic was filtered only by the targets' security groups, which meant those groups had to allow the client CIDR directly, because with client IP preservation the packets arrive with the original source address. An allow rule naming the load balancer's security group does nothing, since there was not one.
NLBs now support security groups, but only when created. You cannot add one later:
If an existing NLB needs one, it has to be replaced. Worth checking before you build.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --name api-nlb --type network \
  --security-groups sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --subnet-mappings 'SubnetId=subnet-0a1b2c3d'

sections.title: Cross-zone load balancing costs money
paragraphs: The default differs between the two load balancer types, and this catches people on their bill.
ALB: cross-zone is on and cannot be turned off, at no charge. NLB: cross-zone is off by default, and enabling it incurs inter-AZ data transfer charges.

With it off, an NLB node only sends traffic to targets in its own availability zone. That is cheaper and keeps latency lowest, but it means uneven distribution when zones hold different numbers of targets, and if a zone has no healthy targets, clients resolving to that node fail.
Keep it off with a balanced number of targets per zone; turn it on when distribution matters more than transfer cost.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 modify-load-balancer-attributes --load-balancer-arn "$NLB_ARN" \
  --attributes Key=load_balancing.cross_zone.enabled,Value=true

sections.title: TLS listeners
paragraphs: An NLB can terminate TLS without becoming an ALB, which is useful for non-HTTP protocols:
Alternatively use TCP on 443 and pass encrypted traffic straight through, terminating on the target, which keeps the connection end-to-end encrypted and is sometimes a compliance requirement.
Terminating TLS at the NLB loses the client IP for the TLS listener unless you enable proxy protocol v2, which prefixes each connection with the original address:
Only enable it if the target application understands proxy protocol. Otherwise it reads the header as the first bytes of your protocol and the connection breaks in a genuinely confusing way.

codeBlock.code:
aws elbv2 create-listener --load-balancer-arn "$NLB_ARN" \
  --protocol TLS --port 443 \
  --certificates CertificateArn="$CERT_ARN" \
  --ssl-policy ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 \
  --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn="$TG_ARN"

sections.title: PrivateLink
paragraphs: An NLB is what you put in front of a service you want to expose to other AWS accounts privately, without VPC peering or public internet:

Consumers create an interface endpoint in their own VPC and reach your service over private addresses. Only an NLB (or a Gateway Load Balancer) can back an endpoint service, so if PrivateLink is on your roadmap, that decides the load balancer type.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint-service-configuration \
  --network-load-balancer-arns "$NLB_ARN" --acceptance-required

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Connections hang with no error. Almost certainly the hairpin problem above, or a target security group that does not allow the client CIDR.
Targets healthy, connections refused. With client IP preservation on, the target security group must allow the client's CIDR, not the load balancer's.
Exactly what it says. Recreate the NLB.
Uneven traffic across targets. Cross-zone load balancing is off, which is the NLB default.

codeBlock.code:
ValidationError: Security groups cannot be added to a network load balancer
after creation

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An EC2 instance registered behind an NLB tries to connect to that NLB's DNS name. The connection hangs with no error and nothing in the logs. Other clients work fine. Why?
A partner requires two fixed IP addresses to allow-list, and the service speaks a custom binary protocol over TCP on port 9000. Which load balancer, and why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: When should I use an NLB instead of an ALB?

When you need any of four things: a static IP address per availability zone for firewall allow-listing, the client's real source IP preserved without relying on headers, a protocol other than HTTP or HTTPS, or the ability to back a PrivateLink endpoint service. Also when throughput and latency are extreme enough that terminating connections at layer 7 is a cost you would rather avoid. For ordinary web traffic where none of those apply, an ALB gives you path and host routing that an NLB fundamentally cannot.
Why do connections through my NLB hang with no error?

Most likely the hairpin problem. With client IP preservation enabled, the default, a target that connects to the NLB in front of it can have that connection routed back to itself, receiving a packet whose source address is its own, which the TCP stack silently drops. Nothing logs an error because nothing refused anything. Disable preserve_client_ip, use an ALB as the NLB's target, or have the instance connect to the service directly rather than through the load balancer.
Does an NLB have a security group?

Now yes, but only if you attach one when the load balancer is created. It cannot be added afterwards, and an existing NLB must be replaced to gain one. Historically NLBs had none at all, which is why so much documentation says traffic must be controlled entirely by the targets' security groups. That distinction matters because with client IP preservation the targets see the original client address, so their rules must allow the client CIDR rather than referencing the load balancer.
Why is traffic uneven across my NLB targets?

Cross-zone load balancing is disabled by default on an NLB, so each node only sends traffic to targets in its own availability zone. If one zone holds four instances and another holds one, the single instance takes a disproportionate share. Enabling cross-zone evens it out but incurs inter-AZ data transfer charges, which an ALB does not, cross-zone is always on there and free. Either keep target counts balanced per zone, or enable it and accept the transfer cost.
How do I preserve the client IP when the NLB terminates TLS?

Enable proxy protocol v2 on the target group. A TLS listener terminates the connection, so the original source address is otherwise lost; proxy protocol prefixes each connection with a header carrying the real client address and port. The important caveat is that the target application must understand proxy protocol, if it does not, it reads the header as the first bytes of your actual protocol and the connection fails in a confusing way. Many web servers and proxies support it with a single configuration flag.
Can an NLB do path-based routing?

No, and it never will. Path-based routing requires parsing HTTP, which is precisely what an NLB does not do. It forwards packets at layer 4 with no knowledge of what they contain. If you need both static IPs and HTTP routing, the standard pattern is an NLB in front of an ALB using --target-type alb: the NLB supplies the fixed addresses, and the ALB behind it does the layer 7 routing.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-auto-scaling.title: AWS Auto Scaling
aws-auto-scaling.subtitle: See what scales on AWS and how: EC2 Auto Scaling vs Application Auto Scaling, scaling ECS, DynamoDB and Aurora, and why right-sizing often beats scaling.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Auto Scaling must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: See what scales on AWS and how: EC2 Auto Scaling vs Application Auto Scaling, scaling ECS, DynamoDB and Aurora, and why right-sizing often beats scaling.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: See what scales on AWS and how: EC2 Auto Scaling vs Application Auto Scaling, scaling ECS, DynamoDB and Aurora, and why right-sizing often beats scaling.
"Auto Scaling" on AWS is not one service. It is two APIs with similar names that people routinely confuse, plus a handful of services that scale themselves.

If a CLI command or IAM policy is not working, checking which of these you are actually using is usually the fastest fix, aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy and aws application-autoscaling put-scaling-policy are different commands with different arguments.

sections.title: Scale out, not up
paragraphs: Two ways to handle more load. Vertical scaling means a bigger instance: simple, requires no application changes, and has a ceiling plus downtime to resize. Horizontal scaling means more instances: no ceiling, no downtime, and it requires the application to tolerate multiple copies.

Auto Scaling on AWS means horizontal, and that imposes one real prerequisite: your application must be stateless. Sessions in memory, uploads on local disk, or a cache on the instance all break the moment a second instance appears or the first is replaced. Put sessions in ElastiCache or a cookie, uploads in S3, and state in a database. Reaching for sticky sessions instead works, and leaves you with uneven load and sessions lost on every scale-in.

sections.title: Scaling EC2
paragraphs: An Auto Scaling group maintains a count of instances between a floor and a ceiling:

Even with no scaling policy at all, that group is doing useful work: it replaces failed instances and keeps capacity spread across availability zones. Self-healing is arguably the bigger benefit, and it is the one people forget when they say they "don't need auto scaling".
Then attach a scaling policy to change the desired count automatically.

codeBlock.code:
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=web-lt,Version='$Latest' \
  --min-size 2 --max-size 10 --desired-capacity 2 \
  --vpc-zone-identifier "subnet-0a1b2c3d,subnet-4e5f6a7b" \
  --target-group-arns "$TG_ARN" \
  --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 180

sections.title: Scaling ECS
paragraphs: Container workloads are where auto scaling genuinely shines, because a task starts in seconds rather than the minutes an EC2 instance needs. Registration comes first, then the policy:

Forgetting register-scalable-target is the most common mistake here. A policy created without it fails, and on EC2 there is no equivalent step, which is exactly why people trip over it when moving to ECS.
On EKS the equivalents are the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for pods and Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler for nodes, both of which sit outside these APIs.

codeBlock.code:
aws application-autoscaling register-scalable-target \
  --service-namespace ecs \
  --resource-id service/prod-cluster/api \
  --scalable-dimension ecs:service:DesiredCount \
  --min-capacity 2 --max-capacity 20

aws application-autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --service-namespace ecs \
  --resource-id service/prod-cluster/api \
  --scalable-dimension ecs:service:DesiredCount \
  --policy-name cpu-target --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-scaling-policy-configuration '{
    "TargetValue": 60.0,
    "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {"PredefinedMetricType": "ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization"}
  }'

sections.title: Scaling DynamoDB
paragraphs: Only relevant in provisioned mode, on-demand scales by itself:

A caveat worth knowing before relying on it: DynamoDB auto scaling reacts over minutes, so a sudden spike throttles before capacity arrives. If your traffic is genuinely spiky, on-demand is the better answer despite the higher per-request price.

codeBlock.code:
aws application-autoscaling register-scalable-target \
  --service-namespace dynamodb \
  --resource-id table/Orders \
  --scalable-dimension dynamodb:table:WriteCapacityUnits \
  --min-capacity 5 --max-capacity 500

sections.title: Scaling Aurora and Lambda
paragraphs: Aurora scales read replicas, not writes. The writer is a single instance, so read scaling is all this offers:

Lambda scales concurrency automatically. What you configure is provisioned concurrency to remove cold starts, and reserved concurrency to cap a function. The latter also protecting a downstream database from being overwhelmed by thousands of simultaneous invocations.

codeBlock.code:
aws application-autoscaling register-scalable-target \
  --service-namespace rds \
  --resource-id cluster:prod-aurora \
  --scalable-dimension rds:cluster:ReadReplicaCount \
  --min-capacity 1 --max-capacity 8

sections.title: Choose the right metric
paragraphs: CPU is the default and frequently the wrong signal. It works for compute-bound work and tells you nothing about a service that is slow because it is waiting on a database.
ALBRequestCountPerTarget is under-used and often the best choice for a web tier: requests per instance maps directly to work arriving, regardless of whether that work is CPU-heavy.
For an SQS consumer, scale on a custom metric of messages per instance. Scaling a queue consumer on CPU means it scales up only once it is already overloaded.

sections.title: Scaling is not a substitute for right-sizing
paragraphs: Auto scaling handles variable load. It does not fix an application that needs eight times the resources it should, and it makes over-provisioning more expensive by multiplying it.

Before adding a scaling policy, check whether the instance type actually matches the workload. A memory-bound service on a compute-optimised instance scales out on CPU that is never the constraint. Compute Optimizer reads real utilisation and recommends types, and acting on that often removes the need to scale at all.
Equally, scaling only saves money if it scales in. A group whose minimum is set to peak capacity is a fixed fleet with extra machinery.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Missing register-scalable-target. Register first, then create the policy.
Set the ceiling first; desired cannot exceed max.
Alarm in ALARM state, nothing happens. Usually a cooldown still in effect, desired already at max, or a service quota on that instance type in the region.

codeBlock.code:
ValidationException: No scalable target registered for service namespace: ecs,
resource ID: service/prod-cluster/api

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Creating a target tracking policy for an ECS service fails with "No scalable target registered for service namespace: ecs". The same approach worked for an EC2 Auto Scaling group. What is different?
An SQS consumer fleet scales on average CPU at 70%. Queue depth grows for twenty minutes during bursts before instances are added. What is the better approach?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between EC2 Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling?

EC2 Auto Scaling manages EC2 instances inside an Auto Scaling group, using the autoscaling API. Application Auto Scaling is a separate service, using the application-autoscaling API, that scales everything else. ECS service task counts, DynamoDB provisioned capacity, Aurora read replicas, Lambda provisioned concurrency, Spot Fleet and more. They have similarly named commands with different arguments, and Application Auto Scaling requires you to register a scalable target before attaching any policy, which EC2 does not.
Do I need Auto Scaling if my traffic is constant?

Probably, though not for scaling. An Auto Scaling group also replaces instances that fail health checks and keeps capacity distributed across availability zones, so a group with min, max and desired all set to the same number still gives you self-healing and zone balance that a manually launched instance does not. Many teams run exactly that configuration deliberately. The scaling policy is a separate decision you can add later.
What metric should I scale on?

Whatever actually correlates with the work arriving. CPU suits compute-bound services and is misleading for anything that spends its time waiting on a database. For a web tier, ALBRequestCountPerTarget is usually better. Requests per instance maps directly to load. For a queue consumer, use backlog per instance or oldest-message age, since CPU only rises once the fleet is already behind. For latency-sensitive services, TargetResponseTime reflects the thing users actually experience.
Why isn't my Auto Scaling group scaling even though the alarm is firing?

Check three things in order. A cooldown or scaling activity still in progress will suppress further action, describe-scaling-activities shows the history and any reason given. The desired capacity may already be at max-size, which silently caps everything. And a service quota on that instance type in the region can prevent launches, which appears as a failed scaling activity rather than an alarm problem. The scaling activity description almost always names the cause.
Does auto scaling save money?

Only if it scales in as readily as it scales out. A group whose minimum equals peak capacity is a fixed fleet with extra moving parts, and it will not save anything. The larger saving usually comes earlier, from right-sizing: a workload on an inappropriate instance family scales out on a metric that was never the real constraint. Check Compute Optimizer's recommendations before adding a policy. Fixing the instance type sometimes removes the need to scale at all.
Can Auto Scaling scale an instance vertically?

No. EC2 Auto Scaling changes how many instances exist, never how large they are, and resizing an instance requires stopping it. If you need a different size, update the launch template and use an instance refresh to roll the group onto the new type. Vertical scaling on AWS is a deliberate change rather than an automatic one. The services that scale a single resource's capacity automatically are the managed ones such as DynamoDB, Aurora Serverless and Lambda.

Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
