sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Set up an Auto Scaling group with launch templates, ELB vs EC2 health checks and grace periods, then deploy with instance refresh and Spot mixed instances.

sections.title: Auto Scaling Groups
paragraphs: An Auto Scaling group keeps a target number of EC2 instances running, replaces ones that fail, and spreads them across availability zones. Even with no scaling policy attached, that self-healing is worth having, which is why a group with min, max and desired all set to the same number is a perfectly sensible production configuration.

sections.title: Launch templates, not launch configurations
paragraphs: Launch configurations are deprecated and cannot be created for accounts that never used them. They were immutable, supported no versioning, and could not express newer features. If you are maintaining any, migrating is overdue.
"HttpTokens": "required" enforces IMDSv2, which closes the SSRF path to instance credentials. Make it a default in every template.
UserData must be base64 encoded, base64 -w0 userdata.sh on Linux, base64 -i userdata.sh on macOS.

Version='$Latest' means new instances always use the newest template version. Convenient, and it means editing a template changes behaviour with no further action, which is not always what you want. $Default pins to a version you promote explicitly, making the template change and the rollout separate steps. For production, pin and promote.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-launch-template --launch-template-name web-lt \
  --version-description v1 \
  --launch-template-data '{
    "ImageId": "ami-0abcdef1234567890",
    "InstanceType": "t3.medium",
    "SecurityGroupIds": ["sg-0123456789abcdef0"],
    "IamInstanceProfile": {"Name": "web-instance-profile"},
    "MetadataOptions": {"HttpTokens": "required"},
    "TagSpecifications": [{"ResourceType":"instance","Tags":[{"Key":"Name","Value":"web"}]}],
    "UserData": "IyEvYmluL2Jhc2gKZWNobyBoZWxsbwo="
  }'

sections.title: Health checks
paragraphs: This is the setting most worth getting right. The default, EC2, only checks whether the hypervisor thinks the instance is running, so an instance whose application has crashed stays in service indefinitely, receiving traffic and failing every request.
ELB makes the group use the load balancer's target health, so an instance failing its HTTP health check is replaced. If you have a load balancer, use it.

The grace period is how long after launch the group ignores health checks. Too short and you get a loop: the instance boots, is not ready, is marked unhealthy, is terminated, and a replacement starts the same cycle. Set it above your genuine boot-to-ready time, and watch out for a group that never stabilises after an AMI change made startup slower.

--default-instance-warmup is the newer, preferred setting: it covers both health checks and metric collection, so a warming instance does not drag the group's average CPU down and trigger further scaling.

codeBlock.code: --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 180

sections.title: Instance refresh
paragraphs: The supported way to roll a fleet onto a new AMI or instance type, without an external deployment tool:

Three preferences earn their place. SkipMatching leaves instances already running the target configuration alone, which turns a re-run into a no-op. AutoRollback reverts to the previous template version if the refresh fails, rather than leaving the group half-migrated. MaxHealthyPercentage above 100 lets the group launch replacements before terminating, so capacity never dips. Worth it if MinHealthyPercentage: 90 would still take you below what you need.

codeBlock.code:
aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --preferences '{
    "MinHealthyPercentage": 90,
    "InstanceWarmup": 180,
    "SkipMatching": true,
    "AutoRollback": true,
    "MaxHealthyPercentage": 110
  }'

sections.title: Lifecycle hooks
paragraphs: Hooks pause an instance at launch or termination so something can act before it proceeds:
Use them to deregister from service discovery, flush logs, or finish in-flight jobs on termination. The critical part is completing the hook when done:

Forget that call and every instance sits in Terminating:Wait for the full heartbeat timeout, which, with --default-result ABANDON, can also strand a group mid-scale. Set CONTINUE as the default result so a broken hook degrades rather than blocks.

codeBlock.code:
aws autoscaling put-lifecycle-hook \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --lifecycle-hook-name drain-connections \
  --lifecycle-transition autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING \
  --heartbeat-timeout 300 --default-result CONTINUE \
  --notification-target-arn "$SNS_ARN" --role-arn "$ROLE_ARN"

sections.title: Termination policies
paragraphs: When scaling in, the group has to choose which instance to remove:
To keep a specific instance, one you are mid-investigation on, use scale-in protection:

codeBlock.code:
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --termination-policies OldestLaunchTemplate Default

sections.title: Mixed instances and Spot
paragraphs: Combining on-demand and Spot across several instance types is where real savings live:

That keeps two on-demand instances as a floor, then fills 75% of anything above with Spot. List several instance types. Spot interruption risk falls sharply with more options, and a single-type Spot group is the configuration that gives Spot its bad reputation.
Capacity rebalancing launches a replacement when AWS signals an upcoming Spot interruption, rather than waiting for the two-minute termination notice.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The template does not exist, the version is wrong, or the name has a typo. describe-launch-template-versions confirms.
The subnet's zone does not offer that type. Remove that subnet or add overrides with types that exist there.
Instances launching and terminating in a loop. Health check grace period shorter than boot time, almost always.
Group stuck at Terminating:Wait. A lifecycle hook that nothing is completing.

codeBlock.code: ValidationError: You must use a valid fully-formed launch template

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: After updating an AMI that made boot take about four minutes, an ASG launches instances that are terminated a couple of minutes later, repeatedly. Health check type is ELB. What is wrong?
An ASG has instances sitting in Terminating:Wait for five minutes before finally terminating. A lifecycle hook was added last week. What is happening?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a launch template and a launch configuration?

Launch configurations are the older, immutable, unversioned mechanism, and they are deprecated. AWS no longer allows new ones in accounts that never used them, and they cannot express newer features such as mixed instance types or IMDSv2 enforcement. Launch templates are versioned, so you can promote or roll back a specific version, and they work with instance refresh and mixed instances policies. Any remaining launch configuration should be migrated; there is no benefit to keeping one.
Why does my Auto Scaling group keep replacing healthy instances?

Usually a health check grace period shorter than the real boot-to-ready time, so instances are judged unhealthy before the application starts serving and terminated in a loop. It often appears after an AMI or application change makes startup slower. Check describe-scaling-activities, which states the reason for each termination. The other cause is a health check path that returns a redirect or 404, which fails even on a fully working instance.
Should health check type be EC2 or ELB?

ELB, whenever there is a load balancer. The EC2 default only considers the instance's own status checks, meaning a host whose application has crashed is still considered healthy and keeps receiving traffic while failing every request. ELB defers to the target group's health, so a failed HTTP check results in replacement. Pair it with a grace period longer than boot time, and a health check endpoint that does not depend on the database.
How do I roll out a new AMI to an Auto Scaling group?

Create a new launch template version with the AMI, then start-instance-refresh with MinHealthyPercentage, InstanceWarmup, SkipMatching and AutoRollback set. The group replaces instances gradually while keeping the healthy proportion above your floor, and reverts automatically if the refresh fails. Setting MaxHealthyPercentage above 100 lets replacements launch before old instances are terminated, so capacity never dips during the roll.
What are lifecycle hooks used for?

Pausing an instance at launch or termination so something can run first. Deregistering from service discovery, uploading final logs, waiting for in-flight jobs to finish, or completing configuration before the instance takes traffic. Whatever handles the hook must call complete-lifecycle-action when done, or the instance waits out the entire heartbeat timeout. Set --default-result CONTINUE so a failure in your handler delays the action rather than abandoning it.
How do I use Spot instances in an Auto Scaling group safely?

Use a mixed instances policy with OnDemandBaseCapacity set to the minimum you must always have, a percentage split above that, and the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy. The single most important detail is listing several instance types in the overrides. Spot interruption risk falls sharply with more options, and a group pinned to one type is what gives Spot its unreliable reputation. Enable capacity rebalancing so replacements launch when AWS signals an upcoming interruption.

keyConcepts.explanation: Compare target tracking, step, scheduled and predictive scaling, pick the right policy, and use warmup and cooldowns to stop flapping and bad scale-in.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Compare target tracking, step, scheduled and predictive scaling, pick the right policy, and use warmup and cooldowns to stop flapping and bad scale-in.

sections.title: Auto Scaling Policies
paragraphs: An Auto Scaling group maintains a desired capacity. A scaling policy is what changes that number. There are five kinds, and the honest summary is that target tracking handles almost everything. The others exist for specific situations.

sections.title: Target tracking
paragraphs: You name a metric and a target value, and AWS manages the alarms, the arithmetic and the scale-in for you:

It creates a pair of CloudWatch alarms behind the scenes and adjusts capacity to hold the metric near the target, scaling out aggressively and in conservatively, which is the behaviour you want and is tedious to implement by hand with step scaling.
For a web tier, requests per instance is usually the better signal than CPU:

That ResourceLabel format is fiddly and a frequent source of errors. It is the ALB and target group portions of their ARNs joined by a /. Read them from describe-target-groups rather than typing them.
Useful when you want one policy adding capacity and something else, a scheduled action, or a more cautious step policy, deciding when to remove it.

Attaching more than one target tracking policy is supported and sensible. The group takes the largest capacity any policy asks for when scaling out, and scales in only when all of them agree. So a CPU policy and a request-count policy together mean either can add capacity, and neither can remove it alone.

sections.title: Step scaling
paragraphs: Step scaling varies the response by how far the metric has breached, which target tracking cannot express:

The bounds are relative to the alarm threshold, not absolute metric values. With a threshold of 60, the first step covers 60 to 80% CPU and adds one instance; the last covers 100% and upwards and adds six. Reading them as absolute values is the usual mistake and produces steps that never fire.
Leave MetricIntervalUpperBound off the last step and MetricIntervalLowerBound off the first, or there is a gap where nothing happens.
You must create and attach the alarm yourself, which is the main cost of step scaling over target tracking.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name web-cpu-high \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --dimensions Name=AutoScalingGroupName,Value=web-asg \
  --statistic Average --period 60 --evaluation-periods 2 \
  --threshold 60 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold

aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --policy-name step-out --policy-type StepScaling \
  --adjustment-type ChangeInCapacity \
  --metric-aggregation-type Average \
  --estimated-instance-warmup 180 \
  --step-adjustments \
    'MetricIntervalLowerBound=0,MetricIntervalUpperBound=20,ScalingAdjustment=1' \
    'MetricIntervalLowerBound=20,MetricIntervalUpperBound=40,ScalingAdjustment=3' \
    'MetricIntervalLowerBound=40,ScalingAdjustment=6'

sections.title: Simple scaling
paragraphs: Simple scaling applies one adjustment, then blocks all scaling for a cooldown period, even if the metric keeps climbing. That single-threaded behaviour is why step scaling replaced it, and there is no remaining reason to choose it.

sections.title: Scheduled scaling
paragraphs: When load follows the clock, there is no reason to wait for a metric to notice:

Two details matter. The recurrence is standard five-field cron, unlike EventBridge's six fields. And --time-zone handles daylight saving properly, so a schedule set in local time does not drift by an hour twice a year, without it, times are UTC.

Scheduled actions raise the floor rather than replacing metric-based policies. Combining a scheduled minimum with target tracking is the standard pattern: guaranteed capacity before the rush, and metric-driven scaling beyond it.

codeBlock.code:
aws autoscaling put-scheduled-update-group-action \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --scheduled-action-name weekday-morning \
  --recurrence '30 7 * * MON-FRI' \
  --min-size 6 --desired-capacity 8 --max-size 20 \
  --time-zone 'Europe/London'

sections.title: Predictive scaling
paragraphs: Predictive scaling reads the last two weeks of history, forecasts the next 48 hours, and provisions ahead of demand:

Start in ForecastOnly. It produces forecasts without acting, so you can compare predictions against what actually happened before letting it provision. Switch to ForecastAndScale once the forecast looks right.

It needs at least 24 hours of data, works only on cyclical patterns, and is genuinely valuable when instances take several minutes to boot. Reactive scaling is always late by however long a launch takes. Always keep target tracking alongside it to handle the unexpected.

sections.title: Cooldowns and warmup
paragraphs: The settings behind most "it scaled too much" complaints.
Cooldown is a period after a scaling activity during which simple scaling does nothing. It does not apply to target tracking or step scaling, so tuning it on a modern setup achieves nothing.

Instance warmup is what matters. A newly launched instance reports low CPU while booting, which drags the group average down and can trigger a scale-in immediately after scaling out. Warmup excludes it from metrics until it is ready:
--default-instance-warmup on the group is the current recommendation and covers every policy. Set it to real boot-to-ready time.

codeBlock.code:
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg --default-instance-warmup 180

sections.title: Flapping
paragraphs: Capacity oscillating up and down usually means one of three things:
describe-scaling-activities shows each decision and its cause, which is where to look rather than guessing:

codeBlock.code:
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg --max-items 10 \
  --query 'Activities[].[StartTime,StatusCode,Cause]' --output table

sections.title: Scale-in is the part that goes wrong
paragraphs: Everyone tests scaling out. Scale-in is where the incidents come from: connections cut mid-request, jobs abandoned half-finished, a cache that has to warm from cold again.

Three safeguards. Set a deregistration delay slightly above your longest request so the load balancer drains connections. Use a lifecycle hook on termination to finish in-flight work. And keep min-size at genuine minimum safe capacity, not at one.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The ALBRequestCountPerTarget label is app/<alb-name>/<alb-id>/targetgroup/<tg-name>/<tg-id>. Build it from the ARNs rather than by hand.
Two steps cover the same interval. Bounds must be contiguous and non-overlapping.
Alarm in ALARM, no scaling activity. Desired capacity is already at max-size, or a service quota is blocking launches. describe-scaling-activities names it.

codeBlock.code: ValidationError: Invalid ResourceLabel format

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A step scaling policy has an alarm threshold of 60% CPU and step adjustments with bounds 70 to 80, 80 to 90, and 90 upwards. Nothing scales even at 95% CPU. Why?

A target tracking policy on ASGAverageCPUUtilization with a target of 25% is adding and removing instances every few minutes. Instances take about three minutes to boot. What is the first thing to fix?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between target tracking and step scaling?

Target tracking takes a metric and a target value and manages everything else. It creates the CloudWatch alarms, works out how much capacity to add or remove, and deliberately scales out faster than it scales in. Step scaling requires you to create the alarm and define adjustments that vary with how far the metric has breached, which is more work but lets you respond more aggressively to a large breach than a small one. Start with target tracking; reach for step scaling only when that graduated response genuinely matters.
Which metric should a scaling policy use?

Whichever tracks arriving work. ASGAverageCPUUtilization suits compute-bound services. ALBRequestCountPerTarget is usually better for a web tier, because requests per instance maps directly to load whether or not it is CPU-heavy. For a queue consumer, use backlog per instance, since CPU only rises once the fleet is already behind. Avoid targets close to idle, around 20% means normal variation crosses the threshold constantly and the group flaps.
Why does my Auto Scaling group keep flapping up and down?

Most often no instance warmup configured. A booting instance reports near-zero CPU, which lowers the group average below target and triggers a scale-in immediately after scaling out. Set --default-instance-warmup to your real boot-to-ready time. The other two causes are a target value close to idle, where ordinary noise crosses it repeatedly, and a metric too spiky to scale on. Both fixed by raising the target into the 40 to 60% range or lengthening the evaluation period.
Can I attach more than one scaling policy to a group?

Yes, and it is a sensible pattern. When several target tracking policies apply, the group scales out to the largest capacity any of them requests, and scales in only when all of them agree it is safe. So a CPU policy and a request-count policy together mean either can add capacity while neither can remove it alone. Combining a scheduled action that raises the floor with target tracking above it is also standard.
Do cooldown periods apply to target tracking policies?

No. Cooldown is a simple scaling concept, and since simple scaling is obsolete, tuning cooldown on a modern configuration achieves nothing. The setting that matters is instance warmup, which excludes newly launched instances from metric aggregation until they are actually serving traffic. --default-instance-warmup on the group is the current recommendation and applies to every policy attached to it.
Is predictive scaling worth using?

It is, on workloads with clear daily or weekly cycles and instances slow enough to boot that reactive scaling is always late. It forecasts from the last fortnight of history and provisions ahead of expected demand, which reactive policies cannot do by definition. Start in ForecastOnly mode and compare its predictions against reality for a week or two before enabling ForecastAndScale, and always keep a target tracking policy alongside it to handle load the forecast did not anticipate.

keyConcepts.explanation: Learn how CloudFront caching works: origin access control for S3, the cache key behind your hit rate, TTL header rules, invalidation costs and error pages.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how CloudFront caching works: origin access control for S3, the cache key behind your hit rate, TTL header rules, invalidation costs and error pages.

sections.title: Amazon CloudFront
paragraphs: CloudFront is a CDN: it caches your content at hundreds of edge locations so a request from Sydney is served from Sydney rather than from your origin in Ireland.
CloudFront: CDN Request Flow
Cache Hit = faster response + lower origin cost

Latency is the obvious benefit. Two less obvious ones often matter more: the origin only sees traffic that actually misses the cache, which can cut its load by an order of magnitude, and data transfer out through CloudFront is cheaper than straight from S3 or EC2, so a well-cached distribution often reduces the bill rather than adding to it.

sections.title: Origins and Origin Access Control
paragraphs: An origin is where CloudFront fetches on a miss: an S3 bucket, an ALB, an API Gateway, or any public HTTP endpoint.

For S3, the important pattern is keeping the bucket completely private and letting only CloudFront read it. Origin Access Control is the current mechanism; Origin Access Identity is its predecessor and still appears in older guides, but OAC supports SSE-KMS and all HTTP methods, so use it for anything new.
The bucket policy then grants CloudFront access, scoped to the one distribution:

Getting this wrong produces a 403 that looks like a CloudFront problem and is a bucket policy problem. Do not enable S3 static website hosting alongside OAC, that endpoint is public HTTP only and bypasses the whole arrangement.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudfront create-origin-access-control \
  --origin-access-control-config '{
    "Name": "site-oac",
    "OriginAccessControlOriginType": "s3",
    "SigningBehavior": "always",
    "SigningProtocol": "sigv4"
  }'

sections.title: The cache key decides your hit rate
paragraphs: This is where most CloudFront disappointment comes from. The cache key is what CloudFront uses to decide whether it already has a response, and anything included in the key fragments the cache.

Forwarding all query strings, all cookies or all headers means a separate cache entry per unique combination. A marketing campaign appending ?utm_source=… to every link creates a fresh cache entry per variant. The content is identical, and your hit rate collapses.
Include in the key only what genuinely changes the response:
Use the managed policies where they fit, Managed-CachingOptimized for static assets, Managed-CachingDisabled for APIs, rather than writing your own from scratch.
Watch the hit rate, which is the single most useful CloudFront metric:
CloudFront metrics live in us-east-1 regardless of where anything else is.

sections.title: TTLs: headers win
paragraphs: CloudFront honours Cache-Control from your origin, and the distribution's TTLs act as bounds:
The clean approach is to control caching at the origin and leave CloudFront's TTLs permissive. Combined with hashed filenames, this removes invalidation from your life entirely:
Fingerprinted assets cache forever because a new build produces a new filename; the HTML that references them is never cached. Nothing needs invalidating on deploy.

codeBlock.code:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable   → /static/app.4f3a1b.js
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate    → /index.html

sections.title: Invalidation is not a deployment strategy
paragraphs: The first 1,000 paths each month are free, then each path costs money, and a wildcard /* counts as one path, which makes it cheaper than listing many files but slower, taking minutes to propagate globally.
Teams that invalidate /* on every deploy are working around a caching strategy that should have used hashed filenames. Reserve invalidation for genuine mistakes.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id E1ABCDEFGHIJKL --paths '/index.html' '/'

sections.title: Custom error pages
paragraphs: Essential for a single-page application, because S3 returns 403 (not 404) for a missing key when using OAC, so any client-side route fails:
Note ErrorCachingMinTTL. The default caches errors for five minutes, so a brief origin outage is served as an error long after the origin recovers. Lower it.

sections.title: HTTPS and the us-east-1 rule
paragraphs: An ACM certificate for CloudFront must be in us-east-1. Not your bucket's region, not your ALB's region, us-east-1, always. It is the most common CloudFront setup error, and a certificate in the wrong region simply does not appear in the list of choices.
Set the viewer policy to redirect and pick a modern security policy:
"Compress": true is free and reduces transfer noticeably for text assets.

codeBlock.code:
aws acm request-certificate --region us-east-1 \
  --domain-name cdn.example.com \
  --validation-method DNS

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: OAC is configured but the bucket policy does not allow cloudfront.amazonaws.com, or the AWS:SourceArn does not match the distribution.
Request it again in us-east-1.
That alternate domain name is attached to another distribution, possibly in another account.
Deploy complete, old content still served. The cache key or TTL, not a CloudFront fault. Check Cache-Control from the origin and whether the asset is fingerprinted.

codeBlock.code: 403 ERROR — The request could not be satisfied. Access Denied

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A distribution serving static assets had a 95% cache hit rate. After a marketing campaign started appending ?utm_source and ?utm_campaign to links, it fell to 20%. The cache policy forwards all query strings. Why?
A team requests an ACM certificate for cdn.example.com in eu-west-1, validates it successfully, and then cannot choose it for their CloudFront distribution. What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does my CloudFront distribution return 403 Access Denied from S3?

Almost always the bucket policy. With Origin Access Control the bucket stays private and must explicitly allow the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal to call s3:GetObject, normally with an AWS:SourceArn condition naming the distribution, and a mismatch there denies every request. Two other causes worth checking: S3 static website hosting enabled alongside OAC, which creates a public HTTP endpoint that bypasses the signing, and an object that genuinely does not exist, since S3 returns 403 rather than 404 when the caller lacks list permission.
How do I improve my CloudFront cache hit ratio?

Reduce what is in the cache key. Forwarding all query strings, cookies or headers creates a separate cache entry per combination, so identical content is fetched repeatedly. Tracking parameters such as utm_source are the classic cause. Set QueryStringBehavior to none for static assets, forward only the parameters that genuinely change the response, and set long Cache-Control max-age values at the origin. The Managed-CachingOptimized policy is a good default for static content.
What is the difference between OAC and OAI?

Origin Access Identity was the original way to keep an S3 bucket private while letting CloudFront read it. Origin Access Control replaces it and is what you should use for anything new: it supports SSE-KMS encrypted objects, all HTTP methods rather than just GET and HEAD, and signs requests with SigV4 scoped to a specific distribution. OAI still works for existing distributions, which is why plenty of older tutorials use it, but there is no reason to choose it today.
How much do CloudFront invalidations cost?

The first 1,000 paths each month are free, and each path after that is charged. A wildcard such as /* counts as a single path, which makes it cheaper than enumerating hundreds of files but slower to propagate, often several minutes. The wider point is that regular invalidation indicates a caching strategy problem: fingerprinted asset filenames combined with non-cached HTML means new deployments are picked up immediately with no invalidation at all.
Why is CloudFront still serving old content after I deployed?

Because the cached object has not expired, which is CloudFront working as configured rather than a fault. Check the Cache-Control header your origin returns, if it says max-age=86400, the edge will hold that object for a day regardless of what you uploaded. The durable fix is content hashing: give built assets names containing a content hash so a new build produces new URLs, and serve the HTML that references them with max-age=0, must-revalidate.
How do I make a single-page application work on CloudFront?

Add custom error responses mapping both 403 and 404 to /index.html with a response code of 200, so client-side routes resolve instead of failing. Both codes are needed because S3 with OAC returns 403 for a missing key rather than 404. Also lower ErrorCachingMinTTL from its five-minute default, otherwise a brief origin problem is cached and served as an error well after the origin has recovered.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

keyConcepts.explanation: Create a CloudFront distribution step by step. Learn behavior precedence, multiple origins, origin groups for failover and Functions vs Lambda@Edge.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create a CloudFront distribution step by step. Learn behavior precedence, multiple origins, origin groups for failover and Functions vs Lambda@Edge.

sections.title: CloudFront Distributions
paragraphs: A distribution is the CloudFront resource itself: the domain name clients hit, the origins it fetches from, and the behaviours deciding how each path is handled. One distribution can front an entire application. Static assets from S3, an API from an ALB, images from a separate bucket, under a single hostname.

sections.title: Creating one
paragraphs: CallerReference is an idempotency token. Reuse the same value and you get the existing distribution rather than a duplicate, which is useful in scripts.
That CachePolicyId is the managed CachingOptimized policy. Use managed policy IDs rather than writing your own unless you genuinely need something different.
DefaultRootObject is what gets served for /. Omitting it means a request to the root returns a directory listing attempt or a 403, which is a five-minute confusion for everyone who forgets it.
Deployment takes a few minutes:

sections.title: Behaviours and precedence
paragraphs: Behaviours map path patterns to origins and caching rules. They are evaluated in order, and the first match wins. Exactly like ALB listener rules, and the source of the same class of bug.
Order matters: put /api/auth/* before /api/* or it will never be reached. The DefaultCacheBehavior is always evaluated last, catching anything unmatched.

Two IDs in that API behaviour do specific jobs. 4135ea2d… is managed CachingDisabled. An API response should not be cached by path alone. 216adef6… is AllViewerExceptHostHeader, which forwards the headers and cookies your API needs (including Authorization) without including them in the cache key. Confusing cache policies with origin request policies is a common mistake: the first decides what forms the cache key, the second decides what reaches the origin.
Also note AllowedMethods. A behaviour permitting only GET and HEAD rejects a POST with a 403, which reads like an authentication failure and is not.

sections.title: Multiple origins and failover
paragraphs: An origin group gives you automatic failover on specified status codes:

Point a behaviour at the group rather than at an origin. Failover triggers on those status codes, connection failures and timeouts, but only for GET, HEAD and OPTIONS, so it does not protect write paths. For anything more sophisticated, Route 53 health-check-based failover is the better tool.

sections.title: Price class
paragraphs: A restricted price class does not make your site unavailable elsewhere. Requests are served from the nearest included edge, so users in Sydney are served from the US with correspondingly higher latency. If your audience is regional, PriceClass_100 is a genuine saving with no functional loss.

codeBlock.code: "PriceClass": "PriceClass_100"

sections.title: Edge functions
paragraphs: Two options, and they are not interchangeable:
CloudFront Functions handle header manipulation, URL rewrites and redirects. The vast majority of real edge logic:
That five-line function is the standard fix for serving a static site with clean directory URLs.
Use Lambda@Edge only when you need to call another service, read a request body, or act on origin responses.

sections.title: Updating a distribution safely
paragraphs: update-distribution replaces the entire configuration. There is no partial update, and omitting a field removes it. The safe procedure is read, modify, write, with the ETag for optimistic locking:
Forgetting --if-match fails; a stale ETag also fails, which is the point. It stops you overwriting someone else's concurrent change.
For risky changes, use a staging distribution with continuous deployment to send a small share of traffic to the new configuration before promoting it:

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudfront get-distribution-config --id E1ABCDEFGHIJKL > dist.json
ETAG=$(python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open('dist.json'))['ETag'])")
python3 -c "
import json
d = json.load(open('dist.json'))['DistributionConfig']
d['Comment'] = 'updated comment'
json.dump(d, open('config.json','w'))
"
aws cloudfront update-distribution --id E1ABCDEFGHIJKL \
  --distribution-config file://config.json --if-match "$ETAG"

sections.title: Deleting one
paragraphs: Deletion needs two steps, and the first is easy to forget:
A Terraform destroy on a distribution takes a surprisingly long time for exactly this reason.

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Disable, and wait for it to finish deploying
aws cloudfront update-distribution --id E1ABCDEFGHIJKL \
  --distribution-config file://disabled.json --if-match "$ETAG"
aws cloudfront wait distribution-deployed --id E1ABCDEFGHIJKL

# 2. Then delete
aws cloudfront delete-distribution --id E1ABCDEFGHIJKL --if-match "$NEW_ETAG"

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Missing or stale --if-match. Re-read the config to get the current ETag.
Disable it and wait for deployment before deleting.
DefaultRootObject must be an object name such as index.html, with no leading slash.
POST returning 403. The matched behaviour's AllowedMethods excludes POST.

codeBlock.code: PreconditionFailed: The request failed because it didn't meet the preconditions

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A distribution has a behaviour for /api/auth/* pointing at an auth origin, listed after an existing /api/* behaviour. Requests to /api/auth/login keep reaching the general API origin. Why?
After running update-distribution with a hand-written config containing only the fields being changed, several unrelated settings were reset to defaults. What went wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How does CloudFront decide which cache behaviour applies?

It evaluates the configured behaviours in order and uses the first whose path pattern matches the request URI, falling back to DefaultCacheBehavior if none do. That means ordering is significant: a broad pattern such as /api/* placed before /api/auth/* means the more specific behaviour is never reached. When a behaviour appears to be ignored, list the behaviours in order before investigating anything else. This is the same precedence model as ALB listener rules.
What is the difference between a cache policy and an origin request policy?

A cache policy decides what forms the cache key, which query strings, headers and cookies make one request different from another, and therefore what gets cached separately. An origin request policy decides what is forwarded to the origin, independent of the cache key. That separation is what lets you send an Authorization header to your API without fragmenting the cache per user. Using CachingDisabled with AllViewerExceptHostHeader is the standard combination for a dynamic API behaviour.
Should I use CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge?

CloudFront Functions for anything that only inspects and rewrites the request or response. Appending index.html to directory URLs, adding security headers, redirecting, normalising a cache key. They run in under a millisecond, cost roughly a sixth as much, and are JavaScript only with no network access. Lambda@Edge is for the cases Functions cannot handle: calling another service, reading a request body, or acting on origin request and response events.
Does a restricted price class make my site unavailable in some regions?

No. A narrower price class removes the more expensive edge locations from consideration, so a viewer in a region you excluded is served from the nearest included location instead. Correctly, just with higher latency. PriceClass_100 covers North America and Europe and is a genuine saving if that is where your audience is. Nothing is blocked, and you can change the class at any time.
Why does my POST request to CloudFront return 403?

Because the matched cache behaviour does not allow the POST method. AllowedMethods defaults to GET and HEAD, and CloudFront rejects anything else with a 403 before the request reaches your origin, which reads like an authentication problem and is not. For a behaviour fronting an API, allow all seven methods, and pair it with the CachingDisabled cache policy since responses to writes should not be cached.
Why does deleting a CloudFront distribution take so long?

Because it is two operations. A distribution must be disabled first, and that change propagates to every edge location before the distribution reaches the Deployed state again, typically several minutes. Only then will delete-distribution accept it. Attempting to delete an enabled distribution returns DistributionNotDisabled. This is also why a terraform destroy involving CloudFront appears to hang: it is waiting through exactly the same sequence.

Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS CloudFront SSL and Custom Domains must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Serve CloudFront on your own domain over HTTPS: request the ACM certificate in us-east-1, validate with DNS, add the alias record and pick a security policy.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Serve CloudFront on your own domain over HTTPS: request the ACM certificate in us-east-1, validate with DNS, add the alias record and pick a security policy.

sections.title: CloudFront SSL and Custom Domains
paragraphs: By default a distribution answers on d1234abcd.cloudfront.net with a certificate AWS provides. Putting it on your own domain over HTTPS takes three things: a certificate in the right region, the domain registered on the distribution, and DNS pointing at it.
The one rule to remember before anything else: the ACM certificate must be in us-east-1.

sections.title: The us-east-1 requirement
paragraphs: CloudFront is a global service whose control plane runs in us-east-1, and it can only attach certificates from that region. This holds regardless of where your bucket, load balancer or anything else lives.

What makes this trip so many people is the failure mode: a certificate in the wrong region is perfectly valid, validates successfully, and simply does not appear in CloudFront's list of choices. Nothing reports an error. If you already have one elsewhere for an ALB, leave it and request a second in us-east-1. ACM certificates are free, and there is no downside to holding both.
Request the wildcard alongside the apex. *.example.com covers www and any future subdomain but not example.com itself, which is why both are listed above.

codeBlock.code:
aws acm request-certificate --region us-east-1 \
  --domain-name example.com \
  --subject-alternative-names 'www.example.com' '*.example.com' \
  --validation-method DNS \
  --query CertificateArn --output text

sections.title: DNS validation
paragraphs: Create that CNAME. In Route 53 one command does it:

Prefer DNS validation over email. It completes in minutes without anyone reading a mailbox, and, the part that matters long term, ACM renews automatically for as long as the validation record stays in place. Deleting that CNAME after validation is a quiet way to break renewal a year later. Leave it.
A certificate stuck in PENDING_VALIDATION is nearly always a missing trailing dot, a record created in the wrong hosted zone, or a subdomain zone that is delegated elsewhere.

codeBlock.code:
aws acm describe-certificate --region us-east-1 \
  --certificate-arn "$CERT_ARN" \
  --query 'Certificate.DomainValidationOptions[].[DomainName,ResourceRecord.Name,ResourceRecord.Value]' \
  --output table

sections.title: Attaching the domain
paragraphs: Two things must both be set: the alternate domain name (CNAME) and the certificate.
CloudFront verifies that the certificate covers every alias, and rejects the update otherwise. Every name in Aliases must be in the certificate's subject or SANs.

sni-only is what you want. The alternative, vip, assigns dedicated IP addresses at a substantial monthly cost per distribution, and exists only for clients too old to support SNI. A population that no longer meaningfully exists.

codeBlock.code:
"Aliases": { "Quantity": 2, "Items": ["example.com", "www.example.com"] },
"ViewerCertificate": {
  "ACMCertificateArn": "arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:123456789012:certificate/…",
  "SSLSupportMethod": "sni-only",
  "MinimumProtocolVersion": "TLSv1.2_2021",
  "CertificateSource": "acm"
}

sections.title: DNS to the distribution
paragraphs: For an apex domain, a CNAME is not allowed by the DNS specification. Route 53's alias record solves this:
Z2FDTNDATAQYW2 is the fixed hosted zone ID for CloudFront. The same for every distribution in every account. Alias records also cost nothing to query, unlike CNAMEs.
Add an AAAA alias with the same target so IPv6 clients resolve too. Forgetting it produces intermittent failures for exactly the users who have IPv6, which is a confusing report to receive.
Outside Route 53, use a CNAME for subdomains and whatever apex-flattening your provider offers (ALIAS, ANAME, or CNAME flattening) for the apex.

sections.title: Security policy
paragraphs: The minimum protocol version sets which TLS versions and ciphers CloudFront accepts from viewers. TLSv1.2_2021 is a sensible modern floor; TLS 1.0 and 1.1 policies still exist and fail most compliance scans. Raising it drops genuinely ancient clients, which is the trade you are making deliberately.
Note it only applies when you use a custom domain with sni-only. On the default *.cloudfront.net name, AWS controls the policy.

codeBlock.code: "MinimumProtocolVersion": "TLSv1.2_2021"

sections.title: Origin-side TLS
paragraphs: The viewer-to-CloudFront leg and the CloudFront-to-origin leg are configured separately, and leaving the second as plain HTTP is a common oversight:
https-only is the right choice for any custom origin. match-viewer sounds appealing and means an HTTP viewer request travels to your origin unencrypted, so avoid it.

The origin's certificate must be publicly trusted and match the origin's domain name. CloudFront will not accept a self-signed certificate, and there is no option to skip verification. A 502 immediately after switching to https-only is usually this.
S3 origins do not need any of it: CloudFront always uses HTTPS to S3.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Almost always the region. Re-request in us-east-1.
That alias is on another distribution, possibly in a different account. CloudFront enforces global uniqueness of alternate domain names. Remove it from the old distribution first.
An alias is missing from the certificate's SANs. Note *.example.com does not cover example.com.
Usually DNS pointing at the distribution before the alias and certificate were attached, so CloudFront answers with its default certificate, which does not match the hostname requested.

codeBlock.code:
InvalidViewerCertificate: The specified SSL certificate doesn't exist,
isn't in us-east-1 region, isn't valid, or doesn't include a valid
certificate chain.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: DNS for shop.example.com was pointed at a CloudFront distribution, but browsers report ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR. The distribution works fine on its cloudfront.net name. What was missed?
An ACM certificate validated by DNS a year ago has failed to renew, and the team tidied up "unused" DNS records a few months back. What happened?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why must a CloudFront certificate be in us-east-1?

Because CloudFront is a global service whose control plane lives in that region, and it can only read ACM certificates from there. It applies no matter where the rest of your infrastructure runs. The confusing part is the failure mode: a certificate requested in another region validates normally and is perfectly usable by regional services such as an ALB, but simply never appears in CloudFront's list, with no error explaining why. Request a separate one in us-east-1; ACM certificates are free.
How do I point my apex domain at CloudFront?

The DNS specification forbids a CNAME at the zone apex, so use a Route 53 alias record of type A pointing at the distribution's domain name, with hosted zone ID Z2FDTNDATAQYW2. The same value for every CloudFront distribution. Add an AAAA alias with the same target so IPv6 clients resolve too. Outside Route 53, use whatever apex flattening your DNS provider offers, commonly called ALIAS, ANAME or CNAME flattening.
Why does CloudFront say CNAMEAlreadyExists?

Alternate domain names are globally unique across all of CloudFront, so the hostname is already attached to another distribution. Frequently an old one in the same account, sometimes one in a different account entirely. Remove the alias from the existing distribution first, wait for that change to deploy, then add it to the new one. If the other distribution is not yours, AWS Support can help verify domain ownership and release it.
Does a wildcard certificate cover my apex domain?

No. *.example.com matches www.example.com and any other single-level subdomain, but not example.com itself, and not a.b.example.com. Request both names on one certificate: --domain-name example.com --subject-alternative-names '*.example.com'. CloudFront validates that the certificate covers every entry in Aliases, so a missing apex is rejected at configuration time rather than causing a mysterious runtime error.
Should I use sni-only or a dedicated IP?

sni-only, essentially always. Server Name Indication lets many distributions share addresses by sending the requested hostname during the TLS handshake, and every browser and client in current use supports it. The dedicated IP option (vip) costs a significant monthly fee per distribution and exists only for clients predating SNI, which in practice means Windows XP and similar. There is no performance or security advantage to it.
Do I need HTTPS between CloudFront and my origin?

Yes for a custom origin. Set OriginProtocolPolicy to https-only. Viewer-side and origin-side TLS are configured separately, so a distribution serving HTTPS to browsers can still be fetching over plain HTTP behind the scenes. Avoid match-viewer, which forwards an HTTP viewer request to the origin unencrypted. The origin's certificate must be publicly trusted and match its hostname, since CloudFront offers no way to skip verification; a 502 right after enabling https-only is usually that. S3 origins always use HTTPS and need no configuration.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-route53.title: AWS Route 53
aws-route53.subtitle: Get DNS working on Route 53: public and private hosted zones, the delegation step people forget, alias records, health checks and how TTL sets failover speed.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Route 53 must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Get DNS working on Route 53: public and private hosted zones, the delegation step people forget, alias records, health checks and how TTL sets failover speed.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Get DNS working on Route 53: public and private hosted zones, the delegation step people forget, alias records, health checks and how TTL sets failover speed.

sections.title: Amazon Route 53
paragraphs: Route 53 is AWS's DNS service, and it does three separable jobs: registering domains, hosting zones that answer queries, and health-checking endpoints so DNS can route around failure.
Route 53: DNS Resolution
Health checks automatically remove unhealthy endpoints from DNS responses

Most confusion comes from mixing up registration and hosting. You can register a domain here and host it elsewhere, or register it elsewhere and host it here, which is the more common arrangement and the one that needs the delegation step below.

sections.title: Hosted zones
paragraphs: Those four name servers are the zone's answer to the world, and nothing works until your registrar points at them. If the domain is registered outside AWS, update the name servers at that registrar. If it is registered in Route 53, this is done for you.

Each hosted zone gets its own unique name server set. Deleting and recreating a zone produces four different names, so an accidental recreate breaks the domain until the registrar is updated again. There is also a monthly charge per hosted zone, which is why duplicate zones for the same domain are worth spotting early:
Two zones for the same domain is a genuinely common cause of "some records work and some do not", only one is authoritative, and you are editing the other.

codeBlock.code:
aws route53 create-hosted-zone --name example.com \
  --caller-reference "$(date +%s)" \
  --hosted-zone-config Comment="production"

sections.title: Alias records
paragraphs: Route 53's most useful non-standard feature. A CNAME cannot exist at a zone apex, which is a DNS protocol constraint rather than an AWS one, so example.com cannot CNAME to a load balancer. An alias record solves it:

Aliases beat CNAMEs in three ways: they work at the apex, they are free to query where CNAME lookups are billed, and EvaluateTargetHealth lets DNS respond to the target's own health without a separate health check.

The HostedZoneId inside AliasTarget is the target service's zone ID, not yours. Some are fixed values, Z2FDTNDATAQYW2 for CloudFront everywhere, while ALB and NLB ids vary by region. Read it rather than guessing:
Always create AAAA aliases alongside A ones. Skipping it breaks IPv6 clients intermittently, which produces confusing reports from a minority of users.

sections.title: TTL decides your failover speed
paragraphs: The TTL on a record is how long resolvers cache it, and it sets a floor on how quickly any DNS-based change can take effect.

Lower TTLs mean more queries and a slightly higher bill; that cost is trivial next to an hour-long outage because a record was cached for 3600 seconds. Drop the TTL to 60 before a planned migration, not during it. Lowering it at cutover time does nothing for resolvers already holding the old value.
Alias records have no TTL of their own; they inherit from the target.

sections.title: Health checks
paragraphs: Checks run from multiple AWS regions, and a target is considered unhealthy only when more than 18% of checkers agree, which prevents a single region's network problem from triggering a failover.

The practical consequence worth planning around: with RequestInterval: 30 and FailureThreshold: 3, detection takes about 90 seconds, and then resolvers still hold the old answer for the record's TTL. DNS failover is a minutes-scale mechanism, not a seconds-scale one. If you need faster, that belongs at the load balancer or in the client.

Health checks are used by routing policies to remove unhealthy endpoints from answers. Two things to watch: the endpoint must be publicly reachable, since checkers come from the internet, a private ALB needs a CloudWatch-alarm-based check instead, and your security groups must allow Route 53's published checker ranges.

codeBlock.code:
aws route53 create-health-check --caller-reference "$(date +%s)" \
  --health-check-config '{
    "Type": "HTTPS",
    "FullyQualifiedDomainName": "origin.example.com",
    "ResourcePath": "/healthz",
    "Port": 443,
    "RequestInterval": 30,
    "FailureThreshold": 3,
    "MeasureLatency": true
  }'

sections.title: Private hosted zones
paragraphs: A zone that resolves only inside associated VPCs:
The VPC needs both enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames set, and a private zone that resolves nowhere is usually one of those being off:

You can have a public and a private zone for the same name, which is split-horizon DNS: inside the VPC, api.example.com resolves to a private address; outside, to a public one. Useful, and confusing to debug. When a record behaves differently depending on where you query from, check for a private zone shadowing the public one.
For resolution between a VPC and on-premises networks, Route 53 Resolver endpoints handle it in both directions.

codeBlock.code:
aws route53 create-hosted-zone --name internal.example.com \
  --caller-reference "$(date +%s)" \
  --vpc VPCRegion=eu-west-1,VPCId=vpc-0abc123 \
  --hosted-zone-config PrivateZone=true

sections.title: Debugging DNS
paragraphs: Ask Route 53 what it would answer, bypassing every cache:
That distinguishes "the record is wrong" from "the record is right and something is caching". Then compare with the outside world:
If test-dns-answer returns the right value and dig does not, the problem is delegation, a duplicate zone, or caching, not your record.

codeBlock.code:
aws route53 test-dns-answer --hosted-zone-id Z1ABCDEFGHIJKL \
  --record-name api.example.com --record-type A

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Use UPSERT rather than CREATE.
Delete every record except the zone's own NS and SOA before deleting the zone.
Records look right, nothing resolves. The registrar is not pointing at this zone's name servers, or there is a second hosted zone for the same domain.

codeBlock.code:
InvalidChangeBatch: RRSet of type CNAME with DNS name example.com. is not
permitted at apex in zone example.com.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A hosted zone for example.com has correct A records, and test-dns-answer returns the right values. From anywhere else, the domain does not resolve at all. What is wrong?
A failover record set with a 30-second health check interval and failure threshold of 3 took roughly fifteen minutes to move traffic during an outage. The record TTL is 900 seconds. Why so slow?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why isn't my Route 53 hosted zone resolving?

Check delegation first. Every hosted zone is assigned four unique name servers, and the domain's registrar must point at exactly those, dig NS example.com shows what the internet is actually being told. The second common cause is duplicate hosted zones for the same domain, where delegation points at one and your records are in the other; list-hosted-zones reveals it. Use test-dns-answer to confirm the zone itself holds the right values, which separates a record problem from a delegation problem.
What is the difference between an alias record and a CNAME?

An alias is a Route 53 extension that points at an AWS resource and is resolved internally, so it can exist at the zone apex where a CNAME cannot, costs nothing to query, and can reflect the target's health via EvaluateTargetHealth. A CNAME is standard DNS, works anywhere except the apex, is billed per query, and simply returns another name for the client to resolve. For AWS targets, ALB, CloudFront, S3 website endpoints, API Gateway, an alias is almost always the right choice.
How do I point my apex domain at a load balancer?

With an alias record, because the DNS specification does not allow a CNAME at the apex. Create an A record for example.com with an AliasTarget whose DNSName is the load balancer's DNS name and whose HostedZoneId is the load balancer's canonical hosted zone ID. Read it from describe-load-balancers --query 'LoadBalancers[0].CanonicalHostedZoneId' rather than guessing, since it differs by region. Add an AAAA alias with the same target for IPv6 clients.
How long does Route 53 failover take?

Longer than most people expect: detection plus caching. Three failed checks at 30-second intervals is about 90 seconds, and the endpoint is only marked unhealthy once more than 18% of Route 53's distributed checkers agree. After that, resolvers continue serving the cached record until its TTL expires. With a 300-second TTL, total failover time is around six or seven minutes. Set TTLs to 60 on records you may need to fail over, and use load balancer health checks where you need sub-minute recovery.
What is a private hosted zone and when would I use one?

A hosted zone that answers only within the VPCs you associate with it, so internal names never appear in public DNS. It is how you give internal services stable names such as db.internal.example.com without exposing your topology. The VPC needs enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames both enabled, which is the usual reason one appears not to work. You can also run a private zone for the same name as a public one, split-horizon DNS, so a hostname resolves to a private address inside and a public one outside.
Why does a record resolve differently inside my VPC than outside?

Almost certainly a private hosted zone for the same domain name associated with that VPC. Route 53 prefers the private zone for queries from inside, so it shadows the public zone entirely for any name it contains, including names it does not define, since the private zone is authoritative for the whole domain. That is split-horizon DNS working as designed, and it is worth checking early whenever DNS behaves differently depending on where you query it from.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create the Route 53 record types you will use: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, CAA and SRV. Covers UPSERT semantics, SPF and DMARC records and common errors.

sections.title: Route 53 Records
paragraphs: A hosted zone is a collection of record sets. Route 53 calls them "record sets" rather than records because one entry can hold several values. An A record with three addresses is one record set, not three records, and that distinction matters when you update them.

sections.title: The change batch API
paragraphs: Every write goes through change-resource-record-sets with a batch of changes, applied atomically:

Use UPSERT, not CREATE. CREATE fails if the record exists, which makes scripts non-idempotent; UPSERT creates or replaces. DELETE requires the record's exact current contents: value, TTL and all, which is why deleting is fiddlier than it looks and another reason to prefer UPSERT.
Because a batch is atomic, one invalid change rejects the whole thing. That is useful: a coordinated cutover of several records happens together or not at all.
Multiple values go in one record set, and DNS returns them in rotating order. Crude round-robin with no health awareness:

sections.title: A and AAAA
paragraphs: If you publish an AAAA record, the service behind it must work over IPv6. Clients with IPv6 connectivity prefer it, so a broken AAAA record produces slow or failing requests for a subset of users while everyone else is fine. One of the more frustrating reports to receive.

sections.title: CNAME, and where it cannot go
paragraphs: Two rules, both from the DNS specification rather than AWS:
No CNAME at the zone apex. example.com cannot be a CNAME, because the apex must hold SOA and NS records and a CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name. Route 53 rejects it explicitly:
Use an alias record instead.

A CNAME cannot share a name with any other record type. So www cannot be both a CNAME and hold a TXT record, which matters when a service asks you to add a verification TXT record on a hostname that is already a CNAME.

codeBlock.code:
{"Name": "www.example.com", "Type": "CNAME", "TTL": 300,
 "ResourceRecords": [{"Value": "example.com"}]}

sections.title: MX, and the mail records that go with it
paragraphs: The number is priority, lowest first. A frequent misreading, since "highest priority" means the smallest number.
Mail needs three more records, and getting them wrong is why your application's email lands in spam:

Only one SPF record per domain. Two TXT records both starting v=spf1 is a permanent error that silently breaks authentication. Combine them into one with multiple include: terms. Note the maximum of ten DNS lookups in an SPF record, which several include: entries can exceed.
Start DMARC at p=none with rua= reporting to see what is being sent as you, then tighten to quarantine and reject once legitimate senders are covered.

sections.title: TXT records and quoting
paragraphs: TXT values must be quoted, and those quotes are part of the value, so in a shell-embedded JSON payload they need escaping, which is where most TXT mistakes come from:
A single string is limited to 255 characters. Longer values are split into multiple quoted strings which receivers concatenate. DKIM keys frequently need this:
Get the quoting wrong and the record exists, looks plausible in the console, and fails validation with no useful error from whichever service is checking it.

codeBlock.code: {"Value": "\"v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all\""}

sections.title: CAA
paragraphs: Restricts which certificate authorities may issue for your domain:

Worth setting, with one caution: a CAA record that omits your CA blocks issuance and renewal. If ACM certificates suddenly fail to validate, check whether someone added a CAA record without including amazon.com.

sections.title: SRV
paragraphs: The four fields are priority, weight, port and target. Used by SIP, XMPP, Minecraft and Kubernetes service discovery.

codeBlock.code:
{"Name": "_sip._tcp.example.com", "Type": "SRV", "TTL": 300,
 "ResourceRecords": [{"Value": "10 60 5060 sipserver.example.com"}]}

sections.title: Listing and auditing
paragraphs: That second query is worth running before any planned cutover. It tells you which records will keep serving stale answers, and for how long.

codeBlock.code:
aws route53 list-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z1ABCDEFGHIJKL \
  --query 'ResourceRecordSets[].[Name,Type,TTL,ResourceRecords[0].Value]' \
  --output table

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: CREATE on an existing record. Use UPSERT.
DELETE needs the exact current value and TTL. Read it with list-resource-record-sets first.
A CNAME cannot coexist with another type at the same name.

codeBlock.code:
InvalidChangeBatch: RRSet of type CNAME with DNS name example.com. is not
permitted at apex in zone example.com.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A domain has one TXT record with "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all" and a second with "v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all". Mail from SES is failing authentication. Why?
A SaaS provider asks for a TXT verification record at www.example.com. That name is already a CNAME to the application. Route 53 refuses to create the TXT record. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between CREATE, UPSERT and DELETE in a change batch?

CREATE adds a record and fails if one already exists with that name and type, which makes scripts non-idempotent. UPSERT creates the record or replaces it entirely, so re-running a deployment is safe. It is the action to use by default. DELETE removes a record but requires you to supply its exact current contents, including every value and the TTL, so it usually means reading the record first. Batches are applied atomically, so an invalid change rejects the whole submission.
Why can't I create a CNAME at my apex domain?

Because the DNS specification forbids it. The zone apex must carry SOA and NS records, and a CNAME cannot coexist with any other record type at the same name, so an apex CNAME is impossible in any DNS system, not just Route 53. The Route 53 answer is an alias record, which behaves like a CNAME pointing at an AWS resource but is resolved internally and returns an address, so it is legal at the apex. It is also free to query and can reflect the target's health.
How do I set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC in Route 53?

SPF is a single TXT record at the apex listing permitted senders, and it must be exactly one record, with multiple include: terms rather than multiple records, since two v=spf1 records is a permanent error. DKIM is normally a set of CNAMEs your mail provider gives you, pointing at keys they host. DMARC is a TXT record at _dmarc.example.com; start at p=none with a rua= reporting address to see what is being sent as your domain, then tighten to quarantine and reject.
Why is my TXT record not being recognised?

Usually quoting. The value must include literal double quotes, which means escaping them inside a JSON change batch, "\"v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all\"". Get it wrong and the record exists, looks plausible, and fails whatever validation is checking it. The other cause is length: a single TXT string is capped at 255 characters, so a longer value such as a DKIM public key must be split into multiple quoted strings within the same record, which receivers concatenate.
What does the number in an MX record mean?

Priority, and lower wins, which is the opposite of how "priority" reads to most people. 1 aspmx.l.google.com is tried before 10 alt2.aspmx.l.google.com, and the higher numbers act as fallbacks. Equal numbers share traffic. All of a domain's MX values belong in a single record set with one value per line, not as separate record sets, since they collectively describe where mail for that domain should go.
Should I add a CAA record?

Yes, with care. A CAA record restricts which certificate authorities may issue certificates for your domain, which limits the damage from a mis-issued certificate. The caution is that omitting a CA you use blocks issuance and renewal, so if you use ACM, include amazon.com and amazontrust.com, and add any other authority in use before publishing the record. Sudden unexplained ACM validation failures are worth checking against CAA before anything else.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Choose a Route 53 routing policy: weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity or multivalue. Learn the Set Identifier rule and why canaries drift.

sections.title: Route 53 Routing Policies
paragraphs: A routing policy decides which answer Route 53 returns when several records share a name. That is how one hostname can serve different users differently, by region, by health, or by a weighting you control.

sections.title: Set Identifier is mandatory
paragraphs: Any policy other than simple requires a SetIdentifier. A unique label distinguishing records that share a name and type. Omitting it is the first error everyone hits:
Route 53 is telling you it cannot hold two records with the same name and type unless each carries a distinct identifier.

codeBlock.code:
InvalidChangeBatch: RRSet of type A with DNS name api.example.com. is not
permitted because a conflicting RRSet exists

sections.title: Weighted
paragraphs: Splits traffic by proportion. The workhorse for canaries and blue-green cutovers:

Weights are relative, not percentages. They are divided by the total, so 90 and 10 gives 90%, and so does 900 and 100. Weight 0 removes a record from consideration unless every record is 0, in which case all are eligible. Setting one side to 0 is the clean way to complete a cutover without deleting anything.
Two caveats worth knowing before you trust a 10% canary.

The split is per DNS query, not per request. A client that resolves once and keeps a connection open sends everything to whichever answer it got, so a small sample can skew badly. Keep TTLs low and give the canary time.

Resolvers cache and clients pool. Real distribution converges on the weights over time but is genuinely noisy at short timescales, which is why weighted DNS is a reasonable canary mechanism and a poor traffic-shaping one. If you need precise percentages, do it at the load balancer with weighted target groups.

sections.title: Failover
paragraphs: An active-passive pair driven by a health check:

The primary must have a health check: either an explicit HealthCheckId or EvaluateTargetHealth on an alias. Without one it is always considered healthy and failover never occurs, which is a configuration that looks complete and does nothing.
The secondary does not need one, and a static S3 maintenance page is a good choice for it: it will be serving precisely when everything else is broken, so it should depend on as little as possible.
Remember the timing from the Route 53 overview: detection is around 90 seconds and cached TTLs add their own delay.

sections.title: Latency
paragraphs: Routes each client to the region with the lowest measured latency from their resolver:
Note Region is an AWS region name, and Route 53 uses its own latency measurements rather than geographic distance, which is usually better, since network paths do not follow maps.

The subtlety: latency is measured to the resolver, not the end user. A client using a distant public resolver can be routed to a distant region. Usually minor, and occasionally the explanation for a puzzling report.

codeBlock.code:
{"Name": "api.example.com", "Type": "A", "SetIdentifier": "eu-west-1",
 "Region": "eu-west-1", "TTL": 60, "ResourceRecords": [{"Value": "203.0.113.10"}]}

sections.title: Geolocation
paragraphs: Routes by where the client appears to be, which is about compliance and content, not performance:
Most specific wins: a German client matches the DE record over the EU one.

Always create a * default record. Without it, a client whose location Route 53 cannot determine receives no answer at all: not a fallback, a NODATA response. This is the most common geolocation mistake and it fails for exactly the users you cannot easily reproduce.
Use geolocation for data residency and licensing. For performance, use latency routing.

sections.title: Geoproximity
paragraphs: Routes by geographic distance, with a bias that expands or shrinks a resource's catchment area:

A positive bias pulls in traffic from further away; a negative one pushes it out. That is the feature. It lets you shift load toward a region with spare capacity without changing anything else. It is the only policy that needs traffic flow policies in the console for the visual editor, though the API works directly.

codeBlock.code:
{"Name": "api.example.com", "Type": "A", "SetIdentifier": "eu-central",
 "GeoProximityLocation": {"AWSRegion": "eu-central-1", "Bias": 40}, …}

sections.title: Multivalue answer
paragraphs: Returns up to eight healthy records at random, with health checking that simple routing lacks:

The difference from a simple record with multiple values is exactly that health awareness: a simple multi-value record keeps returning a dead address, while multivalue omits records whose health check is failing.

It is not a load balancer. There is no connection distribution or session handling, and clients choose from the list themselves. It suits many equivalent endpoints where a real load balancer is unnecessary.

sections.title: Choosing
paragraphs: Policies can be nested through traffic flow, latency routing to pick a region, then weighted within it for a canary, which is where geoproximity's visual editor earns its place.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Missing or duplicate SetIdentifier.
The primary needs a health check or EvaluateTargetHealth.
Geolocation returns nothing for some users. No CountryCode: "*" default record.
Weighted split does not match the weights. Caching and connection reuse. Expect convergence over time, not precision.

codeBlock.code:
InvalidChangeBatch: RRSet of type A with DNS name api.example.com. is not
permitted because a conflicting RRSet exists

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A failover record set has a PRIMARY pointing at an ALB and a SECONDARY pointing at an S3 maintenance page. The primary ALB is down, but traffic keeps going to it. Both records have SetIdentifiers. What is missing?
Geolocation routing sends EU clients to one region and US clients to another. A small number of users report the domain not resolving at all, rather than resolving to the wrong place. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between latency-based and geolocation routing?

Latency routing sends a client to whichever AWS region Route 53 has measured as fastest for their resolver, so it optimises performance and can send a European user to a US region if the network path happens to be better. Geolocation routing sends them strictly by where they appear to be, regardless of speed, which is what you need for data residency, licensing or language. Use latency for performance and geolocation for compliance, and note that only geolocation guarantees which region serves a given country.
How do I do a canary or blue-green deployment with Route 53?

Weighted routing. Create two records with the same name and type, distinct SetIdentifier values, and weights in the ratio you want: 95 and 5 to start. Shift the weights gradually and set one to 0 to complete the cutover, which removes it from consideration without deleting anything. Keep TTLs at 60 so changes take effect quickly. Bear in mind that weights apply per DNS query rather than per request, so short observations are noisy; for precise percentages use weighted target groups on an ALB instead.
Why do my weighted records not split traffic in the ratio I set?

Because weighting applies to DNS answers, not requests. A resolver caches the answer for the TTL and serves it to everyone behind it, and a client that resolves once then reuses a connection sends all its traffic to whichever endpoint it got. Distribution converges on the configured ratio over time but is genuinely uneven at short timescales, especially with large corporate resolvers. Lower TTLs help. For accurate traffic splitting, do it at the load balancer.
What does Set Identifier do in Route 53?

It distinguishes records that share the same name and type, which is what makes any non-simple routing policy possible. Route 53 otherwise refuses to store two A records for api.example.com. The value is an arbitrary label, so use something meaningful like blue, green, eu-west-1 or primary. Omitting it produces a "conflicting RRSet exists" error, which is the most common first error when moving from simple to weighted or failover routing.
When should I use multivalue answer instead of simple routing?

When you have several equivalent endpoints and want unhealthy ones removed from the answers. A simple record holding multiple values returns all of them regardless of state, so a dead address keeps being handed out; multivalue attaches a health check per record and omits the failing ones, returning up to eight at random. It is not a load balancer. There is no connection distribution and clients pick from the list themselves, but it is a cheap improvement over round-robin A records.
What is geoproximity routing's bias for?

It expands or contracts the geographic area a resource serves. A positive bias draws traffic from further away, a negative one pushes nearby traffic to another resource, so you can shift load toward a region with spare capacity, or away from one under pressure, without touching the application. That gradual adjustment is the distinguishing feature versus geolocation, which assigns whole countries or continents. Geoproximity is also where the traffic flow visual editor in the console is genuinely useful.
