Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Learn DynamoDB if you know SQL: partition and sort keys, designing for access patterns first, avoiding hot partitions, conditional writes, streams and TTL.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn DynamoDB if you know SQL: partition and sort keys, designing for access patterns first, avoiding hot partitions, conditional writes, streams and TTL.

sections.title: Amazon DynamoDB
paragraphs: DynamoDB is a managed key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency at effectively any scale. There are no servers, no connection pools and no version upgrades.
DynamoDB: Data Access Model
Query uses an index (fast); Scan reads every item (expensive at scale)

The price of that is a genuine change in how you design. In a relational database you model the data and write whatever queries you need later. In DynamoDB you list your access patterns first and design the table to serve them, because a query the key schema does not support is not slow. It is impossible without scanning the entire table.
If you take one thing from this page: write down your queries before you create the table.

sections.title: Keys decide everything
paragraphs: The partition key (HASH) is hashed to choose which physical partition holds the item. The sort key (RANGE) orders items within that partition, and is what makes range queries possible.
Together they form the primary key and must be unique. A partition key alone is a simple primary key; with a sort key it is composite.
What you can do efficiently:

A query always requires an exact partition key value. "All orders over £100 last month, any customer" is not a query. It is a scan of the whole table, and that is a design problem rather than a tuning problem. Either add a global secondary index or accept that this data belongs in something relational.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb create-table --table-name Orders \
  --attribute-definitions \
    AttributeName=customerId,AttributeType=S \
    AttributeName=orderDate,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema \
    AttributeName=customerId,KeyType=HASH \
    AttributeName=orderDate,KeyType=RANGE \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

sections.title: Choose the partition key for distribution
paragraphs: Data is spread across partitions by the hash of the partition key, so a key with few distinct values concentrates traffic on one partition. That is a hot partition, and it throttles at roughly 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second no matter how much capacity the table has overall.

The symptom is throttling while CloudWatch shows consumed capacity well below provisioned. If a low-cardinality key is unavoidable, write sharding helps, append a random suffix (ORDER#2026-09-16#3) and query all shards in parallel, at the cost of real complexity.

sections.title: On-demand or provisioned
paragraphs: On-demand scales instantly and charges per request. Start here: you cannot get the capacity wrong, and for spiky or unknown traffic it is also cheaper than provisioning for the peak.

Provisioned is cheaper at sustained, predictable volume, often substantially so above roughly 20% steady utilisation, and cheaper again with reserved capacity. Add auto scaling if you use it, or a traffic increase becomes throttling:

Capacity units are worth understanding, because they explain most surprising bills. One WCU is one write of up to 1 KB. One RCU is one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent reads, so the default eventually consistent read is half price. A 10 KB item costs 3 RCUs to read strongly, and 10 WCUs to write.
Transactional reads and writes cost double.

codeBlock.code: aws dynamodb update-table --table-name Orders --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

sections.title: Consistency
paragraphs: Reads are eventually consistent by default, which means a read immediately after a write may return the previous value. Usually irrelevant; occasionally the source of a genuinely baffling bug in a read-after-write flow.
Strongly consistent reads cost twice as much and are not available on global secondary indexes at all. A constraint that occasionally decides a design.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb get-item --table-name Orders \
  --key '{"customerId":{"S":"C-4821"},"orderDate":{"S":"2026-09-16"}}' \
  --consistent-read

sections.title: Conditional writes
paragraphs: The mechanism that makes concurrent access safe, and the one to reach for when building anything idempotent:
That error is the success case when you are deduplicating. It means the item already existed. Combined with an SQS consumer, this is how you make at-least-once delivery harmless.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb put-item --table-name Orders \
  --item '{"customerId":{"S":"C-4821"},"orderDate":{"S":"2026-09-16"},"status":{"S":"placed"}}' \
  --condition-expression 'attribute_not_exists(customerId)'

sections.title: Streams
paragraphs: A change log of every insert, update and delete, retained 24 hours and readable by Lambda. It is how you maintain an aggregate, push changes to OpenSearch, or emit a domain event without the writer knowing about the consumer. NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES costs nothing extra and lets a consumer see what actually changed.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb update-table --table-name Orders \
  --stream-specification StreamEnabled=true,StreamViewType=NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES

sections.title: TTL and backups
paragraphs: TTL deletes expired items free of charge, no write capacity consumed, which makes it far better than a scheduled cleanup job. The attribute must be a Unix epoch in seconds; milliseconds is the usual mistake, and it quietly sets expiry tens of thousands of years away. Deletion is best-effort within about 48 hours of expiry, so filter expired items in your queries rather than trusting the timing.
Point-in-time recovery gives second-level restore for 35 days. Enable it on anything you would miss.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name Sessions \
  --time-to-live-specification 'Enabled=true,AttributeName=expiresAt'

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Throttling. If consumed capacity looks low, it is a hot partition, not a capacity shortfall.
A query without an exact partition key value. Add a GSI or rethink the access pattern.
Every item must carry both key attributes. DynamoDB has no schema beyond the keys, but the keys are mandatory.

codeBlock.code: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A table provisioned for 2,000 WCU is throttling writes, while CloudWatch shows consumed write capacity around 400. The partition key is orderStatus, with values pending, shipped and delivered. What is happening?
A table has partition key customerId and sort key orderDate. The team needs "all orders over £100 placed last month, across all customers". What is the correct assessment?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: When should I use DynamoDB instead of RDS?

Choose DynamoDB when your access patterns are known and key-based, you need predictable single-digit millisecond latency at high scale, and you would rather not manage a database. Choose a relational database when queries are ad hoc, you need joins and aggregations, or reporting matters. Those are precisely what DynamoDB is bad at. The deciding question is usually whether you can enumerate your queries up front: if you can, DynamoDB is excellent; if analysts will invent new ones, it will hurt.
What is the difference between a partition key and a sort key?

The partition key determines which physical partition stores an item, via a hash, so it must have high cardinality to spread load. The sort key orders items within a partition, which is what makes range queries possible. All orders for one customer between two dates, for example. A partition key alone gives you exact-match lookups only; adding a sort key gives you ordering and ranges within each partition. Together they must uniquely identify an item.
Why is DynamoDB throttling when I have provisioned capacity available?

Because capacity is provisioned per table but enforced per partition, at roughly 3,000 read and 1,000 write units each. A low-cardinality partition key concentrates traffic on a few partitions, so those throttle while table-level consumed capacity looks comfortable. Check whether your partition key has few distinct values, status, country, or a date on a write-heavy table are the classic offenders. The fix is a higher-cardinality key, or write sharding with a random suffix if the key cannot change.
Should I use on-demand or provisioned capacity?

Start with on-demand. It scales instantly, cannot be under-provisioned, and for spiky or unpredictable traffic it is genuinely cheaper than provisioning for the peak. Move to provisioned once traffic is steady and predictable, where it can cost substantially less at sustained utilisation, with reserved capacity cheaper still, and always pair it with auto scaling, otherwise growth turns into throttling. Switching between modes is a single update-table call, limited to once every 24 hours.
What is DynamoDB single-table design and do I need it?

Storing several entity types in one table, using generic key names and prefixed values such as CUSTOMER#4821 and ORDER#2026-09-16, so one query can fetch related items together. The benefit is fewer requests and no joins; the cost is a schema that is hard to read and hard to change. It is worth it at high scale with well-understood access patterns. For most applications, separate tables per entity are clearer and the extra request is not the bottleneck. Start there and consolidate only if you measure a reason to.
How does DynamoDB TTL work and why are my items not being deleted?

TTL deletes items whose specified attribute holds a past timestamp, consuming no write capacity, which makes it much better than a cleanup job. Two things commonly go wrong. The attribute must be a Unix epoch in seconds; supplying milliseconds sets expiry far in the future and nothing appears to happen. And deletion is best-effort, typically within 48 hours of expiry rather than immediately, so queries should still filter expired items rather than assuming they are gone.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create a DynamoDB table with the AWS CLI. Choose the key schema you cannot change later, enable deletion protection and PITR, and take on-demand backups.

sections.title: DynamoDB Tables
paragraphs: Creating a DynamoDB table takes one command. Getting it right matters more than usual because the key schema can never be changed, no migration, no ALTER TABLE. Changing a partition key means creating a new table and copying every item across.

Everything else, capacity mode, indexes, streams, TTL, backups, can be changed later. So the decision worth slowing down for is the keys, and that decision comes from your access patterns rather than from the shape of your data.

sections.title: Creating a table
paragraphs: ItemCount and TableSizeBytes update roughly every six hours, so a freshly loaded table reporting zero items is normal rather than a failed import.

This trips up nearly everyone coming from SQL. --attribute-definitions is not a schema. It declares the types of attributes used in keys and indexes, and nothing else. Every other attribute is arbitrary and per-item:
Nothing declared amount, items or giftNote, and the next item need not have them. The corollary is that declaring an attribute you do not use in a key is an error:
Only three key types exist: S (string), N (number) and B (binary).

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb create-table --table-name Orders \
  --attribute-definitions \
    AttributeName=customerId,AttributeType=S \
    AttributeName=orderDate,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema \
    AttributeName=customerId,KeyType=HASH \
    AttributeName=orderDate,KeyType=RANGE \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
  --deletion-protection-enabled \
  --tags Key=Environment,Value=production

sections.title: Turn on deletion protection
paragraphs: A delete-table call is immediate and takes every item with it. Deletion protection costs nothing, and it is the cheapest insurance in DynamoDB. Set it on every table that is not disposable, including in your Terraform or CloudFormation so a destroy in the wrong workspace fails loudly.

codeBlock.code: aws dynamodb update-table --table-name Orders --deletion-protection-enabled

sections.title: Backups: two different things
paragraphs: Point-in-time recovery gives continuous backup with second-level granularity for the last 35 days:
On-demand backups are explicit snapshots that live until you delete them, which is what you want before a risky migration or for retention beyond 35 days:

The constraint that surprises people: a restore always creates a new table. You cannot restore in place. Recovery therefore means restoring alongside, verifying, then repointing the application, so practise it before you need it, and note that indexes, TTL, streams and capacity settings are not all carried over automatically.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb update-continuous-backups --table-name Orders \
  --point-in-time-recovery-specification PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled=true

sections.title: Table classes
paragraphs: STANDARD_INFREQUENT_ACCESS cuts storage cost substantially and raises read and write cost. It pays off when storage dominates the bill. Audit logs, historical events, anything large and rarely read. For a table serving live traffic it usually costs more. Compare TableSizeBytes against consumed capacity before switching.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb update-table --table-name AuditLog \
  --table-class STANDARD_INFREQUENT_ACCESS

sections.title: Global tables
paragraphs: Multi-region, multi-writer replication:

Replication is asynchronous and conflicts resolve last writer wins, by the timestamp DynamoDB records. That is fine for data owned by one region at a time and wrong for anything where two regions might update the same item concurrently, a counter, an inventory level, because one update is simply discarded. Streams must be enabled, and the same key schema applies to every replica.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb update-table --table-name Orders \
  --replica-updates '[{"Create": {"RegionName": "us-east-1"}}]'

sections.title: Loading and exporting in bulk
paragraphs: Import from S3 consumes no write capacity and is dramatically cheaper than looping put-item, but it can only create a new table, not add to an existing one. Export to S3 similarly consumes no read capacity and is the right way to feed Athena or a data pipeline:
Export requires PITR to be enabled.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb import-table \
  --s3-bucket-source S3Bucket=my-imports,S3KeyPrefix=orders/ \
  --input-format DYNAMODB_JSON \
  --table-creation-parameters '{
    "TableName":"OrdersImported",
    "AttributeDefinitions":[{"AttributeName":"customerId","AttributeType":"S"}],
    "KeySchema":[{"AttributeName":"customerId","KeyType":"HASH"}],
    "BillingMode":"PAY_PER_REQUEST"
  }'

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: create-table is not idempotent. Check with describe-table first.
You declared an attribute that is not part of a key or index, or omitted one that is.
Right table name, wrong region. The most common cause by some distance. DynamoDB tables are regional.
Deletion protection is on. That is it working.

codeBlock.code: ResourceInUseException: Table already exists: Orders

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A create-table command declares attribute definitions for customerId, orderDate and amount, with customerId as HASH and orderDate as RANGE. It fails validation. Why?
A faulty deployment corrupted records over two hours. The table has point-in-time recovery enabled. What does recovery actually involve?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Can I change a DynamoDB table's partition key after creating it?

No. The key schema is fixed for the life of the table, and there is no equivalent of ALTER TABLE. Changing it means creating a new table with the new schema and copying every item across, usually by exporting to S3 and importing, which consumes no capacity, or by a Lambda reading the old table's stream during a dual-write migration. This is why enumerating access patterns before creating the table matters so much more here than with a relational database.
What is the difference between attribute definitions and a schema?

AttributeDefinitions declares the data types of attributes that participate in the key schema or an index, and nothing more. Everything else is schemaless: two items in the same table can carry completely different attributes, and nothing needs declaring in advance. That is also why declaring an attribute you do not use in a key causes a validation error. The definitions list and the key schema must correspond exactly.
What is the difference between point-in-time recovery and on-demand backups?

PITR is continuous: once enabled, you can restore to any second within the last 35 days, which is what you want for recovering from a bad deployment. On-demand backups are explicit snapshots that persist until you delete them, so they cover longer retention and deliberate checkpoints such as "before this migration". They are billed differently and serve different purposes; most production tables want PITR always on, plus on-demand backups before risky changes.
Why does describe-table show ItemCount as 0 after I loaded data?

Because ItemCount and TableSizeBytes are updated roughly every six hours rather than in real time. A freshly loaded table legitimately reports zero, and that is not a sign the import failed. For an accurate current count you would have to scan the table with --select COUNT, which consumes read capacity proportional to the table size, usually not worth it just to confirm a load succeeded.
Should I use a DynamoDB global table for multi-region?

Only if you understand the conflict behaviour. Global tables replicate asynchronously and resolve conflicts last-writer-wins, so if two regions update the same item at nearly the same moment, one update is silently discarded. That is fine when each item is effectively owned by one region, user data pinned to a home region, for example, and wrong for counters, inventory levels or anything where a lost update matters. Where it fits, it gives genuine multi-region writes with very little work.
What is the DynamoDB Standard-IA table class for?

Reducing storage cost for data that is rarely read, at the price of higher per-request read and write cost. It suits audit logs, historical events and archives. Tables that are large relative to their traffic. For a table serving live application traffic the extra request cost usually outweighs the storage saving, so compare TableSizeBytes against your consumed capacity before switching. The change is a single update-table call and is reversible.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn DynamoDB Query vs Scan, why filter expressions do not cut cost, how GSIs differ from LSIs, and how to paginate results and use sparse indexes.

sections.title: DynamoDB Queries
paragraphs: There are exactly two ways to read more than one item from DynamoDB, and the gap between them is enormous.
Query reads items with a given partition key. It touches only that partition and bills only for what it reads.
Scan reads every item in the table, then discards what does not match. On a 50 GB table that is 50 GB of read capacity to return three items.
Nearly all DynamoDB performance and cost problems are a Scan where the design should have allowed a Query.

sections.title: Query
paragraphs: Count equal to ScannedCount is what a healthy query looks like. You read exactly what you returned.
The partition key must be an exact match. The sort key supports comparisons, which is where the useful patterns live:
begins_with on the sort key is what makes hierarchical keys work: store ORDER#2026-09-16#A-4821 and you can fetch all of a month's orders with begins_with(sk, "ORDER#2026-09").

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb query --table-name Orders \
  --key-condition-expression 'customerId = :c' \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":c":{"S":"C-4821"}}' \
  --return-consumed-capacity TOTAL

sections.title: Filter expressions do not reduce cost
paragraphs: The single most expensive misunderstanding in DynamoDB.
Three items returned. 847 items read and billed. Filters are applied after the read, on the way out. They shrink the response, never the cost.
A large gap between ScannedCount and Count is the signal that you need an index, not a better filter. Filters are appropriate for trimming a small result set, not for selecting from a large one.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb query --table-name Orders \
  --key-condition-expression 'customerId = :c' \
  --filter-expression 'amount > :min' \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":c":{"S":"C-4821"},":min":{"N":"100"}}' \
  --return-consumed-capacity TOTAL

sections.title: Global secondary indexes
paragraphs: A GSI is a second view of the table with its own partition and sort key, letting you query by something other than the base key.
Note #s. status is a reserved word, and referencing one directly fails:
There are several hundred reserved words including status, name, size, type, year and value. Using #alias with --expression-attribute-names always works, so it is a reasonable default habit.
Four things to know about GSIs:

sections.title: GSI or LSI
paragraphs: Use a GSI. LSIs must be defined when the table is created, can never be added, share the base table's capacity, and impose a hard 10 GB limit per partition key value that will eventually bite. Their only real advantage is strongly consistent reads on an alternate sort key. A narrow requirement.

sections.title: The sparse index trick
paragraphs: A GSI only contains items that have the index's key attributes. That makes it a cheap way to query a small subset of a large table.

Write an unprocessedAt attribute only on orders needing attention, and index on it. The GSI then holds only those items, perhaps a few hundred out of millions, so querying it is fast and cheap regardless of table size. When an order is processed, remove the attribute and it drops out of the index automatically.
This is often a better answer than a status-based index, because a status-index on a table where 99% of rows are complete still carries all of them.

sections.title: Pagination
paragraphs: Every read returns at most 1 MB, regardless of --max-items. If LastEvaluatedKey is present, there is more:

Code that ignores LastEvaluatedKey silently processes the first page and reports success. A genuinely common bug, because it works perfectly until the data grows past 1 MB. Always loop until the key is absent.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb query --table-name Orders \
  --key-condition-expression 'customerId = :c' \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":c":{"S":"C-4821"}}' \
  --exclusive-start-key '{"customerId":{"S":"C-4821"},"orderDate":{"S":"2026-09-10"}}'

sections.title: When a Scan is fine
paragraphs: Scans are not forbidden. They are reasonable on a small table, for a one-off migration, or for an analytics job where cost is understood. Parallelise them when you do:
Add --projection-expression to cut the data transferred, though not the capacity consumed. For genuine analytics, export to S3 and query with Athena instead, export consumes no read capacity at all.

codeBlock.code:
aws dynamodb scan --table-name Orders --total-segments 4 --segment 0 &
aws dynamodb scan --table-name Orders --total-segments 4 --segment 1 &

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: No exact partition key value. This is a Scan, or it needs an index.
Use #n with --expression-attribute-names.
By design. Drop --consistent-read or query the base table.

codeBlock.code: ValidationException: Query condition missed key schema element: customerId

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A query returns 3 items but reports ScannedCount 847 and consumes 106 capacity units. The query uses a key condition on the partition key plus a filter expression on amount. What should change?
An existing production table needs to be queried by a new attribute that is not related to its partition key. Which index type applies?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between Query and Scan in DynamoDB?

Query retrieves items sharing a partition key value, reading only that partition and billing only for what it reads. Scan reads every item in the table and then discards non-matching ones, so it costs capacity proportional to table size no matter how few items come back. On anything beyond a small table the difference is orders of magnitude. If you find yourself scanning in an application code path, the table's keys or indexes do not support the access pattern, that is a design issue rather than something to tune.
Do filter expressions reduce DynamoDB costs?

No, and this is the most expensive misconception in DynamoDB. Filters are evaluated after items are read, so they reduce the size of the response and not the capacity consumed. A query returning 3 items from 847 read is billed for all 847. Compare Count with ScannedCount in the response: a large gap means the access pattern needs an index whose keys match what you are selecting on. Filters are fine for trimming a small result, wrong for selecting from a large one.
What is the difference between a GSI and an LSI?

A global secondary index has its own partition and sort key drawn from any attributes, its own provisioned capacity, and can be created or deleted at any time, but reads are always eventually consistent. A local secondary index must use the table's partition key with a different sort key, can only be created when the table is created, shares the table's capacity, and is limited to 10 GB per partition key value, in exchange for supporting strongly consistent reads. In practice a GSI is almost always the right choice.
Why do I get "Attribute name is a reserved keyword"?

Several hundred words are reserved in DynamoDB expressions, including common ones like status, name, size, type, year and value. Referencing them directly in a key condition, filter or projection fails. Use a placeholder instead: --expression-attribute-names '{"#s":"status"}' and then #s = :val in the expression. Since aliasing always works whether or not the word is reserved, many people alias every attribute name as a matter of habit and avoid the problem entirely.
How does DynamoDB pagination work?

Every Query and Scan returns at most 1 MB of data regardless of any limit you set. When more results exist, the response includes LastEvaluatedKey, which you pass back as ExclusiveStartKey to fetch the next page, repeating until it is absent. Code that reads the first response and stops appears to work perfectly until the data grows past 1 MB, after which it silently processes a fraction of the results. A common and hard-to-spot bug. Always loop.
What is a sparse index and when is it useful?

A secondary index only contains items that actually have the index's key attributes, so if you write an attribute only on items needing attention, the index holds only those. A table with millions of orders can have an index containing the few hundred awaiting review, making that query fast and cheap regardless of table size, and removing the attribute drops the item from the index automatically. It is usually better than a status-based index, where a value like complete covering 99% of rows means the index carries nearly everything.

keyConcepts.explanation: Run ElastiCache well: pick Redis, Valkey or Memcached, start serverless, set eviction policies, implement cache-aside and handle cluster mode and failover.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Run ElastiCache well: pick Redis, Valkey or Memcached, start serverless, set eviction policies, implement cache-aside and handle cluster mode and failover.

sections.title: Amazon ElastiCache
paragraphs: ElastiCache runs managed Redis, Valkey or Memcached, in-memory data stores with sub-millisecond latency. The usual job is taking read load off a database, holding sessions so your application can be stateless, and rate limiting.

The most useful thing to be clear about up front: a cache is not a database. Data in ElastiCache can disappear: a node fails, memory fills and keys are evicted, a maintenance window replaces a node. Anything that must survive belongs in RDS or DynamoDB, with the cache in front of it.

sections.title: Redis, Valkey or Memcached
paragraphs: Choose Redis or Valkey unless you specifically want a simple multi-threaded key-value cache and nothing else. Memcached has no replication, so a node failure loses that node's data with no failover.
Valkey is the open-source fork created after Redis changed licence, is API-compatible, and is priced lower on ElastiCache. For new clusters it is worth considering by default.

sections.title: Serverless is the easy starting point
paragraphs: No node types, no cluster sizing, no patching windows. It scales with demand and bills on storage and compute consumed. For a new workload where you do not yet know the access pattern, it removes every capacity decision.
Provisioned clusters remain cheaper at steady, predictable load, and are what you need for fine control over node types and placement.

codeBlock.code:
aws elasticache create-serverless-cache \
  --serverless-cache-name orders-cache \
  --engine valkey \
  --cache-usage-limits 'DataStorage={Maximum=10,Unit=GB},ECPUPerSecond={Maximum=5000}'

sections.title: Provisioned, with replication
paragraphs: --automatic-failover-enabled with --multi-az-enabled is what makes this production-grade: a primary failure promotes a replica in another availability zone, typically within a minute or two. Without them a node failure is an outage requiring manual intervention.
cache.r7g is Graviton and memory-optimised. Better price-performance than the older m and r generations for almost every cache workload.

codeBlock.code:
aws elasticache create-replication-group \
  --replication-group-id orders-cache \
  --replication-group-description "orders read cache" \
  --engine valkey --cache-node-type cache.r7g.large \
  --num-node-groups 1 --replicas-per-node-group 2 \
  --automatic-failover-enabled --multi-az-enabled \
  --at-rest-encryption-enabled --transit-encryption-enabled \
  --cache-subnet-group-name private-subnets \
  --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0

sections.title: Cluster mode changes your client
paragraphs: The decision with the largest application impact.
Cluster mode disabled gives one shard: a primary plus replicas. Total data is limited to one node's memory. Writes go to the primary, reads can go to replicas.
Cluster mode enabled shards data across multiple node groups, so capacity scales horizontally.
Your client library must support cluster mode, and this is where people get stuck. A standard Redis client connecting to a cluster-mode endpoint receives MOVED redirections it does not understand:
Use the cluster-aware client, redis-py-cluster or redis-py in cluster mode, ioredis with Redis.Cluster, Lettuce for Java, and the configuration endpoint rather than a node address.
Multi-key operations are also constrained: keys touched together must live in the same slot, which means hash tags:
The braces make Redis hash only the enclosed part, so both keys land on the same shard and can be used in one transaction or MGET.
Start with cluster mode disabled unless you know you will exceed one node's memory. Enabling it later requires client changes.

codeBlock.code:
aws elasticache create-replication-group \
  --replication-group-id orders-cache \
  --replication-group-description "sharded" \
  --engine valkey --cache-node-type cache.r7g.large \
  --num-node-groups 3 --replicas-per-node-group 1 \
  --automatic-failover-enabled

sections.title: Eviction policy
paragraphs: What happens when memory fills, and the default is wrong for a cache:
The default volatile-lru only evicts keys that have a TTL, so if your application writes keys without expiry, memory fills and writes start failing:

For a pure cache, allkeys-lru is correct: it always has something to evict. Use allkeys-lfu when a small set of keys is much hotter than the rest. Only use noeviction when losing a key would be a correctness problem, and at that point reconsider whether this should be a cache.
Always set a TTL anyway. It bounds staleness, and it means a key nobody reads disappears rather than occupying memory indefinitely.

codeBlock.code:
aws elasticache modify-cache-parameter-group \
  --cache-parameter-group-name orders-params \
  --parameter-name-values 'ParameterName=maxmemory-policy,ParameterValue=allkeys-lru'

sections.title: Cache-aside
paragraphs: The pattern behind most cache usage:
On write, invalidate rather than update:
Deleting is safer than writing the new value, because a failed cache write leaves stale data indefinitely while a failed delete is corrected by the next read.

Two failure modes worth designing for. A cache stampede happens when a popular key expires and hundreds of requests all miss and hit the database simultaneously. Add jitter to TTLs, or have one request populate while others briefly serve stale. And a cache that must be available for the application to work has become a dependency rather than an optimisation, so make the code path fall back to the database when Redis is unreachable.

sections.title: Failover behaviour
paragraphs: Test this before you need it. During a failover the primary endpoint DNS is repointed, so clients must reconnect and re-resolve. A client caching the resolved address keeps trying a node that is no longer primary, which surfaces as READONLY You can't write against a read only replica.
Most modern clients handle it. Verify yours does, with a real failover test.
Use the reader endpoint to spread reads across replicas, and remember replication is asynchronous, so a read immediately after a write may return the old value.

codeBlock.code:
aws elasticache test-failover --replication-group-id orders-cache \
  --node-group-id 0001

sections.title: Monitoring
paragraphs: A low hit rate usually means TTLs are too short, keys are too specific to be reused, or the cached data is not actually read repeatedly.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/ElastiCache \
  --metric-name DatabaseMemoryUsagePercentage \
  --dimensions Name=ReplicationGroupId,Value=orders-cache \
  --start-time 2026-09-15T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-09-16T00:00:00Z \
  --period 300 --statistics Average

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Memory full and the eviction policy cannot free anything. Set allkeys-lru.
A non-cluster-aware client against a cluster-mode endpoint.
Writing to a replica, or a stale connection after failover.
A multi-key operation across shards. Use hash tags.
Connection timeouts. Security group must allow 6379 from the client, and ElastiCache is not reachable from outside the VPC.

codeBlock.code: (error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Redis cache fills up and writes start failing with "OOM command not allowed when used memory > maxmemory". The application writes many keys without TTLs. What is the fix?
After migrating to a cluster-mode-enabled replication group, the application fails with "MOVED 15495 10.0.1.42:6379". It uses a standard Redis client and the primary node address. What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I use Redis, Valkey or Memcached on ElastiCache?

Redis or Valkey for almost everything. Memcached offers only strings, no replication and no failover, so losing a node loses that node's data with no automatic recovery. It suits a simple multi-threaded key-value cache and little else. Redis adds lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams, pub/sub, optional persistence and automatic failover. Valkey is the open-source fork created after Redis's licence change, is API-compatible, and is priced lower on ElastiCache, which makes it a reasonable default for new clusters.
What is the difference between cluster mode enabled and disabled?

Disabled means a single shard: one primary with replicas, so your dataset must fit in one node's memory. Enabled shards data across several node groups, scaling capacity horizontally. The important consequence is on the client. Cluster mode requires a cluster-aware library and the configuration endpoint, because nodes reply with MOVED redirections for keys they do not own, and multi-key operations need hash tags to keep related keys in the same slot. Start with cluster mode disabled unless you know you will outgrow one node.
Why is ElastiCache rejecting writes when the cache is full?

Because the default eviction policy, volatile-lru, only evicts keys that have a TTL. If your application writes keys without expiry, memory fills with keys the policy will not touch and Redis returns OOM command not allowed. Change maxmemory-policy to allkeys-lru in the parameter group so any key can be evicted, which is the correct behaviour for a cache. Setting TTLs on writes as well bounds staleness and stops unread keys accumulating.
What is the cache-aside pattern?

Read from the cache first; on a miss, read from the database, write the value into the cache with a TTL, and return it. On update, delete the cached key rather than rewriting it. A failed delete is corrected by the next read, whereas a failed write leaves stale data indefinitely. Two things to design for: add jitter to TTLs so a popular key expiring does not send hundreds of simultaneous requests to the database, and make the code fall back to the database when the cache is unreachable.
What happens during an ElastiCache failover?

A replica is promoted and the primary endpoint's DNS is repointed, typically completing within a minute or two when automatic failover and multi-AZ are enabled. Clients must reconnect and re-resolve; one that caches the resolved IP keeps talking to a node that is now a replica and sees READONLY You can't write against a read only replica. Most current client libraries handle this correctly, but verify yours with test-failover before relying on it in production.
Can I store session data in ElastiCache?

Yes, and it is one of the best uses. It lets your application servers be stateless, which is what makes horizontal scaling and rolling deployments work. Just accept the consequence: cache data can be lost to a node failure or eviction, so losing sessions means users are logged out. Enable multi-AZ with automatic failover, set TTLs matching your session lifetime, and if being logged out is unacceptable, either enable Redis persistence or keep a durable copy elsewhere.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Use Amazon SQS well: Standard vs FIFO, a visibility timeout longer than processing time, long polling, idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues, monitoring.

sections.title: Amazon SQS
paragraphs: SQS is a managed queue. A producer writes a message, a consumer reads it, and the two never need to be available at the same time, which is the whole point. A traffic spike becomes a longer queue rather than a stack of failed requests, and a consumer you take down for deployment simply resumes where it left off.
SQS: Message Queue Pattern
Visibility timeout prevents two consumers processing the same message simultaneously

Most of the trouble people have with SQS comes down to three things: choosing Standard when they needed FIFO, setting a visibility timeout shorter than their processing time, and writing consumers that break when a message arrives twice. All three are covered below.

sections.title: Standard or FIFO
paragraphs: A FIFO queue name must end in .fifo, and you cannot convert a queue from one type to the other. The choice is permanent for the life of the queue.

Default to Standard. Its throughput is unbounded and its ordering is good enough for most work. An image to resize or an email to send does not care about sequence. Choose FIFO only when out-of-order processing is genuinely incorrect, such as applying a sequence of updates to the same record.
FIFO ordering is per message group, not per queue, and this is the part that gets missed:

Messages sharing a group id are strictly ordered and processed one at a time; different groups proceed in parallel. Using a single group id for everything serialises the entire queue and throws away your concurrency, which is the usual cause of "FIFO is too slow".

codeBlock.code:
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders.fifo \
  --attributes FifoQueue=true,ContentBasedDeduplication=true

sections.title: Visibility timeout
paragraphs: When a consumer receives a message, SQS hides it from other consumers for the visibility timeout rather than deleting it. The consumer must delete it explicitly once the work is done:
That design is what makes SQS reliable: a consumer that crashes mid-work never deletes the message, so it reappears after the timeout and someone else picks it up.

It is also the most common misconfiguration. The default visibility timeout is 30 seconds. If your handler takes 45, the message becomes visible again while you are still working on it, a second consumer starts the same job, and both finish, so the work happens twice and you may see it a third time. The symptom is duplicate processing that no amount of Standard-queue reasoning explains.
Set it to comfortably more than your worst-case processing time. For long or variable jobs, extend the timeout while working instead of guessing high:
With a Lambda trigger, AWS requires the queue's visibility timeout to be at least six times the function timeout, which accounts for retries within a batch.

codeBlock.code: aws sqs receive-message --queue-url "$Q" --max-number-of-messages 1

sections.title: Long polling
paragraphs: The default of 0 is short polling: every receive-message returns immediately, often empty, and you pay for the request. A consumer loop doing this spends most of its budget asking an empty queue whether anything has arrived.

Long polling holds the connection open for up to 20 seconds and returns as soon as a message appears. It cuts both request cost and latency, and there is essentially no reason not to set it. Note that short polling also samples only a subset of servers, so it can return empty even when messages exist.

codeBlock.code:
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url "$Q" \
  --attributes ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds=20

sections.title: Write idempotent consumers
paragraphs: Standard queues guarantee at-least-once delivery. Duplicates are not an edge case to be prevented. They are documented behaviour, and they also arise from visibility timeouts, retries and network failures on FIFO queues.
The practical requirement is that processing a message twice has the same effect as processing it once. Usually that means a unique key and a conditional write:
"We will just make sure it never delivers twice" is not an available option.

sections.title: Dead-letter queues
paragraphs: A message that keeps failing will keep being retried forever, consuming capacity and often blocking a FIFO message group entirely. A redrive policy moves it aside after a set number of attempts:

The DLQ must be the same type as the source queue. FIFO source, FIFO DLQ. A DLQ nobody watches is worse than none at all, because failures are now silent; alarm on its depth from the moment you create it. The dead-letter queues page covers redrive and replay in detail.

sections.title: What to monitor
paragraphs: Queue depth alone is a poor alarm, because a healthy queue can be deep during a burst and drain fine. Age of the oldest message is the honest signal: if it climbs steadily, consumers cannot keep up. Alarm on DLQ depth above zero separately.

codeBlock.code:
aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$Q" \
  --attribute-names ApproximateNumberOfMessages \
  ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The visibility timeout expired before you called delete-message, so the handle is stale. The work already ran twice. Raise the timeout.
You sent a message to a FIFO queue without a MessageGroupId, which is mandatory there and meaningless on Standard.
FIFO queues are identified by the suffix, and there is no attribute-only way to create one.

codeBlock.code: The receipt handle "AQEBzb..." is not valid for the current visibility timeout

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Standard queue consumer takes about 45 seconds per message. The queue uses default settings. Orders are being processed two or three times each. What is the most likely cause?
A FIFO queue is processing roughly one message at a time despite ten consumers running. Every message is sent with MessageGroupId set to the string "default". What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between SQS and SNS?

SQS is a queue: a message is stored until one consumer reads and deletes it, which suits distributing work among workers. SNS is publish-subscribe: a message is pushed immediately to every subscriber and not retained for a subscriber that is absent, which suits fan-out notification. They are frequently combined. SNS publishes to several SQS queues, giving each consumer its own durable copy, and that fan-out pattern is the standard way to let multiple services react to the same event without coupling them.
Should I use a Standard or FIFO queue?

Standard unless out-of-order processing would actually be wrong. Standard gives effectively unlimited throughput and best-effort ordering, which is fine for independent jobs like resizing an image or sending an email. FIFO caps at 300 messages per second (3,000 with batching) and guarantees ordering within a message group, so it earns its place for sequences of updates to the same entity. The choice is permanent: a queue cannot be converted, and FIFO names must end in .fifo.
Why is my SQS message processed more than once?

Two causes, and both are normal behaviour rather than faults. Standard queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, so occasional duplicates are documented. Far more often, though, the visibility timeout is shorter than the processing time, with the 30-second default and a 45-second handler, the message reappears mid-flight and a second consumer starts the same work. Raise VisibilityTimeout above your worst case, and make the consumer idempotent with a conditional write on a unique key so a duplicate is harmless.
What should the SQS visibility timeout be set to?

Comfortably longer than your worst-case processing time, if p99 handling takes 40 seconds, 120 is a reasonable starting point rather than 45. For jobs with unpredictable duration, call change-message-visibility periodically while working instead of setting one very high value, which would delay retries after a genuine crash. When the consumer is a Lambda function, AWS requires the queue timeout to be at least six times the function timeout to allow for in-batch retries.
How does an SQS dead-letter queue work?

You attach a redrive policy naming a second queue and a maxReceiveCount. Each time a message is received without being deleted, its receive count increases, and once it exceeds the limit SQS moves it to the DLQ instead of making it visible again. That stops one broken message consuming capacity indefinitely or blocking a FIFO group. The DLQ must match the source queue's type, and it needs an alarm on depth above zero. Otherwise you have converted loud failures into silent ones.
Why does my consumer keep returning no messages when the queue is not empty?

Most likely short polling, which is the default. ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds=0 samples a subset of SQS's servers and returns immediately, so it can legitimately come back empty while messages exist elsewhere in the queue. Setting it to 20 enables long polling, which queries all servers and waits for a message to arrive. Lower latency and fewer billable requests. The other explanation is that the messages are in flight rather than available: compare ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible with ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible.

keyConcepts.explanation: Set up an SQS dead-letter queue with a redrive policy, choose maxReceiveCount, inspect failed messages without consuming them and redrive them safely.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Set up an SQS dead-letter queue with a redrive policy, choose maxReceiveCount, inspect failed messages without consuming them and redrive them safely.

A message that cannot be processed will be retried forever. It consumes consumer capacity, fills your logs with the same stack trace, and on a FIFO queue it blocks every other message in its group indefinitely. That single message is a poison pill.
A dead-letter queue is where SQS puts it after a set number of failed attempts, so healthy traffic keeps flowing and the failure becomes something you can inspect at leisure.

sections.title: How a DLQ is wired up
paragraphs: A DLQ is an ordinary queue. What makes it a DLQ is the redrive policy on the source queue pointing at it.
Two constraints worth knowing before you build: the DLQ must be in the same region and account as the source queue, and it must be the same type. A FIFO source needs a FIFO DLQ.

Note the retention period. 1209600 seconds is 14 days, the maximum, and it is the right choice for a DLQ. The default is 4 days, which is easily a long weekend plus a Monday of higher-priority work, after which the evidence is gone.

codeBlock.code:
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders-dlq \
  --attributes MessageRetentionPeriod=1209600

sections.title: What actually triggers a move
paragraphs: SQS counts receives, not failures. Every time a consumer receives a message and does not delete it, because it threw, crashed, timed out, or was killed mid-work, the receive count increases. Once it exceeds maxReceiveCount, the next attempt sends the message to the DLQ instead of making it visible again.
Two consequences follow from that, and both surprise people.

A visibility timeout that is too short burns through the count. If your handler needs 45 seconds and the timeout is 30, each message is received repeatedly while still being processed successfully, so perfectly good messages reach the DLQ. When you find healthy-looking messages in a DLQ, check the visibility timeout before you check the code.
Nothing has to raise an error. A consumer that silently drops a message without deleting it produces exactly the same counter behaviour as one that crashes.

codeBlock.code:
aws sqs receive-message --queue-url "$SRC_URL" \
  --attribute-names ApproximateReceiveCount \
  --message-attribute-names All

sections.title: Choosing maxReceiveCount
paragraphs: The trade is between recovering from transient problems and finding out quickly that something is broken. Set it to 1 and a brief downstream blip dead-letters your traffic; set it to 50 and a genuinely malformed message is retried for half an hour while you wonder why throughput dropped.

If you are retrying largely to ride out downstream outages, prefer a shorter count plus a real backoff strategy. A count of 5 with no delay between attempts exhausts itself in seconds, which is not a retry policy so much as a rapid giving-up.

sections.title: A DLQ nobody watches is worse than no DLQ
paragraphs: Without a DLQ, a failing message is loud: it retries endlessly, floods logs and shows up in your error rate. With a DLQ, it disappears quietly into another queue. That is an improvement only if something tells you.

Threshold zero, not ten. Any message in a DLQ means something failed five times in a row; there is no acceptable background level. Create this alarm in the same change that creates the DLQ, not as a follow-up ticket.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name orders-dlq-not-empty \
  --namespace AWS/SQS \
  --metric-name ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible \
  --dimensions Name=QueueName,Value=orders-dlq \
  --statistic Maximum --period 300 --evaluation-periods 1 \
  --threshold 0 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --alarm-actions "$SNS_TOPIC_ARN"

sections.title: Inspecting without consuming
paragraphs: You want to read a dead-lettered message without starting its clock again. Use a long visibility timeout so it stays put while you look:

--visibility-timeout 0 makes the message immediately available again, which is what you want while investigating. You are reading, not claiming. The SentTimestamp and ApproximateFirstReceiveTimestamp attributes tell you when the message was created and when it first failed, which usually pins the failure to a deployment.

codeBlock.code:
aws sqs receive-message --queue-url "$DLQ_URL" \
  --max-number-of-messages 10 \
  --visibility-timeout 0 \
  --attribute-names All

sections.title: Redriving messages back
paragraphs: Once the bug is fixed, move the messages back to the source queue. The managed redrive does this without a script:
Rate-limit it. Redriving a large backlog at full speed onto a service that has just recovered is a reliable way to knock it over a second time.

Deploy the fix first, and confirm it works on one message before moving thousands. The destination queue is a normal queue, so a still-broken consumer simply dead-letters everything again, this time with the receive count reset.
For a FIFO source you may also need a RedriveAllowPolicy on the DLQ naming which queues are permitted to use it:

codeBlock.code:
aws sqs start-message-move-task \
  --source-arn "$DLQ_ARN" \
  --destination-arn "$SRC_ARN" \
  --max-number-of-messages-per-second 50

sections.title: Do not consume the DLQ automatically
paragraphs: A tempting pattern is a second worker reading the DLQ and retrying. Resist it: you have rebuilt the infinite retry loop the DLQ existed to break, with an extra queue in the middle.

The DLQ is for human attention. What belongs there is an alarm, a dashboard, and enough message metadata to diagnose the failure. Automated handling is reasonable only when it is doing something genuinely different, archiving the payload to S3 for later analysis, or raising a ticket, rather than reprocessing.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The DLQ is in a different account or region. Both must match the source queue.
A FIFO source with a Standard DLQ, or the reverse.
Usually the ARN was built by hand. Read it from get-queue-attributes --attribute-names QueueArn rather than assembling the string.

codeBlock.code:
InvalidParameterValue: Value {...} for parameter RedrivePolicy is invalid.
Reason: Dead letter target owner should be same as the source.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A DLQ is filling with messages that process perfectly when replayed by hand. The queue has maxReceiveCount 5, and the consumer takes around 50 seconds per message. What should you check first?
To avoid manual work, a team adds a worker that reads the DLQ and sends each message back to the source queue immediately. Why is this a poor design?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is an SQS dead-letter queue and why do I need one?

It is a normal queue that receives messages which have failed processing too many times, configured through a redrive policy on the source queue. Without one, a message that cannot be processed is retried indefinitely. Burning consumer capacity, filling logs with the same error, and on a FIFO queue blocking every other message in its group. The DLQ moves that message aside so healthy traffic continues and the failure becomes something you can investigate rather than something that degrades the system.
How do I choose maxReceiveCount?

Three to five suits most workloads. Use one or two when failures are deterministic, a malformed payload will not succeed on the fourth attempt either, and ten or more when your consumer depends on a downstream service that fails transiently and recovers by itself. Higher values delay discovery and let bad messages consume capacity for longer; lower values dead-letter traffic during brief blips. If you are retrying mainly to survive outages, add real backoff rather than simply raising the count.
Why are perfectly valid messages ending up in my dead-letter queue?

Because SQS counts deliveries, not failures. If the visibility timeout is shorter than your processing time, each message is handed out again while the previous consumer is still working on it, and the receive count climbs past maxReceiveCount even though the work succeeds every time. This is the single most common cause of a confusing DLQ. Compare your handler's p99 duration with the queue's VisibilityTimeout before looking anywhere else.
How do I replay messages from a dead-letter queue?

Use the managed redrive: aws sqs start-message-move-task --source-arn "$DLQ_ARN" --destination-arn "$SRC_ARN", with --max-number-of-messages-per-second to rate-limit it. Deploy the fix first and test it against a single message, because the destination is an ordinary queue and a still-broken consumer will simply dead-letter everything again. Rate limiting matters too. Redriving a large backlog at full speed at a service that has just recovered tends to take it down again.
Should something consume the dead-letter queue automatically?

Not to reprocess. Sending messages straight back rebuilds the infinite retry loop the DLQ was created to break, and hides the failure because the queue keeps draining and never trips an alarm. Automation is reasonable when it does something else: archiving payloads to S3 for analysis, emitting a metric, or opening a ticket. Redrive should be a deliberate action taken after a fix is deployed.
What retention period should a dead-letter queue have?

The maximum, 14 days (MessageRetentionPeriod=1209600). The 4-day default is easy to exceed. A failure on Friday evening can expire before anyone looks on Tuesday, taking the only record of what went wrong with it. There is no cost argument against it, since you are charged for requests and storage volume rather than retention window, and a DLQ should be nearly empty in normal operation anyway.

keyConcepts.explanation: Build publish-subscribe messaging with Amazon SNS: set up the SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern, use filter policies and raw message delivery and avoid email traps.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Build publish-subscribe messaging with Amazon SNS: set up the SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern, use filter policies and raw message delivery and avoid email traps.

sections.title: Amazon SNS
paragraphs: SNS is publish-subscribe. A publisher sends one message to a topic, and SNS delivers a copy to every subscriber: a queue, a Lambda function, an HTTPS endpoint, an email address. The publisher never knows who is listening, which is exactly what makes it useful for letting several services react to the same event.

The critical difference from SQS: SNS pushes and does not store. A subscriber that is unavailable when the message is published misses it, aside from limited retries. That single property drives most real SNS design, and it is why the fan-out pattern below exists.

sections.title: Topics and subscriptions
paragraphs: A subscription showing PendingConfirmation instead of an ARN has not been confirmed and receives nothing. For email and HTTPS endpoints, SNS sends a confirmation request the owner must accept. An email subscription silently delivering nothing is almost always this, and the confirmation mail routinely lands in spam. SQS and Lambda subscriptions confirm automatically.

codeBlock.code: aws sns create-topic --name order-events

sections.title: The fan-out pattern
paragraphs: This is the arrangement worth internalising, because it fixes SNS's lack of durability:

Each consumer gets its own queue, so each gets its own durable copy, its own retry behaviour and its own dead-letter queue. A consumer can be down for an hour and catch up; one consumer failing does not affect the others; and adding a fourth is a new queue and a new subscription rather than a change to the publisher.

Subscribing Lambda functions directly to SNS is simpler and gives up all of that. Use direct subscription for genuinely fire-and-forget notifications, and a queue in between whenever the work matters.
The queue needs a policy allowing SNS to write to it:

Missing that policy is the most common fan-out failure. The subscription is created successfully, publishing succeeds, and messages never arrive, because SNS is being denied and nothing in the publish call reveals it.

codeBlock.code:
┌──▶ SQS queue ──▶ billing worker
publisher ──▶ SNS ──┼──▶ SQS queue ──▶ search indexer
                    └──▶ SQS queue ──▶ analytics worker

sections.title: Raw message delivery
paragraphs: By default SNS wraps your payload in an envelope of SNS metadata:
Your actual message is a JSON string inside the Message field, so consumers must parse twice. Worse, message attributes move into the envelope, which means SQS-side filtering on them stops working.

With raw delivery the subscriber receives the payload exactly as published. Enable it on SQS and HTTPS subscriptions unless you specifically need the envelope's metadata. The double-encoded JSON is a frequent source of "the message arrived but my parser broke".

codeBlock.code:
{
  "Type": "Notification",
  "MessageId": "8f3c1e2a-4b7d-11ef-9c2a-0242ac120002",
  "TopicArn": "arn:aws:sns:eu-west-1:123456789012:order-events",
  "Message": "{\"orderId\":\"A-4821\"}",
  "Timestamp": "2026-09-16T09:14:22.481Z"
}

sections.title: Filter policies
paragraphs: Rather than publishing to several topics, publish everything to one and let each subscription choose what it wants:

Filtering happens in SNS, so unmatched messages are never delivered and never billed to the subscriber. By default the policy is evaluated against message attributes, not the body. To filter on body contents, switch the scope:
A filter policy that matches nothing is indistinguishable from a broken subscription, so check NumberOfNotificationsFilteredOut in CloudWatch when messages go missing.

codeBlock.code:
aws sns set-subscription-attributes \
  --subscription-arn "$SUB_ARN" \
  --attribute-name FilterPolicy \
  --attribute-value '{"eventType":["placed","cancelled"],"amount":[{"numeric":[">",100]}]}'

sections.title: FIFO topics
paragraphs: Like FIFO queues, the name must end in .fifo, and ordering is guaranteed per message group rather than per topic. A FIFO topic can only deliver to FIFO SQS queues, not Lambda, not HTTPS, not email. Publishing requires a MessageGroupId.

codeBlock.code:
aws sns create-topic --name order-events.fifo \
  --attributes FifoTopic=true,ContentBasedDeduplication=true

sections.title: Delivery retries
paragraphs: SNS retry behaviour depends entirely on the protocol, which is worth knowing before you rely on it:
For HTTPS endpoints, set a delivery policy and a dead-letter queue on the subscription, or a brief outage at your endpoint silently loses messages:

codeBlock.code:
aws sns set-subscription-attributes --subscription-arn "$SUB_ARN" \
  --attribute-name RedrivePolicy \
  --attribute-value '{"deadLetterTargetArn":"arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-1:123456789012:sns-dlq"}'

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The publisher's IAM policy, or the topic's own access policy, does not permit publishing. Both are checked.
You passed --message-structure json with a payload lacking a default key. Every protocol-specific message object needs default as a fallback.
The endpoint owner has not accepted. Re-request with aws sns confirm-subscription, and check the spam folder for email endpoints.

codeBlock.code: AuthorizationError: User ... is not authorized to perform: SNS:Publish on resource ...

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An SNS topic is subscribed to an SQS queue. The subscription exists with a real ARN, publish calls return a MessageId, and the queue stays empty. What is the most likely cause?
Three services must each react to every "order placed" event. Each may be redeployed independently and must not lose events while restarting. What design fits?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between SNS and SQS?

SNS is push-based publish-subscribe: one message goes to every subscriber immediately and is not retained for a subscriber that is absent. SQS is pull-based queuing: a message waits until a consumer reads and deletes it, and only one consumer gets it. So SNS is for notifying several parties about an event, and SQS is for handing work to a pool of workers. Combining them, SNS fanning out to several SQS queues, gives you both broadcast and durability, and is the usual production pattern.
What is the SNS to SQS fan-out pattern?

Publishing to a single SNS topic that has several SQS queues subscribed, one per consuming service. Each consumer gets its own durable copy, so it can be offline during a deploy and catch up afterwards; each has independent retries and its own dead-letter queue; and adding a consumer means creating a queue and a subscription without touching the publisher. It is the standard way to let multiple services react to one event without coupling them together.
Why is my SNS to SQS subscription not delivering messages?

Nine times out of ten the queue's access policy does not allow sns.amazonaws.com to call sqs:SendMessage on it. Publishing and delivering are authorised separately, so the publish succeeds and returns a MessageId while delivery is silently denied. Add a queue policy granting the SNS service principal, ideally with an aws:SourceArn condition naming the topic, and check the topic's NumberOfNotificationsFailed metric to confirm that was the problem.
What is raw message delivery in SNS?

By default SNS wraps your payload in a JSON envelope containing Type, MessageId, TopicArn and a Message field holding your payload as an escaped string, so consumers have to parse twice, and message attributes move into the envelope where SQS-side filtering cannot see them. Setting RawMessageDelivery to true on an SQS or HTTPS subscription delivers the payload exactly as published. Enable it unless you specifically need the envelope metadata.
How do SNS filter policies work?

A filter policy on a subscription describes which messages that subscriber wants, and SNS evaluates it before delivering, so unmatched messages are never sent and never billed. This lets one topic serve many consumers with different interests instead of maintaining a topic per event type. By default the policy is matched against message attributes, not the body; set FilterPolicyScope to MessageBody to filter on content. Check NumberOfNotificationsFilteredOut when messages seem to disappear.
Why hasn't my email subscription received anything?

Almost certainly because it was never confirmed. SNS sends a confirmation request to email and HTTPS endpoints that the owner must accept, and until then list-subscriptions-by-topic shows PendingConfirmation in place of a subscription ARN and nothing is delivered. The confirmation email frequently lands in spam. SQS and Lambda subscriptions confirm automatically, which is why this only bites on the protocols where a human is involved.

keyConcepts.explanation: Route events with Amazon EventBridge: create buses and rules, write event patterns, schedule jobs, transform input, archive and replay events and add a DLQ.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Route events with Amazon EventBridge: create buses and rules, write event patterns, schedule jobs, transform input, archive and replay events and add a DLQ.

sections.title: Amazon EventBridge
paragraphs: EventBridge is a router for events. Something publishes a JSON event onto a bus, rules match it on content, and matching events are delivered to targets. Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, another bus, an API endpoint.

The difference from SNS is where the routing decision lives. With SNS, a publisher chooses a topic and subscribers take what that topic carries. With EventBridge, publishers emit events onto one bus and each consumer declares a pattern describing what it wants. Adding a consumer with new interests requires no change to the publisher and no new topic.
It was previously called CloudWatch Events, which is why some console URLs, IAM actions and older documentation still say events.

sections.title: Buses
paragraphs: Every account has a default bus, which is where AWS's own service events arrive. Create your own for application events:

Keeping application events off the default bus is worth doing: the default carries a high volume of AWS service noise, and a separate bus gives you cleaner rules, separate archives and its own resource policy for cross-account access.

codeBlock.code:
aws events create-event-bus --name order-events
aws events list-event-buses --query 'EventBuses[].Name' --output table

sections.title: Events and patterns
paragraphs: An event is JSON with a small required envelope:
Check FailedEntryCount. put-events returns HTTP 200 even when individual entries fail, so a script that only checks the exit code reports success while dropping events.
A rule matches on structure and values:
Pattern matching rules that catch people out:
Test before deploying:

sections.title: AWS service events
paragraphs: The default bus receives events from AWS itself, which lets you react to infrastructure changes without polling:

Useful examples: an ECS task stopping unexpectedly, a CodePipeline stage failing, an S3 object being created, a GuardDuty finding, an RDS snapshot completing, an AWS Health event announcing planned maintenance. The aws.health source in particular is worth a rule. It is how you find out about scheduled hardware retirement before it happens rather than afterwards.

sections.title: Scheduled rules
paragraphs: EventBridge cron has six fields, not five, the extra one is year, and the day-of-week field uses ? where the other day field is specified. A five-field expression is rejected, which is the usual first error. All schedules are UTC.
rate(5 minutes) is simpler where you just need an interval.

For anything non-trivial, prefer EventBridge Scheduler, the newer dedicated service: it supports time zones with automatic daylight-saving handling, one-off schedules, and flexible time windows to avoid every schedule firing at exactly the same second.

codeBlock.code:
aws events put-rule --name nightly-report \
  --schedule-expression 'cron(0 3 * * ? *)'

sections.title: Transforming the input
paragraphs: Targets often want a different shape from the event. An input transformer reshapes it without a Lambda in the middle:

sections.title: Failures go to the target's DLQ
paragraphs: This is the part that most often gets missed. If a target fails, EventBridge retries for up to 24 hours and then discards the event. There is no queue holding it, and nothing tells you.
Attach a dead-letter queue per target:
Then alarm on that queue's depth. Without it, a broken target loses events quietly for as long as it stays broken.

sections.title: Archive and replay
paragraphs: EventBridge can retain matching events and replay them later. Genuinely useful after fixing a consumer bug, and a capability SNS does not have:
Use FilterArns to replay into one rule rather than every rule on the bus, or every consumer reprocesses everything.

codeBlock.code:
aws events create-archive --archive-name order-archive \
  --event-source-arn "arn:aws:events:eu-west-1:123456789012:event-bus/order-events" \
  --retention-days 30

aws events start-replay --replay-name reprocess-sept \
  --event-source-arn "arn:aws:events:eu-west-1:123456789012:archive/order-archive" \
  --event-start-time 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z \
  --event-end-time 2026-09-02T00:00:00Z \
  --destination '{"Arn":"arn:aws:events:eu-west-1:123456789012:event-bus/order-events","FilterArns":["arn:aws:events:eu-west-1:123456789012:rule/order-events/high-value-orders"]}'

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Five cron fields instead of six, or a missing ? in the day-of-week position.
The caller lacks events:PutEvents on that bus, or the bus resource policy denies the source account.

Rule exists, target never fires, no errors anywhere. Nearly always the pattern. Run test-event-pattern against a real event. The usual culprits are DetailType instead of detail-type, or a typo in source that makes the pattern match nothing.

codeBlock.code: ValidationException: Parameter ScheduleExpression is not valid

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A rule on a custom bus has a pattern of {"source":["orders.api"],"DetailType":["OrderPlaced"]}. Events are published successfully with FailedEntryCount 0, but the Lambda target is never invoked and no errors appear. What is wrong?
A Lambda target was broken for three hours. Afterwards, the events from that window are nowhere to be found and no alarm fired. What was missing?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between EventBridge and SNS?

Both deliver events to multiple consumers; they differ in who decides routing. With SNS the publisher picks a topic and subscribers accept whatever that topic carries, so a new consumer with different interests usually means a new topic. With EventBridge, publishers emit onto a bus and each consumer writes a pattern describing the events it wants, matched on content. EventBridge also integrates with AWS service events, supports scheduling, and offers archive and replay. SNS has lower latency and higher throughput, and remains the better fit for simple fan-out to queues.
Why is my EventBridge rule not triggering?

Test the pattern first: aws events test-event-pattern --event-pattern file://p.json --event file://e.json returns true or false in one call. The usual cause is field naming, put-events takes DetailType and Detail, while patterns match the delivered event's lowercase detail-type and detail, so a pattern using the PascalCase names matches nothing without erroring. Also confirm the rule is on the right bus, that it is enabled, and that the target's resource policy allows EventBridge to invoke it.
How do I schedule something with EventBridge cron?

--schedule-expression 'cron(0 3 * * ? *)' runs at 03:00 UTC daily. EventBridge cron has six fields rather than the usual five, minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week, year, and requires ? in whichever day field you are not specifying. All times are UTC, with no daylight-saving handling. For anything involving time zones, one-off schedules or jitter, use EventBridge Scheduler instead, which is a separate and more capable service.
What happens if an EventBridge target fails?

EventBridge retries with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours, then discards the event permanently. It is a router and retains nothing. That means an outage longer than the retry window silently loses events, with no backlog to notice afterwards. Attach a DeadLetterConfig to each target so undeliverable events land in an SQS queue, set a RetryPolicy to control attempts, and alarm on the DLQ depth. Creating an archive additionally lets you replay a time window after fixing the cause.
Should I use the default event bus or create my own?

Create your own for application events. The default bus carries every AWS service event in the account, which is a high volume of noise to write rules against, and mixing your events into it makes archives and rule management harder. A custom bus gives you a clean namespace, its own archive and retention, and a resource policy you can use to grant specific accounts permission to publish. Keep the default bus for reacting to AWS service events.
How does EventBridge archive and replay work?

An archive retains events matching an optional pattern for a retention period you set, and a replay re-publishes them onto the bus for a chosen time range. It is the main operational advantage over SNS: after fixing a consumer bug you can reprocess exactly the events that were mishandled. Use the FilterArns field on the replay to target specific rules. Replaying onto the whole bus makes every consumer reprocess everything, which is rarely what you want.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
