verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Step Functions must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Orchestrate workflows with AWS Step Functions: Standard vs Express (a 100x cost gap), retries and catchers, Map state parallelism and debugging failed runs.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Orchestrate workflows with AWS Step Functions: Standard vs Express (a 100x cost gap), retries and catchers, Map state parallelism and debugging failed runs.

Step Functions runs a workflow as a state machine defined in JSON. Each state calls a service, branches, waits, or runs work in parallel, and the service handles retries, error paths, timeouts and state between steps.

The point is what it removes. A multi-step process chained together with Lambdas invoking Lambdas needs retry logic in every function, has no record of where an execution got to, and fails in ways nobody can reconstruct afterwards. Step Functions makes the orchestration declarative and gives you a visual history of every execution.

sections.title: Standard or Express
paragraphs: Decide this first. It cannot be changed after creation, and the cost difference is roughly two orders of magnitude.
Standard suits long-running business processes where you need auditability and exactly-once behaviour: order fulfilment, approval flows, ETL.

Express suits high-volume short-lived work: per-request processing, streaming transformations. Because it bills on duration rather than transitions, a workflow with many quick steps is dramatically cheaper. A busy Standard workflow at scale produces genuinely startling bills, because every transition is chargeable.
Express is at-least-once, so its steps must be idempotent.

sections.title: A state machine
paragraphs: That RefundAndFail path is the saga pattern: when a later step fails, run compensating actions for the earlier ones. Distributed transactions do not exist across AWS services, so compensation is how you get consistency, and having it declared in the workflow rather than buried in a function is much of the value.

sections.title: Retries and catchers
paragraphs: Retry re-attempts the same state; Catch routes to a different state when retries are exhausted. Both match on error names.
Order matters. The first matching rule wins, so specific errors go before States.ALL.
JitterStrategy: FULL randomises the delay, which matters when many executions retry simultaneously against the same downstream service; without it they retry in lockstep and keep it overloaded.

Built-in error names worth knowing: States.Timeout, States.TaskFailed, States.Permissions, States.ExceedToleratedFailureThreshold. A Lambda throwing a custom exception surfaces as that exception's name, which is how ValidationError above is matched.
Always set TimeoutSeconds on a Task. Without it a Standard workflow can wait a year for a state that will never complete, and you pay for the wait.

sections.title: Input and output processing
paragraphs: The field that causes most confusion. Four filters apply in order:

The .$ suffix means "this value is a path, not a literal", "Payload.$": "$" passes the whole input, while "Payload": "$" passes the literal string $. Forgetting the .$ is a frequent and confusing bug.

ResultPath: "$.validation" merges the result into the existing state under that key. Omitting ResultPath replaces the entire state with the task's output, which silently loses everything upstream. The usual cause of "my data disappeared halfway through".
ResultSelector is worth using on Lambda tasks to strip the SDK envelope, so downstream states see your payload rather than $.Payload.… everywhere.

sections.title: Map state for parallel work
paragraphs: Set MaxConcurrency. The default is unlimited, so a Map over 10,000 items launches 10,000 concurrent Lambdas, which exhausts your account concurrency, throttles every other function, and often overwhelms whatever database they all connect to. This is one of the easier ways to cause a self-inflicted outage.
ToleratedFailurePercentage lets a batch job survive a few bad items rather than failing entirely.
For very large datasets, distributed map mode reads directly from S3 and runs up to 10,000 parallel child executions, escaping the 256 KB payload limit that inline mode inherits.

sections.title: Direct SDK integrations
paragraphs: Step Functions can call most AWS APIs directly, with no Lambda:

Over 200 services are available this way. Every Lambda you remove is a cold start, a deployment artefact and a per-invocation charge you no longer have, and for a straightforward "write this to DynamoDB" step, the function was never doing anything else.

sections.title: Waiting for something external
paragraphs: The workflow pauses, costing nothing while waiting, until something calls back with the token:
This is how human approval steps work, and a Standard workflow can wait up to a year. $$ accesses the execution context; $$.Task.Token is the callback token.

sections.title: Debugging an execution
paragraphs: Execution names must be unique for 90 days, which is why a timestamp is appended.

--reverse-order puts the failure first, which is almost always what you want. The cause field carries the actual error from the underlying service, that is where the answer is, not in the state machine definition.

codeBlock.code:
aws stepfunctions start-execution --state-machine-arn "$SM_ARN" \
  --input '{"orderId":"A-4821"}' --name "order-A-4821-$(date +%s)"

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The execution role lacks permission for that service. Step Functions needs its own role; the Lambda's role is separate.
Payload between states exceeded 256 KB. Pass an S3 reference instead of the data itself.
That execution name was used within the last 90 days.
The task exceeded TimeoutSeconds, or a Lambda exceeded its own timeout.

codeBlock.code: States.Permissions: The state machine does not have permission to invoke

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Map state processes a 12,000-item array by invoking a Lambda per item. On first run, unrelated Lambda functions across the account began throttling. What was misconfigured?
A workflow passes an order object through three tasks. By the third, the original order fields are gone and only the second task's output remains. No errors occurred. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between Standard and Express workflows?

Standard bills per state transition, runs up to a year, keeps a full queryable execution history for 90 days, and guarantees exactly-once execution. Express bills on requests and duration, is capped at five minutes, logs only to CloudWatch, and is at-least-once, so its steps must be idempotent. At high volume Express costs on the order of 1% of Standard, because a Standard workflow with many quick steps pays for every transition. The type is fixed at creation, so choose deliberately.
When should I use Step Functions instead of chaining Lambdas?

When the process has more than two or three steps, needs retries with backoff, has error paths that differ by failure type, or when you will later be asked what happened to a specific execution. Chained Lambdas put retry logic in every function, keep no record of progress, and are very hard to reconstruct after a failure. Step Functions makes all of that declarative and gives you a visual history per execution. For a single function reacting to an event, it is unnecessary overhead.
How do retries work in Step Functions?

Each state can carry a Retry array matching on error names, with IntervalSeconds, MaxAttempts, BackoffRate and optionally MaxDelaySeconds and JitterStrategy. Rules are evaluated in order and the first match wins, so list specific errors before States.ALL. Catch is the companion: when retries are exhausted it routes to another state rather than failing the execution. Set JitterStrategy: FULL when many executions may retry at once, so they do not hammer a recovering service in lockstep.
Why did my workflow lose data between states?

Because a task without ResultPath replaces the entire state with its own output, discarding everything upstream. Set ResultPath to a key such as "$.payment" so the result is merged in rather than substituted. ResultSelector is worth adding on Lambda tasks too, to strip the invocation envelope so downstream states read your fields directly instead of reaching into $.Payload. Neither produces an error when wrong, which is what makes it confusing to diagnose.
Can Step Functions call AWS services without a Lambda?

Yes, and it should. Optimised integrations exist for common targets such as SQS, SNS, DynamoDB, ECS and Lambda itself, and the generic aws-sdk: integration covers over 200 services and thousands of API actions. A task that only writes to DynamoDB or publishes to SNS needs no function at all. Removing it eliminates a cold start, a deployment artefact and a per-invocation charge. Reserve Lambda for steps that contain real logic.
How do I debug a failed Step Functions execution?

aws stepfunctions get-execution-history --execution-arn <arn> --reverse-order puts the failure first, and the taskFailedEventDetails.cause field carries the underlying service's actual error, that is where the answer is, not in the definition. The console's graph view highlights the failed state and shows input and output at each step, which is usually faster for a one-off. States.Permissions means the state machine's execution role is missing something, which is a separate role from any Lambda's.

Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

keyConcepts.explanation: Choose between API Gateway HTTP, REST and WebSocket APIs, then create an HTTP API with stages, throttling and a custom domain. Includes the 70% price gap.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Choose between API Gateway HTTP, REST and WebSocket APIs, then create an HTTP API with stages, throttling and a custom domain. Includes the 70% price gap.

sections.title: Amazon API Gateway
paragraphs: API Gateway sits in front of your backend and handles the things every API needs: routing, authentication, throttling, request validation, TLS, and logging.

The first decision matters more than anything else on this page, and it is not the one people expect: there are three different products called API Gateway, with different features, different APIs and a substantial price difference.

sections.title: HTTP, REST or WebSocket
paragraphs: Start with HTTP API. It is roughly 70% cheaper, measurably faster, and simpler to configure. For a typical Lambda- or container-backed JSON API it does everything needed, and its built-in JWT authorizer means Cognito or Auth0 integration without writing a custom authorizer.

Move to REST API only for a specific feature: API keys and usage plans for third-party consumers, request validation at the gateway, WAF, private endpoints inside a VPC, or response caching. Those are real reasons, but pick them deliberately rather than by default, because "REST" sounds like the standard choice and is the expensive one.
WebSocket APIs are for persistent bidirectional connections. Chat, live dashboards, notifications.

sections.title: Creating an HTTP API
paragraphs: That single command creates the API, a default route, a Lambda proxy integration and an auto-deploying default stage. For anything beyond a prototype, be explicit:

CORS on an HTTP API is configuration, not code. Set it here and the gateway answers preflight requests itself. On a REST API you configure a mock OPTIONS method instead, which is one of the genuine ergonomic differences.

codeBlock.code:
aws apigatewayv2 create-api \
  --name orders-api --protocol-type HTTP \
  --target "arn:aws:lambda:eu-west-1:123456789012:function:orders"

sections.title: Stages
paragraphs: A stage is a deployed snapshot with its own URL, throttle limits, logging and variables:
--auto-deploy publishes changes immediately. Convenient in development and usually wrong in production, where you want a deliberate deployment step.
REST APIs differ here in a way that catches people constantly: changes do nothing until you create a deployment.
Editing a REST API and wondering why the behaviour has not changed is almost always a missing deployment.
Stage variables let one configuration serve several environments:

codeBlock.code:
aws apigatewayv2 create-stage --api-id "$API_ID" --stage-name prod \
  --auto-deploy \
  --default-route-settings 'ThrottlingBurstLimit=200,ThrottlingRateLimit=100,DetailedMetricsEnabled=true'

sections.title: Throttling and quotas
paragraphs: Two different mechanisms, frequently conflated.
Throttling is rate limiting, applied per stage or per route, and it protects your backend:

Rate limit is steady-state requests per second; burst limit is the token bucket depth for spikes. Exceeding either returns 429 Too Many Requests, and the account-level default of 10,000 requests per second across all APIs in a region is worth knowing before a launch.

Usage plans and API keys are quotas per consumer, requests per day or month, and they are REST API only. If you need to give partners individual keys with monthly limits, that alone justifies REST API.
An important caveat: API keys identify a caller for metering; they are not authentication. Anyone with the key has whatever access the API grants. Use an authorizer for identity.

codeBlock.code:
aws apigatewayv2 update-stage --api-id "$API_ID" --stage-name prod \
  --route-settings '{"GET /orders/{id}": {"ThrottlingRateLimit": 50, "ThrottlingBurstLimit": 100}}'

sections.title: Custom domains
paragraphs: The certificate region differs from CloudFront: a regional endpoint needs the certificate in the same region as the API, while an edge-optimised endpoint needs it in us-east-1. Getting this backwards is a common first-time error.
API mappings are what remove the stage name from your URLs, so consumers call api.example.com/v1/orders rather than the default abc123.execute-api.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/prod/orders.

codeBlock.code:
aws apigatewayv2 create-domain-name --domain-name api.example.com \
  --domain-name-configurations 'CertificateArn=arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:…,EndpointType=REGIONAL,SecurityPolicy=TLS_1_2'

aws apigatewayv2 create-api-mapping --domain-name api.example.com \
  --api-id "$API_ID" --stage prod --api-mapping-key v1

sections.title: Logging
paragraphs: Metrics are on by default; access logs are not, and they are what you will want during an incident:
$context.integrationErrorMessage is the field worth including above all others. When the gateway returns a 502, that is where the actual reason appears.
$context.responseLatency versus $context.integrationLatency separates gateway overhead from backend time, which settles most "the API is slow" arguments.

codeBlock.code:
aws apigatewayv2 update-stage --api-id "$API_ID" --stage-name prod \
  --access-log-settings 'DestinationArn=arn:aws:logs:eu-west-1:123456789012:log-group:/aws/apigw/orders,Format={"requestId":"$context.requestId","ip":"$context.identity.sourceIp","route":"$context.routeKey","status":"$context.status","integrationStatus":"$context.integrationStatus","integrationError":"$context.integrationErrorMessage","latency":"$context.responseLatency"}'

sections.title: API Gateway or an ALB
paragraphs: A reasonable question, since both can front a service:

The deciding factor at scale is usually cost shape: API Gateway charges per request with no hourly fee, while an ALB charges by the hour plus capacity units. Low or spiky traffic favours API Gateway; sustained high volume favours an ALB, and the crossover arrives sooner than most people expect.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: A 502 from a Lambda integration, almost always a malformed response shape. See API Gateway and Lambda. Check integrationErrorMessage in the access log.
Misleading: it usually means the path does not match any route, not an auth problem. Check the route key and whether the stage is in the URL.
A 429 from stage, route or account-level throttling.
REST API changes have no effect. No deployment was created.

codeBlock.code: {"message":"Internal server error"}

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team edits a REST API's integration in the console, saves successfully, and the deployed endpoint keeps behaving as before. No errors appear anywhere. What is missing?
A new JSON API is backed by Lambda, authenticates with Cognito JWTs, and must issue individual keys to partners with monthly request quotas. Which API type fits?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between HTTP API and REST API in API Gateway?

They are separate products with separate APIs. HTTP API is newer, roughly 70% cheaper per request, lower latency, and includes a built-in JWT authorizer, which covers most Lambda- or container-backed JSON APIs. REST API is older and more featureful: API keys and usage plans, request validation at the gateway, WAF integration, private VPC endpoints, response caching and mapping templates. Start with HTTP API and choose REST when you specifically need one of those, rather than because "REST" sounds like the default.
Why do my API Gateway changes not take effect?

On a REST API, because configuration and what is serving traffic are separate: a stage continues serving the last deployment until you run create-deployment for it. Nothing errors, so the change simply appears to be ignored. HTTP APIs avoid this when the stage is created with --auto-deploy. If you are moving between the two types, this is the difference that bites first.
What does "Missing Authentication Token" mean?

Usually that the request path does not match any configured route, despite the message pointing at authentication. API Gateway returns it for an unmatched path on a REST API, so the likely causes are a typo in the path, a missing stage name in the URL (/prod/orders rather than /orders on a default endpoint), or a method that is not configured on an otherwise valid resource. Check the route or resource definition before investigating authorizers.
How does API Gateway throttling work?

Two levels, which are easy to conflate. Stage and route throttling limit requests per second with a burst allowance, protecting your backend. Exceeding either returns 429. Usage plans, available only on REST APIs, meter individual consumers by API key with daily or monthly quotas. There is also an account-level default of 10,000 requests per second across all APIs in a region, which is worth raising before a launch rather than during one.
Should I use API Gateway or an Application Load Balancer?

API Gateway when the backend is Lambda, when you need per-consumer keys and quotas, request validation or transformation, or when traffic is low and spiky. It charges per request with no hourly fee. An ALB when the backend is containers or EC2 and traffic is high and steady, since its hourly plus capacity pricing is cheaper at sustained volume. The crossover point arrives sooner than most people expect, so it is worth modelling if you are anywhere near it.
Do API keys secure my API?

No. An API key identifies a caller so you can meter and throttle them; it is not authentication and should not be treated as a secret that grants access. Anyone holding the key has whatever access the API allows. Use a JWT authorizer, IAM authorisation, or a Lambda authorizer for identity and permissions, and use API keys alongside them purely for usage plans and quotas.

Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.

keyConcepts.explanation: Build an API Gateway REST API with resources, mapping templates and request validation, then add API keys, usage plans, caching and OpenAPI import.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Build an API Gateway REST API with resources, mapping templates and request validation, then add API keys, usage plans, caching and OpenAPI import.

sections.title: API Gateway REST APIs
paragraphs: A REST API costs roughly three and a half times what an HTTP API does, so it is worth being clear about what you get for the difference. This page covers exactly that: the features that justify choosing REST, and how to use them.
If none of these apply to you, use an HTTP API.

sections.title: Resources and methods
paragraphs: A REST API is a tree of resources, each carrying methods:

Building this by hand is laborious, which is why most REST APIs are defined in OpenAPI or CloudFormation and imported. A {proxy+} greedy path catches everything below a point and hands routing to your backend, which cuts the resource tree down dramatically when you do not need per-path gateway behaviour.

codeBlock.code:
REST_ID=$(aws apigateway create-rest-api --name orders-api \
  --endpoint-configuration types=REGIONAL --query id --output text)

ROOT=$(aws apigateway get-resources --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" \
  --query 'items[0].id' --output text)

ORDERS=$(aws apigateway create-resource --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" \
  --parent-id "$ROOT" --path-part orders --query id --output text)

ORDER=$(aws apigateway create-resource --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" \
  --parent-id "$ORDERS" --path-part '{orderId}' --query id --output text)

aws apigateway put-method --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" --resource-id "$ORDER" \
  --http-method GET --authorization-type NONE \
  --request-parameters 'method.request.path.orderId=true'

sections.title: Integration types
paragraphs: AWS_PROXY is the sensible default. See API Gateway and Lambda. The non-proxy AWS type is what enables direct service integrations without a Lambda at all:

That puts a request straight onto an SQS queue with no Lambda in between, no cold start, no function to maintain, and nothing to pay per invocation. The same pattern works for DynamoDB, Step Functions, Kinesis and EventBridge. It is one of the genuinely good reasons to use a REST API.
MOCK integrations are how you stub an endpoint before the backend exists, and how CORS preflight is implemented on a REST API.

codeBlock.code:
aws apigateway put-integration --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" --resource-id "$ORDERS" \
  --http-method POST --type AWS \
  --integration-http-method POST \
  --uri "arn:aws:apigateway:eu-west-1:sqs:path/123456789012/orders" \
  --credentials "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/apigw-sqs-role" \
  --request-parameters 'integration.request.header.Content-Type='"'"'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'"'"'' \
  --request-templates '{"application/json":"Action=SendMessage&MessageBody=$util.urlEncode($input.body)"}'

sections.title: Mapping templates
paragraphs: Mapping templates transform requests and responses using VTL. They are powerful, and they are also code that lives in your infrastructure configuration rather than your repository, so use them for genuine adaptation, not business logic.
Useful $input methods: $input.params('name') reads a path, query or header parameter; $input.json('$') inserts the body as JSON; $input.path('$.field') extracts one value.
The most common legitimate use is mapping a backend error to a proper status code:

selectionPattern is a regex matched against the integration's error output, which is how a Lambda throwing "not found" becomes a 404 rather than a 502. Note it matches the error message, which makes it brittle. Another argument for AWS_PROXY, where your function sets the status code directly.

codeBlock.code:
## Request template
{
  "orderId": "$input.params('orderId')",
  "body": $input.json('$'),
  "requestId": "$context.requestId",
  "caller": "$context.identity.sourceIp"
}

sections.title: Request validation
paragraphs: Rejecting bad requests at the gateway means your backend is never invoked, so you do not pay for it and do not have to write the checks:

A failing request gets a 400 without reaching Lambda. This is REST-only and one of its better features, though the error message it returns is terse, so an API with human consumers usually wants friendlier validation in the application as well.

codeBlock.code:
MODEL=$(aws apigateway create-model --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" \
  --name CreateOrder --content-type application/json \
  --schema '{
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-04/schema#",
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["customerId", "items"],
    "properties": {
      "customerId": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^C-[0-9]+$"},
      "items": {"type": "array", "minItems": 1}
    }
  }' --query name --output text)

VALIDATOR=$(aws apigateway create-request-validator --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" \
  --name body-and-params --validate-request-body --validate-request-parameters \
  --query id --output text)

aws apigateway put-method --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" --resource-id "$ORDERS" \
  --http-method POST --authorization-type NONE \
  --request-validator-id "$VALIDATOR" \
  --request-models '{"application/json":"CreateOrder"}'

sections.title: API keys and usage plans
paragraphs: The feature most often responsible for choosing REST. Keys identify consumers; usage plans meter them:
Then require the key on each method:
Setting apiKeyRequired is the step people forget. Creating keys and plans without it produces an API that happily serves anyone, with the keys metering nobody.
Consumers send the key in the x-api-key header. And again: a key is not authentication. It identifies a caller for metering, nothing more.

codeBlock.code:
KEY_ID=$(aws apigateway create-api-key --name partner-acme --enabled \
  --query id --output text)

PLAN_ID=$(aws apigateway create-usage-plan --name partner-tier \
  --throttle 'rateLimit=10,burstLimit=20' \
  --quota 'limit=10000,period=MONTH,offset=0' \
  --api-stages "apiId=$REST_ID,stage=prod" \
  --query id --output text)

aws apigateway create-usage-plan-key --usage-plan-id "$PLAN_ID" \
  --key-id "$KEY_ID" --key-type API_KEY

sections.title: Caching
paragraphs: Worth knowing two things. The cache is provisioned capacity billed per hour, not per request, so a small cache on a low-traffic API can cost more than the requests it saves. And by default the cache key is the full request path. Enable caching per method and choose cache key parameters deliberately, or authenticated responses can be served to the wrong caller, which is a genuine security bug rather than a performance one.

codeBlock.code:
aws apigateway update-stage --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" --stage-name prod \
  --patch-operations \
    'op=replace,path=/cacheClusterEnabled,value=true' \
    'op=replace,path=/cacheClusterSize,value=0.5' \
    'op=replace,path=/*/*/caching/enabled,value=true' \
    'op=replace,path=/*/*/caching/ttlInSeconds,value=300'

sections.title: Private endpoints
paragraphs: A REST API reachable only from inside your VPCs:
A private API also needs a resource policy allowing the endpoint, or every request is denied:

codeBlock.code:
aws apigateway create-rest-api --name internal-api \
  --endpoint-configuration types=PRIVATE

aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.execute-api \
  --vpc-id vpc-0abc123 --subnet-ids subnet-0a1b2c3d

sections.title: OpenAPI import and canary deployments
paragraphs: Defining the API as a spec and importing it is far more maintainable than clicking through resources, and it gives you a reviewable diff.
REST APIs also support canary deployments natively:

codeBlock.code:
aws apigateway import-rest-api --body 'fileb://openapi.yaml'
aws apigateway put-rest-api --rest-api-id "$REST_ID" --mode overwrite --body 'fileb://openapi.yaml'

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: With a private API, the resource policy does not allow your VPC endpoint. Otherwise, a missing or invalid x-api-key on a method requiring one.
Request validation rejected it against the model. The response is deliberately terse.
The gateway lacks lambda:InvokeFunction. Add a resource-based permission on the function.
Everything returns the old behaviour. No create-deployment after the change.

codeBlock.code: {"message":"Forbidden"}

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: API keys and a usage plan with a monthly quota are configured and attached to the prod stage. Requests without any key still succeed, and usage reports show nothing. What was missed?
A Lambda function behind API Gateway does nothing but forward the request body to an SQS queue. It adds cold starts and cost. What is the REST API feature that removes it?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What can a REST API do that an HTTP API cannot?

Five things worth the price difference: API keys with usage plans for per-consumer quotas, request validation against a JSON Schema model at the gateway, WAF integration, private endpoints reachable only inside a VPC, and response caching. It also supports mapping templates and direct AWS service integrations, which let you call SQS or DynamoDB without a Lambda. If none of those apply, an HTTP API does the same job for roughly 30% of the cost and slightly lower latency.
What are mapping templates and should I use them?

VTL templates that transform a request before it reaches the backend, or a response before it returns. They are genuinely useful for adapting between an external API contract and an internal service shape, and for calling AWS services directly with no Lambda. They are also code living in infrastructure configuration rather than a repository, with limited testing options, so keep them to adaptation and avoid business logic. With AWS_PROXY integrations you rarely need them at all.
How do API keys and usage plans actually work?

An API key identifies a consumer, and a usage plan attaches throttle rates and a daily or monthly quota to one or more API stages. You create the key, create the plan, associate them, and then, the step most often missed, set apiKeyRequired to true on each method that should enforce it. Consumers send the key in the x-api-key header. Keys identify and meter callers; they are not authentication, so pair them with an authorizer for identity.
Is API Gateway caching worth enabling?

Sometimes, and check the arithmetic first. The cache is provisioned capacity billed per hour regardless of traffic, so on a low-volume API it can easily cost more than the backend calls it avoids. The bigger caution is correctness: the default cache key is the request path, so enabling caching on an endpoint whose response depends on the caller can serve one user's data to another. Enable it per method and set cache key parameters explicitly.
How do I make a private API Gateway work?

Create the API with --endpoint-configuration types=PRIVATE, create an interface VPC endpoint for com.amazonaws.<region>.execute-api, and attach a resource policy to the API allowing execute-api:Invoke with an aws:SourceVpce condition naming that endpoint. The resource policy is the part that catches people, without it every request returns Forbidden, because a private API denies everything by default. The endpoint also needs private DNS enabled for the standard hostname to resolve inside the VPC.
Should I define my REST API in OpenAPI?

Yes, for anything beyond a prototype. Building resources and methods through the console or individual CLI calls is slow, error-prone and produces no reviewable artefact. put-rest-api --mode overwrite --body fileb://openapi.yaml applies a spec as the whole definition, so the API is version-controlled, diffable in a pull request and reproducible in another account. AWS-specific integration details go in x-amazon-apigateway-* extensions within the same document.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-api-gateway-lambda.title: AWS API Gateway and Lambda
aws-api-gateway-lambda.subtitle: Connect API Gateway to Lambda with proxy integration and return the response shape that avoids a 502. Covers payload v1 vs v2, CORS and the 29-second limit.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS API Gateway and Lambda must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Connect API Gateway to Lambda with proxy integration and return the response shape that avoids a 502. Covers payload v1 vs v2, CORS and the 29-second limit.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Connect API Gateway to Lambda with proxy integration and return the response shape that avoids a 502. Covers payload v1 vs v2, CORS and the 29-second limit.

sections.title: API Gateway and Lambda
paragraphs: The most common serverless pattern on AWS, and the source of one error more than any other: {"message": "Internal server error"} with a 502, caused not by your code failing but by returning the wrong shape.
This page is mostly about getting that shape right.

sections.title: Proxy integration
paragraphs: With AWS_PROXY, API Gateway passes the entire request to your function and expects the entire HTTP response back. Your function handles routing, status codes and headers.

The alternative, non-proxy AWS integration, uses mapping templates to shape both directions. It lets you keep transformation out of your code, at the cost of VTL in your infrastructure config and error mapping that depends on matching error strings. Use proxy unless you have a specific reason not to.

codeBlock.code:
aws apigatewayv2 create-integration --api-id "$API_ID" \
  --integration-type AWS_PROXY \
  --payload-format-version 2.0 \
  --integration-uri "arn:aws:lambda:eu-west-1:123456789012:function:orders" \
  --timeout-in-millis 29000

sections.title: The response shape
paragraphs: This is the whole ball game. A proxy integration requires an object with specific keys, and anything else is a 502:
Three rules that cause nearly every 502:
body must be a string. Returning a dict is the single most common mistake, json.dumps() it.
statusCode must be present and an integer. "200" as a string fails.
An unhandled exception is a 502, not a 500 with your error. Catch and return deliberately:
The gateway's error message never tells you which of these it was. The function's CloudWatch log does, which is why the log group is the first place to look, not the gateway.

sections.title: Payload format 1.0 vs 2.0
paragraphs: HTTP APIs default to 2.0, REST APIs are always 1.0, and the event structures differ in ways that break code moved between them:

That last row is a real trap. Under 2.0, a function returning a plain object with no statusCode is treated as a successful JSON body with status 200, so a function that silently returns the wrong thing looks like it works. Under 1.0 the same return is a 502. Set statusCode explicitly either way.
Header names arrive lowercased, and event["headers"] in 2.0 joins multiple values with commas rather than providing a multi-value map.
Pin the format explicitly rather than relying on defaults:

codeBlock.code: --payload-format-version 2.0

sections.title: Permissions
paragraphs: API Gateway needs permission to invoke the function. This is a resource-based policy on the Lambda, not an execution role:
Creating the integration in the console adds this automatically; creating it with the CLI, Terraform or CloudFormation does not, which is why a hand-built integration fails with:
Keep --source-arn scoped to your API. A wildcard principal with no source restriction lets any API Gateway in any account invoke your function.

codeBlock.code:
aws lambda add-permission --function-name orders \
  --statement-id apigw-invoke \
  --action lambda:InvokeFunction \
  --principal apigateway.amazonaws.com \
  --source-arn "arn:aws:execute-api:eu-west-1:123456789012:$API_ID/*/*"

sections.title: CORS
paragraphs: Handled in two places, and getting it half right is worse than not doing it at all.
Preflight (OPTIONS), on an HTTP API this is configuration, and the gateway answers without invoking Lambda:
Actual responses: your function must still return the headers, because CORS applies to every response, not just the preflight:

The classic symptom is a request that works in curl and fails in the browser with a CORS error, because the error response lacks the headers even though the success response has them. Return CORS headers on error paths too, or a 500 becomes an unhelpful CORS message that hides the real problem.
AllowCredentials=true cannot be combined with AllowOrigins=*; browsers reject it.

codeBlock.code:
aws apigatewayv2 update-api --api-id "$API_ID" \
  --cors-configuration 'AllowOrigins=https://app.example.com,AllowMethods=GET,POST,PUT,DELETE,OPTIONS,AllowHeaders=content-type,authorization,AllowCredentials=true,MaxAge=300'

sections.title: Timeouts
paragraphs: Two limits, and the smaller one wins:

So a Lambda configured for five minutes behind API Gateway is cut off at 29 seconds, and the client gets a 504 while the function keeps running and billing. Configure the function timeout below the gateway's:
For genuinely long work, return 202 immediately and do the work asynchronously, put a message on SQS or start a Step Functions execution, then let the client poll or receive a webhook.

codeBlock.code: aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name orders --timeout 25

sections.title: Cold starts
paragraphs: A first invocation pays initialisation cost: container start, runtime boot, then your module-level code. Three things help, in order of effect:
Move work to module scope. Clients created inside the handler are rebuilt on every invocation:
Keep the package small. A 200 MB deployment package initialises slower than a 5 MB one. Bundle only what you import.
Provisioned concurrency removes cold starts for a fixed hourly cost:
It requires a version or alias, not $LATEST. Use it for latency-sensitive user-facing paths and not for everything, since you pay whether or not the capacity is used.

codeBlock.code:
import boto3
ddb = boto3.resource("dynamodb")          # once per container
table = ddb.Table("Orders")

def handler(event, context):
    return table.get_item(Key={...})      # reuses the connection

sections.title: Debugging a 502
paragraphs: No Lambda log at all means permissions. A log showing a successful run means the response shape is wrong. A log showing an exception means the code failed, and the 502 is hiding it, which is why you should catch exceptions and return a real status code.

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Did the function even run?
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/orders --since 10m --follow

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Missing lambda:add-permission for apigateway.amazonaws.com.
504 at 29 seconds. Lower the function timeout and make long work asynchronous.
Works in curl, CORS error in the browser. Error responses are missing CORS headers.

codeBlock.code: {"message":"Internal server error"}

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Lambda behind API Gateway logs a successful execution and returns {"statusCode": 200, "body": {"orderId": "A-4821"}}. The client receives 502 Internal server error. Why?

An API returns data correctly via curl. From the browser, successful requests work but any request that errors shows a CORS error instead of the error message. CORS is configured on the HTTP API. What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does API Gateway return "Internal server error" when my Lambda works?

That message is a 502, and it usually means the response shape is wrong rather than the code failing. The three causes, in order: body returned as an object instead of a JSON string, a missing or non-integer statusCode, and an unhandled exception, which API Gateway converts to a 502 rather than surfacing your error. Check the function's CloudWatch log first: a successful run with a 502 at the client points at the response shape, and no log at all points at a missing invoke permission.
What is the difference between payload format 1.0 and 2.0?

They are different event and response contracts. Under 1.0 the method is event["httpMethod"] and the path is event["path"]; under 2.0 they move to event["requestContext"]["http"]["method"] and event["rawPath"], cookies get their own array, and statusCode becomes optional in the response. HTTP APIs default to 2.0 and REST APIs are always 1.0, so code moved between them breaks. Pin --payload-format-version explicitly, and always set statusCode, under 2.0 its absence silently produces a 200.
Why does my integration fail with "Invalid permissions on Lambda function"?

API Gateway needs a resource-based policy on the function allowing apigateway.amazonaws.com to call lambda:InvokeFunction. Creating the integration in the console adds it for you; creating it via CLI, Terraform or CloudFormation does not, which is why this appears in infrastructure-as-code setups and not in console experiments. Add it with aws lambda add-permission, scoping --source-arn to your API so other accounts cannot invoke the function.
How do I fix CORS with API Gateway and Lambda?

Two halves. Configure CORS on the API so the gateway answers OPTIONS preflight requests itself. Then have your function return Access-Control-Allow-Origin on every response, including errors, with a proxy integration the gateway does not add headers to your responses. The tell-tale symptom of getting only the first half right is an API that works in curl and shows CORS errors in the browser whenever something fails, because the error response lacks the headers.
What is the maximum timeout for API Gateway with Lambda?

29 seconds, and it is a hard limit on REST APIs that no support request will raise. Lambda itself allows up to 15 minutes, so a long-running function behind a gateway is cut off at 29 seconds while continuing to run and bill. Set the function timeout below the gateway's, 25 seconds is a sensible ceiling, and for genuinely long work, return 202 immediately after queueing to SQS or starting a Step Functions execution, then let the client poll or receive a callback.
How do I reduce Lambda cold starts behind API Gateway?

In order of effect: initialise SDK clients and database connections at module scope so they persist across invocations in the same container; keep the deployment package small, since initialisation time scales with what has to be loaded; and use provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive paths, which eliminates cold starts entirely for a fixed hourly cost and requires a version or alias rather than $LATEST. Choosing a faster-starting runtime also helps, though rarely enough to justify a rewrite on its own.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-ecr.title: AWS ECR
aws-ecr.subtitle: Push, pull and secure Docker images in Amazon ECR. Authenticate with the AWS CLI, tag images, set lifecycle policies, enable scanning and fix common errors.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS ECR must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Push, pull and secure Docker images in Amazon ECR. Authenticate with the AWS CLI, tag images, set lifecycle policies, enable scanning and fix common errors.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Push, pull and secure Docker images in Amazon ECR. Authenticate with the AWS CLI, tag images, set lifecycle policies, enable scanning and fix common errors.

sections.title: Amazon ECR
paragraphs: Amazon ECR is AWS's private container registry. Its real advantage over Docker Hub isn't features. It's that authentication runs through IAM, so the same roles that govern the rest of your infrastructure govern who can push and pull images, and pulls from inside AWS don't cross the internet or hit rate limits.
You'll spend most of your ECR time on four things: authenticating, tagging correctly, stopping storage costs from creeping, and reading scan results.

sections.title: Repositories
paragraphs: An ECR repository holds all the tags for one image. It's regional, and the name is part of the image URI:

IMMUTABLE is the setting worth arguing for. With mutable tags, someone can push a different image over 1.4.2 and every future pull silently gets different bytes, which makes rollbacks unreliable and incident timelines impossible to reconstruct. Immutability makes that push fail instead.

codeBlock.code:
<account-id>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/<repository>:<tag>
111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2

sections.title: Authenticating
paragraphs: ECR doesn't use a static username and password. You exchange IAM credentials for a token that lasts 12 hours:
The username is literally the string AWS, that's not a placeholder. And the registry argument is the host only, with no repository path and no https://.

Two mistakes account for most login failures. Passing the region of one registry while logging into another gives you a token that's valid but for the wrong endpoint. And a token acquired 13 hours ago in a long-running CI agent will fail with a 401 that reads like a permissions problem but isn't, re-authenticate on every job rather than caching the login.

codeBlock.code:
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 \
  | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

sections.title: Pushing an image
paragraphs: If you skip step 2, Docker tries to push to Docker Hub and fails with a denied error that says nothing about ECR.
Tag with something traceable. A commit SHA is the most useful default, because it maps a running container back to exact source:
Never deploy :latest. It's mutable by definition, so two deploys of "latest" can run different code, and a rollback has nothing to roll back to.

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Build
docker build -t payments-api:1.4.2 .

# 2. Tag with the full registry URI. This is the step people forget
docker tag payments-api:1.4.2 \
  111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2

# 3. Push
docker push 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api:1.4.2

sections.title: Lifecycle policies
paragraphs: ECR charges $0.10 per GB per month, and image layers accumulate faster than anyone expects. A CI pipeline pushing on every commit will produce thousands of images a year. Lifecycle policies expire them automatically.

Rules evaluate in priority order and an image is expired by the first matching rule, so put your "keep" rules at lower priority numbers than your broad cleanup rules. Run the preview before applying. There is no undelete.

sections.title: Image scanning
paragraphs: ECR scans images for known CVEs. Basic scanning is free and runs on push; enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector, costs more, and continuously rescans as new vulnerabilities are published, which matters, because an image that was clean when built is not clean forever.
Gate your pipeline on it, but gate on severity rather than any finding at all. A policy of "zero vulnerabilities" gets switched off within a month:

Most findings come from the base image, so switching from a full distribution base to a slim or distroless one usually removes more CVEs than any amount of dependency patching. This is one of the clearest payoffs of a good multi-stage build.

codeBlock.code:
aws ecr describe-image-scan-findings \
  --repository-name payments-api \
  --image-id imageTag=1.4.2 \
  --query 'imageScanFindings.findingSeverityCounts'

sections.title: Permissions
paragraphs: Two policy types apply, and both must allow the action:
A minimal pull-only IAM policy:

ecr:GetAuthorizationToken must be granted on *. It's an account-level call, not a repository-level one. Scoping it to a repository ARN silently breaks authentication, and it's a common cause of "it works for me but not in CI".

Repository policies are how you share images across accounts. A shared build account pushes once; every environment account pulls from it, so the artifact that reaches production is the exact one that passed tests.

sections.title: Pull through cache
paragraphs: Pull through cache mirrors upstream registries (Docker Hub, ECR Public, quay.io, GitHub) into your own ECR on first pull. It removes Docker Hub rate limits from your builds and keeps working if the upstream is down:
Then pull 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/docker-hub/library/nginx:1.27 instead of nginx:1.27.

codeBlock.code:
aws ecr create-pull-through-cache-rule \
  --ecr-repository-prefix docker-hub \
  --upstream-registry-url registry-1.docker.io \
  --credential-arn arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:111122223333:secret:ecr-pullthroughcache/dockerhub

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A CI role has ecr:GetAuthorizationToken scoped to a specific repository ARN, plus full push permissions on that repository. The docker login step fails. Why?
A repository has rule priority 1 expiring any image older than 30 days, and rule priority 2 keeping the 10 most recent tagged releases. Release images are disappearing. What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does docker push to ECR fail with "denied: requested access to the resource is denied"?

Nearly always one of two things. Either the image wasn't tagged with the full registry URI, docker tag myapp:1.0 111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:1.0, in which case Docker is trying to push to Docker Hub, or the repository doesn't exist yet. ECR never creates repositories implicitly on push, unlike Docker Hub. Create it first with aws ecr create-repository, and confirm your docker login used the same account and region as the tag.
How long does ECR authentication last?

Twelve hours. aws ecr get-login-password exchanges your IAM credentials for a token with that lifetime. For CI this is usually invisible because each job authenticates fresh, but long-running agents that cache a login will start failing with 401 errors partway through the day. Authenticate at the start of every job rather than treating login as one-time setup.
Should I use ECR or Docker Hub?

For anything running on AWS, ECR. Authentication uses IAM instead of a separate credential set, pulls from within AWS stay on the AWS network and avoid Docker Hub's rate limits, and images sit inside your account's security and compliance boundary. Docker Hub still makes sense for publicly distributed images where you want easy anonymous pulls. Pull through cache gives you a middle path: mirror the upstream images you depend on into ECR automatically.
How do I stop ECR storage costs from growing?

Set a lifecycle policy on every repository at creation time. Storage is $0.10 per GB per month and a pipeline that pushes on each commit accumulates quickly. A practical pair of rules: expire untagged images after 7 days, and keep only the most recent 10 to 20 tagged releases. Always run start-lifecycle-policy-preview first, because expiry is permanent and a mis-ordered rule can delete images you meant to keep.
Can another AWS account pull images from my ECR repository?

Yes, through a repository policy that names the other account as a principal and allows the pull actions, ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer, ecr:BatchGetImage, and ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability. The pulling account also needs ecr:GetAuthorizationToken in its own IAM policies. This is the standard shared-build-account pattern: one account builds and pushes, environment accounts pull, and the artifact promoted to production is byte-identical to the one tested.
What is the difference between basic and enhanced image scanning?

Basic scanning is free, runs on push, and checks operating system packages against a CVE database. Enhanced scanning is powered by Amazon Inspector, costs per image, and additionally inspects application-language dependencies while continuously rescanning stored images as new vulnerabilities are disclosed. That continuous part is the real difference. An image that scanned clean six months ago may have several critical findings today, and only enhanced scanning tells you.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-eks.title: AWS EKS
aws-eks.subtitle: Understand how Amazon EKS runs Kubernetes on AWS: what AWS manages, node options, access entries, IRSA vs Pod Identity, add-ons and networking pitfalls.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS EKS must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Understand how Amazon EKS runs Kubernetes on AWS: what AWS manages, node options, access entries, IRSA vs Pod Identity, add-ons and networking pitfalls.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand how Amazon EKS runs Kubernetes on AWS: what AWS manages, node options, access entries, IRSA vs Pod Identity, add-ons and networking pitfalls.

sections.title: Amazon EKS
paragraphs: Amazon EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you. AWS operates the API server and etcd across three Availability Zones, patches them, and backs them with an SLA. You keep everything above that line: worker capacity, networking, add-ons, and access control.

That split is the whole point, and it's also where most of the surprises live. A cluster comes up in fifteen minutes; making it production-ready takes considerably longer, because the pieces EKS doesn't manage are the ones that cause outages.
EKS: Managed Kubernetes Architecture
AWS manages the control plane HA. You only pay for worker nodes

sections.title: What AWS runs and what you run
paragraphs: The control plane costs $0.10/hour per cluster, about $73/month, before you run a single pod. That's per cluster, so the "one cluster per team per environment" pattern gets expensive quickly. Nodes, load balancers, and data transfer are all billed separately.

sections.title: Creating a cluster
paragraphs: eksctl is the fastest path. It's a community tool, not an AWS product, but it's the de facto standard and it provisions the VPC, IAM roles, and node group in one command:
Expect cluster creation to take 15 to 20 minutes. The control plane alone is roughly 10 of those.
For anything real, define the cluster in a config file so it's reviewable and reproducible:

Two things in that file matter more than they look. privateNetworking: true keeps nodes off public subnets. Nodes should never have public IPs. And enabling audit logging from day one means you have the logs when you need them; turning it on after an incident is too late.

codeBlock.code:
# Simplest possible cluster. Fine for learning, not for production
eksctl create cluster \
  --name demo \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --nodes 2 \
  --node-type t3.medium

# Point kubectl at it (eksctl does this automatically; this is the manual form)
aws eks update-kubeconfig --region us-east-1 --name demo

kubectl get nodes -o wide

sections.title: Choosing how nodes run
paragraphs: Managed node groups are the default answer. Fargate is genuinely useful for CI runners and one-off jobs, but the "no DaemonSets" limitation catches teams out. Most observability agents ship as DaemonSets and simply won't run there.

For scaling, Karpenter has largely replaced the Cluster Autoscaler on new clusters. Cluster Autoscaler adjusts node group sizes; Karpenter provisions right-sized instances directly from the EC2 API, which packs workloads better and responds faster.

sections.title: Access control: two systems, not one
paragraphs: This is the part that confuses nearly everyone. Getting a pod or a person into an EKS cluster involves two separate permission systems, and both must allow the action.
An IAM administrator with AdministratorAccess is not automatically a cluster admin. They need a mapping.

Historically that mapping lived in the aws-auth ConfigMap: a single YAML object in kube-system that, if you corrupted it, locked everyone out of the cluster with no recovery path short of AWS Support. Access entries replaced it and are now the recommended approach:

If you're on a cluster still using aws-auth, migrating is worth doing. Set the cluster's authentication mode to API_AND_CONFIG_MAP, create access entries alongside the existing ConfigMap, verify, then switch to API.

codeBlock.code:
# Grant an IAM role cluster-admin via the EKS API, no ConfigMap editing
aws eks create-access-entry \
  --cluster-name production \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/PlatformTeam \
  --type STANDARD

aws eks associate-access-policy \
  --cluster-name production \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/PlatformTeam \
  --access-scope type=cluster \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy

sections.title: Giving pods AWS permissions
paragraphs: Never attach application permissions to the node's instance profile. Every pod on that node inherits them, so one compromised container gets whatever the node has.
There are two correct approaches:
IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) uses an OIDC provider on the cluster. The service account carries an annotation, and the pod receives a scoped token:

EKS Pod Identity is the newer option and simpler to operate. It needs the eks-pod-identity-agent add-on, but it drops the per-cluster OIDC trust-policy setup, which makes roles reusable across clusters:
For a new cluster, prefer Pod Identity. IRSA remains the right choice if you need to reuse roles outside EKS or you're on a region or version where Pod Identity isn't available.

codeBlock.code:
eksctl create iamserviceaccount \
  --cluster production \
  --namespace payments \
  --name payments-api \
  --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess \
  --approve

sections.title: Networking, and the mistake everyone makes once
paragraphs: The AWS VPC CNI gives every pod a real VPC IP address from your subnets. That's excellent for observability and security groups, and it means you can run out of IP addresses in a way you never would on other Kubernetes distributions.
A t3.medium supports 17 pods. Not because of CPU or memory, because of ENI limits. Teams routinely provision a /24 subnet, scale to 40 pods, and hit failed to assign an IP address to container.
Two fixes: size subnets generously from the start (a /20 per AZ is not excessive), and enable prefix delegation, which assigns /28 blocks per ENI and raises that t3.medium from 17 pods to 110.
Load balancer placement depends on subnet tags. Miss these and your Ingress will sit in pending with no useful error:

codeBlock.code:
# Check what's actually available before you scale
aws ec2 describe-subnets \
  --filters "Name=tag:kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb,Values=1" \
  --query 'Subnets[].{ID:SubnetId,AZ:AvailabilityZone,Free:AvailableIpAddressCount}' \
  --output table

sections.title: Upgrades
paragraphs: EKS supports each Kubernetes version for about 14 months, then moves it to extended support at a significantly higher hourly rate. Clusters left unattended eventually get force-upgraded.
Upgrade order matters:
Before any upgrade, check for removed APIs. This is the single most common cause of a broken upgrade:
Set a PodDisruptionBudget on anything that matters, or a node drain will take all your replicas down at once.

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Control plane first. One minor version at a time, no skipping
eksctl upgrade cluster --name production --version 1.32 --approve

# 2. Core add-ons
eksctl utils update-coredns --cluster production --approve
eksctl utils update-kube-proxy --cluster production --approve

# 3. Nodes last
eksctl upgrade nodegroup --cluster production --name general

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An engineer has the IAM AdministratorAccess policy but gets "error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)" when running kubectl. Why?

A deployment scales from 10 to 40 replicas. New pods stay in ContainerCreating with "failed to assign an IP address to container", but nodes show plenty of free CPU and memory. What is the most likely cause?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How much does an EKS cluster cost?

The control plane is $0.10 per hour, roughly $73 per month, per cluster. On top of that you pay for worker nodes (EC2 or Fargate), EBS volumes, load balancers, NAT gateway data processing, and cross-AZ traffic. A small production cluster with three m6i.large nodes and a NAT gateway typically lands somewhere around $300 to 400 per month. Clusters on extended support versions cost considerably more per hour, which is a deliberate nudge to keep current.
What is the difference between IRSA and EKS Pod Identity?

Both give pods scoped AWS permissions without using the node's instance profile. IRSA uses an OIDC provider per cluster, so each IAM role's trust policy references that specific cluster. Reusing a role across clusters means editing trust policies. Pod Identity uses an agent add-on and a simple association API instead, so the same role works across clusters unchanged. Pod Identity is simpler to operate and is the better default for new clusters; IRSA is still needed for some cross-account patterns and in places where Pod Identity isn't yet available.
Why do my pods fail with "failed to assign an IP address to container"?

The VPC CNI allocates each pod a real IP from your subnets, so you've exhausted either the subnet's addresses or the instance's ENI limit. Check free addresses with aws ec2 describe-subnets. Fix it by enabling prefix delegation on the VPC CNI, which assigns /28 blocks per ENI and raises pod density dramatically, and by using larger subnets. A /20 per Availability Zone is a reasonable starting point.
Why is my Ingress stuck in pending?

Almost always subnet tags. The AWS Load Balancer Controller discovers where to place a load balancer by looking for kubernetes.io/role/elb=1 on public subnets and kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb=1 on private ones. Without those tags it has nowhere to put the load balancer and fails quietly. Check the controller's logs, kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/aws-load-balancer-controller, which will say it couldn't discover subnets. The other common cause is that the controller isn't installed at all; EKS does not ship it by default.
Do I need eksctl, or can I use Terraform?

Either works, and for anything long-lived Terraform is usually the better answer because the cluster then lives alongside the rest of your infrastructure in the same state and review process. eksctl is faster for learning and for throwaway clusters, and it handles a lot of IAM and VPC wiring for you. Many teams use eksctl to explore and Terraform to run production.
Can I run an EKS cluster without any EC2 instances?

Yes. Fargate profiles run pods on AWS-managed capacity with no nodes to patch, and EKS Auto Mode goes further by managing compute for you. The Fargate constraints are real, though: no DaemonSets, no privileged containers, no EBS volume mounts, and a per-pod cost that's higher than equivalent EC2 for steady workloads. Because most monitoring and logging agents are DaemonSets, fully serverless clusters usually need a different observability approach.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create an EKS cluster that works the first time: avoid IAM lockouts with access entries vs aws-auth, tag subnets correctly and plan for the VPC CNI IP limit.

EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you. Highly available across three availability zones, patched and backed by an SLA. For a fixed hourly charge per cluster. You supply the worker nodes and everything above them.

What makes EKS different from other managed Kubernetes is the IAM-to-Kubernetes boundary. AWS authenticates you; Kubernetes RBAC authorises you; and the mapping between the two is where almost every new cluster goes wrong.

sections.title: Create the cluster
paragraphs: eksctl is the pragmatic choice. It creates the VPC, subnets, IAM roles and node groups that a cluster needs, which by hand is a long afternoon:
Expect 15 to 20 minutes. The equivalent with the AWS CLI is aws eks create-cluster plus separately creating the VPC, both IAM roles, the OIDC provider and the node groups.

withOIDC: true matters more than it looks. It creates the OIDC identity provider that IRSA depends on, and without it pods cannot assume IAM roles. You end up putting access keys in secrets, which is the thing IRSA exists to prevent. Adding it later is possible and easy to forget.

codeBlock.code:
# cluster.yaml
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig

metadata:
  name: prod
  region: eu-west-1
  version: "1.31"

iam:
  withOIDC: true                 # required for IRSA

vpc:
  cidr: 10.0.0.0/16
  clusterEndpoints:
    publicAccess: true
    privateAccess: true

addons:
  - name: vpc-cni
    version: latest
    configurationValues: '{"env":{"ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION":"true"}}'
  - name: coredns
  - name: kube-proxy
  - name: aws-ebs-csi-driver
    wellKnownPolicies:
      ebsCSIController: true

managedNodeGroups:
  - name: general
    instanceTypes: ["m6i.large", "m6a.large"]
    minSize: 2
    maxSize: 10
    desiredCapacity: 3
    privateNetworking: true
    volumeSize: 50
    volumeType: gp3

sections.title: The access problem
paragraphs: The most common EKS experience: create a cluster, hand it to a colleague, and they get
The cluster creator is granted admin implicitly. Nobody else has any access at all until you grant it, and the error gives no hint as to why.
There are two mechanisms. Access entries are the current approach and far better:
The aws-auth ConfigMap is the older mechanism, still present on many clusters:

Editing it is genuinely dangerous. A malformed entry locks everyone out of the cluster, including you, and recovery means the original creator identity or AWS Support. Access entries exist precisely because of that failure mode. Set the cluster's authentication mode to API_AND_CONFIG_MAP and migrate.

Note a subtlety that wastes a lot of time: IAM roles are matched by the role ARN, not the assumed-role session ARN. Mapping arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/Admin/user does not work; map arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/Admin.

codeBlock.code: error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)

sections.title: Subnet tagging
paragraphs: EKS discovers subnets by tag. Missing tags produce a cluster that works until you create a LoadBalancer service or an Ingress, which then never gets an address:
eksctl applies these. A cluster built into a pre-existing VPC by hand frequently does not have them, and the symptom, a service stuck in <pending> with no events explaining it, points nowhere useful.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-tags --resources subnet-0a1b2c3d \
  --tags Key=kubernetes.io/role/elb,Value=1

sections.title: The CNI IP address limit
paragraphs: The constraint that catches teams at exactly the wrong moment.

The AWS VPC CNI gives every pod a real VPC IP address, which is excellent for networking and means pod density is capped by how many IPs an instance type supports. An m6i.large supports 3 network interfaces with 10 addresses each: 29 usable, minus some for the node itself.
Pods then sit in Pending with:
Two fixes. Prefix delegation assigns /28 prefixes instead of individual addresses, raising an m6i.large from 29 pods to around 110:
Or size your subnets properly. A /24 per subnet runs out quickly when every pod consumes an address. Plan the VPC CIDR around peak pod count, not node count.

codeBlock.code: kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PODS:.status.allocatable.pods

sections.title: Endpoint access
paragraphs: Public and private both enabled, with the public side restricted to your office and CI ranges, is the arrangement that works for most teams. Private-only is a genuine trap: kubectl then only works from inside the VPC or over a VPN, and it is easy to enable while working from an EC2 host and lose access from your laptop.

codeBlock.code:
aws eks update-cluster-config --name prod \
  --resources-vpc-config endpointPublicAccess=true,endpointPrivateAccess=true,publicAccessCidrs=203.0.113.0/24

sections.title: Add-ons
paragraphs: Managed add-ons let AWS handle version compatibility:

Four are effectively required. vpc-cni, coredns and kube-proxy come with the cluster. aws-ebs-csi-driver does not, and since Kubernetes 1.23 it is what actually provisions EBS volumes, so without it every PersistentVolumeClaim sits Pending forever with no obvious cause. It is the single most common "my cluster is broken" after a fresh install.
Worth adding beyond those: AWS Load Balancer Controller for Ingress, and either Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler for node scaling.

codeBlock.code:
aws eks describe-addon-versions --addon-name vpc-cni \
  --kubernetes-version 1.31 --query 'addons[0].addonVersions[0].addonVersion'

aws eks create-addon --cluster-name prod --addon-name aws-ebs-csi-driver \
  --service-account-role-arn "$EBS_CSI_ROLE_ARN" \
  --resolve-conflicts OVERWRITE

sections.title: Upgrades
paragraphs: The order is fixed: control plane, then add-ons, then nodes. You cannot skip minor versions, so 1.29 to 1.32 is three sequential upgrades.
Before each one, check for deprecated APIs. An upgrade that removes an API version your manifests use breaks them with no warning:
EKS supports each version for a limited window and then force-upgrades you, with extended support billed at a much higher hourly rate. Falling behind is expensive as well as risky.

codeBlock.code: aws eks update-cluster-version --name prod --kubernetes-version 1.32

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: No access entry or aws-auth mapping for your principal. Also check you are in the right account and region.
CNI IP exhaustion. Enable prefix delegation.
The EBS CSI driver add-on is missing.
A LoadBalancer service stuck at <pending>. Subnet tags missing, or no AWS Load Balancer Controller.
kubectl times out. Private-only endpoint, and you are outside the VPC.

codeBlock.code: error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A new EKS cluster works for the engineer who created it. A teammate with AdministratorAccess in the same account runs kubectl get nodes and receives "You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)". Why?
Pods are Pending with "0/4 nodes are available: 4 Too many pods." The nodes are m6i.large with CPU and memory largely unused. What is the constraint?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why do I get "You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)" on EKS?

Because your IAM principal is not mapped to anything in Kubernetes. EKS uses IAM for authentication and Kubernetes RBAC for authorisation, and only the identity that created the cluster is granted admin automatically, even an account administrator is unauthorised until mapped. Create an access entry for the principal and associate a cluster access policy. Two gotchas: map the IAM role ARN rather than the assumed-role session ARN, and confirm you are targeting the right account and region.
What is the difference between access entries and the aws-auth ConfigMap?

aws-auth is the original mechanism: a ConfigMap in kube-system mapping IAM ARNs to Kubernetes users and groups. It is edited with kubectl, has no validation, and a malformed entry can lock every user out of the cluster with recovery requiring the original creator identity or AWS Support. Access entries are the API-based replacement. Managed with aws eks commands, validated, auditable through CloudTrail, and manageable before anyone can reach the cluster. Use access entries; migrate existing clusters by setting authentication mode to API_AND_CONFIG_MAP.
Why are my pods stuck in Pending with "Too many pods"?

The AWS VPC CNI assigns each pod a real VPC IP address, so pods per node is limited by the instance type's network interface capacity rather than by CPU or memory. An m6i.large allows roughly 29. Enable prefix delegation with ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true on the aws-node DaemonSet, which allocates /28 prefixes and raises the figure to around 110. Also check subnet sizing: with an address per pod, a /24 exhausts far sooner than node counts suggest.
Why is my PersistentVolumeClaim stuck in Pending on EKS?

Almost certainly the EBS CSI driver is not installed. Since Kubernetes 1.23 the in-tree EBS provisioner has been removed, so the aws-ebs-csi-driver add-on is what actually creates volumes, and a new cluster does not include it. Add it with aws eks create-addon --addon-name aws-ebs-csi-driver, giving it an IRSA role with the necessary EC2 permissions. This is the most frequent "my fresh cluster is broken" cause after access problems.
Why is my LoadBalancer service stuck in pending?

Usually subnet tags. EKS discovers which subnets to place load balancers in by tag, kubernetes.io/role/elb on public subnets and kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb on private ones, and without them nothing is provisioned and the events say very little. eksctl applies these automatically, so it mainly affects clusters built into an existing VPC. The second cause is the AWS Load Balancer Controller not being installed, which is required for Ingress resources and for LoadBalancer services of type NLB.
How do I upgrade an EKS cluster safely?

In order: control plane, then add-ons, then nodes, and one minor version at a time, since skipping is not permitted. Before each step, check for deprecated API usage with the apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis metric, because an upgrade that removes an API your manifests still use breaks them without warning. Test in a non-production cluster first. Falling behind is costly as well as risky: EKS force-upgrades unsupported versions, and extended support is billed at a substantially higher hourly rate.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
