sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Run EKS worker nodes : managed node groups vs Fargate, why Karpenter beats Cluster Autoscaler, taints, Spot interruptions and nodes that will not join.

sections.title: EKS Node Groups
paragraphs: The control plane is AWS's problem. The nodes are yours, and how you run them determines your cost, your upgrade pain and how quickly pods get scheduled.

sections.title: Three ways to run workers
paragraphs: Managed node groups are the default choice. AWS handles the Auto Scaling group, the AMI, and a graceful drain-and-replace upgrade.
Self-managed is for what managed cannot express: a custom AMI with specific kernel settings, unusual GPU configurations, or Windows in older setups.

Fargate removes nodes entirely, and its limitations are what decide it. No DaemonSets, so any log shipper, security agent or service mesh sidecar delivered that way does not run. No privileged containers, no host networking, and a maximum of 4 vCPU and 30 GB per pod. It suits bursty, isolated workloads; it rarely suits a general-purpose cluster.

sections.title: A managed node group
paragraphs: List several instance types. It widens the pool the group can draw from, which matters for capacity during a busy period and enormously for Spot.

Include a version in the name. Node group configuration is largely immutable. Instance types, AMI family and subnets cannot be changed after creation, so "upgrading" often means creating general-v2, migrating, and deleting general. A name without a version makes that awkward.

codeBlock.code:
eksctl create nodegroup --config-file=- <<'EOF'
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
metadata:
  name: prod
  region: eu-west-1
managedNodeGroups:
  - name: general-v2
    instanceTypes: ["m6i.large", "m6a.large", "m5.large"]
    minSize: 2
    maxSize: 20
    desiredCapacity: 3
    privateNetworking: true
    volumeSize: 100
    volumeType: gp3
    amiFamily: AmazonLinux2023
    labels:
      workload: general
    updateConfig:
      maxUnavailablePercentage: 25
    iam:
      withAddonPolicies:
        cloudWatch: true
EOF

sections.title: Taints and labels
paragraphs: Labels attract pods; taints repel them. Together they keep workloads where they belong:

The taint is what stops ordinary pods landing on expensive GPU instances. Without it the scheduler treats them as general capacity and you pay GPU rates to run a web service. A mistake that shows up on the bill rather than in any alert.

codeBlock.code:
managedNodeGroups:
  - name: gpu
    instanceTypes: ["g5.xlarge"]
    labels:
      workload: ml
      nvidia.com/gpu: "true"
    taints:
      - key: nvidia.com/gpu
        value: "true"
        effect: NoSchedule

sections.title: Karpenter over Cluster Autoscaler
paragraphs: For node scaling there are two options, and they are not close any more.
Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the desired capacity of existing node groups. It can only launch instance types those groups already define, needs a group per instance shape, and takes several minutes.
Karpenter watches unschedulable pods and launches instances chosen to fit them, right-sizing automatically, consolidating underused nodes, and provisioning in under a minute.

Rather than enumerating instance types, you describe acceptable characteristics and let Karpenter pick. consolidationPolicy then actively repacks pods onto fewer nodes and terminates the remainder, which is where most of the saving comes from. Cluster Autoscaler only scales down nodes that are already nearly empty.
Keep a small managed node group for Karpenter itself and CoreDNS. Karpenter cannot provision the nodes it runs on.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: ["spot", "on-demand"]
        - key: kubernetes.io/arch
          operator: In
          values: ["amd64", "arm64"]
        - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category
          operator: In
          values: ["c", "m", "r"]
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
  limits:
    cpu: 1000
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 30s

sections.title: Spot instances
paragraphs: Spot is where cluster cost drops by 60 to 90%, and it is safe for stateless workloads given three things.
Diversify. Accept many instance types and families so an interruption in one pool is absorbed elsewhere. A Spot node group pinned to a single type is what gives Spot its reputation.

Handle interruptions. AWS gives a two-minute warning; something must cordon and drain the node. Karpenter handles this natively via an SQS queue; with managed node groups, run the AWS Node Termination Handler.
Set PodDisruptionBudgets, or a drain can evict every replica at once:
Mix capacity types rather than going all-Spot: a baseline of on-demand for the workloads that must not move, Spot for everything else.

codeBlock.code:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api

sections.title: Upgrading nodes
paragraphs: AWS cordons each node, drains it respecting PodDisruptionBudgets, waits, then terminates it.

That respect for PDBs is a double edge. A PDB that can never be satisfied, minAvailable: 1 on a single-replica Deployment, blocks the drain indefinitely, and the upgrade hangs for hours before failing:
Before any upgrade, check for PDBs that cannot be met:
ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS: 0 is the row that will stop your upgrade. --force skips PDBs entirely, which gets the upgrade moving and causes the outage the PDB existed to prevent.
Set maxUnavailablePercentage to control the pace: 25% replaces a quarter of the group at a time, which is much faster than the default of one node while still being gradual.

codeBlock.code:
aws eks update-nodegroup-version --cluster-name prod \
  --nodegroup-name general --kubernetes-version 1.32

sections.title: Diagnosing a node that will not join
paragraphs: A node that launches but never appears in kubectl get nodes is nearly always one of four things:
describe-nodegroup's health.issues usually names it directly, and is faster than reading instance logs.
For a node that joined and later went NotReady, look at the kubelet:
DiskPressure is common and usually means image accumulation. Set imageGCHighThresholdPercent or use larger root volumes.

codeBlock.code:
kubectl get nodes
aws eks describe-nodegroup --cluster-name prod --nodegroup-name general \
  --query 'nodegroup.health.issues'

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: IAM, networking, security groups or bootstrap user data.
An unsatisfiable PodDisruptionBudget. Fix the PDB or the replica count.
The pod lacks a toleration for a tainted node group.
Nodes at Ready but pods stay Pending. Often CNI IP exhaustion rather than a node problem.

codeBlock.code: NodeCreationFailure: Instances failed to join the kubernetes cluster

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A managed node group upgrade stalls, then fails with "pods that cannot be evicted". One namespace has a single-replica Deployment with a PodDisruptionBudget of minAvailable: 1. What is happening?
A g5.xlarge node group was added for machine learning. Ordinary web pods are now scheduling onto it and the bill has risen sharply. The node group has the label workload: ml. What is missing?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between managed node groups, self-managed nodes and Fargate?

Managed node groups have AWS run the Auto Scaling group, supply the AMI and orchestrate graceful upgrades. The right default. Self-managed nodes give you full control of the AMI, user data and lifecycle, which you need for custom kernels or unusual hardware. Fargate removes nodes entirely and charges per pod, but supports no DaemonSets, no privileged containers and no host networking, and caps a pod at 4 vCPU and 30 GB. That DaemonSet restriction alone rules Fargate out for most clusters running log shippers or security agents.
Should I use Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler?

Karpenter, on new clusters. Cluster Autoscaler only adjusts the size of node groups you have already defined, so it can only launch instance types those groups specify and needs a group per shape. Karpenter looks at pending pods and provisions instances that fit them, in under a minute, choosing from broad requirements rather than a fixed list, and it consolidates underused nodes, which is where most of the cost saving comes from. Keep a small managed node group for Karpenter itself and CoreDNS.
How do I run Spot instances safely on EKS?

Three things together. Diversify across many instance types and families so one pool's interruption is absorbed elsewhere. A single-type Spot group is what earns Spot its bad reputation. Handle the two-minute interruption notice by cordoning and draining, which Karpenter does natively and managed node groups need the AWS Node Termination Handler for. And set PodDisruptionBudgets so a drain cannot evict every replica at once. Keep a baseline of on-demand capacity for anything that must not move.
Why won't my EKS nodes join the cluster?

Four causes cover nearly all of it, and aws eks describe-nodegroup --query 'nodegroup.health.issues' usually names the right one. The node IAM role may be missing AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly or AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy. A private subnet may have no NAT gateway or VPC endpoints, leaving nodes unable to reach the EKS API or ECR. Security groups may not permit cluster-to-node traffic both ways. Or a custom launch template's user data may not invoke the bootstrap script.
What is the difference between a taint and a label on a node group?

A label is descriptive. It lets a pod request that node through a nodeSelector or affinity rule, and does nothing otherwise. A taint is restrictive: it prevents any pod without a matching toleration from being scheduled there. Labels alone on an expensive node group are not enough, because the scheduler sees untainted capacity and uses it, so ordinary pods land on GPU instances. Use both: a taint to keep others out, and a label plus nodeSelector to draw the intended workload in.
How do I upgrade EKS nodes without downtime?

Use update-nodegroup-version, which cordons, drains respecting PodDisruptionBudgets, and replaces each node. Before starting, run kubectl get pdb -A and fix any budget showing ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS: 0, since that blocks the drain indefinitely and the upgrade eventually fails. Set maxUnavailablePercentage to around 25 so the rollout is gradual but not glacial. Avoid --force: it ignores PDBs and produces the outage they were protecting against.

quickReference.command: kubectl describe node ip-10-0-1-42.ec2.internal | grep -A10 Conditions

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand AWS CloudFormation: template anatomy, deploying stacks, change sets, drift detection and stuck stacks, plus CloudFormation vs Terraform.

CloudFormation is AWS's native infrastructure-as-code service. You describe resources in a YAML or JSON template, and CloudFormation works out the order to create them, tracks what it created in a stack, and can tear the whole thing down again.

Its defining characteristic, for better and worse, is that the state lives in AWS. There's no state file to store, lock, or accidentally commit. In exchange, you get whatever recovery options AWS gives you when a stack wedges, and no more.

sections.title: Template anatomy
paragraphs: Only Resources is required. The pieces that earn their place quickly:

DeletionPolicy: Retain on stateful resources is the single most valuable line in that template. Without it, deleting a stack deletes the bucket and everything in it. UpdateReplacePolicy covers the sneakier case: a property change that forces replacement rather than an in-place update.

codeBlock.code:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Payments service networking

Parameters:
  Environment:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, staging, prod]
    Description: Deployment environment

Mappings:
  EnvConfig:
    dev:     { InstanceType: t3.small }
    staging: { InstanceType: t3.medium }
    prod:    { InstanceType: m6i.large }

Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Environment, prod]

Resources:
  AppBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'payments-${Environment}-${AWS::AccountId}'
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: !If [IsProd, Enabled, Suspended]
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true

Outputs:
  BucketName:
    Value: !Ref AppBucket
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-BucketName'

sections.title: Deploying
paragraphs: aws cloudformation deploy is the command to use. It creates the stack if it doesn't exist and updates it if it does:

--capabilities is mandatory whenever a template creates IAM resources. It's an explicit acknowledgement that you're about to grant permissions, CAPABILITY_IAM for unnamed roles, CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM when you set a role name yourself.
Validate before you deploy:
That only checks syntax. For real linting, deprecated properties, invalid values, security issues, use cfn-lint, which catches far more:

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudformation deploy \
  --template-file template.yaml \
  --stack-name payments-network-prod \
  --parameter-overrides Environment=prod \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM \
  --tags Service=payments Environment=prod

sections.title: Change sets
paragraphs: Never update a production stack without previewing the plan. A change set is CloudFormation's equivalent of terraform plan:

Replacement: True is the column that matters. It means CloudFormation will create a new resource and delete the old one. On a database or an EBS volume, that is data loss delivered by an apparently routine property change. Read every change set for that column before executing.
aws cloudformation deploy --no-execute-changeset produces the same preview in one step.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudformation create-change-set \
  --stack-name payments-network-prod \
  --change-set-name review-$(date +%s) \
  --template-body file://template.yaml \
  --parameters ParameterKey=Environment,ParameterValue=prod \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM

aws cloudformation describe-change-set \
  --stack-name payments-network-prod \
  --change-set-name review-1757600000 \
  --query 'Changes[].ResourceChange.{Action:Action,Resource:LogicalResourceId,Replacement:Replacement}' \
  --output table

sections.title: When a stack gets stuck
paragraphs: This is where CloudFormation's managed state cuts both ways.
UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED is the one that hurts. An update failed, the rollback also failed, and the stack now accepts no further updates. Recovery:
Skipped resources drift out of CloudFormation's view, so you must reconcile them by hand afterwards.

DELETE_FAILED is usually a dependency CloudFormation didn't create: a non-empty S3 bucket, an ENI still attached, a security group referenced by something outside the stack. Empty or detach it, then retry the delete.
Rollback on create failure deletes everything, which makes debugging awkward. Disable it while iterating:

codeBlock.code:
# Skip the resources that cannot roll back
aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback \
  --stack-name payments-network-prod \
  --resources-to-skip AppDatabase

sections.title: Drift detection
paragraphs: Someone will change something in the console. Drift detection finds it:
Run it on a schedule via EventBridge rather than only during incidents. Be aware that drift detection doesn't support every resource type, so a clean report is reassuring rather than conclusive.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name payments-network-prod

aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource-drifts \
  --stack-name payments-network-prod \
  --stack-resource-drift-status-filters MODIFIED DELETED

sections.title: Structuring larger systems
paragraphs: Don't put everything in one template. A 3,000-line template is slow to deploy, dangerous to change, and impossible to review.
Nested stacks compose child templates into a parent, sharing a lifecycle:

Cross-stack references with Export/ImportValue link independent stacks, but the coupling is rigid: you cannot delete or modify an exported value while another stack imports it, and untangling that in production is genuinely painful. Prefer passing values as parameters, or reading them from Parameter Store, unless you specifically want that hard dependency.
StackSets deploy one template across many accounts and regions, which is how you roll out baseline guardrails to an entire AWS Organization.

codeBlock.code:
Resources:
  Network:
    Type: AWS::CloudFormation::Stack
    Properties:
      TemplateURL: https://s3.amazonaws.com/my-templates/network.yaml
      Parameters:
        Environment: !Ref Environment

sections.title: CloudFormation or Terraform?
paragraphs: Choose CloudFormation if you're AWS-only, want no state to manage, or need StackSets for organisation-wide rollouts. Choose Terraform if you touch more than one provider, or you want the ability to surgically repair state. The UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED situation has no real Terraform equivalent because you can always edit state directly.

If YAML is the sticking point rather than the engine, AWS CDK lets you write TypeScript or Python that synthesises CloudFormation templates, giving you loops, types, and testing while keeping managed state.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A change set for a production stack shows Modify on an RDS instance with Replacement: True. What will happen if you execute it?
A networking stack exports SubnetId. Updating it to rename that export fails with "Export cannot be updated as it is in use". Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I fix a stack stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED?

Run aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback --stack-name <name>. If it fails again, add --resources-to-skip with the logical IDs of the resources blocking the rollback, which you can find in describe-stack-events. Skipping means CloudFormation stops tracking their real state, so afterwards you must inspect those resources and either bring them back in line with the template or import them again. The usual root causes are a resource deleted outside CloudFormation and an IAM permission that was revoked mid-update.
What is the difference between a change set and just deploying?

A change set computes what would change and shows it without applying anything, the same role terraform plan plays. It tells you which resources are added, modified or deleted and, critically, which will be replaced rather than updated in place. Deploying without one means finding out at execution time, which on a stateful resource can mean discovering the replacement after the original is gone.
Does deleting a CloudFormation stack delete my data?

Yes, by default. Deleting a stack deletes every resource it created, including S3 buckets, RDS instances and EBS volumes. Protect anything stateful with DeletionPolicy: Retain (keep the resource, orphaned from the stack) or DeletionPolicy: Snapshot where supported. Add UpdateReplacePolicy too, since a replacement during an update deletes the original by a different code path that DeletionPolicy alone does not cover. Enabling termination protection on the stack adds another safeguard.
CloudFormation or Terraform, which should I learn?

Terraform if you only learn one, because it works across AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Datadog and hundreds of other providers, and the skill transfers between employers. CloudFormation is worth knowing if you are in an AWS-only environment, particularly for StackSets, which deploy a template across every account in an Organization with no equivalent in open-source Terraform. Many AWS teams run both: CloudFormation or CDK for account baselines, Terraform for application infrastructure.
Why does my template fail with "Requires capabilities: [CAPABILITY_IAM]"?

The template creates IAM resources, a role, policy, user or instance profile, and CloudFormation requires you to acknowledge that explicitly rather than granting permissions as an invisible side effect. Add --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM, or CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM if any IAM resource has an explicit name. A third value, CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND, is needed for templates using macros or transforms such as AWS SAM.
How do I split a large template without creating a mess?

Nested stacks are the tighter option: a parent template declares AWS::CloudFormation::Stack children, they deploy and delete as one unit, and values pass down as parameters. Independent stacks linked by Export/ImportValue are more loosely coupled on the surface but create a dependency that blocks the exporting stack from changing while consumers exist. For most teams the cleanest pattern is independent stacks that pass values as parameters or read them from Parameter Store, keeping stacks genuinely separable.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Recover a CloudFormation stack stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED or ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, then prevent repeats with change sets, drift checks and delete policies.

sections.title: CloudFormation Stacks
paragraphs: A stack is a set of AWS resources managed as one unit, created from a template. Create the stack and the resources appear in dependency order; delete it and they are removed in reverse. That atomicity is the point, and the failure modes below are what you spend your time on.

sections.title: Create, and watch it properly
paragraphs: When something fails, the stack events hold the answer, and the first failure is the one that matters, since everything after it is consequence:

--capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM is required for any template creating roles or policies, and CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM when those have explicit names. It exists so a template cannot quietly grant itself permissions you did not review.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudformation create-stack --stack-name orders-api \
  --template-body file://template.yaml \
  --parameters ParameterKey=Environment,ParameterValue=prod \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM \
  --enable-termination-protection \
  --tags Key=Owner,Value=platform

sections.title: Never update without a change set
paragraphs: update-stack applies changes immediately. A change set shows you what it would do first, and the distinction that matters is Replacement. A resource being deleted and recreated rather than modified in place.
Replacement: True on a database, a table or a volume means the existing one is deleted and a new empty one created. The stack update reports success and the data is gone.

Changing a DynamoDB table's key schema, an RDS instance's identifier, or an EC2 instance's availability zone all trigger replacement. Reading this table before every production update is the single most valuable CloudFormation habit.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudformation create-change-set --stack-name orders-api \
  --change-set-name review-$(date +%s) \
  --template-body file://template.yaml \
  --parameters ParameterKey=Environment,ParameterValue=prod \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM

sections.title: The two rollback states you will meet
paragraphs: ROLLBACK_COMPLETE: the stack's first creation failed and rolled back. It cannot be updated, only deleted:
Delete it and create again. This only happens on initial creation; a failed update produces UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, which is a healthy state.
UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED: worse. An update failed, and the rollback failed too, so the stack is stuck and refuses everything.
If a specific resource cannot roll back, typically one deleted outside CloudFormation, or a security group with a dependency that no longer exists. Skip it and reconcile by hand:
Skipped resources leave the stack's view of reality wrong, so follow up with drift detection.
To avoid the state entirely, keep --on-failure ROLLBACK (the default) and disable rollback only when you genuinely want to inspect a half-built stack:

codeBlock.code:
An error occurred (ValidationError): Stack:arn:... is in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE
state and can not be updated.

sections.title: Protecting what matters
paragraphs: Termination protection blocks delete-stack entirely. Enable it on anything stateful.
DeletionPolicy protects individual resources even when the stack goes:
UpdateReplacePolicy is the one people omit, and it is the one that saves you. It covers the replacement case above, where the stack is not being deleted but the resource is.
A stack policy can deny updates to specific resources:

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudformation update-termination-protection \
  --stack-name orders-api --enable-termination-protection

sections.title: Drift
paragraphs: Resources changed outside CloudFormation, a console edit during an incident, another tool, are drift, and CloudFormation neither notices nor corrects it until the next update, which may overwrite the fix or fail confusingly.

Detection is asynchronous, so poll describe-stack-drift-detection-status with the returned id. Run it before any significant update to a stack you do not fully control, and on a schedule for production.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name orders-api
aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource-drifts --stack-name orders-api \
  --stack-resource-drift-status-filters MODIFIED DELETED \
  --query 'StackResourceDrifts[].[LogicalResourceId,StackResourceDriftStatus]' --output table

sections.title: Cross-stack references
paragraphs: Two ways to share values, with very different consequences.
Exports and Fn::ImportValue create a hard dependency:
An exported value cannot be changed or deleted while anything imports it, so the networking stack becomes effectively frozen. That is sometimes protection and often an obstacle.
SSM Parameter Store is looser and usually better:
No hard coupling, and the consumer picks up changes on its next update.

codeBlock.code:
# networking stack
Outputs:
  VpcId:
    Value: !Ref Vpc
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-VpcId'

sections.title: Nested stacks or StackSets
paragraphs: Different problems, frequently confused.

Nested stacks break one large template into reusable components deployed together as a parent and children. They keep templates under the 500-resource and 1 MB limits and allow reuse. The cost is worse error messages. A failure inside a child surfaces as a generic failure on the parent, so you follow the event chain down.
StackSets deploy the same stack across many accounts and regions:

With Organizations integration, service-managed StackSets deploy automatically to new accounts as they are created, which is how a baseline of logging, guardrails and IAM roles lands everywhere without anyone remembering to apply it.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudformation create-stack-instances --stack-set-name baseline-guardrails \
  --deployment-targets OrganizationalUnitIds=ou-abc1-12345678 \
  --regions eu-west-1 us-east-1 \
  --operation-preferences FailureTolerancePercentage=10,MaxConcurrentPercentage=25

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Failed initial creation. Delete and recreate.
CloudFormation sees no difference. Real when nothing changed; misleading when you edited a file you are not actually submitting.
Remove the import first, or use SSM parameters instead.
Something outside the stack owns that name. Use import-stacks-to-stack-set or create-change-set --import-existing-resources to adopt it rather than renaming.

codeBlock.code: Stack ... is in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE state and can not be updated.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A CloudFormation update changed a DynamoDB table's partition key. The stack reported UPDATE_COMPLETE and the table is now empty. What would have prevented this?

A networking stack exports its VPC ID, and three application stacks import it. Attempts to update the networking stack fail with "Export cannot be updated as it is in use". What is the underlying issue?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a change set and why should I always use one?

A change set is a preview: CloudFormation compares your new template against the deployed stack and lists what it would add, modify or delete, without doing any of it. The column that matters is Replacement, True means a resource will be deleted and recreated rather than modified, so a database or table would come back empty while the update reports success. Reading that list before every production update is the single most valuable CloudFormation habit, and it costs one extra command.
How do I fix a stack stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED?

Run aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback. If a particular resource is what blocks it, commonly one deleted outside CloudFormation, or a security group whose dependency has gone. Add --resources-to-skip naming those logical IDs, which lets the rollback finish while leaving those resources unmanaged. Afterwards run drift detection, because skipping resources means the stack's view of reality is now wrong and the next update may behave unexpectedly.
Why can't I update a stack in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE?

Because that state means the stack's very first creation failed and was rolled back, so there is no previously working configuration to update from. CloudFormation only allows deleting it. Delete the stack and create it again with the corrected template. A stack that has succeeded at least once never enters this state; a failed update leaves UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, which is perfectly updatable.
What is CloudFormation drift and how do I handle it?

Drift is a difference between what the template says and what actually exists, caused by changes made outside CloudFormation. A console edit during an incident, or another tool touching the same resources. CloudFormation does not notice or correct it automatically, so the next update may overwrite the manual fix or fail in a confusing way. Run detect-stack-drift before significant updates and on a schedule for production, then either bring the change into the template or revert it.
When should I use nested stacks versus StackSets?

They solve unrelated problems. Nested stacks split one large deployment into reusable child templates deployed together, keeping you under the resource and template size limits and allowing components to be shared between stacks. StackSets deploy the same stack to many accounts and regions at once, which is how organisation-wide baselines are applied, and with Organizations integration, new accounts receive them automatically as they are created.
How do I stop CloudFormation deleting my database?

Two settings, both needed. DeletionPolicy: Retain keeps the resource when the stack is deleted. UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain keeps it when an update would otherwise replace it. The case people forget, because the stack is not being deleted and the loss still happens. Add termination protection on the stack itself, and a stack policy denying Update:Replace on the specific resource if you want a hard block rather than a retained orphan.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Write maintainable CloudFormation templates with typed parameters, intrinsic functions, conditions, DependsOn and custom resources, then lint with cfn-lint.

sections.title: CloudFormation Templates
paragraphs: A template declares what should exist; CloudFormation works out how to get there. This page is about writing ones that are still readable a year later. The mechanics of operating stacks are covered separately.
Use YAML. It supports comments, the short-form functions (!Ref, !Sub) are far more readable than their JSON equivalents, and multi-line strings work properly.

sections.title: Structure
paragraphs: Only Resources is mandatory. Everything else earns its place.

codeBlock.code:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Orders API infrastructure

Parameters:
  Environment:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, staging, prod]
    Description: Deployment environment

  DbPassword:
    Type: AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<String>
    Default: /orders/db-password
    NoEcho: true

  VpcId:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPC::Id

Mappings:
  EnvConfig:
    dev:      { InstanceType: t3.small,  MinSize: 1, MultiAZ: false }
    staging:  { InstanceType: t3.medium, MinSize: 2, MultiAZ: false }
    prod:     { InstanceType: m6i.large, MinSize: 3, MultiAZ: true }

Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Environment, prod]

Resources:
  Database:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    DeletionPolicy: Snapshot
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot
    Properties:
      DBInstanceClass: !FindInMap [EnvConfig, !Ref Environment, InstanceType]
      MultiAZ: !FindInMap [EnvConfig, !Ref Environment, MultiAZ]
      MasterUserPassword: !Ref DbPassword
      BackupRetentionPeriod: !If [IsProd, 30, 1]
      DeletionProtection: !If [IsProd, true, false]

Outputs:
  DatabaseEndpoint:
    Value: !GetAtt Database.Endpoint.Address
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-DbEndpoint'

sections.title: Parameter types do validation for you
paragraphs: The most under-used feature in CloudFormation. A typed parameter is validated before the stack starts changing anything, rather than failing halfway through:

Typing a subnet as String means a typo fails during creation, after other resources exist. Typing it as AWS::EC2::Subnet::Id means it fails immediately with a clear message, and the console gives a dropdown.

AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<String> is the one worth adopting as a habit: the template references a parameter path, and the value is fetched at deploy time, so secrets and environment-specific values never appear in the template or in version control.
Add NoEcho: true to anything sensitive so it is masked in the console, events and API responses.

codeBlock.code:
AllowedCidr:
    Type: String
    AllowedPattern: '^(\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}/\d{1,2}$'
    ConstraintDescription: Must be a valid CIDR block

sections.title: Intrinsic functions
paragraphs: !Ref returns the "main" value. For a parameter its value, for most resources the physical ID, though what exactly that means varies by type. Check the documentation rather than assuming.
!GetAtt returns a specific attribute:
!Sub substitutes variables into a string, and should be your default over !Join:
!Sub also reaches attributes directly with ${Resource.Attribute}, and a literal ${ is escaped as ${!.

Pseudo-parameters are always available: AWS::Region, AWS::AccountId, AWS::StackName, AWS::Partition, AWS::NoValue. Use AWS::Partition rather than hardcoding aws in ARNs if anything might run in GovCloud or China.
!Ref AWS::NoValue removes a property entirely, which is how you make one conditional:

codeBlock.code:
!GetAtt Database.Endpoint.Address
!GetAtt LambdaRole.Arn

sections.title: Conditions
paragraphs: A resource with a false Condition is not created at all. This keeps one template serving every environment, which is much better than three templates that drift apart.

Beyond a handful of conditions, though, readability collapses. That is usually the point at which CDK or a templating layer is the better answer, because real conditionals in a programming language beat nested !If expressions.

codeBlock.code:
Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Environment, prod]
  IsNotDev: !Not [!Equals [!Ref Environment, dev]]
  NeedsBackup: !Or [!Condition IsProd, !Condition IsNotDev]

Resources:
  ReadReplica:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Condition: IsProd
    Properties:
      SourceDBInstanceIdentifier: !Ref Database

sections.title: Dependencies
paragraphs: CloudFormation infers ordering from !Ref and !GetAtt, if resource A references B, B is created first. Most of the time you need nothing else.
DependsOn is for ordering CloudFormation cannot see:

An EC2 instance downloading packages depends on the internet gateway being attached, but nothing in its properties references it, so without DependsOn the instance may launch first and its user data fails silently.

Overusing DependsOn is its own problem: it serialises creation that could have run in parallel and makes the dependency graph harder to reason about. Add it when you have a real ordering requirement, not defensively.

codeBlock.code:
Instance:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Instance
    DependsOn: GatewayAttachment      # needs internet access to bootstrap

sections.title: Custom resources
paragraphs: For anything CloudFormation does not support natively:

The Lambda receives Create, Update and Delete events and must signal back to a presigned URL. If it does not, because it timed out, crashed, or returned without responding, CloudFormation waits the full hour before failing.
Two rules make them survivable: always respond, including from your exception handler, and handle Delete as a no-op rather than an error if the thing is already gone, or stack deletion hangs forever.
Where possible, prefer a module or an AWS-provided resource type over writing one.

codeBlock.code:
DnsValidation:
    Type: Custom::DnsValidator
    Properties:
      ServiceToken: !GetAtt ValidatorFunction.Arn
      DomainName: !Ref DomainName

sections.title: Lint before you deploy
paragraphs: cfn-lint catches misspelled properties, invalid values, missing required fields and unreachable conditions. The things that otherwise fail ten minutes into a deploy. Run it in CI.
aws cloudformation validate-template only checks that the template parses, which is much weaker.
cfn-guard enforces policy, "every S3 bucket must have encryption", "no security group may allow 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22", as a check rather than a review comment.

codeBlock.code: cfn-lint template.yaml

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: A !Ref to something that does not exist. Usually a typo in a logical ID, which are case-sensitive.
!Condition is required when referencing one condition from another. A plain !Ref does not work there.
A typed parameter doing its job before anything was created.
The Lambda did not signal back. Check its logs and make sure every path responds.

codeBlock.code:
Template format error: Unresolved resource dependencies [VpcId] in the
Resources block

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A template creates a VPC, an internet gateway, a gateway attachment and an EC2 instance whose user data installs packages. The stack succeeds but the instance has no packages. Nothing references the attachment. What is missing?
A template has BackupRetension instead of BackupRetentionPeriod. aws cloudformation validate-template reports no problems. Where would this be caught before deploying?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I write CloudFormation templates in YAML or JSON?

YAML. It supports comments, which JSON does not and which templates badly need; the short-form intrinsic functions (!Ref, !Sub, !GetAtt) are far more readable than {"Fn::Sub": …}; and multi-line strings for user data and policies work properly. JSON is only preferable when a template is machine-generated. Both express exactly the same thing, and cfn-flip converts between them if you inherit the wrong one.
What is the difference between !Ref and !GetAtt?

!Ref returns a resource's default identifier, which varies by type: a bucket name for an S3 bucket, an instance ID for EC2, the value itself for a parameter. !GetAtt returns a named attribute, such as !GetAtt Database.Endpoint.Address or !GetAtt Role.Arn. When you need an ARN, an endpoint or anything other than the primary identifier, it is !GetAtt. Since what !Ref returns differs per resource type, check the documentation rather than assuming.
Why should I use typed parameters like AWS::EC2::Subnet::Id?

Because they are validated before CloudFormation changes anything. A subnet declared as String accepts a typo and fails partway through creation, after other resources exist and with a rollback to sit through; declared as AWS::EC2::Subnet::Id it fails immediately with a clear message, and the console offers a dropdown. AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<String> goes further by resolving a value from Parameter Store at deploy time, keeping secrets and per-environment settings out of the template entirely.
When do I need DependsOn?

Only when a real ordering requirement exists that no property expresses. CloudFormation derives ordering from !Ref and !GetAtt, so most dependencies are already handled. The classic exception is an EC2 instance whose user data needs internet access, which depends on the internet gateway attachment without referencing it. Adding DependsOn defensively serialises resources that could have been created in parallel, making deployments slower and the dependency graph harder to reason about.
What is a custom resource and what usually goes wrong?

A hook that lets a Lambda function do something CloudFormation does not natively support, receiving Create, Update and Delete events as part of the stack lifecycle. The thing that goes wrong is not signalling back: the function must POST a response to a presigned URL, and if it times out or throws before doing so, CloudFormation waits a full hour before failing. Always respond from the exception handler too, and treat Delete on something already absent as success, or stack deletion hangs.
How do I validate a CloudFormation template before deploying?

cfn-lint template.yaml is the real check. It validates property names and values against the resource specification and catches misspellings, missing required fields, bad enum values and unused parameters, with line numbers. aws cloudformation validate-template only confirms the document parses, so it passes templates that will certainly fail. Add cfn-guard if you want policy enforcement, such as requiring encryption on every bucket or forbidding 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22. Run all of it in CI.

quickReference.explanation: Core command for AWS CloudFormation Templates

Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Deploy an app with Elastic Beanstalk without managing servers. Compare deployment policies and downtime tradeoffs, blue-green URL swaps and .ebextensions.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Deploy an app with Elastic Beanstalk without managing servers. Compare deployment policies and downtime tradeoffs, blue-green URL swaps and .ebextensions.

Beanstalk takes your application code and creates everything needed to run it. EC2 instances, an Auto Scaling group, a load balancer, security groups, CloudWatch alarms, from a single command. It is a platform-as-a-service layer over ordinary AWS resources.

The crucial property, and the reason it is still worth knowing: everything Beanstalk creates is a normal AWS resource in your account. You can inspect the Auto Scaling group, adjust the security groups, and see exactly what it built. That makes it a much gentler starting point than a fully opaque platform, and it means the exit path is understood rather than a rewrite.

sections.title: Deploying
paragraphs: A Procfile tells Beanstalk how to start the application, and defining it explicitly avoids relying on platform defaults that change between versions:

codeBlock.code:
eb init orders-api --platform python-3.12 --region eu-west-1
eb create prod-env --instance-types t3.small --min-instances 2 --max-instances 8
eb deploy
eb open

sections.title: Environment types
paragraphs: Web server environments sit behind a load balancer and serve HTTP. Worker environments have no load balancer; instead a daemon on each instance reads from an SQS queue and POSTs each message to your application on localhost.
That worker pattern is genuinely useful. Background jobs scale independently of the web tier, and your application only needs to handle an HTTP POST rather than integrate an SQS client.

A single-instance environment (--single) has no load balancer, which saves the hourly charge and is right for development. It also means no zero-downtime deployments and no redundancy, so it is not a production configuration.

codeBlock.code: eb create worker-env --tier worker

sections.title: Deployment policies matter
paragraphs: This is the setting that determines whether a deploy causes an outage, and the default is not the safe one.
All at once is the default and takes the whole environment down during the deploy. Fine for development, wrong for anything users touch.
Rolling updates instances in batches, so capacity drops while a batch is out. Rolling with additional batch launches extra instances first, keeping full capacity throughout.

Immutable launches a complete new Auto Scaling group, waits for it to pass health checks, then swaps and terminates the old one. It costs double for a few minutes and it is the safest option. A failed deploy leaves the original instances untouched and rolls back automatically. For production it is the one to choose.
Traffic splitting is a canary: a percentage of requests go to new instances for an evaluation period, and it rolls back automatically if health degrades.

codeBlock.code:
aws elasticbeanstalk update-environment --environment-name prod-env \
  --option-settings \
    Namespace=aws:elasticbeanstalk:command,OptionName=DeploymentPolicy,Value=Immutable \
    Namespace=aws:elasticbeanstalk:command,OptionName=Timeout,Value=1800

sections.title: Blue-green by swapping URLs
paragraphs: Beanstalk's built-in blue-green is a CNAME swap between two environments:

The swap is near-instant and reversible by swapping back. A far better rollback story than redeploying. Two caveats. It is DNS, so clients holding a cached record keep hitting the old environment until the TTL expires. And a database inside the environment does not come along, which leads to the next point.

codeBlock.code:
eb create prod-env-v2 --cname orders-api-v2
eb deploy prod-env-v2
# test prod-env-v2 thoroughly
eb swap prod-env --destination-name prod-env-v2

sections.title: Never put the database in the environment
paragraphs: Beanstalk offers to create an RDS instance inside the environment. Do not accept for anything you care about.

The database then shares the environment's lifecycle: terminate the environment and the database goes with it. It also cannot be shared with another environment, which breaks blue-green entirely. The new environment has no data.
Create RDS separately and pass the endpoint in:
This is the most consequential Beanstalk mistake, and it is presented as a convenient default during setup.

codeBlock.code: eb setenv DATABASE_URL="postgresql://app@orders-db.abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/orders"

sections.title: Configuration with .ebextensions
paragraphs: YAML files in .ebextensions/ customise the environment:
leader_only: true is essential for migrations. Without it every instance runs the migration simultaneously, which at best is wasteful and at worst corrupts data.
Files are processed in alphabetical order, so prefix them with numbers. On Amazon Linux 2 and later, platform hooks in .platform/hooks/ are the newer mechanism and are preferred for scripts.
Beware that .ebextensions can create arbitrary CloudFormation resources. Powerful, and a common way for a Beanstalk environment to become something nobody understands.

codeBlock.code:
# .ebextensions/01-options.config
option_settings:
  aws:elasticbeanstalk:application:environment:
    PYTHONPATH: /var/app/current
  aws:autoscaling:asg:
    MinSize: 2
    MaxSize: 8
  aws:elasticbeanstalk:environment:
    LoadBalancerType: application
  aws:elbv2:loadbalancer:
    IdleTimeout: 120
  aws:autoscaling:trigger:
    MeasureName: CPUUtilization
    UpperThreshold: 70
    LowerThreshold: 30

packages:
  yum:
    postgresql-devel: []

container_commands:
  01_migrate:
    command: "python manage.py migrate --noinput"
    leader_only: true

sections.title: Health
paragraphs: Enhanced health monitoring reads application response codes and latency rather than just EC2 status checks, and it is what makes Degraded meaningful. Enable it.

An environment that goes Severe immediately after a deploy is usually the application failing to bind to the expected port. Beanstalk's nginx proxies to port 8000 on most platforms, and an app listening on 3000 or on 127.0.0.1 fails health checks while appearing to run.

codeBlock.code: eb health --refresh

sections.title: When to move on
paragraphs: Beanstalk suits a single application, a small team, and conventional web or worker workloads. It is the fastest route from code to a production-shaped deployment on AWS.

Move on when you need several services deployed independently (ECS or EKS), fine-grained infrastructure control (CDK or Terraform), or when you find yourself writing enough .ebextensions to constitute an infrastructure codebase, at which point the abstraction is costing more than it saves.
The exit is genuinely manageable, because the underlying resources were always ordinary AWS resources. That is a real argument for starting here rather than avoiding it.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Constrain the environment to zones that offer the type.
The application is not serving on the expected port, or crashed on start. eb logs --all and check the bind address.
Read the CloudFormation events for the real cause; Beanstalk's message is a wrapper.
Deploy succeeds, old code still served. The version was not deployed to that environment, or a cached artefact. eb appversion lists what exists.

codeBlock.code:
ERROR: Your requested instance type (t3.small) is not supported in your
requested Availability Zone

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team creates a second environment for blue-green, deploys to it, and finds it has an empty database. The original environment's RDS instance was created through Beanstalk during setup. What went wrong?
A production Beanstalk deploy caused about four minutes of complete unavailability. The environment has four instances behind a load balancer and default settings. What should change?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is Elastic Beanstalk and how does it differ from ECS or Lambda?

Beanstalk is a platform-as-a-service layer that provisions EC2 instances, an Auto Scaling group, a load balancer and monitoring from your application code, so you deploy code rather than infrastructure. ECS runs containers you have built and gives you far more control over networking, task placement and scaling. Lambda removes servers entirely and charges per invocation. Beanstalk sits between "just run my app" and "I want to configure everything", and unlike a closed platform, everything it creates is a standard AWS resource you can inspect and eventually take over.
Which Elastic Beanstalk deployment policy should I use?

Immutable for production. It launches an entirely new Auto Scaling group, waits for health checks to pass, then swaps traffic and terminates the old instances, so a failed deploy leaves the originals serving and rolls back automatically, at the cost of running double capacity for a few minutes. "All at once" is the default and takes the whole environment down, which is only acceptable in development. "Rolling with additional batch" is the middle ground, preserving full capacity without doubling it.
Should I let Beanstalk create my RDS database?

No, for anything beyond a throwaway environment. A database created inside the environment shares its lifecycle, so terminating the environment deletes it, and it cannot be shared with a second environment, which makes blue-green deployments impossible, since the new environment comes up with no data. Create RDS separately and pass the connection string in with eb setenv. Migrating away later means a snapshot, a restore outside Beanstalk and a repoint, so it is much easier to get right initially.
How does blue-green deployment work in Elastic Beanstalk?

You run two environments and exchange their CNAMEs with eb swap. Deploy to the idle environment, test it properly on its own URL, then swap, which is near-instant and reversible by swapping back, giving a far better rollback than redeploying. Two things to understand: it is DNS, so clients holding a cached record continue hitting the old environment until the TTL expires, and the database must live outside both environments or the new one has nothing to serve.
What are .ebextensions and when should I use them?

YAML configuration files in an .ebextensions/ directory that customise the environment. Option settings, packages to install, files to write, and commands to run during deployment. The one setting worth memorising is leader_only: true on container_commands that run migrations, since without it every instance runs them simultaneously. On Amazon Linux 2 and later, .platform/hooks/ is the newer mechanism and is preferred for scripts. Be wary of growing them into an infrastructure codebase, which is usually the signal to move to CDK or Terraform.
Why does my environment show Severe right after deploying?

Most often the application is not listening where Beanstalk expects. The platform's nginx proxies to a specific port, 8000 on most, 5000 on some, so an app bound to 3000, or bound to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0, fails every health check while the process itself is running fine. Run eb logs --all and check the bind address and port first. The other frequent cause is a crash during startup from a missing environment variable, which the application log will show directly.

Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Use AWS KMS correctly: why key policies come before IAM, AWS managed vs customer managed keys, envelope encryption, encryption context, rotation and grants.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Use AWS KMS correctly: why key policies come before IAM, AWS managed vs customer managed keys, envelope encryption, encryption context, rotation and grants.

KMS creates and controls encryption keys. The keys themselves never leave the service. You send data or a data key to KMS and it returns the encrypted or decrypted result, so the key material is never in your application's memory or your logs.
AWS Security Services Overview
Almost everything that goes wrong with KMS comes down to one thing that works differently from the rest of AWS: a key policy is required, and IAM alone is not enough.

sections.title: The key policy rule
paragraphs: For most AWS resources, an IAM policy granting access is sufficient. For KMS it is not. Every key has a key policy, and access requires permission from both the key policy and IAM, unless the key policy explicitly delegates to IAM.
That delegation is what the default key policy does:

Principal: root here does not mean the root user. It means "this account", and it allows IAM policies in the account to grant access to this key. Remove that statement and IAM becomes irrelevant, only principals named directly in the key policy can use the key, and an administrator with AdministratorAccess cannot.
That is also how a key gets orphaned. A key policy naming only a deleted role locks the key permanently, and recovery requires AWS Support.
A more careful policy separates administration from use:

Note the separation: an administrator can manage the key and cannot decrypt with it. kms:ViaService restricts use to requests arriving through a named service, so the role can decrypt S3 objects and cannot call kms:Decrypt directly on arbitrary ciphertext.

sections.title: Which key type
paragraphs: AWS managed keys, aws/s3, aws/rds, appear automatically and cost nothing, which makes them the right default for encryption-at-rest where you have no specific access requirement.

Create a customer managed key when you need to control who can decrypt independently of who can read the resource, share access with another account, prove key control for compliance, or audit key usage separately.
Always create an alias. Key IDs are opaque UUIDs, and referencing alias/orders throughout your infrastructure means the underlying key can be rotated or replaced without changing anything else.

codeBlock.code:
aws kms create-key --description "orders app" \
  --key-usage ENCRYPT_DECRYPT --key-spec SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT \
  --policy file://key-policy.json

aws kms create-alias --alias-name alias/orders --target-key-id "$KEY_ID"

sections.title: Envelope encryption
paragraphs: KMS will not encrypt more than 4 KB directly. That limit is deliberate: it pushes you toward envelope encryption, which is how every AWS service does it.

You get the same key twice: plaintext to encrypt your data locally, and encrypted to store alongside it. Use the plaintext, discard it from memory, and keep the ciphertext. To decrypt later, send the ciphertext to kms:Decrypt to recover the plaintext key.
The point is that bulk encryption happens locally at full speed, and KMS is only involved for the small key, so you are not limited by KMS throughput or charged per megabyte.

Use the AWS Encryption SDK rather than implementing this yourself. It handles the format, the algorithm choices and data key caching, which matters: a high-volume application calling generate-data-key per object hits KMS request throttling and accumulates real cost.

codeBlock.code: aws kms generate-data-key --key-id alias/orders --key-spec AES_256

sections.title: Encryption context
paragraphs: An underused feature that prevents a whole class of mistake:

The context is additional authenticated data, not secret, but cryptographically bound to the ciphertext. Decryption must supply exactly the same context or it fails, so ciphertext encrypted for one tenant cannot be decrypted in another tenant's context even by a caller with full key access.
It also appears in CloudTrail, which makes key usage auditable in terms of what was accessed rather than just how often.

codeBlock.code:
aws kms encrypt --key-id alias/orders \
  --plaintext fileb://data.bin \
  --encryption-context 'tenant=acme,purpose=orders'

sections.title: Rotation
paragraphs: Automatic rotation generates new key material annually while keeping all previous material, so old ciphertext still decrypts with no re-encryption. The key ID and ARN do not change, so nothing in your infrastructure needs updating.

This is genuinely free of operational cost, and there is no reason not to enable it on every customer managed key. Note it does not apply to imported key material or asymmetric keys. Those need manual rotation with a new key and an alias update.

codeBlock.code: aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id alias/orders --rotation-period-in-days 365

sections.title: Deletion has a waiting period
paragraphs: Minimum seven days, maximum thirty. The delay exists because deleting a key destroys every piece of data encrypted with it, permanently. There is no recovery, no support escalation, nothing.
Before scheduling deletion, confirm nothing uses the key:
Disabling the key first is the safer approach. It produces immediate, visible failures rather than a silent countdown, and it is reversible.

codeBlock.code:
aws kms schedule-key-deletion --key-id "$KEY_ID" --pending-window-in-days 30
aws kms cancel-key-deletion --key-id "$KEY_ID"

sections.title: Cross-account access
paragraphs: Two sides, and missing either produces the same AccessDenied:
On the key policy, allow the other account:
In the other account, an IAM policy must also grant those actions on the key ARN. The key policy permits it; IAM in the consuming account still has to allow it.
For temporary or programmatic delegation, grants are better than editing the policy:
Grants can be revoked individually without touching the key policy, which makes them safer for automation.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Deliberately vague, so it does not reveal whether the key exists. Check, in order: the key policy allows your principal, your IAM policy allows the action, you are in the right region, and any kms:ViaService or encryption context condition is satisfied.
Usually a missing or mismatched encryption context, or ciphertext from a different key.
Cancel the deletion. The key is unusable until you do.
Too many KMS requests. Use data key caching rather than requesting a key per operation.

codeBlock.code:
An error occurred (AccessDeniedException) when calling the Decrypt operation:
The ciphertext refers to a customer master key that does not exist, does not
exist in this region, or you are not allowed to access.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A role with AdministratorAccess gets AccessDeniedException calling kms:Decrypt on a customer managed key. The key exists in the same region and account. What is the most likely cause?
A service encrypting thousands of small records per second calls kms:GenerateDataKey for each one and starts hitting ThrottlingException. What is the correct fix?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why do I get AccessDenied on KMS when my IAM policy allows it?

Because KMS requires permission from both the key policy and IAM. Unlike most AWS resources, an IAM policy granting kms:Decrypt does nothing unless the key policy also permits that principal, usually via the default statement allowing the account root, which delegates authority to IAM. Check the key policy first with get-key-policy, then your IAM policy, then whether you are in the right region, and finally any kms:ViaService or encryption context conditions attached to the grant.
What is the difference between AWS managed and customer managed keys?

AWS managed keys such as aws/s3 are created automatically the first time a service needs one, cost nothing, rotate yearly and cannot be modified, shared across accounts or deleted. Customer managed keys cost about a dollar a month each and give you a key policy you control, configurable rotation, cross-account sharing, grants and independent audit. Use AWS managed keys for straightforward encryption at rest; create a customer managed key when access control, cross-account sharing or compliance evidence matters.
What is envelope encryption and why does KMS use it?

KMS refuses to encrypt more than 4 KB directly, which forces the pattern: ask for a data key, receive it in both plaintext and encrypted form, encrypt your data locally with the plaintext copy, discard that copy from memory, and store the encrypted key alongside the ciphertext. To decrypt, send the encrypted key back to KMS. Bulk encryption then runs locally at full speed with KMS only handling a small key, so throughput is not limited and you are not billed per megabyte.
Should I enable automatic key rotation?

Yes, on every customer managed key. Rotation generates fresh key material annually while retaining all previous material, so existing ciphertext continues to decrypt with no re-encryption and the key ID, ARN and alias are unchanged. Nothing in your infrastructure needs to know it happened. There is no meaningful cost or operational burden. It does not cover imported key material or asymmetric keys, which require creating a new key and repointing the alias manually.
What happens if I delete a KMS key?

Every piece of data encrypted with it becomes permanently unrecoverable. There is no restore, no support escalation and no backup of the key material. That is why deletion is scheduled with a mandatory waiting period of seven to thirty days rather than executed immediately, and why cancel-key-deletion exists. Disable the key first instead: it produces immediate, visible failures from anything still using it, and is instantly reversible, which is a far better way to discover an unknown dependency than a silent countdown.
How do I give another AWS account access to my KMS key?

Both sides must allow it. Add a statement to the key policy naming the other account as principal and listing the permitted actions, and have an IAM policy in that account grant the same actions on the key's ARN. Missing either produces an identical access denied error, which makes it slow to diagnose. For temporary or programmatic access, a grant is preferable to editing the key policy. It can be created and revoked independently without risking a policy change that locks people out.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-secrets-manager.title: AWS Secrets Manager
aws-secrets-manager.subtitle: Store, rotate and read secrets with AWS Secrets Manager. Covers resource policies, automatic rotation, caching, recovery windows, cost and Parameter Store.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Secrets Manager must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Store, rotate and read secrets with AWS Secrets Manager. Covers resource policies, automatic rotation, caching, recovery windows, cost and Parameter Store.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Store, rotate and read secrets with AWS Secrets Manager. Covers resource policies, automatic rotation, caching, recovery windows, cost and Parameter Store.

Secrets Manager stores credentials encrypted with KMS, controls access through IAM, logs every read to CloudTrail, and, the part that justifies its price, rotates supported secrets automatically without anyone touching a config file.
That last capability is the deciding factor. If you don't need rotation, Parameter Store does the same job for free.

sections.title: Creating a secret
paragraphs: Note the six random characters AWS appends to the ARN. They're deliberate: they stop a deleted secret's name from being immediately reusable by someone who might inherit its permissions. It also means you can't construct a secret ARN by hand, if you're writing IAM policies, either look the ARN up or end the resource with a wildcard: arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:111122223333:secret:prod/payments/db-*.
Store JSON rather than a bare string. Rotation functions expect structured fields, and it lets one secret carry the host and port alongside the credentials.
Use a naming convention with a path-like shape, <env>/<service>/<purpose>, because IAM policies can then grant a service everything under its own prefix:

codeBlock.code:
aws secretsmanager create-secret \
  --name prod/payments/db \
  --description "Aurora credentials for the payments service" \
  --secret-string '{"username":"payments","password":"REPLACE_ME","host":"db.internal","port":5432}'

sections.title: Reading a secret
paragraphs: In application code, retrieve at startup and cache, never call Secrets Manager on every request:

API calls cost $0.05 per 10,000, which sounds trivial until a service handling 500 requests per second fetches on every one, that's about $65 a month to read a value that changes quarterly. Worse, you'll hit the API throttling limit and take an outage. AWS publishes language-specific caching libraries that handle refresh-on-rotation properly; use one rather than the naive dictionary above if your secrets actually rotate.

On Kubernetes, mount secrets through the Secrets Store CSI driver with the AWS provider instead of calling the API from application code. On ECS, reference the secret ARN directly in the task definition and let the agent inject it as an environment variable:
The trailing :password:: selects a single JSON key, so the container gets just that value rather than the whole document.

codeBlock.code:
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value \
  --secret-id prod/payments/db \
  --query SecretString --output text

sections.title: Rotation
paragraphs: Rotation is the feature you're paying for. Secrets Manager invokes a Lambda function on a schedule that creates a new credential, tests it, and promotes it, while the old one stays valid until the switch completes, so running applications don't break.
For RDS, Aurora, Redshift and DocumentDB, AWS supplies the rotation function:
Rotation moves version staging labels rather than overwriting anything:

There are two strategies. Single-user rotation changes the password on one database user; there's a brief window where a cached old password fails, so applications need retry logic. Alternating-user rotation maintains two users and swaps between them, which removes that window entirely. Use alternating users for anything that can't tolerate a failed connection.

Test rotation before trusting it. A rotation function that can't reach the database, wrong subnet, missing security group rule, fails silently on a schedule, and you find out months later when someone checks:

codeBlock.code:
aws secretsmanager rotate-secret \
  --secret-id prod/payments/db \
  --rotation-lambda-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:111122223333:function:SecretsManagerRDSPostgreSQLRotationSingleUser \
  --rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=30

sections.title: Deletion has a waiting period
paragraphs: Secrets don't delete immediately. The minimum recovery window is 7 days and the default is 30. During that window the secret is unreadable but restorable:
--force-delete-without-recovery skips the window and is irreversible. It also blocks reusing that name for the duration, which trips up teardown-and-recreate scripts in test environments.

codeBlock.code:
aws secretsmanager delete-secret \
  --secret-id prod/payments/db \
  --recovery-window-in-days 30

sections.title: Secrets Manager or Parameter Store?
paragraphs: The honest guidance: use Parameter Store for configuration and for secrets you rotate manually or rarely. API keys, webhook tokens, third-party credentials. Use Secrets Manager for database credentials, anything that must rotate on a schedule, and anything shared across accounts. At $0.40 per secret per month, putting 200 config values in Secrets Manager costs $960 a year for something Parameter Store does for nothing.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A policy allows secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:111122223333:secret:prod/payments/db". The application still gets AccessDenied. Why?
A payment service cannot tolerate a single failed database connection. Which rotation strategy fits?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I use Secrets Manager or Parameter Store?

Use Parameter Store for configuration values and for secrets you rarely rotate. It stores SecureStrings encrypted with KMS at no cost in the Standard tier. Use Secrets Manager when you need automatic rotation, cross-account sharing via resource policies, values larger than 4 KB, or a managed rotation function for RDS and Aurora. The cost difference is the deciding factor at scale: Secrets Manager is $0.40 per secret per month, so a few hundred values add up quickly for a capability many of them don't need.
How much does Secrets Manager cost?

$0.40 per secret per month, prorated hourly, plus $0.05 per 10,000 API calls. Ten database credentials is about $4 a month, which is nothing. The cost trap is API calls from an application that fetches on every request instead of caching, at high request rates that runs into tens of dollars a month and will hit API throttling limits before it hits your budget.
Why does my application get ResourceNotFoundException for a secret that exists?

Usually a region mismatch. Secrets are regional, and the SDK defaults to whatever region the environment supplies, which may not be where the secret lives. Set the region explicitly in the client. The other frequent cause is a partially-created secret in a CreateSecret that failed, or a secret that's inside its deletion recovery window. During that window it exists but is unreadable, and describe-secret will show a DeletedDate.
Can I recover a deleted secret?

Yes, if it was deleted with a recovery window. The default is 30 days and the minimum is 7, and aws secretsmanager restore-secret --secret-id <name> brings it back within that period. If it was deleted with --force-delete-without-recovery, it is gone permanently. That flag also reserves the name for a period, which is a common source of failures in scripts that tear down and recreate test environments.
How do I inject a secret into a container without calling the API in my code?

On ECS, reference the secret ARN in the task definition's secrets block and the agent injects it as an environment variable at start-up; appending :key:: to the ARN pulls a single field out of a JSON secret. On EKS, use the Secrets Store CSI driver with the AWS provider, which mounts the secret as a file and can sync it to a native Kubernetes Secret. Both approaches keep the credential out of your image, out of your source, and out of application code.
What happens to running applications while a secret rotates?

Rotation promotes a new version by moving the AWSCURRENT staging label; the previous version keeps the AWSPREVIOUS label and remains readable. With alternating-user rotation both credentials authenticate successfully throughout, so nothing fails. With single-user rotation there is a brief window where a cached old password is rejected, so applications need to catch authentication failures, re-read the secret, and retry. This is the main reason to prefer alternating users for anything latency- or availability-sensitive.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
