verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS WAF and Shield must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Set up AWS WAF without blocking users: build a web ACL, run rules in count mode first, add rate limiting, handle false positives and weigh Shield Advanced.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Set up AWS WAF without blocking users: build a web ACL, run rules in count mode first, add rate limiting, handle false positives and weigh Shield Advanced.
Two different products at two different layers.

Shield Standard is automatic, free, and defends every AWS account against network and transport layer attacks. SYN floods, reflection attacks, volumetric traffic. You are already protected and there is nothing to configure.

WAF inspects HTTP requests and decides what to allow, block, count or challenge. It handles the application layer: SQL injection, cross-site scripting, bad bots, and the request floods that look like legitimate traffic.
Shield Advanced is a paid subscription adding response support, cost protection and enhanced detection.
The failure mode that matters is not being attacked. It is blocking your own users, which is why count mode below is the most important section on this page.

sections.title: A web ACL
paragraphs: --scope REGIONAL for an ALB, API Gateway or AppSync. --scope CLOUDFRONT for CloudFront, and that one must be created in us-east-1, the same rule as CloudFront certificates.
A web ACL that exists but is associated with nothing inspects nothing. That is an easy state to leave things in after a Terraform apply that created the ACL and not the association.

codeBlock.code:
aws wafv2 create-web-acl --name prod-acl --scope REGIONAL \
  --region eu-west-1 \
  --default-action Allow={} \
  --visibility-config 'SampledRequestsEnabled=true,CloudWatchMetricsEnabled=true,MetricName=prodAcl' \
  --rules file://rules.json

sections.title: Rules evaluate in priority order
paragraphs: Lowest priority number first, and evaluation stops at the first terminating action. An Allow at priority 0 for your monitoring IPs means nothing below can block them, which is what you want, and equally what makes a careless broad Allow dangerous, since it skips every rule beneath it.
Put explicit allows for known-good traffic first, then rate limiting, then managed rule groups, then your own custom rules.

sections.title: Count mode first. Always.
paragraphs: Deploying a managed rule group straight to Block is how you take your own site down.

AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet blocks request bodies over 8 KB by default, so a file upload, a large JSON payload or a long form submission is rejected with a 403 that looks nothing like a WAF problem. SQLiRule matches on patterns that legitimate content contains: a blog post about SQL, a password containing --, a search for O'Brien.
Set the whole group to count, leave it for a week, and look at what it would have blocked:

Then switch the group to block and override the individual rules that produced false positives, as SizeRestrictions_BODY is overridden above. Overriding one rule is far better than disabling the group.

codeBlock.code: "OverrideAction": { "Count": {} }

sections.title: Rate limiting
paragraphs: The rule that stops most real problems. Credential stuffing, scraping, accidental client loops:

The ScopeDownStatement is what makes this usable: a strict limit applies only to the login endpoint while normal browsing is untouched. A single global rate limit either allows too much on sensitive endpoints or blocks legitimate heavy users elsewhere.
Aggregating by IP is crude when clients sit behind corporate NAT or a mobile carrier. AggregateKeyType can instead use a header, a cookie or a JA3 fingerprint, which handles that far better.

sections.title: Logging
paragraphs: The log group name must begin with aws-waf-logs-, which is an easy thing to get wrong and produces a validation error rather than silence.
Redact sensitive headers. Without it, authorization and cookie values land in your logs, which turns a debugging aid into a credential store.
Without logging you cannot tune rules, cannot investigate a complaint, and cannot tell whether a 403 came from WAF or your application. Enable it before you enable blocking.

sections.title: What Shield Advanced actually buys
paragraphs: At roughly $3,000 a month with a one-year commitment, plus data transfer, the question is what you get beyond the free Shield Standard.
Cost protection. If an attack scales your infrastructure, Auto Scaling launching instances, CloudFront serving attack traffic, AWS credits the charges. On a large estate this alone can justify it.
The Shield Response Team. Direct access during an attack, and with proactive engagement enabled they contact you rather than waiting.
Health-based detection. Attaching a Route 53 health check lets Shield distinguish an attack from a traffic spike, which reduces false positives significantly.
Free WAF. WAF charges are included, which offsets part of the cost for a heavy user.

For most organisations Shield Standard plus a well-tuned WAF is the right answer. Shield Advanced makes sense when downtime is measured in large sums per hour, when you are a plausible target, or when the cost protection covers the subscription on its own.

sections.title: Bot Control and account takeover
paragraphs: Bot Control identifies known bots and distinguishes verified crawlers from impersonators. It costs meaningfully more than standard WAF rules and is priced per request, so scope it down to the paths that need it.
AWSManagedRulesATPRuleSet targets credential stuffing specifically, inspecting login requests for stolen credentials and unusual patterns. Both are worth count mode before blocking.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Usually a CLOUDFRONT scope ACL created outside us-east-1, or a regional ACL being associated with a CloudFront distribution.
A web ACL has a capacity budget in WCUs, and managed rule groups consume a lot. Remove unused groups or request an increase.
The resource is in a different region, or the ACL was never associated.
Legitimate users getting 403. A managed rule false positive. Check the WAF logs for terminatingRuleId before anything else.

codeBlock.code:
WAFInvalidParameterException: Error reason: The ARN isn't valid.
A valid ARN begins with arn: and includes other information separated by colons or slashes.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: After enabling AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet in block mode, file uploads started failing with 403 while everything else works. What is the cause and the right fix?

A single rate-based rule of 2,000 requests per five minutes per IP is applied to the whole site. Credential stuffing on /api/login continues, while some corporate customers behind NAT are being blocked. What should change?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between AWS WAF and AWS Shield?

They operate at different layers. Shield defends against network and transport attacks, SYN floods, UDP reflection, volumetric traffic, and Shield Standard is automatic and free on every account. WAF inspects HTTP requests and enforces rules about their content: SQL injection patterns, cross-site scripting, bot signatures, request rates. Shield Standard handles the traffic that never reaches your application; WAF handles the requests that do. Shield Advanced is a paid tier adding cost protection, response team access and health-based detection.
Why is my WAF blocking legitimate traffic?

Almost certainly a managed rule group deployed straight to block. AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet rejects request bodies over 8 KB, which breaks uploads, and its injection rules match patterns that ordinary content contains: an apostrophe in a name, a double dash in a password, a blog post discussing SQL. Check the WAF logs for terminatingRuleId to identify which rule fired, then use RuleActionOverrides to set just that rule to Count. Deploy new groups in count mode for a week before blocking.
What is WAF count mode and why does it matter?

Count mode evaluates rules and records matches without blocking anything, so you can see exactly what a rule would have rejected before it affects users. It is the single most important WAF practice, because the realistic risk is not an attacker getting through. It is a managed rule quietly returning 403 to your own customers while your application logs show nothing. Run new rule groups in count for a week, query the logs for what matched, override the false positives, then switch to block.
How do I rate limit only my login endpoint?

Add a ScopeDownStatement to the rate-based rule, matching the URI path, so the limit applies only to requests to that path. A strict limit of around 100 requests per five minutes per IP is reasonable on /api/login and would be absurd applied site-wide. For clients sharing an address through corporate NAT or mobile carriers, change AggregateKeyType from IP to a header, cookie or JA3 fingerprint so one shared address does not lock out an entire office.
Is Shield Advanced worth the cost?

At roughly $3,000 a month on an annual commitment, it depends on what an hour of downtime costs you. The strongest argument is cost protection, if an attack drives Auto Scaling or CloudFront charges up, AWS credits them, which on a large estate can exceed the subscription. Beyond that you get the Shield Response Team during an incident, proactive engagement, health-based detection that distinguishes attacks from traffic spikes, and WAF charges included. For most organisations, Shield Standard plus a well-tuned WAF is sufficient.
Why does my WAF web ACL not seem to do anything?

Three things to check. It may never have been associated with a resource. Creating a web ACL and associating it are separate operations, and infrastructure code frequently does the first without the second. Its scope may be wrong: CLOUDFRONT ACLs must be created in us-east-1, and a REGIONAL ACL cannot protect a distribution. Or the rules may be in count mode, recording matches without blocking. aws wafv2 get-web-acl shows the rules and actions, and the CloudWatch metrics show whether it is evaluating anything at all.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Go beyond the 90-day event history: create a multi-region CloudTrail trail, log management and data events, validate log files and query logs with Athena.

CloudTrail records API activity in your account: who called what, when, from which IP, with which credentials, and whether it succeeded. It is the answer to "who deleted that?" and the evidence auditors ask for.
It is on by default, and the default is weaker than most people assume.

sections.title: Event history is not a trail
paragraphs: Every account has Event history: the last 90 days of management events, queryable in the console and CLI, at no cost and with nothing to configure.
Three things it does not give you, all of which matter:
A trail delivers events to S3 and fixes all three. Creating one is the first thing to do in a new account.
start-logging is a separate call. A trail created without it exists, appears configured, and records nothing. A quietly bad outcome for something whose entire purpose is evidence.
--is-multi-region-trail matters too: a single-region trail misses activity elsewhere, and an attacker operating in an unused region leaves no trace.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=DeleteBucket \
  --start-time 2026-09-01 \
  --query 'Events[].[EventTime,Username,CloudTrailEvent]' --output text

sections.title: Management and data events
paragraphs: Data events are off because the volume is enormous. A busy S3 bucket generates orders of magnitude more GetObject calls than your account generates management events, and billing is per event.
Enable them selectively rather than globally:
That records writes to one sensitive bucket and ignores everything else. Enabling data events for all S3 buckets in a data-heavy account is a genuinely expensive mistake, and it is one checkbox away.

sections.title: Reading an event
paragraphs: The fields that answer real questions:

userIdentity.type: Root is worth alarming on unconditionally. AssumedRole means a role, and sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName tells you which one. sourceIPAddress: an AWS service appears as a service name rather than an address. errorCode: present on denied calls, which is how you spot enumeration attempts. mfaAuthenticated: whether MFA was used, frequently a compliance requirement.
The session name (ci-run-8123 above) is chosen by whoever assumed the role, so setting it meaningfully in your CI pipeline pays off later.

sections.title: Querying at scale
paragraphs: lookup-events is fine for a single question and useless across months of data. Two better options.
Athena over the S3 bucket is the established approach:
Partition the table by region and date, or every query scans the entire history and the Athena bill becomes its own problem.
CloudTrail Lake is the managed alternative. A queryable event store with retention up to ten years and no S3 or Athena setup:
It costs more per ingested event than S3 storage but removes the plumbing. For a small team wanting queryable audit history without maintaining a data pipeline, it is usually the better trade.

codeBlock.code:
SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn, eventname, sourceipaddress, errorcode
FROM cloudtrail_logs
WHERE eventname IN ('DeleteBucket','PutBucketPolicy','DeleteDBInstance')
  AND from_iso8601_timestamp(eventtime) > current_timestamp - interval '7' day
ORDER BY eventtime DESC;

sections.title: Alerting on what matters
paragraphs: A trail nobody reads is compliance decoration. Send events to CloudWatch Logs and alarm on the few that are always worth waking up for:

Worth alarming on: root account usage, ConsoleLogin without MFA, changes to CloudTrail itself (StopLogging, DeleteTrail), IAM policy changes, security group changes opening 0.0.0.0/0, and KMS key deletion scheduling.
StopLogging deserves special attention. Disabling the audit log is a standard early step in an intrusion, and it is the one alarm that must not depend on the trail still working.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudtrail update-trail --name org-trail \
  --cloud-watch-logs-log-group-arn "$LOG_GROUP_ARN" \
  --cloud-watch-logs-role-arn "$ROLE_ARN"

aws logs put-metric-filter \
  --log-group-name /aws/cloudtrail/org-trail \
  --filter-name root-usage \
  --filter-pattern '{ $.userIdentity.type = "Root" && $.eventType != "AwsServiceEvent" }' \
  --metric-transformations metricName=RootAccountUsage,metricNamespace=Security,metricValue=1

sections.title: Integrity and protection
paragraphs: Log file validation writes signed digest files hourly, so you can prove logs have not been altered or deleted. It costs nothing and is the difference between logs and evidence.
Protect the bucket properly:
Logs an attacker can delete are not an audit trail.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudtrail validate-logs --trail-arn "$TRAIL_ARN" \
  --start-time 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z

sections.title: Organisation trails
paragraphs: One trail covering every account in an organisation, created from the management account:

Member accounts cannot disable or delete it, which is precisely the point. It removes the possibility of an account operator turning off their own auditing. New accounts are covered automatically as they join. This is the correct baseline for any multi-account setup.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name org-trail \
  --s3-bucket-name central-cloudtrail-logs \
  --is-organization-trail --is-multi-region-trail \
  --enable-log-file-validation

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The bucket policy must allow cloudtrail.amazonaws.com to call s3:PutObject with the expected s3:x-amz-acl condition, and s3:GetBucketAcl.
Trails are regional objects even when multi-region. Check the region.
A trail exists and the bucket is empty. start-logging was never called, or the KMS key policy does not allow CloudTrail.
Events appear ~15 minutes late. Normal. CloudTrail delivery is not real time, which is why critical alarms go through CloudWatch Logs rather than polling S3.

codeBlock.code:
InsufficientS3BucketPolicyException: Incorrect S3 bucket policy is detected
for bucket: my-cloudtrail-logs

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A trail was created four months ago with a valid S3 bucket and correct policy. During an investigation the bucket is found to be empty, and get-trail-status shows IsLogging false. What happened?
After enabling data events for all S3 buckets, CloudTrail costs rise sharply. The account stores millions of objects read continuously by an application. What is the right adjustment?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between CloudTrail Event history and a trail?

Event history is enabled automatically and holds the last 90 days of management events, queryable in the console and via lookup-events at no cost. A trail delivers events to an S3 bucket you control, with no retention limit, optional data events, log file validation and the ability to query at scale. Anything beyond casual investigation needs a trail. Event history cannot answer a question about an incident discovered four months later, and it never contained data events at all.
What is the difference between management events and data events?

Management events record control-plane operations: creating an instance, changing a bucket policy, assuming a role. Data events record data-plane access: reading an S3 object, writing a DynamoDB item, invoking a Lambda. Management events are on by default and the first copy is free. Data events are off by default and billed per event, because their volume is orders of magnitude higher. A read-heavy account can generate millions a day. Enable them selectively with advanced event selectors scoped to sensitive resources.
Why is my CloudTrail bucket empty?

Most often because start-logging was never called. Creating a trail does not start it, and everything else looks correctly configured. Check get-trail-status, which reports IsLogging and the last delivery time. The other causes are an S3 bucket policy that does not allow cloudtrail.amazonaws.com to write, or a KMS key policy that does not permit CloudTrail to encrypt. Also note delivery takes up to about 15 minutes, so a brand new trail legitimately looks empty at first.
How do I query CloudTrail logs efficiently?

Not with lookup-events, which is fine for one question and impractical across months. Either create an Athena table over the S3 bucket. Partitioned by region and date, or every query scans your whole history, or use CloudTrail Lake, a managed event store with SQL querying and retention up to ten years. Lake costs more per ingested event but removes the pipeline entirely, which usually makes it the better choice for a team that would otherwise not build one.
What CloudTrail events should I alarm on?

A short list covers most real value: any root account usage, ConsoleLogin without MFA, StopLogging and DeleteTrail, IAM policy and user changes, security group rules opening 0.0.0.0/0, and ScheduleKeyDeletion on KMS keys. StopLogging matters most. Disabling the audit trail is a standard early step in an intrusion. Deliver the trail to CloudWatch Logs and use metric filters, since polling S3 adds delay to exactly the alerts that need to be prompt.
How do I stop someone deleting the CloudTrail logs?

Put them in a separate AWS account, so compromising the audited account does not reach its own evidence. Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, which makes objects undeletable even by root for the retention period. Add versioning, MFA delete, and a bucket policy denying delete actions. Turn on log file validation so any tampering is detectable through the signed hourly digests. An organisation trail created from the management account is the final piece, since member accounts cannot disable it.

aws-config.subtitle: Use AWS Config for continuous compliance: turn on the recorder, apply managed rules and conformance packs, auto-remediate with SSM and compare with CloudTrail.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Config must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Use AWS Config for continuous compliance: turn on the recorder, apply managed rules and conformance packs, auto-remediate with SSM and compare with CloudTrail.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Use AWS Config for continuous compliance: turn on the recorder, apply managed rules and conformance packs, auto-remediate with SSM and compare with CloudTrail.

Config records what your AWS resources look like over time and continuously evaluates them against rules. CloudTrail tells you someone called AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress; Config tells you the security group now allows 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22, that this is non-compliant, and what it looked like before.
The two answer different questions, who did it and what is it now, and a mature setup uses both.

sections.title: Turn on the recorder
paragraphs: Nothing happens until a configuration recorder and a delivery channel exist:

includeGlobalResourceTypes covers IAM, which is not regional. Enable it in one region only. Enabling it everywhere records every IAM change once per region and multiplies that portion of the bill for no benefit.

sections.title: Cost is the thing people get wrong
paragraphs: Config bills per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation. Both sound small and both scale with change.

An Auto Scaling group replacing instances continuously, a busy EKS cluster, or anything creating and destroying resources on a loop generates configuration items constantly, and with allSupported: true you record every one.
If the bill surprises you, record selectively:

You can also exclude high-churn types while keeping everything else, and set periodic rather than continuous recording for types that change constantly. Start broad, look at the bill after a month, then narrow.

codeBlock.code:
aws configservice put-configuration-recorder \
  --configuration-recorder name=default,roleARN="$CONFIG_ROLE_ARN" \
  --recording-group '{
    "allSupported": false,
    "resourceTypes": ["AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup","AWS::IAM::Role","AWS::IAM::Policy",
                      "AWS::S3::Bucket","AWS::RDS::DBInstance","AWS::KMS::Key"]
  }'

sections.title: Rules
paragraphs: A rule evaluates resources and marks them COMPLIANT or NON_COMPLIANT. Around 300 managed rules cover most common requirements:

Rules are either change-triggered, evaluating when a resource changes, or periodic, running on a schedule. Change-triggered is what gives you near-real-time detection; periodic covers things with no configuration change to hook, such as "an access key older than 90 days".
For requirements no managed rule covers, write a custom rule, as a Lambda, or more simply with Guard syntax:
Guard rules need no Lambda to deploy, maintain or pay for.

sections.title: Conformance packs
paragraphs: A pack is a collection of rules deployed as a unit, and AWS publishes packs mapped to real frameworks. CIS, PCI DSS, HIPAA, NIST:

Deploying one across an organisation is how a baseline reaches every account, including accounts created later. Expect a large initial non-compliance count. Treat it as a backlog to work through rather than a signal to disable the pack.

codeBlock.code:
aws configservice put-conformance-pack \
  --conformance-pack-name cis-foundations \
  --template-s3-uri s3://aws-config-conformance-packs/Operational-Best-Practices-for-CIS-AWS-v1.4-Level1.yaml \
  --delivery-s3-bucket my-config-history

sections.title: Automatic remediation
paragraphs: This is where Config becomes useful rather than merely informative. Attach an SSM Automation document to a rule:
A public bucket is now private within minutes of becoming public, without anyone reading a dashboard.

Introduce automatic remediation carefully. Start with "Automatic": false, which makes remediation a one-click manual action, and watch what it would have done for a couple of weeks. An over-eager rule that revokes a security group rule something legitimately depends on causes an outage, and does so at the moment nobody expects a change.
Good candidates: making buckets private, enabling encryption, removing 0.0.0.0/0 SSH rules, enabling versioning. Poor candidates: anything terminating resources or altering networking.

sections.title: The configuration timeline
paragraphs: The feature that repays enabling Config on its own:

Every recorded change is a snapshot you can diff, so "what did this look like before Tuesday's incident" is a query rather than an archaeology exercise. Combined with CloudTrail's record of who made the call, that is a complete answer.
Advanced queries work across your whole inventory in SQL:
That is also a genuinely good inventory tool. Finding every unencrypted volume or every instance of a retired type across accounts.

codeBlock.code:
aws configservice get-resource-config-history \
  --resource-type AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup \
  --resource-id sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --limit 5 \
  --query 'configurationItems[].[configurationItemCaptureTime,configurationItemStatus]' \
  --output table

sections.title: Aggregators
paragraphs: For multi-account estates, an aggregator gives one view:
Compliance across every account and region in one place, which is the only practical way to answer "are we compliant" at organisational scale.

codeBlock.code:
aws configservice put-configuration-aggregator \
  --configuration-aggregator-name org-wide \
  --organization-aggregation-source \
    'RoleArn=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ConfigAggregator,AllAwsRegions=true'

sections.title: Config, CloudTrail or Security Hub
paragraphs: They stack rather than compete. Security Hub consumes Config rule results alongside other sources and presents one prioritised view, which is where a team with several security services should be looking.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The recorder is not started. start-configuration-recorder first.
The bucket policy must allow the Config service principal to write, with the expected ACL condition.
Rules stuck at NOT_APPLICABLE. No resources of that type exist, or the recorder is not recording that type. Likely with a restricted resourceTypes list.
A surprising bill. allSupported: true plus high-churn resources, or global resource types recorded in every region.

codeBlock.code:
NoAvailableConfigurationRecorderException: Configuration recorder is not
available to put configuration rule

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An S3 bucket became publicly readable overnight. You need both who made the change and what the bucket policy looked like before it. Which services answer which half?
A rule with automatic remediation revoked a security group rule that an internal service depended on, causing an outage. How should automatic remediation be introduced?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between AWS Config and CloudTrail?

CloudTrail is an API audit log: who called what, when, from which IP and whether it succeeded. Config is a configuration database: what each resource currently looks like, what it looked like previously, and whether it complies with your rules. So CloudTrail answers "who opened that security group" and Config answers "what does the security group allow now, and what did it allow yesterday". They overlap in an investigation and neither replaces the other.
Why is AWS Config expensive?

Because it bills per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation, and both scale with how much your infrastructure changes. An Auto Scaling group cycling instances, a busy container platform, or anything creating and destroying resources continuously generates configuration items constantly, and allSupported: true records every one. Narrow the recorded resource types to what you actually evaluate, exclude high-churn types, and enable global resource types such as IAM in a single region rather than all of them.
How do Config rules work?

Each rule evaluates resources and marks them compliant or non-compliant. Change-triggered rules run when a resource configuration changes, giving near-real-time detection; periodic rules run on a schedule and cover things with no configuration change to hook, such as an access key exceeding an age limit. AWS provides around 300 managed rules covering most common requirements, and you can write custom rules either as a Lambda function or with Guard policy syntax, which requires no Lambda at all.
Can AWS Config fix problems automatically?

Yes, by attaching an SSM Automation document to a rule as a remediation configuration, so a bucket that becomes public is made private within minutes without anyone reading a dashboard. Introduce it carefully: begin with Automatic: false, which makes remediation a reviewed one-click action, and watch what it would have changed before enabling automation. Suitable candidates are making buckets private, enabling encryption and removing open SSH rules; anything that terminates resources or alters networking should stay manual.
What is a conformance pack?

A collection of Config rules and remediation actions deployed and managed as a single unit, defined as a template. AWS publishes packs mapped to recognised frameworks including CIS, PCI DSS, HIPAA and NIST, so adopting a baseline is one deployment rather than dozens of individual rules. Deployed across an organisation, a pack applies to every account including ones created afterwards. Expect a high initial non-compliance count and treat it as a backlog rather than a reason to remove the pack.
Do I need Config if I already have Security Hub?

Security Hub depends on Config for many of its checks, so the question does not quite separate them. Its CIS and foundational security standards are implemented as Config rules, and disabling the recorder leaves those unable to evaluate. What Security Hub adds is aggregation: findings from Config, GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and third-party tools in one prioritised view across accounts. Config remains the source of configuration history and the mechanism for your own rules and remediation.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Set up Systems Manager and fix managed instances that do not appear, then use Run Command, Patch Manager, State Manager and Automation to manage a fleet.

Systems Manager is a collection of loosely related tools for operating servers: running commands across a fleet, patching, storing configuration, maintaining desired state, and connecting to instances without SSH.
Systems Manager: Management Channels
No inbound ports required. SSM Agent initiates outbound HTTPS to the SSM service
Everything depends on one thing working first, and it is where almost all Systems Manager time is spent.

sections.title: Getting instances to appear
paragraphs: An empty list means the prerequisites are not met. There are exactly three, and they are the answer to nearly every "SSM does not see my instance" question:
1. The agent must be running. Amazon Linux 2023, Amazon Linux 2, Ubuntu 16.04+ and Windows Server AMIs include it. Other images need it installed.
2. The instance profile needs AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore:
This is the most common cause. An instance with no instance profile at all, or one missing this policy, never registers and reports nothing.

3. Network access to the SSM endpoints. The agent makes outbound connections. It never receives inbound traffic, so no security group ingress rule is needed. A private subnet therefore needs either a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints:

All three endpoints are required. ssmmessages handles Session Manager and ec2messages handles Run Command, so omitting one produces a partially working setup. The instance appears in the console but sessions fail, which is a confusing place to end up. The endpoint security group must allow inbound 443 from the instances.
If an instance still does not appear, read the agent log:

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm describe-instance-information \
  --query 'InstanceInformationList[].[InstanceId,PingStatus,AgentVersion,PlatformName]' \
  --output table

sections.title: Run Command
paragraphs: Execute a command across a fleet without SSH:

Two parameters make this safe on a real fleet. --max-concurrency 10% runs on a tenth of the targets at a time rather than all at once. --max-errors 2 halts the whole operation after two failures, so a broken command does not roll across production.
Targeting by tag rather than instance ID means the command automatically covers instances that did not exist when you wrote it.
Every invocation is recorded in CloudTrail with the calling identity, which is a real advantage over SSH: there is an audit trail of who ran what, without needing to collect shell history.

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm send-command \
  --document-name AWS-RunShellScript \
  --targets 'Key=tag:Environment,Values=production' \
  --parameters 'commands=["systemctl restart nginx","systemctl is-active nginx"]' \
  --max-concurrency 10% --max-errors 2 \
  --comment "restart nginx after config change" \
  --output-s3-bucket-name my-ssm-output

sections.title: Parameter Store
paragraphs: Configuration and secrets, with a hierarchy:

--with-decryption is required for SecureString values, and the caller needs kms:Decrypt on the key. A missing KMS permission here is a frequent and confusing failure, because the parameter read itself is authorised.
Use a consistent hierarchy (/env/app/key), since IAM policies can then scope to a path prefix:

Parameter Store for configuration and for secrets you rotate manually. Secrets Manager when you want automatic rotation. Particularly for RDS, where the integration handles the database side too. Paying per secret for values that never rotate is waste; managing manual rotation of a database password is worse.

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm put-parameter --name /prod/orders/db-host \
  --value "orders.abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com" --type String

aws ssm put-parameter --name /prod/orders/db-password \
  --value 'correct-horse-battery-staple' --type SecureString --key-id alias/orders

aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /prod/orders --recursive --with-decryption \
  --query 'Parameters[].[Name,Value]' --output table

sections.title: Patch Manager
paragraphs: ApproveAfterDays=7 is the setting worth understanding: patches are approved automatically a week after release, which gives time for a bad patch to be withdrawn while keeping you current. Zero days means installing everything immediately; never approving means an unpatched fleet.
Patching runs in a maintenance window:
--cutoff 1 stops new tasks starting in the final hour, so long-running work does not get cut off at the window's close.
Scan-only mode (Operation=Scan) reports compliance without installing anything, which is the right way to start.

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm create-patch-baseline --name prod-linux \
  --operating-system AMAZON_LINUX_2023 \
  --approval-rules 'PatchRules=[{
    PatchFilterGroup={PatchFilters=[{Key=CLASSIFICATION,Values=[Security,Bugfix]},{Key=SEVERITY,Values=[Critical,Important]}]},
    ApproveAfterDays=7,
    ComplianceLevel=CRITICAL
  }]'

sections.title: State Manager
paragraphs: Where Run Command is a one-off, State Manager enforces continuously:

That reapplies every thirty minutes, so an instance that drifts, or a new one that launches, converges without anyone noticing. It is lightweight configuration management for teams not running Ansible or Puppet, and it does not need an agent beyond the one already there.

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm create-association --name AWS-RunShellScript \
  --targets 'Key=tag:Environment,Values=production' \
  --parameters 'commands=["systemctl enable --now amazon-cloudwatch-agent"]' \
  --schedule-expression "rate(30 minutes)" \
  --association-name ensure-cloudwatch-agent \
  --compliance-severity MEDIUM

sections.title: Automation
paragraphs: Multi-step runbooks combining AWS API calls, commands and approvals:

AWS provides many pre-built documents, and Automation is what Config auto-remediation invokes. Custom runbooks can include an aws:approve step that pauses for a human, which turns a risky manual procedure into a repeatable one with an audit trail.

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm start-automation-execution \
  --document-name AWS-RestartEC2Instance \
  --parameters 'InstanceId=i-0123456789abcdef0'

sections.title: Inventory and Compliance
paragraphs: Inventory collects installed applications, network configuration, Windows updates and custom attributes across the fleet, queryable through Resource Data Sync into S3 and Athena. "Which instances have this vulnerable package" becomes a query rather than a broadcast command.

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm create-association --name AWS-GatherSoftwareInventory \
  --targets 'Key=InstanceIds,Values=*' \
  --schedule-expression "rate(1 day)"

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The instance is not registered with SSM. Check the three prerequisites.
Wrong region, wrong path, or no ssm:GetParameter permission on that path. A denied read looks identical to a missing parameter.
Reading a SecureString needs KMS permission as well as SSM permission.
Instance in Fleet Manager but sessions fail. The ssmmessages endpoint is missing.

codeBlock.code: An error occurred (InvalidInstanceId) when calling the SendCommand operation

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An EC2 instance in a private subnet runs the SSM agent and has a NAT gateway for outbound access, but never appears in describe-instance-instance-information. What is most likely missing?
A team needs to store an RDS master password that should rotate every 30 days without manual work. Which service, and why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why don't my instances appear in Systems Manager?

Three prerequisites, and one of them is missing. The SSM agent must be running. It is preinstalled on Amazon Linux, recent Ubuntu and Windows AMIs but not everything. The instance profile must include AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, which is the most common omission. And the instance needs outbound network access to the ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages endpoints, via NAT gateway, internet gateway or VPC endpoints. Check /var/log/amazon/ssm/amazon-ssm-agent.log on the instance; it names the failure directly.
Which VPC endpoints does Systems Manager need?

Three interface endpoints: com.amazonaws.<region>.ssm, .ssmmessages and .ec2messages. Creating only the first gives a partially working setup where instances register and appear in the console while Session Manager and Run Command fail. A confusing state to debug. ssmmessages carries Session Manager traffic and ec2messages carries Run Command. The endpoint security group must allow inbound 443 from the instance security group, and private DNS should be enabled.
What is the difference between Parameter Store and Secrets Manager?

Parameter Store is free at the standard tier, stores configuration and encrypted SecureString values, and has no rotation capability. Secrets Manager costs roughly 40 cents per secret per month and adds automatic rotation through Lambda, cross-account access via resource policies, random password generation and a larger size limit. Use Parameter Store for configuration and for secrets you rotate manually, and Secrets Manager where automatic rotation matters. Particularly for RDS, where the built-in integration updates the database and the stored secret together.
How do I run a command on many instances safely?

Target by tag rather than instance ID, so new instances are included automatically, and set --max-concurrency to a percentage such as 10% so the command rolls out gradually rather than hitting the whole fleet at once. Set --max-errors to a small number so the operation stops after a few failures instead of propagating a broken command everywhere. Send output to S3 or CloudWatch Logs, since inline output is truncated. Every invocation is recorded in CloudTrail with the calling identity.
What does State Manager do that Run Command does not?

Run Command executes once; State Manager enforces continuously. An association reapplies its document on a schedule, every thirty minutes, daily, whatever you set, so an instance whose configuration drifts is corrected, and a newly launched instance matching the target tags converges without anyone doing anything. It is lightweight configuration management using the agent you already have, which is often enough for teams not running Ansible or Puppet.
How should I configure Patch Manager?

Create a patch baseline filtered to the classifications and severities you care about, with ApproveAfterDays set to around seven. Patches are then adopted automatically a week after release, which leaves time for a bad one to be withdrawn while keeping the fleet current. Run patching inside a maintenance window with a cutoff so long tasks are not truncated at the end. Start in scan-only mode to see compliance without installing anything, and check describe-instance-patch-states-for-patch-group for the resulting picture.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS SSM Session Manager must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Get a shell on EC2 with Session Manager and no SSH, bastion or open ports. Meet the prerequisites, log sessions for audit and port-forward to a database.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Get a shell on EC2 with Session Manager and no SSH, bastion or open ports. Meet the prerequisites, log sessions for audit and port-forward to a database.

sections.title: Session Manager
paragraphs: Session Manager gives you an interactive shell on an EC2 instance with no SSH port open, no key pairs, and no bastion host. The connection is outbound from the instance to AWS, and you connect through the AWS API.

That removes a lot at once: no port 22 in any security group, no keys to distribute, rotate or revoke when someone leaves, no bastion to patch and pay for, and no public subnet needed for access. Authorisation is IAM, and every session is recorded in CloudTrail against a real identity rather than a shared key.

sections.title: Connecting
paragraphs: The CLI needs the Session Manager plugin installed locally, which is a separate download from the AWS CLI itself, SessionManagerPlugin is not found is the error when it is missing.

Prerequisites are the same three as Systems Manager generally: the agent running, AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore on the instance profile, and outbound access to the ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages endpoints. ssmmessages is the one that matters here. An instance that shows up in Fleet Manager but fails to start a session is almost always missing that endpoint.
Online means a session should work. Anything else is a prerequisite problem.

codeBlock.code: aws ssm start-session --target i-0123456789abcdef0

sections.title: Then close port 22
paragraphs: The benefit is not realised until you actually remove SSH access:

An instance reachable through Session Manager and SSH still has the bastion, the keys and the open port to manage. Removing 22 entirely is the point, and it lets instances live in private subnets with no inbound rules at all.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

sections.title: Log every session
paragraphs: Without this you have replaced auditable SSH with unauditable shell access, which is a step backwards:

That records every keystroke and every byte of output to S3 and CloudWatch Logs. cloudWatchStreamingEnabled sends output continuously rather than only at session end, so a session that is killed still leaves a record, which is precisely the session you would want to read.
kmsKeyId also enables end-to-end encryption of the session itself, beyond the TLS that is always present.
idleSessionTimeout and maxSessionDuration close forgotten sessions, which is both a security improvement and a way to stop a dangling session holding things open.

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm create-document --name SSM-SessionManagerRunShell \
  --document-type Session --document-format JSON --content '{
  "schemaVersion": "1.0",
  "description": "Session preferences",
  "sessionType": "Standard_Stream",
  "inputs": {
    "s3BucketName": "my-session-logs",
    "s3EncryptionEnabled": true,
    "cloudWatchLogGroupName": "/aws/ssm/sessions",
    "cloudWatchEncryptionEnabled": true,
    "cloudWatchStreamingEnabled": true,
    "kmsKeyId": "alias/session-manager",
    "idleSessionTimeout": "20",
    "maxSessionDuration": "120",
    "runAsEnabled": true,
    "runAsDefaultUser": "ssm-user",
    "shellProfile": { "linux": "cd /home/ssm-user && bash" }
  }
}'

sections.title: Port forwarding is the underrated feature
paragraphs: Session Manager can tunnel a port, which gives you private database access with no bastion and no VPN:

The second form is the one worth knowing. The database stays in a private subnet with no public access, the EC2 instance is only a relay, and your local tooling, psql, a GUI client, a migration script, connects to localhost. No bastion, no VPN client, and the whole thing is authorised by IAM and logged.

codeBlock.code:
# Forward a port on an instance
aws ssm start-session --target i-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSession \
  --parameters '{"portNumber":["8080"],"localPortNumber":["9090"]}'

sections.title: SSH over Session Manager
paragraphs: Existing SSH-based tooling can keep working while port 22 stays closed. Add to ~/.ssh/config:
This still uses SSH keys on the instance, so it is a transitional arrangement rather than the end state, but it means Ansible, scp and rsync work without an open port while you migrate.

codeBlock.code:
Host i-* mi-*
  ProxyCommand sh -c "aws ssm start-session --target %h --document-name AWS-StartSSHSession --parameters 'portNumber=%p'"

sections.title: Restricting who can connect where
paragraphs: An IAM policy scoped by tag is the usual approach:
The second statement is easy to miss: without it a user can start a session and not end their own. The ${aws:username}-* pattern confines them to their own sessions.
You can also restrict which documents may be used, which is how you allow shell access while forbidding port forwarding, or the reverse.

sections.title: Who is connected right now
paragraphs: Worth an alarm: a session started against a production instance outside change hours is something you want to know about while it is happening.

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm describe-sessions --state Active \
  --query 'Sessions[].[SessionId,Owner,Target,StartDate]' --output table

sections.title: The ssm-user
paragraphs: Sessions run as ssm-user, created automatically by the agent, with passwordless sudo on Linux by default.

That default deserves attention. Anyone who can start a session has root, so the access control is entirely in IAM, which is fine when IAM is scoped properly and not fine when everyone has ssm:StartSession on *. To remove it:
Or set runAsDefaultUser in the session document to connect as a specific less-privileged account instead.

codeBlock.code: sudo rm /etc/sudoers.d/ssm-agent-users

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: The agent is not reporting. Check the three prerequisites, and specifically the ssmmessages endpoint.
Install the plugin locally; it is separate from the AWS CLI.
Missing ssm:StartSession, or a tag condition on the policy that this instance does not satisfy.
Session starts and immediately closes. Usually a broken shellProfile in the session document, or a missing shell on a minimal AMI.

codeBlock.code:
An error occurred (TargetNotConnected) when calling the StartSession operation:
i-0123456789abcdef0 is not connected.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An instance in a private subnet appears in Systems Manager with PingStatus Online, but start-session fails with TargetNotConnected. VPC endpoints exist for ssm and ec2messages. What is missing?
A developer needs to run psql against an RDS instance in a private subnet with no public access. There is no VPN and the team wants no bastion. What works?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How is Session Manager more secure than SSH with a bastion?

Three ways. No inbound port is open anywhere. The agent connects outbound, so instances can sit in private subnets with no ingress rules at all. There are no key pairs to distribute, rotate or revoke, because authorisation is IAM and access disappears when the identity does. And every session is attributable to a real principal in CloudTrail, with full keystroke and output logging available, rather than a shared key whose use you can only infer. You also stop patching and paying for a bastion.
Why does start-session fail with TargetNotConnected?

The agent is not reporting to SSM. Check the three prerequisites: the agent is running, the instance profile has AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, and there is network access to the SSM endpoints. When the instance appears in Fleet Manager as Online but sessions specifically fail, it is almost always the ssmmessages VPC endpoint, that one carries session traffic, while ssm handles registration, so a partial endpoint set produces exactly this.
How do I log Session Manager sessions?

Create or edit the SSM-SessionManagerRunShell session document with s3BucketName and cloudWatchLogGroupName, and set cloudWatchStreamingEnabled to true so output is written continuously rather than only when the session ends. Otherwise a session that is killed leaves no record, which is the one you would most want. Add a kmsKeyId for end-to-end session encryption, and set idleSessionTimeout and maxSessionDuration to close forgotten sessions.
Can I use Session Manager to reach a private RDS database?

Yes, and it is the feature most worth knowing. Use AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost with the database hostname and port, plus a local port. The session tunnels through an EC2 instance that can reach the database, and your local psql, GUI client or migration tool connects to localhost. The database needs no public access and there is no bastion or VPN involved, while authorisation stays in IAM and the session is logged.
Can I still use SSH and SCP with Session Manager?

Yes. Add a ProxyCommand entry to ~/.ssh/config using the AWS-StartSSHSession document, and ssh, scp, rsync and Ansible work against instance IDs with port 22 closed to the network. It does still rely on SSH keys on the instance, so treat it as a transition rather than the destination, but it means existing tooling keeps working immediately rather than blocking the removal of your bastion.
Does Session Manager give users root access?

By default, effectively yes. Sessions run as ssm-user, which the agent creates with passwordless sudo on Linux. That makes IAM the entire access control: anyone with ssm:StartSession on an instance has root on it. Scope the permission by tag so people can only reach the environments they should, and either remove /etc/sudoers.d/ssm-agent-users or set runAsDefaultUser in the session document to connect as a less-privileged account where full root is not warranted.

keyConcepts.explanation: Store configuration and secrets in SSM Parameter Store with SecureString encryption, path hierarchies, versions, labels, standard vs advanced tiers and cost.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Store configuration and secrets in SSM Parameter Store with SecureString encryption, path hierarchies, versions, labels, standard vs advanced tiers and cost.

Parameter Store is the part of AWS Systems Manager that holds configuration values and secrets. It encrypts SecureString parameters with KMS, versions every change, controls access through IAM, and, unlike Secrets Manager, the Standard tier costs nothing.
For most teams it should be the default place configuration lives, with Secrets Manager reserved for the specific cases that need automatic rotation.

sections.title: Parameter types
paragraphs: Without --key-id, SecureString uses the AWS-managed alias/aws/ssm key. That works, but a customer-managed key is better for anything sensitive: you get your own key policy as a second access control layer, and key usage shows up separately in CloudTrail. The trade-off is that readers then need kms:Decrypt on that key in addition to the SSM permission. A very common cause of confusing AccessDeniedException errors.
Updating an existing parameter requires --overwrite, which is a deliberate guard against accidental clobbering:

codeBlock.code:
# Plain configuration
aws ssm put-parameter \
  --name /prod/payments/log-level \
  --value info \
  --type String

# An encrypted secret
aws ssm put-parameter \
  --name /prod/payments/api-key \
  --value "sk_live_xxxxxxxx" \
  --type SecureString \
  --key-id alias/payments-kms

sections.title: Hierarchies are the main design decision
paragraphs: Parameter names are paths, and getting the hierarchy right is what makes Parameter Store pleasant rather than tedious. Put the environment first:
Environment-first means one IAM statement scopes a role to exactly its own environment:
Note the ARN has no slash between parameter and the leading /prod. It reads parameter/prod/.... Adding one produces a policy that silently matches nothing.
It also means an application can load its whole configuration in one call:
--with-decryption is required for SecureString values; without it you get the ciphertext back and a confusing runtime failure.
Loading by path is the pattern to build on, because adding a parameter needs no code change:

Use the paginator. get_parameters_by_path returns at most 10 results per call, and code that ignores NextToken works fine in staging with eight parameters and truncates silently in production with thirty.

codeBlock.code:
/prod/payments/db-host
/prod/payments/db-password
/prod/payments/log-level
/staging/payments/db-host

sections.title: Versions and labels
paragraphs: Every write creates a new version, and old versions stay readable, which makes rollback trivial:
Labels give versions readable names, so a deployment can reference :live and you promote by moving the label rather than editing values:

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm get-parameter-history --name /prod/payments/log-level \
  --query 'Parameters[].{Version:Version,Value:Value,Date:LastModifiedDate}' --output table

# Pin a specific version
aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/payments/log-level:3

sections.title: Standard vs advanced tier
paragraphs: Standard covers almost everything. Move to advanced when a value exceeds 4 KB, typically a certificate or a large JSON blob, or when you want parameter policies, which can expire a parameter automatically or emit an EventBridge notification when one hasn't changed in N days. That second policy is a genuinely useful way to catch credentials nobody has rotated.

sections.title: Throughput
paragraphs: The default API limit is modest, and applications that read parameters on every request will hit ThrottlingException under load. The fixes, in order of preference: cache in the application, fetch by path once at start-up rather than per parameter, and only then consider paying for higher throughput.

On Lambda, the AWS Parameters and Secrets Extension is the clean answer. It runs a local caching layer so repeated reads never leave the execution environment. On ECS, reference parameters directly in the task definition:

sections.title: Integration worth knowing
paragraphs: Parameter Store publishes AWS-managed public parameters, which removes a whole category of hardcoded values. The latest Amazon Linux AMI ID, for example:
Terraform and CloudFormation can both resolve parameters at deploy time, so an AMI ID never needs to be pasted into a template again.

codeBlock.code:
aws ssm get-parameter \
  --name /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 \
  --query Parameter.Value --output text

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A role has ssm:GetParameter on the correct ARN, but reading a SecureString encrypted with a customer-managed key returns AccessDeniedException. What is missing?
A service loads config with get-parameters-by-path. Staging has 8 parameters and works. Production has 30 and the service starts with several values missing, but no error. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Is Parameter Store really free?

The Standard tier is free for storage and for standard-throughput API calls, up to 10,000 parameters per account per region. You pay only for KMS usage on SecureString operations, which is negligible for normal access patterns. The Advanced tier costs $0.05 per parameter per month and raises the value size limit to 8 KB, the count to 100,000, and adds parameter policies. Higher-throughput API access is a separate paid option in both tiers.
When should I use Secrets Manager instead?

When you need automatic rotation with a managed function, RDS, Aurora, Redshift and DocumentDB credentials being the clear cases, or cross-account access via resource policies, or values larger than 4 KB without moving to the advanced tier. Everything else belongs in Parameter Store. Putting a few hundred configuration values in Secrets Manager at $0.40 each per month costs real money for a rotation feature those values never use.
How do I read a SecureString value?

Pass --with-decryption to get-parameter or get-parameters-by-path. Without it the API returns the encrypted value and your application fails somewhere later with a confusing error. The caller needs both the SSM read permission and kms:Decrypt on the key that encrypted the parameter; with the default alias/aws/ssm key the second part is implicit, but a customer-managed key must grant it explicitly.
Why does my IAM policy for Parameter Store not work?

Check the ARN format first. It is arn:aws:ssm:<region>:<account>:parameter/prod/payments/*. There is no slash between parameter and the parameter path, so the leading slash of the name is the separator. Writing parameter//prod/... produces a policy that matches nothing and denies without explanation. The second thing to check is whether the parameter is a SecureString needing a separate kms:Decrypt grant.
Can I roll back a parameter change?

Yes. Every put-parameter creates a new version and previous versions remain readable indefinitely. Use get-parameter-history to see what changed and when, then read a specific version with --name /path/to/param:3. For a cleaner workflow, apply a label such as live to the known-good version and have deployments read :live, so promoting and rolling back are label moves rather than value edits.
How do I stop hardcoding AMI IDs?

AWS publishes public parameters under /aws/service/, including the latest AMI for each distribution. For example /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64. Read it with get-parameter, or reference it directly from CloudFormation and Terraform so templates resolve the current AMI at deploy time instead of carrying an ID that goes stale and becomes a security liability.

keyConcepts.explanation: Set up multi-account AWS with Organizations. Learn why separate accounts beat separate VPCs, how to design OUs, create accounts and use consolidated billing.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Set up multi-account AWS with Organizations. Learn why separate accounts beat separate VPCs, how to design OUs, create accounts and use consolidated billing.
Organizations groups multiple AWS accounts under one management account, with consolidated billing, centralised policy and shared service configuration.

The question it answers is why you would want many accounts at all. The answer is that an AWS account is the strongest isolation boundary AWS offers. Service quotas are per account, a blast radius stops at the account edge, IAM cannot accidentally reach across one, and billing separates without tag discipline. Separating production from development with VPCs and IAM policies in one account is possible and considerably weaker. One over-broad policy and the separation is gone.

sections.title: Structure
paragraphs: ALL, not CONSOLIDATED_BILLING. The billing-only feature set gives you a shared invoice and nothing else, no service control policies, no delegated administration, no organisation-wide CloudTrail. Upgrading later requires every member account to accept, which is tedious.
A structure that works for most organisations:

Organise by what policy should apply, not by team. Teams reorganise; the distinction between production and non-production does not. An OU structure mirroring your org chart needs rebuilding after every reorganisation, and policies attached to it move with people rather than with risk.
Keep the hierarchy shallow. Policies inherit down, and debugging an effective policy through five nested levels is genuinely unpleasant.

codeBlock.code: aws organizations create-organization --feature-set ALL

sections.title: The management account
paragraphs: Three rules, and they are widely broken.

Run no workloads in it. Nothing. It is where organisation-wide policy lives, and it is the one account service control policies cannot restrict. An SCP never applies to the management account, so it has no guardrails at all.
Lock it down. Hardware MFA on root, root credentials in a safe, no IAM users, access only via a break-glass role that alarms when assumed.
Do not use it as the security account. Delegate to a separate one:

Delegated administration lets a dedicated security account manage GuardDuty, Security Hub, Config, IAM Access Analyzer and others across the organisation, so day-to-day security work never requires touching the management account.

codeBlock.code:
aws organizations register-delegated-administrator \
  --account-id 210987654321 \
  --service-principal guardduty.amazonaws.com

sections.title: Creating accounts
paragraphs: Two practical points.

Every account needs a unique email address, and it cannot be reused even after an account is closed. Use a plus-addressed or distribution-list scheme, aws-prod-payments@example.com, pointing at a group rather than an individual. An account whose root email belongs to someone who has left is a genuine problem.

OrganizationAccountAccessRole is created automatically and trusts the management account, which is how you get into a new account initially. It grants full administrator access, so treat assuming it as a privileged operation and alarm on it.
Move the account into the right OU immediately, since it lands under the root where fewer policies apply:

codeBlock.code:
aws organizations create-account \
  --email aws-prod-payments@example.com \
  --account-name "Payments Production" \
  --role-name OrganizationAccountAccessRole \
  --iam-user-access-to-billing DENY

sections.title: Billing
paragraphs: Consolidated billing is the most immediately visible benefit, and it does more than combine invoices.
Volume discounts aggregate. Tiered pricing for S3 and data transfer is calculated across the whole organisation, so ten accounts each using 20 TB are priced as 200 TB.

Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are shared by default. An unused reservation in one account automatically applies to matching usage in another. That is usually what you want, and occasionally not. A team that bought reservations from its own budget may be subsidising another. Turn sharing off per account where it matters:
Cost allocation tags must be activated in the management account before they appear in reports:
Tags applied for months before activation produce no historical data, which is a common and irritating discovery.

codeBlock.code:
aws organizations disable-aws-service-access \
  --service-principal ram.amazonaws.com    # example: RAM sharing

sections.title: Control Tower
paragraphs: Control Tower is a managed layer over Organizations that sets up a landing zone: the OU structure, a log archive and audit account, organisation CloudTrail, Config with conformance packs, IAM Identity Center and a set of guardrails.
Use it for a new organisation. It produces a sound structure in an afternoon rather than weeks, and encodes AWS's current recommendations.

Two caveats worth knowing before committing. It is opinionated about structure, and fighting it is unpleasant. And enrolling existing accounts with established configurations can be awkward, sometimes requiring changes you would not otherwise make. For a greenfield organisation it is the obvious choice; for a large existing estate, evaluate carefully.

sections.title: Closing accounts
paragraphs: The account enters a 90-day suspended state before final closure, during which it can be reopened. Its resources stop and its root email remains unusable for a new account permanently.

The pattern worth adopting instead is a Suspended OU with a deny-all SCP. Move the account there, let it sit with everything blocked, and confirm nothing broke before closing it properly. Closure is irreversible after 90 days, and the data goes with it.
There is also a quota on how many accounts can be closed in a rolling 30-day period, which surprises teams doing a large cleanup.

codeBlock.code: aws organizations close-account --account-id 210987654321

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Organizations APIs largely work only from the management account, or from a delegated administrator for that specific service.
A soft quota. Request an increase; new organisations start with a low limit.
That email belongs to an existing or previously closed AWS account. Addresses are never released.
An SCP has no effect on the management account. By design. It cannot be restricted.

codeBlock.code: AccessDeniedException: You don't have permissions to access this resource.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An SCP denying the creation of unencrypted S3 buckets is attached to the root and works everywhere except one account, where unencrypted buckets can still be created. That account is the management account. Why?
A company with six product teams is designing its OU structure. Reorganisations happen roughly annually. What structure will age best?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why use multiple AWS accounts instead of one with separate VPCs?

Because an account is the strongest isolation boundary AWS provides. Service quotas apply per account, so one team cannot exhaust another's Lambda concurrency. A compromise or a runaway script stops at the account edge. IAM policies cannot accidentally grant access across accounts the way an over-broad policy can within one. And costs separate without relying on tag discipline. VPC and IAM separation inside a single account is workable and materially weaker. One mistaken wildcard undoes it.
How should I structure organizational units?

By the policies that should apply, not by team. A structure of Security, Infrastructure, Workloads split into Prod and NonProd, plus Sandbox and Suspended, reflects genuine differences in what should be permitted and survives reorganisations. An OU per team means restructuring the hierarchy and its attached policies whenever the company reshuffles. Express team ownership through tags and account names instead, and keep the tree shallow. Inherited policies across many levels are hard to reason about.
What should the management account be used for?

Organisation management and nothing else. No workloads, no data, no shared services. The reason is that service control policies never apply to it, so it has no guardrails at all. A mistake there has no safety net. Lock root with hardware MFA, store the credentials physically, create no IAM users, and access it only through a break-glass role that raises an alarm when assumed. Delegate GuardDuty, Security Hub, Config and similar services to a dedicated security account.
What does consolidated billing actually save?

More than a single invoice. Volume discount tiers for services such as S3 and data transfer are calculated across the whole organisation, so many accounts' usage aggregates into cheaper tiers. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are shared by default, meaning an unused reservation in one account automatically covers matching usage in another. That sharing is usually desirable and occasionally not, if a team purchased reservations from its own budget. It can be disabled per account.
Should I use AWS Control Tower?

For a new organisation, yes. It sets up a landing zone. OU structure, log archive and audit accounts, organisation CloudTrail, Config with conformance packs, IAM Identity Center and guardrails, in an afternoon rather than weeks of assembly, and it encodes AWS's current recommendations. The caveats are that it is opinionated about structure and unpleasant to fight, and that enrolling existing accounts with established configurations can be awkward. For a large existing estate, evaluate before committing.
What happens when I close an AWS account?

It enters a suspended state for 90 days during which it can be reopened, then closes permanently along with its data. The root email address is consumed forever and cannot be used for a new account, even after closure. There is also a quota on closures within a rolling 30-day window, which catches teams doing bulk cleanup. The safer pattern is a Suspended OU with a deny-all SCP: move the account there, confirm over some weeks that nothing depended on it, and only then close.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
