Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Write service control policies that restrict without breaking things: deny lists over allow lists, why an SCP grants nothing, break-glass roles and testing.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Write service control policies that restrict without breaking things: deny lists over allow lists, why an SCP grants nothing, break-glass roles and testing.

sections.title: Service Control Policies
paragraphs: An SCP sets the maximum permissions available in an account. It is a ceiling, not a grant, and that distinction is the source of nearly every SCP problem.
Two rules to hold on to:

An SCP never grants anything. A principal's effective permissions are the intersection of the SCP and their IAM policy. Both must allow an action; either can deny it. An SCP permitting s3:* gives nobody S3 access. IAM still has to grant it.
SCPs never apply to the management account. No exceptions, which is why nothing should run there.

sections.title: Allow lists and deny lists
paragraphs: Every OU and account starts with FullAWSAccess attached, an allow-everything policy. That is what makes a deny list possible: keep FullAWSAccess and attach policies that carve exceptions out of it.

An allow list means removing FullAWSAccess and enumerating everything permitted. It is more restrictive and considerably more work. A service you forgot is simply unavailable, with an error that does not mention SCPs.
Use deny lists. Allow lists are defensible in a tightly regulated environment and will otherwise consume your time in a permanent game of catch-up.

sections.title: Policies worth having
paragraphs: Restrict regions. Reduces attack surface and stops resources appearing where nobody is looking:

The NotAction list is essential. Global services have endpoints in us-east-1, so a naive region restriction breaks IAM, Route 53, CloudFront and support cases, and the resulting errors give no clue that a region policy is responsible.
Protect security infrastructure:
Prevent IAM user creation, pushing everyone to federated access with short-lived credentials:

sections.title: Always exempt a break-glass role
paragraphs: Every restrictive SCP should exclude at least one role, or you can lock yourself out of your own account with no way back except AWS Support:

That role should exist in every account, be assumable only from the management account, require MFA, and raise an alarm whenever it is used. The alarm is what keeps it from becoming an ordinary administrative path.
Note the deliberate use of ArnNotLike with aws:PrincipalArn rather than aws:PrincipalType. A role session ARN differs from the role ARN, and wildcards handle that.

sections.title: Test before attaching broadly
paragraphs: An SCP mistake affects every account beneath its attachment point, and the errors it produces are not obviously SCP-related. The safe sequence:
One sandbox account first.
Check what a principal can actually do:
Look for the actions in use before denying them, so the policy reflects reality rather than assumption:
Then widen to a non-production OU, and only afterwards to production.

codeBlock.code: aws organizations attach-policy --policy-id p-abc123 --target-id 210987654321

sections.title: Diagnosing an SCP denial
paragraphs: The error does not say "an SCP blocked this", which makes this one of the harder AWS things to debug:

That trailing phrase, "with an explicit deny in a service control policy", is the one reliable indicator, and it is easy to miss at the end of a long message. Not every SCP denial includes it, though: an implicit denial under an allow-list SCP produces an ordinary access denied with no explanation at all.
Work up the tree: policies attached to the account, its OU, parent OUs, and the root all combine, and a deny anywhere wins.

codeBlock.code:
An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the CreateBucket operation:
User: arn:aws:sts::210987654321:assumed-role/AppRole/session is not authorized
to perform: s3:CreateBucket with an explicit deny in a service control policy

sections.title: Resource control policies
paragraphs: RCPs are the newer counterpart and worth knowing about. An SCP limits what principals in your accounts can do; an RCP limits what can be done to resources in your accounts, including by principals outside the organisation.

That prevents any external account accessing your S3 buckets or assuming your roles, regardless of what a resource policy in a member account says. It closes a gap SCPs cannot: an SCP cannot stop someone in a member account writing a bucket policy that grants access to an outside party.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Found it. Work out which policy in the chain contains it.
Five SCPs per entity and a 5,120-byte limit per policy. Consolidate statements.
SCPs must be enabled for the root first, and the organisation needs --feature-set ALL.
A policy appears to have no effect. The target is the management account, which is exempt, or an inherited Allow is not what you think. SCPs filter, they never grant.

codeBlock.code:
... is not authorized to perform: <action> with an explicit deny in a
service control policy

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team attaches an SCP allowing s3:* and ec2:* to their OU, expecting developers to gain those permissions. Nobody can do anything new. Why?
An SCP denying all actions outside eu-west-1 is attached. Immediately, IAM role creation, Route 53 changes and support case creation all fail. What is wrong with the policy?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Do SCPs grant permissions?

No, and assuming otherwise causes most SCP confusion. An SCP defines the maximum set of actions available in an account; actual permissions still come from IAM policies, and a principal can act only where both allow it. So attaching an SCP permitting s3:* gives nobody S3 access. Worse, replacing the default FullAWSAccess with a narrow allow list silently removes everything not enumerated, so a policy intended to grant can end up restricting far more than expected.
What is the difference between an allow list and a deny list SCP?

A deny list keeps FullAWSAccess attached and adds policies that deny specific actions, so everything remains permitted except what you have carved out. An allow list removes FullAWSAccess and enumerates every permitted action, blocking everything else. Deny lists are far easier to live with: a service you did not think of still works. Allow lists are more restrictive and appropriate in tightly regulated environments, but they turn every new service adoption into a policy change, and the failures give no hint of the cause.
Why doesn't my SCP affect the management account?

Because the management account is exempt from all SCPs by design. The reasoning is that it must always retain the ability to manage the organisation, including removing a policy that has locked every other account out. The consequence is that it has no guardrails at all, which is the reason to run no workloads there, keep no data in it, lock root away with hardware MFA, and delegate security services to a separate account.
How do I know whether an SCP is blocking my request?

Look for the phrase "with an explicit deny in a service control policy" at the end of the access denied message. It is the one reliable indicator and easy to miss. An implicit denial under an allow-list SCP produces no such hint, just an ordinary access denied. Use list-policies-for-target and describe-effective-policy for the account to see every applicable policy, remembering that policies attached to the account, its OU, parent OUs and the root all combine, and a deny anywhere wins.
How do I avoid locking myself out with an SCP?

Exempt a break-glass role from every restrictive statement using a condition on aws:PrincipalArn, and make sure that role exists in every account, is assumable only from the management account, requires MFA and raises an alarm when used. Test policies on a single sandbox account first, then a non-production OU, then production. And check CloudTrail for real usage of the actions you plan to deny. A restriction that looks obviously safe often turns out to block an automation nobody remembered.
What is the difference between an SCP and a resource control policy?

An SCP limits what principals in your accounts may do. An RCP limits what may be done to resources in your accounts, including by principals outside the organisation entirely. That closes a real gap: an SCP cannot stop someone in a member account writing a bucket policy granting access to an external AWS account, because the restriction applies to your principals rather than to the resource. An RCP denying access to anything without your aws:PrincipalOrgID blocks that regardless of what the resource policy says.

Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Create and mount Amazon EFS across instances and containers. Covers mount targets per AZ, the forgotten security group rule, throughput modes and EFS vs EBS.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create and mount Amazon EFS across instances and containers. Covers mount targets per AZ, the forgotten security group rule, throughput modes and EFS vs EBS.

sections.title: Amazon EFS
paragraphs: EFS is a managed NFS filesystem that many instances, containers or Lambda functions can mount at the same time, all reading and writing the same files. It grows and shrinks automatically and spans availability zones.
That concurrent access is the whole reason to choose it. An EBS volume attaches to one instance and lives in one availability zone; EFS is reachable from every instance in the VPC.

sections.title: Create and mount
paragraphs: A mount target is needed in every availability zone you will mount from. This is not optional, and an instance in an AZ without one simply cannot connect:
Use amazon-efs-utils rather than mounting NFS directly. It handles TLS in transit, IAM authorisation, and retries. A plain mount -t nfs4 works and gives you none of that.
_netdev waits for networking before mounting, without which boot can hang. noresvport lets the client reconnect after a network interruption rather than holding a dead session.

codeBlock.code:
aws efs create-file-system \
  --creation-token orders-shared \
  --encrypted --kms-key-id alias/aws/elasticfilesystem \
  --throughput-mode elastic \
  --tags Key=Name,Value=orders-shared

sections.title: The security group rule everyone forgets
paragraphs: An EFS mount that hangs and eventually times out is, almost every time, the security group:

The mount target's security group must allow inbound TCP 2049 (NFS) from the client's security group. Nothing reports this, mount simply sits there for a minute or two and then fails with a timeout, which is a slow way to discover a firewall rule.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --protocol tcp --port 2049 --source-group sg-0fedcba9876543210

sections.title: Throughput modes matter more than you expect
paragraphs: This is where EFS goes wrong in production, and the default is the problem.

Bursting was the historical default and is a trap for small filesystems. Baseline throughput is about 50 KiB/s per GiB stored, so a 10 GiB filesystem gets roughly 0.5 MiB/s sustained. It accumulates burst credits while idle and spends them under load, so everything is fast for a while, then abruptly is not.
A BurstCreditBalance trending toward zero is the warning, and exhausting it produces a filesystem that has become mysteriously slow with no change on your side. Alarm on it, or use Elastic:

Elastic is the right default now. It scales up to gigabytes per second with no credits to track, and you pay for what you read and write. For a spiky or small workload it is usually cheaper than provisioning, and it removes an entire failure mode.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace AWS/EFS --metric-name BurstCreditBalance \
  --dimensions Name=FileSystemId,Value=fs-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --start-time 2026-09-15T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-09-16T00:00:00Z \
  --period 3600 --statistics Minimum

sections.title: EFS is not fast for small files
paragraphs: Worth being blunt, because it disappoints people. EFS is a network filesystem, so every operation crosses the network. Latency per operation is orders of magnitude higher than a local EBS volume.

That makes it poor for anything metadata-heavy: node_modules, a Git working tree, a compiler's intermediate files, an application's local cache. npm install on EFS is painfully slow, and no throughput setting fixes it, because the constraint is operation latency rather than bandwidth.

General Purpose performance mode gives the lowest latency and is right for almost everything. Max I/O raises throughput at the cost of higher per-operation latency, and only pays off for genuinely parallel workloads across many instances.
Use EFS for shared state that must be shared. Keep build artefacts and caches on local storage.

sections.title: Access points
paragraphs: An access point enforces a directory and a POSIX identity, so a client cannot reach outside its own subtree:

Two reasons this matters. It makes multi-tenant use safe, since every client is confined to its path regardless of what it asks for. And it creates the root directory with the right ownership automatically, which removes the usual permission fight when several containers share a filesystem.
Access points are also required for Lambda, and the standard approach on EKS via the EFS CSI driver.

codeBlock.code:
aws efs create-access-point --file-system-id fs-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --posix-user 'Uid=1000,Gid=1000' \
  --root-directory 'Path=/tenant-a,CreationInfo={OwnerUid=1000,OwnerGid=1000,Permissions=0755}' \
  --tags Key=Name,Value=tenant-a

sections.title: Cost control with lifecycle policies
paragraphs: EFS Standard storage is considerably more expensive per GiB than EBS or S3, so lifecycle management is not optional on any growing filesystem:

Infrequent Access costs a fraction of Standard with a per-access read charge; Archive is cheaper still. TransitionToPrimaryStorageClass=AFTER_1_ACCESS moves a file back on first read, so genuinely active data does not stay in a class that charges per access.
For a filesystem holding years of documents that are rarely re-read, this is frequently the difference between a sensible bill and an alarming one.

codeBlock.code:
aws efs put-lifecycle-configuration --file-system-id fs-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --lifecycle-policies \
    'TransitionToIA=AFTER_30_DAYS' \
    'TransitionToArchive=AFTER_90_DAYS' \
    'TransitionToPrimaryStorageClass=AFTER_1_ACCESS'

sections.title: IAM authorisation
paragraphs: Mounting with -o iam uses the instance role rather than relying purely on network reachability, so a filesystem policy can require authenticated access and deny anonymous mounts. Combined with tls, that gives encryption in transit and identity on every mount.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Security group missing inbound 2049, or no mount target in this availability zone.
The filesystem policy or access point is refusing. Check -o iam and the instance role.
amazon-efs-utils is not installed, so -t efs is unrecognised.
Everything suddenly slow. Burst credits exhausted. Check BurstCreditBalance and switch to Elastic.
Permission denied writing to a new filesystem. The root is owned by root with mode 755. Use an access point with CreationInfo, or chown it once from a client.

codeBlock.code: mount.nfs4: Connection timed out

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A 20 GiB EFS filesystem performed well for weeks, then throughput collapsed with no configuration or code change. It uses Bursting throughput mode. What happened?
mount -t efs on an instance in the same VPC hangs for about two minutes and fails with "Connection timed out". A mount target exists in the instance's availability zone. What should you check?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: When should I use EFS instead of EBS or S3?

EFS when multiple instances or containers must read and write the same files simultaneously. Shared uploads, a CMS content directory, a workspace several workers process. EBS when a single instance needs a fast block device: databases, boot volumes, anything latency-sensitive. S3 when you want objects rather than a filesystem, at the lowest cost and highest durability, accessed over HTTP. Choosing EFS for single-instance storage means paying considerably more per GiB for network latency you did not need.
Why does my EFS mount time out?

Almost always the security group. The mount target needs an inbound rule allowing TCP 2049 from the client's security group, and without it packets are dropped silently while mount waits out its timeout. Nothing in the error mentions a firewall. The other cause is no mount target in the instance's availability zone, since mount targets are per-AZ and an instance cannot use one elsewhere. describe-mount-targets shows which zones are covered.
What is the difference between Bursting and Elastic throughput?

Bursting ties baseline throughput to how much data is stored, around 50 KiB/s per GiB, and funds short bursts from credits that accrue while idle. That works for large filesystems and starves small ones, which fail suddenly when credits reach zero with nothing having changed. Elastic scales automatically to gigabytes per second and charges for what you actually read and write. Elastic is the sensible default; if you remain on Bursting, alarm on BurstCreditBalance.
Why is EFS slow for my application?

Because it is a network filesystem, so every file operation incurs network latency that a local EBS volume does not. Workloads dominated by many small operations, node_modules, a Git working tree, compiler intermediates, an application cache, are badly affected, and no throughput setting fixes it since the constraint is per-operation latency rather than bandwidth. Keep build artefacts and caches on local storage and use EFS only for state that genuinely needs sharing.
What are EFS access points for?

An access point pins a mount to a specific directory and POSIX user and group, so a client is confined to its own subtree no matter what path it requests, which is what makes multi-tenant use safe. It also creates that directory with the ownership and permissions you specify, removing the usual permission struggle when several containers share a filesystem. They are required for Lambda and are the standard approach for Kubernetes through the EFS CSI driver.
How do I stop EFS costs growing?

Set a lifecycle configuration. EFS Standard is expensive per GiB relative to EBS or S3, and Infrequent Access costs a fraction of it with a small per-read charge, while Archive is cheaper again. Transitioning after 30 and 90 days respectively, with TransitionToPrimaryStorageClass=AFTER_1_ACCESS so genuinely active files move back, usually cuts the bill substantially on any filesystem accumulating data that is rarely re-read.

aws-ebs-deep-dive.subtitle: Choose and tune EBS volumes: gp3 vs gp2, io2 Block Express, why the instance type caps throughput, fast snapshot restore, safe resizing and encryption.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS EBS Deep Dive must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Choose and tune EBS volumes: gp3 vs gp2, io2 Block Express, why the instance type caps throughput, fast snapshot restore, safe resizing and encryption.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Choose and tune EBS volumes: gp3 vs gp2, io2 Block Express, why the instance type caps throughput, fast snapshot restore, safe resizing and encryption.

sections.title: EBS Deep Dive
paragraphs: EBS provides block storage for EC2. Volumes that behave like disks, persist independently of the instance, and are replicated within a single availability zone.
Two things account for most EBS disappointment: still using gp2, and not realising that the instance type caps what any volume can deliver.

sections.title: Volume types
paragraphs: gp2's performance is tied to size: 3 IOPS per GiB, so 3,000 IOPS requires a 1,000 GiB volume whether or not you need the space. Below 1,000 GiB it relies on burst credits, which behave exactly like EFS bursting. Fine until they run out, then abruptly slow.
gp3 decouples the two. Every gp3 volume starts at 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size, and you provision more independently.

gp3 is also about 20% cheaper per GiB than gp2, and the conversion happens online with no downtime and no snapshot. A 100 GiB gp2 volume delivers 300 baseline IOPS; the same volume as gp3 delivers 3,000 for less money.
This is the single easiest cost-and-performance improvement available in most AWS accounts, and it is frequently untouched because nothing surfaces it.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --volume-type gp3 --iops 3000 --throughput 125

sections.title: The instance type is the real limit
paragraphs: Provisioning 16,000 IOPS on a volume attached to an instance that supports 6,000 achieves nothing, and nothing warns you.

Note baseline versus maximum: smaller instances burst their EBS bandwidth too, so sustained performance is the baseline figure. An m6i.large sustains about 81 MiB/s regardless of how the volume is configured.
Check this before provisioning IOPS. Paying for 10,000 IOPS on an instance that sustains 3,600 is pure waste, and "the volume is fast enough but the application is slow" is usually this.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types m6i.large \
  --query 'InstanceTypes[0].EbsInfo.EbsOptimizedInfo' --output table

sections.title: Snapshots
paragraphs: Snapshots are incremental and stored in S3. The first captures every used block; later ones store only changes, though each remains independently restorable. Deleting an old snapshot never breaks a newer one.
For a multi-volume instance, snapshot them together so they are mutually consistent:
Automate retention with Data Lifecycle Manager rather than a cron job:

The trap that catches people during a recovery. A volume created from a snapshot is available immediately, but blocks are fetched from S3 on first access, so early reads are dramatically slower than normal, exactly when you are trying to get a service back.

Fast snapshot restore removes the penalty at an hourly cost per snapshot per AZ. Enable it on the snapshots your recovery plan depends on, not all of them, and if you cannot, pre-warm by reading the volume through before putting it in service.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --description "pre-migration $(date -I)" \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=snapshot,Tags=[{Key=Retain,Value=30d}]'

sections.title: Resizing
paragraphs: Volumes grow online, and cannot shrink:
The filesystem does not grow by itself. The volume is bigger and df shows the old size until you extend it:
Forgetting this step is why "I resized the volume and the disk is still full" is such a common report.
A volume cannot be modified again for six hours after a change, which is worth knowing before an emergency resize.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --size 200
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query 'VolumesModifications[0].[ModificationState,Progress]'

sections.title: Encryption
paragraphs: Set this in every account and region. It costs nothing and removes the possibility of an unencrypted volume being created by accident.
An existing unencrypted volume cannot be encrypted in place. The path is snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption, create a new volume, swap it in:
That requires downtime for the swap, which is the argument for enabling encryption by default before you have volumes to migrate.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default
aws ec2 modify-ebs-default-kms-key-id --kms-key-id alias/ebs

sections.title: Multi-attach
paragraphs: io1 and io2 volumes can attach to up to 16 instances in the same availability zone:

This does not give you a shared filesystem. Two instances mounting ext4 on the same volume will corrupt it, because neither knows about the other's writes. It requires a cluster-aware filesystem such as GFS2 or an application managing its own locking.
If you want shared file storage, that is EFS.

codeBlock.code:
aws ec2 create-volume --volume-type io2 --size 100 --iops 10000 \
  --multi-attach-enabled --availability-zone eu-west-1a

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Detach first, or use multi-attach if the volume type and filesystem support it.
gp3 caps at 500 IOPS per GiB, io2 at 500 as well within its own limits. Increase the size or lower the IOPS.
Six-hour cooldown between modifications.
df shows the old size after resizing. Extend the filesystem.
A snapshot restore is slow. Blocks are being lazily loaded. Fast snapshot restore, or pre-warm.

codeBlock.code: VolumeInUse: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is already attached to an instance

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A gp3 volume is raised from 3,000 to 12,000 IOPS on an m6i.large instance. Database performance does not improve measurably. Why?
A volume was resized from 50 GiB to 200 GiB and the modification shows as completed. df -h still reports 50G with no free space. What is missing?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I use gp2 or gp3?

gp3, without qualification. gp2 ties IOPS to volume size at 3 per GiB and relies on burst credits below 1,000 GiB, so a 100 GiB volume has a 300 IOPS baseline. Every gp3 volume starts at 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size, lets you provision more independently, and costs roughly 20% less per GiB. Conversion is a single modify-volume call, happens online with no downtime, and needs no snapshot. Auditing an account for gp2 volumes is usually the cheapest performance win available.
Why doesn't increasing IOPS improve performance?

Because the instance type has its own EBS limits and the effective figure is the lower of the two. An m6i.large sustains around 3,600 IOPS and 81 MiB/s, so provisioning 12,000 on the volume adds cost and nothing else. Check describe-instance-types with the EbsInfo.EbsOptimizedInfo query, and pay attention to baseline versus maximum. Smaller instances burst their EBS bandwidth, so sustained workloads should be sized against the baseline number.
How do EBS snapshots work and is deleting old ones safe?

Snapshots are incremental: the first stores every used block, subsequent ones store only changed blocks, and all of them reference a shared set of blocks in S3. Each snapshot is independently restorable, and deleting one never invalidates another. AWS retains any blocks still needed by remaining snapshots. So a retention policy that keeps the last seven daily snapshots works exactly as expected. Use Data Lifecycle Manager to automate creation and expiry rather than scripting it.
Why is a volume restored from a snapshot slow?

Because blocks are pulled from S3 lazily, on first access, so a volume is usable immediately but reads of not-yet-loaded blocks are much slower than normal, which lands precisely during a recovery. Fast snapshot restore eliminates the penalty for an hourly charge per snapshot per availability zone; enable it on the snapshots your recovery plan actually depends on. Without it, read the volume through with dd or fio before putting it into service.
How do I resize an EBS volume?

aws ec2 modify-volume --size N grows it online, and volumes cannot shrink. The step people miss is that the filesystem does not grow with the device: run growpart if the device is partitioned, then resize2fs for ext4 or xfs_growfs -d for xfs, both of which work on a mounted filesystem. lsblk shows the device size and df the filesystem size, so comparing them confirms which half is outstanding. A volume cannot be modified again for six hours.
Can I encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume?

Not in place. Take a snapshot, copy the snapshot with --encrypted and your KMS key, create a volume from the encrypted copy, then detach the old volume and attach the new one, which means downtime for the swap. That is the argument for running enable-ebs-encryption-by-default in every account and region now: it costs nothing, prevents unencrypted volumes being created accidentally, and saves you this migration entirely.

Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Choose between Kinesis Data Streams, Firehose, SQS and MSK. Learn shards, hot partition keys, consumer lag, enhanced fan-out and how to reshard a busy stream.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Choose between Kinesis Data Streams, Firehose, SQS and MSK. Learn shards, hot partition keys, consumer lag, enhanced fan-out and how to reshard a busy stream.

sections.title: Amazon Kinesis
paragraphs: Kinesis is a family of services for streaming data. Two of them matter for most work, and choosing wrongly costs a lot of unnecessary effort.
Data Streams is a durable, ordered, replayable log. Records persist for 24 hours by default and up to a year, multiple consumers read independently, and each can re-read from any point.
Data Firehose is a managed delivery pipeline. It buffers records and writes them to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or an HTTP endpoint with no code, no shards and no consumers to run.

If your goal is "get this data into S3", use Firehose. People reach for Data Streams, write a consumer, manage shards and reimplement batching. All to do what Firehose does with a configuration block.

sections.title: Firehose first
paragraphs: Two details worth getting right.

The Hive-style prefix (year=…/month=…/day=…) makes the output directly partitionable by Athena and Glue, so queries scan one day rather than the whole bucket. Retrofitting partitioning later means rewriting the object layout.

Buffering hints trade latency for cost and query efficiency. 128 MB or 300 seconds produces fewer, larger objects. Cheaper to store and far faster to query. A one-minute buffer produces many small files, which is the classic mistake that makes an Athena table slow.
DataFormatConversionConfiguration converts JSON to Parquet in flight, typically cutting both storage and query cost by an order of magnitude for analytical use.

codeBlock.code:
aws firehose create-delivery-stream \
  --delivery-stream-name events-to-s3 \
  --delivery-stream-type DirectPut \
  --extended-s3-destination-configuration '{
    "RoleARN": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/FirehoseRole",
    "BucketARN": "arn:aws:s3:::my-events",
    "Prefix": "events/year=!{timestamp:yyyy}/month=!{timestamp:MM}/day=!{timestamp:dd}/",
    "ErrorOutputPrefix": "errors/",
    "BufferingHints": { "SizeInMBs": 128, "IntervalInSeconds": 300 },
    "CompressionFormat": "GZIP",
    "DataFormatConversionConfiguration": { "Enabled": true }
  }'

sections.title: Data Streams and shards
paragraphs: Use Data Streams when you need multiple independent consumers, replay, ordering per key, or sub-second processing.
Start on-demand. It scales automatically and removes shard management entirely. Provisioned is cheaper at steady high volume, and requires you to get the shard count right:
A shard is the unit of capacity: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records per second in, 2 MB/s out. Those limits are per shard, so total capacity is shards multiplied by the limit.

codeBlock.code: aws kinesis create-stream --stream-name orders --stream-mode-details StreamMode=ON_DEMAND

sections.title: The partition key decides everything
paragraphs: Records are assigned to shards by a hash of the partition key, so a low-cardinality key concentrates traffic on one shard, a hot shard, which throttles while the others sit idle.

That last row is the real trade. Ordering is guaranteed only within a shard, so records sharing a partition key are ordered relative to each other. Using a random key gives perfect distribution and no ordering at all. Fine for independent events, wrong for a sequence of updates to the same entity.
One shard named while others are fine is a hot key, not insufficient capacity.

codeBlock.code:
aws kinesis put-record --stream-name orders \
  --partition-key "customer-4821" \
  --data "$(echo -n '{"event":"placed"}' | base64)"

sections.title: Consumer lag is the metric that matters
paragraphs: IteratorAgeMilliseconds is how old the records being processed are. Steady near zero means consumers keep up; rising means they do not, and if it reaches the retention period, data is lost permanently. Records expire before anyone reads them.
This is the single most important Kinesis alarm. Set it well below retention, so a few hours of climbing lag is a page rather than a postmortem.
When lag rises, the usual causes are a slow consumer, too few shards for the volume, or a hot shard where one consumer is overwhelmed while others idle.

codeBlock.code:
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/Kinesis \
  --metric-name GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds \
  --dimensions Name=StreamName,Value=orders \
  --start-time 2026-09-15T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-09-16T00:00:00Z \
  --period 300 --statistics Maximum

sections.title: Consumers
paragraphs: Lambda is the simplest:
Four of those options prevent real problems.

--bisect-batch-on-function-error splits a failing batch to isolate the bad record. Without it, one unparseable record fails its batch repeatedly and blocks that shard until the record expires: a poison pill that stalls the stream for up to the retention period.
--maximum-retry-attempts and --maximum-record-age-in-seconds bound how long a bad record is retried.
--destination-config sends failures to a DLQ instead of discarding them.
--parallelization-factor runs several concurrent invocations per shard, preserving order per partition key while raising throughput.
By default Lambda processes one batch per shard at a time, so throughput is bounded by shard count multiplied by how fast your function runs.

codeBlock.code:
aws lambda create-event-source-mapping \
  --function-name process-orders \
  --event-source-arn "$STREAM_ARN" \
  --starting-position LATEST \
  --batch-size 100 \
  --maximum-retry-attempts 3 \
  --maximum-record-age-in-seconds 3600 \
  --bisect-batch-on-function-error \
  --parallelization-factor 4 \
  --destination-config '{"OnFailure":{"Destination":"arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-1:123456789012:kinesis-dlq"}}'

sections.title: Enhanced fan-out
paragraphs: Standard consumers share the shard's 2 MB/s read limit, so five consumers get 400 KB/s each. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own dedicated 2 MB/s and pushes records rather than being polled:
It costs more per consumer-shard-hour and drops propagation delay to around 70 ms. Worth it beyond two or three consumers, or where latency matters.

codeBlock.code:
aws kinesis register-stream-consumer \
  --stream-arn "$STREAM_ARN" --consumer-name analytics

sections.title: Kinesis, SQS or MSK
paragraphs: Choose SQS for distributing work among workers where each message is handled once. Choose Kinesis when several systems need the same stream, or you need replay. Choose MSK when you already have Kafka expertise and tooling, or need portability off AWS. Accepting considerably more operational work.
The common mistake is using Kinesis as a work queue. If each record has exactly one consumer and you never replay, SQS is simpler, cheaper and has dead-letter handling built in.

sections.title: Resharding
paragraphs: Resharding is online but not free: old shards enter a CLOSED state that consumers must drain before reading the new ones, and the KCL and Lambda handle that automatically while custom consumers often do not. Doubling or halving is the cleanest change.
This is the main reason on-demand mode is a good default. It removes resharding from your operational surface entirely.

codeBlock.code:
aws kinesis update-shard-count --stream-name orders \
  --target-shard-count 8 --scaling-type UNIFORM_SCALING

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: A hot partition key if one shard is named; genuine under-provisioning if all are.
A shard iterator was held longer than five minutes. Fetch a fresh one.
Resharding in progress; wait for ACTIVE.
Lambda stops processing one shard. A poison record blocking the batch. Enable bisect-on-error and a failure destination.
Records missing. IteratorAgeMilliseconds reached retention and they expired unread.

codeBlock.code: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException: Rate exceeded for shard shardId-…

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A four-shard stream throttles with ProvisionedThroughputExceededException naming shardId-000000000002 while the other three show low utilisation. Records use eventType as the partition key, with four possible values. What is wrong?

A Lambda consumer processes three of four shards normally. The fourth has made no progress for hours and its iterator age keeps climbing. Logs show the same batch failing repeatedly. What is happening and what fixes it?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between Kinesis Data Streams and Data Firehose?

Data Streams is a durable, replayable log: records persist for 24 hours up to a year, several consumers read independently, and each tracks its own position so it can re-read. Firehose is a managed delivery pipeline that buffers records and writes them to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or an HTTP endpoint with no consumers to write or shards to manage. If the goal is getting data into S3, use Firehose. Building that on Data Streams means reimplementing batching, compression and partitioning that Firehose does with configuration.
When should I use Kinesis instead of SQS?

When several independent systems need the same records, or when you need to replay history. SQS delivers each message to one consumer and deletes it, with no replay; Kinesis keeps records for the retention period and lets every consumer read them at its own pace from any point. If each record has exactly one consumer and you never need to re-read, SQS is simpler, cheaper, and has dead-letter handling built in. Using Kinesis as a work queue is a common and avoidable mistake.
How do I choose a Kinesis partition key?

Pick something with high cardinality so records spread evenly across shards. A customer, device or session identifier. Low-cardinality keys such as an event type concentrate traffic on a few shards, which throttle while the rest idle, and total stream capacity does not help because limits are per shard. The trade-off to understand is ordering: records are ordered only within a shard, so a random key gives perfect distribution and no ordering guarantees at all. Choose the key whose ordering you actually need.
What does IteratorAgeMilliseconds mean and why alarm on it?

It is how old the records your consumers are currently processing are. Effectively consumer lag. Steady near zero means processing keeps pace with ingestion. A rising value means it does not, and if the age reaches the stream's retention period, records expire before anyone reads them and the data is gone permanently. That makes it the most important Kinesis alarm: set the threshold well below retention so a few hours of growing lag is something you act on rather than discover afterwards.
Why did my Lambda consumer stop processing one shard?

Almost certainly a poison record. Kinesis processing is ordered per shard, so Lambda will not skip past a batch that keeps failing, by default it retries until the records expire, blocking that shard for up to the retention period. Enable --bisect-batch-on-function-error so the batch is split to isolate the offending record, set --maximum-retry-attempts and --maximum-record-age-in-seconds to bound the retrying, and add a --destination-config failure destination so the bad record is captured rather than lost.
What is enhanced fan-out and do I need it?

Standard consumers share a shard's 2 MB/s read throughput, so five consumers get roughly 400 KB/s each and compete for it. Enhanced fan-out registers a consumer for its own dedicated 2 MB/s per shard and pushes records rather than being polled, cutting propagation delay to around 70 milliseconds. It costs more per consumer-shard-hour, so it earns its place beyond two or three consumers or where latency genuinely matters. With one consumer, standard polling is fine.

verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS Athena must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Query S3 with SQL using Athena and keep the bill low. Learn partitioning, partition projection, why Parquet beats JSON and how to cap bytes scanned per query.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Query S3 with SQL using Athena and keep the bill low. Learn partitioning, partition projection, why Parquet beats JSON and how to cap bytes scanned per query.

sections.title: Amazon Athena
paragraphs: Athena runs SQL directly against files in S3. There is no cluster to provision and nothing to load. You define a table describing where the data is and what shape it has, then query it.

You pay per terabyte scanned. That single fact should shape every decision you make about it, because the difference between a well-organised table and a careless one is routinely a factor of a hundred in both cost and query time.

sections.title: A table over S3
paragraphs: The table is metadata in the Glue Data Catalog. Nothing is copied, and dropping the table deletes no data.

codeBlock.code:
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE events (
  event_time  timestamp,
  user_id     string,
  event_type  string,
  amount      double
)
PARTITIONED BY (year string, month string, day string)
STORED AS PARQUET
LOCATION 's3://my-events/events/'
TBLPROPERTIES ('parquet.compression' = 'SNAPPY');

sections.title: Partitioning is the whole game
paragraphs: Without partitions, every query reads every file:
With partitions and a matching S3 layout, Athena reads only the relevant prefixes:
That key=value directory naming is the Hive convention Athena understands, and it is why Firehose prefixes should be configured that way from the start.
New partitions are not discovered automatically:

MSCK REPAIR scans the whole location, which becomes slow once you have thousands of partitions. Partition projection avoids it entirely by telling Athena how to compute partition values rather than look them up:
No metadata store lookups, no repair command, no partition registration. For any time-partitioned dataset this is the right configuration and it is widely unknown.

codeBlock.code:
-- Scans the entire dataset. Could be terabytes
SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE year = '2026' AND month = '09';

sections.title: File format matters as much as partitioning
paragraphs: Parquet is columnar, so selecting three columns of forty reads only those three. It also carries statistics per row group, letting Athena skip blocks that cannot match a predicate.
Converting once pays for itself immediately:
A CTAS statement like that is also how you build a summary table from an expensive query, so repeated dashboards read a small aggregate rather than the raw data each time.
Avoid many small files. Thousands of tiny objects cost more in overhead than a few large ones. Aim for 128 MB or larger per file, which is what generous Firehose buffering produces.

codeBlock.code:
CREATE TABLE events_parquet
WITH (
  format = 'PARQUET',
  parquet_compression = 'SNAPPY',
  partitioned_by = ARRAY['year','month','day'],
  external_location = 's3://my-events/parquet/'
) AS
SELECT event_time, user_id, event_type, amount, year, month, day
FROM events_json;

sections.title: Writing queries that scan less
paragraphs: Always filter on partition columns. A WHERE on a non-partition column filters after reading:
Never SELECT * on a columnar table. It defeats the format's main advantage.
LIMIT does not reduce the scan in most cases, which surprises people. An aggregate still reads everything it needs; the limit applies to output rows.
Check what a query actually cost:

sections.title: Put a limit on it before someone runs a bad query
paragraphs: A single careless query against an unpartitioned multi-terabyte table is an expensive accident. Workgroups let you cap it:

BytesScannedCutoffPerQuery at 100 GB cancels anything exceeding it. Set this on every workgroup before giving anyone access. It is the one control that turns a potential surprise bill into an error message.
Separate workgroups also give per-team cost attribution and separate result locations.

codeBlock.code:
aws athena create-work-group --name analysts \
  --configuration '{
    "ResultConfiguration": {"OutputLocation": "s3://my-athena-results/analysts/"},
    "BytesScannedCutoffPerQuery": 107374182400,
    "EnforceWorkGroupConfiguration": true,
    "PublishCloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true
  }'

sections.title: Querying AWS's own logs
paragraphs: Two tables worth having ready.
ALB access logs, where the separate timing fields are what settle "is it us or the balancer":
Both should be partitioned. An unpartitioned CloudTrail table over a year of organisation-wide logs is exactly the query that produces an unpleasant bill.

codeBlock.code:
SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn, eventname, sourceipaddress, errorcode
FROM cloudtrail_logs
WHERE eventname IN ('DeleteBucket','PutBucketPolicy','StopLogging')
  AND year='2026' AND month='09'
ORDER BY eventtime DESC;

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: A column type changed between partitions. Either correct the data or define the column as string and cast in the query.
A row does not match the declared schema, commonly a null in a numeric column, or a header row in a CSV. skip.header.line.count handles the latter.
Too much data for the query plan, often a large join or window function. Filter harder, or use CTAS to materialise an intermediate result.
Athena needs read on the data bucket, write on the results bucket, and Glue catalog permissions. All three.
Query returns zero rows but the data is there. Partitions were never added. Run MSCK REPAIR TABLE or enable partition projection.

codeBlock.code:
HIVE_PARTITION_SCHEMA_MISMATCH: There is a mismatch between the table and
partition schemas.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE user_id = 'u-4821' LIMIT 10 scanned 4 TB on a table partitioned by year, month and day. Why did LIMIT not help?
A table receives a new daily partition from Firehose. Queries return nothing until someone remembers to run MSCK REPAIR TABLE, which now takes several minutes. What is the better approach?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How is Athena billed and how do I reduce the cost?

Per terabyte of data scanned, with no charge for idle time. Everything that reduces bytes read therefore reduces cost: partition the data and filter on partition columns so only relevant prefixes are read, store it as Parquet with Snappy so only the columns you select are touched, avoid SELECT *, and consolidate small files into ones of 128 MB or more. Converting a JSON dataset to partitioned Parquet commonly cuts a scan by two orders of magnitude.
Why does my Athena query return no rows when the data exists in S3?

Because the partitions are not registered. A partitioned table only knows about partitions recorded in the Glue catalog, so data written to a new prefix is invisible until MSCK REPAIR TABLE runs or the partition is added with ALTER TABLE ADD PARTITION. The better fix is partition projection, which lets Athena compute partition locations from a template so new data is queryable immediately with no registration step. Also check the S3 prefix uses key=value naming.
What is partition projection and why should I use it?

It tells Athena the types, ranges and location template of your partition columns, so it derives the S3 path for a queried partition arithmetically instead of looking it up. That removes MSCK REPAIR TABLE from your workflow entirely, makes new data queryable as soon as it lands, and avoids the catalog growing to thousands of partition entries, which is what makes repair slow over time. For any time-based dataset written continuously it is the right configuration.
Should I convert my data to Parquet?

Almost certainly. Parquet is columnar, so a query selecting three of forty columns reads only those three, and it stores per-row-group statistics that let Athena skip blocks which cannot satisfy a predicate. Against uncompressed JSON the reduction in bytes scanned is frequently around a hundredfold, which shows up directly in both cost and query time. A single CTAS statement converts and partitions an existing table, and it usually pays for itself within days.
How do I stop someone running an expensive query?

Set BytesScannedCutoffPerQuery on the workgroup, which cancels any query exceeding the limit: 100 GB is a reasonable starting point for interactive use. Do this before granting access rather than afterwards, because a single SELECT * against an unpartitioned multi-terabyte table is otherwise a real and unpleasant bill. Separate workgroups per team also give you cost attribution and independent result locations, and EnforceWorkGroupConfiguration stops users overriding the settings.
Can I use Athena to query CloudTrail and load balancer logs?

Yes, and it is one of its best uses. Both produce large volumes of S3 data nobody wants to load into a database. AWS documents the table definitions, and the console can generate them. The essential part is partitioning by date: an unpartitioned CloudTrail table over a year of organisation-wide logs will scan everything on every query. For ALB logs, the separate request_processing_time and target_processing_time fields are what let you establish whether latency is in the balancer or your application.

aws-codedeploy.subtitle: Run blue-green and canary deployments to EC2, Lambda and ECS with CodeDeploy. Write the appspec file, add lifecycle hooks and roll back on CloudWatch alarms.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS CodeDeploy must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Run blue-green and canary deployments to EC2, Lambda and ECS with CodeDeploy. Write the appspec file, add lifecycle hooks and roll back on CloudWatch alarms.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Run blue-green and canary deployments to EC2, Lambda and ECS with CodeDeploy. Write the appspec file, add lifecycle hooks and roll back on CloudWatch alarms.

CodeDeploy orchestrates deployments to EC2, on-premises servers, Lambda and ECS. What it adds over copying files or updating a service is controlled traffic shifting with automatic rollback. A canary that watches an alarm and reverts itself if the alarm fires.

The three compute platforms behave quite differently, which is worth knowing before reading further: EC2 deployments run scripts on the instances, while Lambda and ECS deployments shift traffic between versions and run no scripts on any host.

sections.title: The appspec file
paragraphs: For EC2, appspec.yml at the root of your bundle describes what to copy and which scripts to run:
For Lambda and ECS it is JSON or YAML naming versions rather than scripts:

The lifecycle detail that causes the most confusion. ApplicationStop executes from the previously deployed revision, not the one you are deploying, because the old version is what is running and needs stopping.

So a broken ApplicationStop script blocks every future deployment, and fixing it in the new revision does not help, since the old one still runs. Recovery means either deploying with --ignore-application-stop-failures or removing the agent's stored revision on the instance:
Keep ApplicationStop scripts trivial and idempotent, systemctl stop app || true rather than anything that can fail.

codeBlock.code:
version: 0.0
os: linux
files:
  - source: /
    destination: /var/www/app
    overwrite: true
permissions:
  - object: /var/www/app
    owner: app
    group: app
    mode: 755
hooks:
  ApplicationStop:
    - location: scripts/stop.sh
      timeout: 60
      runas: root
  BeforeInstall:
    - location: scripts/backup.sh
      timeout: 120
  AfterInstall:
    - location: scripts/install-deps.sh
      timeout: 300
  ApplicationStart:
    - location: scripts/start.sh
      timeout: 60
  ValidateService:
    - location: scripts/healthcheck.sh
      timeout: 120

sections.title: Deployment configurations
paragraphs: EC2 in-place updates instances in batches:
EC2 blue-green provisions a replacement fleet, shifts the load balancer, then terminates the original. Safer, and it needs double capacity briefly.
Lambda and ECS shift traffic between versions:
A canary is only useful if something is watching, which is the next section.

sections.title: Automatic rollback is the point
paragraphs: DEPLOYMENT_STOP_ON_ALARM with a real alarm is what makes this worth using. Without it, a canary sends 10% of traffic to a broken version for five minutes and then confidently promotes it to 100%.
Pick alarms that reflect user experience, 5xx rate, p99 latency, a business metric, not CPU. A deployment that raises the error rate should roll back; one that raises CPU by 10% probably should not.
terminationWaitTimeInMinutes: 30 keeps the old fleet alive after the switch, so a manual rollback is immediate rather than a redeploy.

sections.title: Lifecycle hooks for validation
paragraphs: Hooks are where a deployment becomes more than a file copy. On Lambda and ECS they are Lambda functions that must report back:
The function must call put_lifecycle_event_hook_execution_status. A hook that returns without reporting leaves the deployment waiting until it times out. An hour by default, which looks like a hang.
BeforeAllowTraffic runs against the new version before any real traffic reaches it, which is the right place for a smoke test. AfterAllowTraffic runs once traffic is shifted.

codeBlock.code:
import boto3
cd = boto3.client('codedeploy')

def handler(event, context):
    deployment_id = event['DeploymentId']
    hook_id = event['LifecycleEventHookExecutionId']
    try:
        assert smoke_test_passes()
        status = 'Succeeded'
    except Exception:
        status = 'Failed'
    cd.put_lifecycle_event_hook_execution_status(
        deploymentId=deployment_id,
        lifecycleEventHookExecutionId=hook_id,
        status=status,
    )

sections.title: The two EC2 prerequisites
paragraphs: Almost every EC2 CodeDeploy failure is one of these.
The agent must be installed and running:
An instance without a running agent is simply skipped or fails with no useful message. Install it via user data, bake it into the AMI, or deploy it with State Manager.

The instance profile needs S3 read access to the artefact bucket. The agent pulls the bundle itself using the instance role, so a missing s3:GetObject produces a download failure that reads like a CodeDeploy problem.
Deployment groups target instances by tag or Auto Scaling group:
Targeting an Auto Scaling group means instances launched later receive the current revision automatically, which is what you want.

codeBlock.code:
sudo systemctl status codedeploy-agent
sudo tail -100 /var/log/aws/codedeploy-agent/codedeploy-agent.log

sections.title: Diagnosing a failure
paragraphs: That last query names the failing lifecycle event and its diagnostic output, including the script's exit code and last lines of stdout, which is the fastest route to the cause. For EC2, follow up in the agent log on the instance.

codeBlock.code:
aws deploy get-deployment --deployment-id d-ABCDEF123 \
  --query 'deploymentInfo.[status,errorInformation]'

aws deploy list-deployment-targets --deployment-id d-ABCDEF123

aws deploy get-deployment-target --deployment-id d-ABCDEF123 \
  --target-id "i-0123456789abcdef0" \
  --query 'deploymentTarget.instanceTarget.lifecycleEvents[?status==`Failed`]'

sections.title: Do you need CodeDeploy?
paragraphs: Worth asking honestly.

For ECS, the built-in rolling update handles most deployments without CodeDeploy. Add CodeDeploy when you want genuine blue-green with traffic shifting, canary percentages and automatic rollback on alarms.
For Lambda, SAM's DeploymentPreference configures CodeDeploy for you in five lines, which is much easier than assembling it directly.

For EC2, CodeDeploy is a reasonable choice, though an immutable approach using an Auto Scaling group instance refresh with a new AMI is often simpler and avoids maintaining deployment scripts on instances entirely.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: CodeDeploy will not overwrite files it did not place. Set overwrite: true in appspec.yml, or clean the directory in BeforeInstall.
Read the diagnostic output from get-deployment-target. Also check the script is executable and has LF line endings. A CRLF script fails with a confusing "not found".
Exceeded the deployment group's minimum healthy hosts. Look at one failing instance's lifecycle events.
Deployment hangs, then times out. A Lambda hook that never reported its status, or an ApplicationStop script waiting on something.

codeBlock.code:
The deployment failed because a specified file already exists at this location:
/var/www/app/index.html

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: An ApplicationStop script has a bug that causes it to exit non-zero. The fix is committed and a new revision deployed, but every deployment still fails at ApplicationStop. Why?
A CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes deployment sent 10% of traffic to a version returning 500s, then promoted it to 100%. What was missing?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between in-place and blue-green deployment in CodeDeploy?

In-place updates the application on existing instances, in batches you configure, no extra capacity needed, but instances are briefly out of service and rollback means deploying the previous revision again. Blue-green provisions a replacement set of instances, shifts the load balancer to them once healthy, and terminates the original after a wait period, so rollback is switching back, which is near-instant. Blue-green costs double capacity briefly and is the safer choice for anything user-facing.
Why does my deployment keep failing at ApplicationStop?

Because ApplicationStop runs from the previously deployed revision, not the one being deployed. Its job is to stop what is currently running. A broken stop script therefore blocks every subsequent deployment, and fixing it in the new revision changes nothing until you get past it once. Deploy with --ignore-application-stop-failures to break the cycle. Keep these scripts trivial and idempotent, such as systemctl stop app || true, precisely because of this property.
How do I set up automatic rollback?

Two parts, and both are required. Set --auto-rollback-configuration with the events that should trigger it, including DEPLOYMENT_STOP_ON_ALARM, and set --alarm-configuration listing CloudWatch alarms to watch. Without the alarms, a canary shifts traffic, waits its interval and promotes regardless of what happened. Choose alarms reflecting user experience, error rate, p99 latency, a conversion metric, rather than CPU, which moves for reasons unrelated to whether the deployment is good.
Why is my CodeDeploy deployment stuck and eventually timing out?

On Lambda or ECS, almost always a lifecycle hook function that never reported its result. A hook Lambda must call put_lifecycle_event_hook_execution_status with Succeeded or Failed; returning without doing so leaves CodeDeploy waiting until the hook times out, which defaults to an hour and looks like a hang. Make sure the call happens in the failure path too. On EC2, the equivalent cause is a script waiting on something that never completes.
What does the CodeDeploy agent need on EC2?

Two things, and they account for most EC2 failures. The agent itself must be installed and running, check systemctl status codedeploy-agent and its log under /var/log/aws/codedeploy-agent/, and the instance profile must allow s3:GetObject on the artefact bucket, because the agent downloads the bundle itself using the instance role. Install the agent through user data, a baked AMI, or Systems Manager State Manager so newly launched instances always have it.
Do I need CodeDeploy for ECS?

Not for ordinary deployments. ECS's built-in rolling update replaces tasks gradually and handles most cases. CodeDeploy earns its place when you want genuine blue-green with two target groups, canary or linear traffic shifting by percentage, lifecycle hooks running validation before traffic arrives, and automatic rollback driven by CloudWatch alarms. For Lambda, SAM's DeploymentPreference configures the same machinery in a few lines and is much easier than wiring it up directly.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-codecommit.title: AWS CodeCommit
aws-codecommit.subtitle: CodeCommit no longer accepts new customers. See what that means for existing repositories and how to migrate to GitHub or GitLab with your history intact.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS CodeCommit must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: CodeCommit no longer accepts new customers. See what that means for existing repositories and how to migrate to GitHub or GitLab with your history intact.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: CodeCommit no longer accepts new customers. See what that means for existing repositories and how to migrate to GitHub or GitLab with your history intact.

CodeCommit is closed to new customers. Since mid-2024, AWS has not onboarded new accounts to it, if your account has never created a CodeCommit repository, you cannot start now, and the service does not appear as an option. Accounts with prior usage keep full access, and AWS continues to operate and support existing repositories.

So this page is for two audiences: teams operating a repository they already have, and teams deciding whether to keep it. If you are choosing a Git host today, the answer is GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, and the migration section below is probably the part you want.

There is no announced end-of-life date. Existing repositories are not at immediate risk, but a service receiving no new customers is unlikely to receive significant new features either, which is the practical consideration.

sections.title: Why it was used
paragraphs: It is worth being fair about the genuine advantages, because they are the things you lose by migrating.

IAM as the only access control. No separate user directory, no SSO integration to maintain, no license seats. Someone who leaves loses repository access when their IAM identity is removed, with nothing else to remember.
Nothing leaves your account. For organisations where code cannot sit with a third party, that is occasionally a hard requirement rather than a preference.
No per-user cost beyond a small free tier, and traffic to other AWS services stays inside AWS.

Against that: no pull request experience comparable to GitHub or GitLab, no built-in CI beyond CodePipeline, no issue tracking, no package registry, and an ecosystem of integrations that is essentially empty.

sections.title: Working with an existing repository
paragraphs: The cleanest authentication is git-remote-codecommit, which uses your normal AWS credentials, including SSO and assumed roles, with no separate Git credentials to create:

That codecommit:: URL form is the one to use. HTTPS Git credentials are generated per IAM user, which does not work with SSO or roles at all, and SSH keys mean uploading a public key to each IAM user. Both are legacy approaches that exist because git-remote-codecommit came later.

codeBlock.code:
pip install git-remote-codecommit
git clone codecommit::eu-west-1://orders-api

sections.title: Approval rules are the closest thing to branch protection
paragraphs: Note what this does not do: it requires approvals on pull requests, and it does not prevent a direct push to main. For that you need an IAM policy denying the push:
That two-part arrangement, approval rule template plus IAM deny, is the CodeCommit equivalent of a single "protect this branch" checkbox elsewhere, and it is a fair illustration of the ergonomic gap.

codeBlock.code:
aws codecommit create-approval-rule-template \
  --approval-rule-template-name require-two-reviews \
  --approval-rule-template-content '{
    "Version": "2018-11-08",
    "DestinationReferences": ["refs/heads/main"],
    "Statements": [{
      "Type": "Approvers",
      "NumberOfApprovalsNeeded": 2,
      "ApprovalPoolMembers": ["arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/Developer/*"]
    }]
  }'

aws codecommit associate-approval-rule-template-with-repository \
  --approval-rule-template-name require-two-reviews \
  --repository-name orders-api

sections.title: Triggers and notifications
paragraphs: EventBridge is the better route for anything beyond SNS, since it can target Lambda, Step Functions or a pipeline directly:

codeBlock.code:
aws codecommit put-repository-triggers --repository-name orders-api \
  --triggers '[{
    "name": "build-on-main",
    "destinationArn": "arn:aws:sns:eu-west-1:123456789012:builds",
    "branches": ["main"],
    "events": ["updateReference"]
  }]'

sections.title: Migrating out, with history intact
paragraphs: A Git repository is self-contained, so moving the code itself is genuinely easy. --mirror carries every branch, tag and ref:
Verify nothing was left behind:
For a large repository, or one with LFS objects, fetch LFS content explicitly first:

What does not migrate is the part that takes the time: pull requests and their comments, approval rule templates, repository triggers, and any IAM policies granting access. Plan for rewriting the access model rather than translating it. CodeCommit's IAM-based permissions have no direct equivalent in a system with its own user and team model.
Sequence that works well: mirror the repository, set up CI on the new host and confirm it passes, switch developers over, leave CodeCommit read-only for a few weeks as a fallback, then archive it.

codeBlock.code:
git clone --mirror codecommit::eu-west-1://orders-api orders-api.git
cd orders-api.git

git remote set-url --push origin git@github.com:acme/orders-api.git
git push --mirror

sections.title: Where to go
paragraphs: If keeping code inside your AWS account is a hard requirement, GitLab or GitHub Enterprise Server can be self-hosted on EC2, which trades a managed service for an operational burden, and is worth costing properly before choosing it.
All of the alternatives integrate with CodePipeline and CodeBuild through CodeStar Connections, so an AWS-based pipeline does not need rebuilding:
The connection requires a one-time authorisation in the console, which is the only manual step.

codeBlock.code:
aws codestar-connections create-connection \
  --provider-type GitHub --connection-name github-acme

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Expired credentials, a missing IAM permission, or HTTPS Git credentials being used with an assumed role, which does not work. Use git-remote-codecommit.
git-remote-codecommit is not installed, so Git does not recognise the helper.
If your account has no CodeCommit history, this is the service being closed to new customers rather than a policy problem.

codeBlock.code:
fatal: unable to access 'https://git-codecommit.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/v1/repos/orders-api/':
The requested URL returned error: 403

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team starting a new project on AWS wants to know whether to use CodeCommit for its IAM integration. What is the correct advice?
A team plans to migrate three CodeCommit repositories to GitHub and expects the commit history to be the difficult part. What should they actually budget time for?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Can I still use AWS CodeCommit?

Only if your AWS account already used it. AWS stopped onboarding new customers in mid-2024, so an account with no prior CodeCommit repositories cannot create one, CreateRepository is refused. Accounts with existing usage keep full access to create and operate repositories, and AWS continues to run and support the service with no announced end-of-life. The practical implication is that a service closed to new customers is unlikely to gain significant new features.
Should I migrate away from CodeCommit?

Not urgently, but plan for it. Existing repositories keep working and there is no announced shutdown, so this is not a fire. What you are giving up by staying is feature development, third-party integrations and the pull request experience that GitHub and GitLab have continued improving. If your repositories are active and your team spends time in code review, migrating is worth scheduling. If they hold stable code that rarely changes, leaving them alone is defensible.
How do I authenticate to CodeCommit properly?

Install git-remote-codecommit and clone with the codecommit::region://repo URL form. It uses your normal AWS credential chain, so SSO, assumed roles and named profiles all work. The older options, HTTPS Git credentials and SSH keys, are generated per IAM user, which means they do not work with SSO or role assumption at all, and they exist mainly because the credential helper arrived later. The codecommit:: form is the one to standardise on.
How do I protect the main branch in CodeCommit?

Two separate pieces, which is one of the clearer ergonomic gaps. An approval rule template associated with the repository requires a number of approvals on pull requests targeting refs/heads/main. That alone does not stop a direct push, so you also need an IAM policy denying codecommit:GitPush and codecommit:DeleteBranch on that reference, using the codecommit:References condition key. Elsewhere this is a single checkbox.
How do I migrate a CodeCommit repository to GitHub without losing history?

git clone --mirror codecommit::eu-west-1://repo, then set the push URL to the new host and git push --mirror. That transfers every commit, branch and tag with unchanged hashes, and usually takes minutes. Verify by comparing git ls-remote output from both hosts. If the repository uses Git LFS, run git lfs fetch --all and git lfs push --all separately, since mirror does not carry LFS objects.
What does not transfer when migrating from CodeCommit?

Everything except the Git data. Pull requests and their review comments stay behind, as do approval rule templates, repository triggers and any notification rules. The access model needs rebuilding too, because CodeCommit permissions are IAM policies while GitHub and GitLab have their own users, teams and roles. There is no translation. Budget time for that rather than for the code, keep the old repository read-only for a few weeks as a fallback, and use CodeStar Connections so existing CodePipeline setups keep working.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
