aws-cdk.subtitle: Define AWS infrastructure in TypeScript or Python with CDK. Learn the three construct levels, bootstrapping, cdk diff, escape hatches and CDK vs Terraform.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS CDK must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Define AWS infrastructure in TypeScript or Python with CDK. Learn the three construct levels, bootstrapping, cdk diff, escape hatches and CDK vs Terraform.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Define AWS infrastructure in TypeScript or Python with CDK. Learn the three construct levels, bootstrapping, cdk diff, escape hatches and CDK vs Terraform.

The CDK lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Java, Go or C#, and synthesises it to CloudFormation. You get loops, conditionals, functions, types and unit tests, and deployment remains ordinary CloudFormation, with the same change sets, rollbacks and drift behaviour.
The trade is that an abstraction which generates 400 lines of CloudFormation from 10 lines of TypeScript is wonderful until you need to know exactly what it produced.

sections.title: A stack
paragraphs: The line doing the most work is table.grantReadData(fn). It writes an IAM policy scoped to exactly that table and exactly the read actions, and attaches it to the function's role. Hand-written equivalents are usually broader than they need to be, because getting the action list right is tedious, and the grant* methods are, for many teams, the strongest single argument for the CDK.

sections.title: Three levels of construct
paragraphs: L2 is the right default. L1 constructs are always available for a service the CDK has not modelled yet, since they are generated from the CloudFormation specification.

L3 patterns such as ApplicationLoadBalancedFargateService create a VPC, cluster, service, load balancer, security groups and log groups from one declaration. They are excellent for prototypes and a liability when you need to change one detail they did not expose, at which point you are reaching for escape hatches to modify something a simple L2 stack would have made explicit.

sections.title: Bootstrap first
paragraphs: This creates the S3 bucket, ECR repository and IAM roles the CDK needs for deployment. Every account and region combination needs it once, and forgetting is the first error everyone hits:
The bootstrap stack is versioned, and an old one causes confusing failures after a CDK upgrade, re-running the command updates it.

codeBlock.code: cdk bootstrap aws://123456789012/eu-west-1

sections.title: cdk diff is the important command
paragraphs: requires replacement is the line to read before every production deploy, for the same reason as a CloudFormation change set: the resource will be destroyed and recreated, and the deployment will report success.
cdk diff also summarises IAM and security group changes separately, and cdk deploy pauses for confirmation when either changes, which is a good default to leave on.
To see the generated CloudFormation:
Worth doing when a construct behaves unexpectedly. It is the only way to know what was actually created.

codeBlock.code: cdk diff

sections.title: Escape hatches
paragraphs: When an L2 construct does not expose a property, drop to the underlying L1 resource rather than abandoning the construct:
You can also add raw CloudFormation the CDK has no construct for:
Escape hatches are a feature, not a workaround. They mean the CDK is never a dead end. They are also a signal: needing several on one construct usually means an L1 resource would be clearer.

sections.title: Removal policy
paragraphs: Defaults differ by resource and are easy to get wrong. A DynamoDB table or S3 bucket defaults to DESTROY in a CDK stack, so cdk destroy on a development stack takes the data with it. Set RETAIN explicitly on anything stateful.
autoDeleteObjects: true on a bucket creates a custom resource that empties it on delete. Convenient for genuinely disposable buckets, and exactly what you do not want in production.

codeBlock.code: removalPolicy: cdk.RemovalPolicy.RETAIN,

sections.title: Testing
paragraphs: Real unit tests against infrastructure, which is a genuine advantage over templates:
Snapshot tests catch unintended changes across a whole stack:
They are noisy, a CDK version bump changes hashes and logical IDs, but they do surface the thing you did not mean to change.

sections.title: Aspects for org-wide rules
paragraphs: An Aspect visits every construct in a tree, which is how you enforce a policy across a whole app:
addError fails the synth, so the rule is enforced before anything is deployed rather than flagged in review.

sections.title: CDK, Terraform, or CloudFormation
paragraphs: Pick the CDK when you are AWS-only, your team is comfortable in one of its languages, and IAM correctness matters. Pick Terraform when you manage more than AWS or already have an estate in it. Note also CDK for Terraform, which uses CDK constructs to emit Terraform. Worth knowing exists.

The honest CDK caveats: logical IDs are derived from the construct tree, so renaming or moving a construct destroys and recreates the resource; upgrades between major versions have been disruptive; and debugging sometimes means reading synthesised CloudFormation, which defeats some of the abstraction.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: Run cdk bootstrap for that account and region.
Two stacks in different accounts or regions referencing each other directly. Pass values explicitly or use SSM.
Construct IDs must be unique within a scope.
A resource was replaced unexpectedly. A construct was renamed or moved in the tree, changing its logical ID.

codeBlock.code: This stack uses assets, so the toolkit stack must be deployed

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A developer renames a construct from new dynamodb.Table(this, "Orders", …) to "OrdersTable" for clarity. The deploy succeeds and the table is empty. Why?
An L2 construct does not expose a property that the underlying CloudFormation resource supports. What is the right approach?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between L1, L2 and L3 constructs?

L1 constructs (CfnBucket, CfnTable) map one-to-one onto CloudFormation resources with no defaults, and are generated from the resource specification so they cover every service immediately. L2 constructs (Bucket, Table) add sensible defaults, type safety and helper methods such as grantRead, and are what you should use by default. L3 constructs are opinionated patterns combining several resources, an entire load-balanced Fargate service from one declaration, which are excellent when the pattern fits and awkward when you need to change something they do not expose.
Do I need to run cdk bootstrap?

Yes, once per account and region combination, before the first deployment there. It creates the S3 bucket, ECR repository and IAM roles the CDK uses to stage assets and execute deployments. Skipping it produces an error explicitly telling you to run it, which makes it a brief rather than mysterious problem. The bootstrap stack is versioned too, so re-run it after a major CDK upgrade. An outdated bootstrap causes confusing failures that look unrelated.
Why did renaming a construct delete my resource?

Because the CloudFormation logical ID is derived from the construct's path in the tree. Changing the construct ID, or moving it under a different parent, produces a different logical ID, so CloudFormation sees a new resource to create and an old one that has vanished from the template, and deletes it. For stateful resources this loses data while the deploy reports success. Always check cdk diff before deploying, and set removalPolicy: RETAIN so the original survives if it happens.
How do I set a property the CDK construct does not support?

Use an escape hatch. Cast the construct's node.defaultChild to its L1 type and call addPropertyOverride('Path.To.Property', value), or addOverride for anything outside Properties. This works for any property the underlying CloudFormation resource accepts, including ones the L2 API has not caught up with, and it keeps the construct's defaults and grant helpers intact. It is a supported pattern rather than a hack, though several overrides on one construct suggests using the L1 resource directly would be clearer.
Should I use CDK or Terraform?

CDK when you are AWS-only, your team is fluent in TypeScript or Python, and you value the grant* methods that generate least-privilege IAM automatically, that last point prevents a whole class of over-permissive policy. Terraform when you manage more than AWS, already have an estate in it, or prefer explicit configuration over generated abstraction. Terraform's state management is more work; CDK's generated output is more opaque when debugging. CDK for Terraform also exists, combining CDK constructs with Terraform providers.
Can I write tests for CDK infrastructure?

Yes, and it is one of the better reasons to choose it. The aws-cdk-lib/assertions module synthesises a stack in memory and lets you assert on the result, hasResourceProperties to check a table has point-in-time recovery, resourceCountIs to catch accidental duplication, or searching the generated IAM policies to prove a function cannot write where it should only read. Snapshot tests catch unintended changes across a whole stack, though they are noisy across CDK version bumps.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

aws-sam.title: AWS SAM
aws-sam.subtitle: Build and deploy serverless apps with AWS SAM: write the template shorthand, run sam build and sam deploy --guided, test with sam local and compare with CDK.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing AWS SAM must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Aws documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Aws in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Build and deploy serverless apps with AWS SAM: write the template shorthand, run sam build and sam deploy --guided, test with sam local and compare with CDK.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Aws.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Build and deploy serverless apps with AWS SAM: write the template shorthand, run sam build and sam deploy --guided, test with sam local and compare with CDK.

SAM is a shorthand for CloudFormation aimed at serverless applications, plus a CLI that builds, tests and deploys them. A AWS::Serverless::Function resource expands into a Lambda function, an IAM role, a log group and any triggers you declared. Perhaps forty lines of CloudFormation from ten lines of SAM.
That is the whole proposition: it is CloudFormation, so anything CloudFormation can express you can drop into the same template, and the stack behaves like any other.

sections.title: A template
paragraphs: The Transform line is what makes it SAM. Without it, CloudFormation does not recognise AWS::Serverless::* and the deploy fails with an unknown resource type.
Three parts of that template are doing real work.
Globals applies defaults to every function, which stops the same six properties being repeated per function. It is the main reason a SAM template with ten functions stays readable.

Policies with a policy template: DynamoDBReadPolicy here. Generates a least-privilege role scoped to that table. It is markedly better than the common habit of attaching a broad managed policy, and there are around sixty templates covering the usual combinations.

Events creates the trigger and the permission. Declaring an HttpApi event wires the route and adds the resource-based policy that API Gateway needs to invoke the function. The permission people forget when building integrations by hand.
Architectures: [arm64] is worth making a default: Graviton Lambda is around 20% cheaper and usually slightly faster.

codeBlock.code:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Description: Orders API

Globals:
  Function:
    Runtime: python3.12
    Timeout: 25
    MemorySize: 512
    Architectures: [arm64]
    Tracing: Active
    Environment:
      Variables:
        TABLE_NAME: !Ref OrdersTable
    LoggingConfig:
      LogFormat: JSON

Resources:
  OrdersApi:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::HttpApi
    Properties:
      StageName: prod
      CorsConfiguration:
        AllowOrigins: ['https://app.example.com']
        AllowMethods: [GET, POST, OPTIONS]
        AllowHeaders: [content-type, authorization]

  GetOrderFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      CodeUri: src/get_order/
      Handler: app.handler
      Policies:
        - DynamoDBReadPolicy:
            TableName: !Ref OrdersTable
      Events:
        Api:
          Type: HttpApi
          Properties:
            ApiId: !Ref OrdersApi
            Path: /orders/{id}
            Method: GET

  OrdersTable:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::SimpleTable
    Properties:
      PrimaryKey: { Name: orderId, Type: String }
      BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST

Outputs:
  ApiUrl:
    Value: !Sub 'https://${OrdersApi}.execute-api.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com/prod'

sections.title: Build and deploy
paragraphs: --use-container builds inside a Lambda-like Docker image, which matters for any dependency with native extensions. Building psycopg2 or numpy on macOS and deploying to Lambda produces an import error at runtime. An architecture and libc mismatch of the same family as exec format error. If your dependencies are pure Python or JavaScript you can skip it; if they are not, use it always and in CI.
The guided deploy asks for a stack name, region and parameters, then writes samconfig.toml:

After that, sam deploy alone is enough, and sam deploy --config-env prod targets the other environment. Commit samconfig.toml. It is the difference between a reproducible deploy and one that depends on what someone typed.
CAPABILITY_IAM is required because SAM creates roles. A template with named roles needs CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM instead, which is a common first deploy failure.

codeBlock.code: sam build --use-container

sections.title: Testing locally
paragraphs: That last command is more useful than it looks: it produces a correctly shaped event for the trigger you name, so you are testing against the real payload structure rather than one you guessed. It covers S3, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB streams and dozens more.

What local testing genuinely gives you is fast iteration on handler logic and confidence in the event shape. What it does not give you is IAM, sam local uses your credentials, so a function that works locally can fail deployed because its role lacks a permission. Local success is not a permissions test.
For iterating against real AWS rather than a local emulation:

sam sync pushes code changes directly to the function, skipping CloudFormation for code-only edits. A few seconds instead of a couple of minutes. It is explicitly for development: it can leave the stack differing from the template, so deploy properly before anything else depends on it.

codeBlock.code: sam local invoke GetOrderFunction --event events/get_order.json

sections.title: Safe deployments
paragraphs: SAM exposes CodeDeploy's traffic shifting as a few lines:

That publishes a version, shifts 10% of traffic for five minutes, watches the alarm, and rolls back automatically if it fires. Getting equivalent behaviour by hand means versions, aliases, a CodeDeploy application and a deployment group. This is the clearest case where SAM's shorthand earns its keep.

codeBlock.code:
GetOrderFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      AutoPublishAlias: live
      DeploymentPreference:
        Type: Canary10Percent5Minutes
        Alarms:
          - !Ref ErrorRateAlarm
        Hooks:
          PreTraffic: !Ref SmokeTestFunction

sections.title: SAM, CDK, Terraform or Serverless Framework
paragraphs: Choose SAM when the application is serverless and AWS-only and you want the shortest path from template to deployed stack, with local testing included. Choose CDK when you want real language constructs and are building more than functions, and note the two interoperate, since sam local can test a CDK-synthesised template. Choose Terraform when serverless is a small part of a larger estate you already manage there.

sections.title: Common errors
paragraphs: sam build was not run, or CodeUri points somewhere that does not exist. Deploy from .aws-sam/build, which sam deploy does automatically after a build.
Add --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM, or CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM if roles are named.
A property is misspelled or in the wrong place. The message lists the offending path; sam validate --lint catches most of these before deploying.

Handler does not match the file and function. It is <file>.<function> relative to CodeUri, with no .py extension. The other cause is a native dependency built for the wrong platform, which sam build --use-container fixes.

paragraphs: A function runs correctly under sam local invoke but fails deployed with AccessDeniedException on a DynamoDB call. The template builds and deploys without error. What explains it?
A Python function using a library with compiled C extensions imports fine on a developer's Mac but fails deployed with Unable to import module. sam build was run without flags. What fixes it?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between SAM and CloudFormation?

SAM is CloudFormation with a transform that expands serverless shorthand. AWS::Serverless::Function becomes a Lambda function, an execution role, a log group and any triggers you declared, so ten lines produce what would otherwise take forty. Because the result is a normal CloudFormation stack, you can mix ordinary resources into the same template and manage it with the usual tooling. The SAM CLI adds the parts CloudFormation lacks for serverless: building dependencies, local invocation and log tailing.
Should I use SAM or CDK?

SAM when the application is serverless, AWS-only, and you want the shortest path from template to deployment with local testing included. CDK when you are building broader infrastructure and want real programming-language constructs, loops and abstractions rather than YAML. CDK has a steeper learning curve and its synthesised output is harder to read, which matters when debugging. They also interoperate, sam local can test a template CDK synthesised, so the choice is less final than it appears.
When do I need sam build --use-container?

Whenever a dependency includes compiled code. A plain sam build installs packages with your local toolchain, so anything with C extensions is built for your operating system and architecture and fails to import in Lambda. Building inside a Lambda-like container produces artefacts for the right architecture and C library. Pure Python or JavaScript dependencies do not need it, but using it consistently, and in CI, makes builds reproducible rather than dependent on whose machine ran them.
Does sam local test my IAM permissions?

No, and this is the most important limitation to know. sam local runs the handler using your own credentials, which are typically much broader than the function's execution role, so a missing permission passes locally and fails on the first deployed invocation. Local testing validates handler logic and that you are handling the real event shape; authorisation has to be tested against a deployed stack. Use policy templates in the template to keep the role least-privilege rather than guessing.
What does sam sync do and is it safe?

sam sync --watch pushes code changes straight to the deployed functions, bypassing CloudFormation for code-only edits. Seconds instead of a couple of minutes. It is explicitly a development tool: because it skips the stack, the deployed state can drift from the template, so anything shared or production-facing should go through sam deploy. Used on your own development stack it removes most of the friction that makes people avoid deploying to real AWS while iterating.
How do I do canary deployments with SAM?

Add AutoPublishAlias and a DeploymentPreference block to the function. SAM publishes a new version on each deploy, points the alias at it gradually according to the strategy you name, Canary10Percent5Minutes, Linear10PercentEvery1Minute and similar, watches any CloudWatch alarms you list, and rolls back automatically if one fires. Hooks can run pre-traffic and post-traffic validation functions. Building the equivalent by hand means versions, aliases, a CodeDeploy application and a deployment group.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
